Client Education

  • Report: breast lumps, tenderness, or discharge; depression or suicidal thoughts; difficulty with sexual function that persists; rash or allergic reaction
  • Take at the same time each day — patience needed (months for full effect)
  • Do NOT crush or break tablets
  • Pregnant women must not handle broken or crushed tablets (skin absorption — fetal harm)
  • Use a condom during sex if female partner is pregnant (small amounts in semen)
  • Sexual side effects (↓ libido, erectile dysfunction, ↓ ejaculate volume) may occur and may persist after discontinuation
  • Do NOT donate blood for at least 1 month after stopping (protect pregnant transfusion recipients)
  • Tell providers about finasteride — affects PSA interpretation
  • Hair loss may resume within a year of stopping
Worked Example Sildenafil (PDE5 Inhibitor) Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract · Men’s health section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor — inhibits PDE5, increasing cyclic GMP → smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation
  • In the penis: enhances nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation → increased blood flow → erection (with sexual stimulation)
  • In pulmonary vasculature: vasodilation (for pulmonary hypertension)

Therapeutic Use

  • Erectile dysfunction (ED)
  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension (Revatio brand)
  • Requires sexual stimulation to produce erection (does not work alone)

Complications

  • Severe/fatal hypotension with nitrates (absolute contraindication)
  • Priapism — erection > 4 hr; medical emergency (tissue damage)
  • Headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion
  • Visual disturbances — blue-tinged vision, light sensitivity; rare: NAION (sudden vision loss)
  • Sudden hearing loss (rare)
  • Hypotension, dizziness, syncope
  • MI/arrhythmia in cardiac-compromised clients during sexual activity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent nitrates (any form) or riociguat — ABSOLUTE contraindication (fatal hypotension)
  • Severe cardiovascular disease; unstable angina; recent MI/stroke
  • Severe hepatic/renal impairment (dose adjust)
  • Hypotension (< 90/50)
  • Retinitis pigmentosa
  • Caution with alpha blockers (additive hypotension)
  • History of NAION

Interactions

  • Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide) — CONTRAINDICATED (fatal hypotension)
  • Alpha blockers (tamsulosin, doxazosin) — additive hypotension; separate dosing/start low
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin, grapefruit) — increase sildenafil levels (reduce dose)
  • Other antihypertensives — additive hypotension
  • Riociguat — contraindicated

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved erectile function (ED indication)
  • Improved exercise capacity and reduced symptoms (pulmonary hypertension)
  • No hypotensive events or priapism
  • No visual/hearing complications
  • Tolerable side effects

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • ED: 50 mg (range 25–100 mg) about 30–60 min before sexual activity; max once daily
  • Pulmonary HTN: 20 mg three times daily (different dosing)
  • High-fat meals delay absorption
  • Reduce dose with CYP3A4 inhibitors, hepatic/renal impairment, older adults

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify NO nitrate use (scheduled or PRN, including recreational “poppers”) — absolute contraindication
  • Assess cardiovascular status (sexual activity is cardiac stress)
  • Review medications for alpha blockers, CYP3A4 inhibitors
  • Baseline BP; monitor for hypotension
  • Educate on priapism emergency
  • Counsel on visual/hearing changes
  • For pulmonary HTN use: different dosing and monitoring

Client Education

  • NEVER take with nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide) or chest-pain medications containing nitrates — can cause fatal blood pressure drop
  • Requires sexual stimulation to work; takes ~30–60 min
  • Take no more than once daily
  • Seek emergency care for an erection lasting more than 4 hours (priapism)
  • Stop and seek care for sudden vision or hearing loss, chest pain during activity
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Limit alcohol (worsens hypotension and ED)
  • Tell all providers you take this (interaction with nitrates in emergencies)
  • Sexual activity is exertion — discuss cardiac safety with provider if heart disease
  • Rise slowly (dizziness)
Worked Example Tamsulosin (Flomax) Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract · Men’s health section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Tamsulosin (Flomax)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective alpha-1A adrenergic antagonist — targets receptors in the prostate and bladder neck
  • Relaxes smooth muscle in prostate and bladder neck → improved urine flow
  • More uroselective than older alpha blockers → less effect on blood pressure (but still some)
  • Does NOT shrink the prostate (symptomatic relief only)

Therapeutic Use

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — relieve urinary symptoms
  • Off-label: facilitate passage of ureteral/kidney stones (medical expulsive therapy)

Complications

  • Orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, syncope (especially first dose)
  • Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome (IFIS) — complicates cataract surgery; must inform ophthalmologist
  • Retrograde/abnormal ejaculation
  • Nasal congestion, headache
  • Priapism (rare)
  • Reflex tachycardia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to tamsulosin or sulfa (some caution)
  • History of orthostatic hypotension/syncope
  • Planned cataract surgery (IFIS — inform surgeon)
  • Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors (additive hypotension)
  • Concurrent strong CYP3A4/2D6 inhibitors
  • Older adults — fall risk

Interactions

  • PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) — additive hypotension
  • Other antihypertensives, alpha blockers — additive hypotension
  • Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole) and CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine) — increase tamsulosin levels
  • Cimetidine — increases levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved urinary flow rate
  • Reduced BPH symptoms: hesitancy, frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream
  • Reduced post-void residual
  • No symptomatic hypotension or falls
  • Improved quality of life (AUA symptom score)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral capsule
  • Dose: 0.4 mg PO once daily; may increase to 0.8 mg
  • Take 30 minutes after the same meal each day (consistent)
  • Swallow whole — do not crush, chew, or open capsule
  • Take first dose at bedtime to reduce first-dose hypotension risk (per some protocols)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and orthostatic BP (sitting/standing)
  • Fall precautions, especially first dose and dose increases
  • Ask about planned cataract surgery (IFIS); notify ophthalmologist if so
  • Review for PDE5 inhibitors and antihypertensives
  • Assess urinary symptoms and response
  • Educate on consistent timing (after same meal)
  • Rule out prostate cancer (BPH symptoms overlap; check PSA/DRE per provider)

Client Education

  • Take 30 minutes after the same meal daily
  • Swallow capsule whole; do not crush or chew
  • Rise slowly from sitting/lying (dizziness, especially first doses)
  • If dizzy, sit or lie down; avoid driving after first dose until response known
  • Tell your eye surgeon you take this if you have cataract surgery (floppy iris syndrome)
  • May cause abnormal/retrograde ejaculation (harmless but report concerns)
  • Do not combine with ED medications without provider approval (low BP)
  • Continue medication — it manages symptoms but does not cure BPH
  • Report fainting, prolonged erection, or worsening urinary symptoms
  • Keep follow-up for prostate evaluation
Worked Example Methylergonovine Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Methylergonovine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Methylergonovine is an ergot alkaloid uterine stimulant:

  • Stimulates contraction of uterine smooth muscle directly
  • Produces sustained tetanic contractions (NOT rhythmic like oxytocin) → compress uterine vessels → control bleeding
  • Also causes peripheral vasoconstriction (cause of HTN side effect)
  • Onset: PO 5-15 min, IM 2-5 min, IV immediate
  • Duration: 3 hr (PO/IM), 45 min (IV)

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage caused by uterine atony after delivery of the placenta.
  • Promotes a firm, contracted uterus and compresses uterine vessels to reduce excessive postpartum bleeding.
  • Not used to induce or augment labor because sustained tetanic contractions can compromise uteroplacental blood flow before delivery.

Complications

  • Hypertensive crisis: severe headache, nausea/vomiting, markedly increased BP, blurred vision, or seizure risk.
  • Peripheral and coronary vasoconstriction can cause chest pain, palpitations, cold or numb extremities, vasospasm, and ischemia.
  • Common effects include uterine cramping, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, and increased blood pressure.
  • Can suppress lactation and pass into breast milk; avoid breastfeeding during therapy as directed.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Contraindicated during pregnancy and labor before delivery; give only after delivery of the placenta for postpartum bleeding control.
  • Avoid with hypertension, preeclampsia/eclampsia, or significant cardiac disease because vasoconstriction can precipitate severe hypertension or ischemia.
  • Use cautiously with severe renal or hepatic disease and sepsis, and monitor BP/HR before each dose.
  • Avoid additive vasoconstriction or ergot toxicity with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, triptans, other ergots, sympathomimetics, beta blockers, and tobacco exposure.

Interactions

  • Vasoconstrictors, other sympathomimetics → severe HTN
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors) → ↑ ergot toxicity (vasospasm, ischemia)
  • Beta-blockers (esp. propranolol) → ↑ vasoconstriction → peripheral ischemia
  • Triptans, other ergots → additive vasoconstriction (avoid)
  • Tobacco → ↑ vasoconstriction

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Firm, contracted uterus on palpation (no boggy uterus)
  • ↓ uterine bleeding, normal lochia rubra → serosa progression
  • Stable vital signs (BP, HR, no signs of shock)
  • Adequate uterine involution (descending fundal height postpartum)
  • No signs of ergot toxicity: chest pain, severe HA, vision changes, peripheral coldness/numbness

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IM (most common in postpartum), oral, IV (only in emergency, with caution)
  • Postpartum: 0.2 mg IM after delivery of placenta; may repeat q2-4h up to 5 doses
  • Oral maintenance: 0.2 mg PO q6-8h × up to 7 days
  • IV use ONLY in life-threatening emergencies due to severe HTN risk
  • Assess BP and HR BEFORE each dose; hold if BP > 140/90 or per protocol
  • Monitor uterine fundus (firmness, position, lochia)
  • Have calcium gluconate available (used for ergot poisoning vasospasm)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor vital signs for increase in blood pressure.
  • Monitor for manifestations of hypertensive crisis (headache, nausea, vomiting, and increased blood pressure).
  • Monitor for uterine tone and vaginal bleeding.
  • Provide emergency interventions.

Client Education

  • Report: chest pain, severe headache, blurred vision, numbness or tingling in fingers/toes, calf pain, palpitations, sudden cold extremities
  • This medication helps control postpartum bleeding by keeping the uterus contracted
  • You may experience cramping (sign it's working — uterus contracting)
  • Common side effects: nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, ↑ BP
  • Avoid smoking (worsens vasoconstriction)
  • Do NOT breastfeed while taking — can suppress milk supply and pass to infant
  • Limit caffeine
  • Inform all providers if planning future pregnancy (do not use during pregnancy)
Worked Example Oxytocin (Pitocin) Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery · Stimulants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Oxytocin (Pitocin)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Synthetic oxytocin — stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction (mimics endogenous oxytocin)
  • Increases frequency, duration, and force of contractions
  • Also stimulates milk ejection (let-down reflex)
  • HIGH-ALERT MEDICATION

Therapeutic Use

  • Labor induction (initiate labor) and augmentation (strengthen existing labor)
  • Postpartum hemorrhage prevention/control (uterine atony) — promotes uterine involution
  • Management of incomplete/inevitable abortion
  • Milk let-down (rarely used)

Complications

  • Uterine hyperstimulation/tachysystole → reduced placental perfusion → fetal distress (late decelerations, bradycardia)
  • Uterine rupture (especially with prior cesarean, grand multiparity)
  • Water intoxication / hyponatremia (oxytocin has antidiuretic effect at high doses) → seizures
  • Maternal hypotension (rapid IV)
  • Postpartum hemorrhage (after prolonged use — uterine fatigue)
  • Fetal: hypoxia, acidosis from reduced perfusion

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)
  • Fetal malpresentation, fetal distress (when delivery not imminent)
  • Placenta previa, vasa previa
  • Prior classical cesarean or uterine surgery (rupture risk)
  • Active genital herpes
  • Hypertonic uterine activity
  • Use only with continuous fetal/uterine monitoring

Interactions

  • Vasopressors / sympathomimetics — severe hypertension (oxytocin + ephedrine)
  • Prostaglandins (cervical ripening agents) — do not give concurrently; space dosing (additive uterine stimulation)
  • Other uterotonics — additive effect
  • Inhalational anesthetics — may reduce oxytocin effect, cause hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Adequate labor pattern: contractions every 2–3 min, lasting 45–60 sec, moderate-strong, with uterine rest between
  • Progressive cervical dilation and fetal descent
  • Reassuring fetal heart rate pattern
  • Postpartum: firm, contracted uterus; controlled bleeding
  • No hyperstimulation or fetal distress

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV infusion (induction/augmentation) via pump on a SECONDARY line; IM/IV (postpartum)
  • Always given as a secondary (piggyback) infusion at the port closest to the client — so it can be stopped quickly
  • Start low; titrate by milliunits/min per protocol based on contraction pattern and FHR
  • Continuous electronic fetal monitoring required
  • Postpartum: 10–40 units in IV fluids, or 10 units IM
  • High-alert: independent double-check; infusion pump mandatory

Nursing Interventions

  • Continuous fetal heart rate AND uterine contraction monitoring
  • Assess contraction frequency, duration, intensity, and resting tone
  • STOP oxytocin immediately for: tachysystole (> 5 contractions/10 min), contractions > 90 sec, inadequate uterine rest, or non-reassuring FHR (late decels, bradycardia)
  • If stopping: reposition (left side), IV fluid bolus, oxygen, notify provider; terbutaline may be ordered
  • Monitor maternal vitals, I&O (water intoxication)
  • Postpartum: assess fundal firmness and bleeding
  • High-alert medication: independent double-check; piggyback setup

Client Education

  • Oxytocin stimulates/strengthens contractions to help labor progress
  • Continuous monitoring of the baby’s heart rate and your contractions is necessary
  • Report contractions that feel constant or extremely painful without rest between
  • The medication can be stopped quickly if needed
  • Postpartum: oxytocin helps the uterus contract to control bleeding
  • Report increased bleeding, severe headache, or feeling unwell
  • Expect frequent assessment of your uterus and bleeding after delivery
Worked Example Terbutaline (Tocolytic) Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Terbutaline (Brethine)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Beta-2 adrenergic agonist — relaxes uterine smooth muscle (tocolytic)
  • Suppresses uterine contractions in preterm labor
  • Also bronchodilates (originally an asthma drug)
  • Buys time for antenatal corticosteroids (fetal lung maturity) and maternal transfer

Therapeutic Use

  • Short-term suppression of preterm labor (tocolysis) — typically ≤ 48–72 hours
  • Uterine hyperstimulation/tachysystole (to relax uterus, e.g., during oxytocin-induced distress)
  • Off-label in OB; also asthma/bronchospasm

Complications

  • Maternal tachycardia, palpitations (beta-1 cross-stimulation)
  • FDA BLACK BOX: not for prolonged tocolysis (> 48–72 hr) — risk of maternal cardiac events and death; injectable not for outpatient/home use
  • Pulmonary edema (especially with fluid overload, multiple gestation)
  • Hyperglycemia (maternal); neonatal hypoglycemia
  • Hypokalemia
  • Tremor, nervousness, headache
  • Fetal tachycardia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Maternal cardiac disease, arrhythmias
  • Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism
  • Poorly controlled diabetes
  • Severe preeclampsia/eclampsia
  • Conditions where prolonging pregnancy is dangerous (chorioamnionitis, abruption, fetal demise, severe IUGR)
  • Gestational age where tocolysis not beneficial (≥ 34 weeks typically)

Interactions

  • Other beta agonists, sympathomimetics — additive cardiac effects
  • Beta blockers — antagonize tocolytic effect
  • Corticosteroids (often co-administered for fetal lung maturity) — additive hyperglycemia, pulmonary edema risk
  • Magnesium sulfate (another tocolytic) — additive effects; monitoring
  • Potassium-wasting drugs — additive hypokalemia

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Decreased frequency/intensity of uterine contractions
  • Cessation or slowing of preterm labor
  • Time gained for corticosteroid course (fetal lung maturity)
  • No maternal cardiac or pulmonary complications
  • Stable maternal/fetal status

Medication Administration

  • Route: subcutaneous (acute tocolysis) or IV; oral form not recommended for maintenance tocolysis
  • SC: 0.25 mg every 20 min to 3 hr (hold for maternal HR > 120)
  • Short-term only (≤ 48–72 hr) per black box warning
  • Continuous maternal and fetal monitoring during administration

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor maternal heart rate — HOLD if > 120 bpm; assess for arrhythmias, chest pain
  • Continuous fetal heart rate and contraction monitoring
  • Assess for pulmonary edema (dyspnea, crackles, chest tightness) — limit IV fluids; monitor I&O
  • Monitor blood glucose (maternal hyperglycemia) and potassium
  • Assess deep tendon reflexes if also on magnesium
  • Prepare for neonatal care (hypoglycemia)
  • Coordinate antenatal corticosteroid administration

Client Education

  • This medication relaxes the uterus to temporarily stop preterm contractions
  • Expect a faster heartbeat, jitteriness, or tremor (common; report if severe)
  • Report chest pain, difficulty breathing, severe palpitations immediately
  • Report return of regular contractions, leaking fluid, or vaginal bleeding
  • Used short-term to gain time for steroids that help the baby’s lungs mature
  • Continuous monitoring of you and the baby is necessary
  • Diabetic clients: blood sugar may rise
  • Rest as directed; report any concerning symptoms
Worked Example Etanercept Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Etanercept
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Etanercept is a TNF-alpha inhibitor (biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug — DMARD):

  • Soluble fusion protein that binds and inactivates tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)
  • TNF-α is a major proinflammatory cytokine driving autoimmune joint and skin disease
  • Reduces inflammation and tissue damage in chronic inflammatory conditions
  • Slows or prevents structural joint damage (disease-modifying)
  • Onset: weeks to months for full clinical effect

Therapeutic Use

Etanercept is a biologic DMARD classified as a tumor necrosis factor antagonist. It suppresses manifestations of moderate to severe RA and slows the progression of the disorder.

Complications

  • Severe infections, including tuberculosis or reactivation of hepatitis B
  • Heart failure
  • Severe skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  • Hematologic disorders

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active infection (sepsis, TB, opportunistic infections) — TNF inhibition impairs defense
  • Latent TB — screen with PPD or IGRA before initiation; treat if positive
  • Hepatitis B carrier status — risk of reactivation
  • Demyelinating disease (MS) — may worsen
  • Heart failure (NYHA III-IV) — TNF inhibitors may worsen HF
  • Hypersensitivity to etanercept
  • Live vaccines (during therapy and prior) — avoid; complete vaccinations BEFORE starting
  • Caution: history of malignancy, especially lymphoma
  • Pregnancy Cat B (limited data, but generally avoided unless benefit clearly outweighs)

Interactions

  • Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, zoster, intranasal flu, yellow fever) — AVOID
  • Other biologics, anakinra, abatacept → ↑ infection risk; do not combine
  • Cyclophosphamide → ↑ malignancy risk
  • Methotrexate — often combined intentionally for RA (safe)
  • Inactivated vaccines (e.g., flu shot) — give before therapy if possible; may be less effective during

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • RA: ↓ joint pain, stiffness, swelling, fatigue; ↑ function; ↓ ESR/CRP; slowed radiographic progression
  • Psoriasis: clearer skin, ↓ plaque coverage and severity (PASI score improvement)
  • Ankylosing spondylitis: ↓ back pain and stiffness, ↑ spinal mobility
  • No serious infections (sepsis, opportunistic, TB reactivation)
  • No new malignancies
  • No worsening of HF or demyelinating disease

Medication Administration

  • Teach clients to administer by subcutaneous injection twice weekly.
  • Discard solutions that are discolored or that contain particulate matter.
  • Monitor for injection-site reactions, and report them to provider.
  • Rotate injection sites.
  • Avoid skin areas that are bruised or reddened when injecting.

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct clients to monitor for infection, and to report sore throat and other manifestations.
  • Discuss reasons for TB testing and possible hepatitis B testing.
  • Clients should notify the provider for edema, shortness of breath, and other manifestations of heart failure.
  • Report skin rash to provider.
  • Report easy bruising, bleeding, or unusual fatigue to provider.

Client Education

  • Report: signs of infection (fever, persistent cough, fatigue, weight loss, painful urination, skin infections — any), shortness of breath, new neurologic symptoms (numbness, weakness, vision changes), unusual bruising or bleeding, new lumps or skin changes, severe injection site reaction
  • Avoid people with active infections; practice good hygiene
  • Avoid live vaccines while on therapy and for some time after
  • Get all recommended NON-live vaccines (annual flu shot, pneumococcal)
  • Refrigerate medication; warm to room temperature 15-30 min before injecting
  • Rotate injection sites; injection site reactions are common but should be mild
  • Inform ALL providers (especially dentists, surgeons) before any procedure
  • Keep all lab appointments (CBC, LFTs, TB screening as ordered)
  • Discuss any planned pregnancy or surgery with rheumatology
Worked Example Alendronate Ch 34 — Bone Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Alendronate
Review Module Chapter
Ch 34 — Bone Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Alendronate is a bisphosphonate used to treat osteoporosis:

  • Binds to hydroxyapatite in bone, where it is taken up by osteoclasts during bone resorption
  • Inhibits osteoclast activity → ↓ bone resorption → ↑ bone mineral density
  • Helps preserve bone structure and reduce fracture risk
  • Poor oral bioavailability (~0.7%); food and beverages ↓ absorption significantly
  • Long retention in bone (years)

Therapeutic Use

In this client who is at high risk for osteoporosis, the purpose of alendronate is to prevent osteoporosis from occurring by decreasing resorption of bone. The medication also is used to treat existing osteoporosis and Paget's disease.

Complications

Alendronate can cause esophagitis and esophageal ulceration; other GI effects (nausea, diarrhea, and constipation); muscle pain; and visual disturbances. Rarely, it can cause atraumatic femoral fracture.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Esophageal abnormalities (strictures, achalasia) that delay esophageal emptying
  • Inability to stand/sit upright for at least 30 minutes
  • Hypocalcemia (correct before initiating)
  • Severe renal impairment (CrCl < 35)
  • Pregnancy Cat C
  • Caution: GI disease (gastritis, ulcers, dysphagia)
  • Caution: invasive dental procedures planned (osteonecrosis of jaw risk)

Interactions

  • Calcium, iron, magnesium, antacids, food → significantly ↓ absorption — separate by at least 30 min (preferably take alendronate first, on empty stomach)
  • Coffee, juice, milk → ↓ absorption — water only
  • NSAIDs → ↑ GI ulcer/erosion risk
  • Aspirin → ↑ GI adverse effects
  • Aminoglycosides → additive hypocalcemia
  • Other bisphosphonates → not used concurrently

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↑ bone mineral density on DEXA scan (every 1-2 years)
  • ↓ risk of vertebral, hip, and non-vertebral fractures
  • Resolution of bone pain (if Paget disease)
  • No serious adverse events: no atypical femoral fractures, no osteonecrosis of jaw, no severe esophageal injury

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Treatment dose: 10 mg PO daily OR 70 mg PO once weekly
  • Prevention dose: 5 mg daily OR 35 mg weekly
  • Strict administration protocol:
    • Take FIRST THING in the morning, on an EMPTY stomach
    • With 6-8 oz of PLAIN WATER only (no coffee, juice, mineral water)
    • Swallow whole — do NOT chew, crush, or suck
    • Remain upright (sit or stand) for at least 30 minutes AND until first food/drink of the day
    • Wait 30 min before eating, drinking other beverages, or taking other medications
  • Ensure adequate calcium (1,200 mg) and vitamin D (800-1,000 IU) intake
  • Consider drug holiday after 3-5 years (per provider) to reduce long-term complications

Nursing Interventions

Diagnostic tests: Blood calcium, bone density scans Nursing interventions

  • Assess the client's ability to follow administration directions (must be able to sit upright or stand for at least 30 min after taking alendronate).
  • Teach the client to take this medication first thing in the morning with at least 240 mL (8 oz) water and wait 30 min before eating or drinking anything else or taking any other medications or supplements.
  • Teach the client other ways to help prevent osteoporosis, such as performing weight-bearing exercises daily and obtaining adequate amounts of calcium and vitamin D.

Client Education

  • Report: heartburn, difficulty swallowing, chest pain when swallowing, thigh or groin pain (atypical fracture), jaw pain, severe muscle/bone/joint pain
  • Strict morning routine:
    • First thing in morning, before any food, drink, or other medication
    • Take with 6-8 oz plain water ONLY
    • Stand or sit upright for ≥ 30 min and until you eat your first meal
    • Do not lie down during this time
  • Take calcium (1,200 mg/day) and vitamin D (800-1,000 IU/day) — but separate from alendronate by ≥ 30 min
  • Continue weight-bearing exercise (walking, dancing, light resistance)
  • Tell dentist about alendronate BEFORE any dental work; have dental exam before starting
  • Stop smoking; limit alcohol (bone loss)
  • Discuss any planned pregnancy with provider
Worked Example Calcitonin (Salmon) Ch 34 — Bone Disorders · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Calcitonin-Salmon (Miacalcin, Fortical)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 34 — Bone Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Hormone — inhibits osteoclast activity (reduces bone resorption)
  • Promotes renal excretion of calcium → lowers serum calcium
  • Salmon calcitonin is more potent than human form
  • Has analgesic properties for acute vertebral fracture pain

Therapeutic Use

  • Postmenopausal osteoporosis (second-line; bisphosphonates preferred)
  • Paget’s disease of bone
  • Hypercalcemia (rapid, short-term lowering)
  • Acute pain from osteoporotic vertebral fractures

Complications

  • Nasal effects (nasal spray) — rhinitis, irritation, dryness, epistaxis
  • Nausea, flushing (injectable more common)
  • Hypocalcemia — tetany, paresthesias (monitor)
  • Possible increased malignancy risk with long-term use (FDA review)
  • Hypersensitivity/allergic reactions (salmon protein)
  • Injection site reactions

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to salmon calcitonin (skin test if high-risk)
  • Pre-existing hypocalcemia
  • Long-term use weighed against possible malignancy risk
  • Pregnancy/lactation — caution
  • Nasal pathology (for nasal spray)

Interactions

  • Lithium — calcitonin may reduce lithium levels
  • Other calcium-lowering agents — additive hypocalcemia
  • Bisphosphonates — additive bone effects (usually sequential, not combined)
  • Few major interactions overall

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced bone pain (vertebral fractures)
  • Lowered serum calcium (hypercalcemia)
  • Reduced bone turnover markers (Paget’s)
  • Stabilized/improved bone density (osteoporosis — modest)
  • No hypocalcemia symptoms

Medication Administration

  • Routes: intranasal spray, subcutaneous/IM injection
  • Nasal: 1 spray (200 units) once daily, alternating nostrils each day
  • Prime the nasal pump before first use
  • Ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake
  • Bedtime dosing reduces nausea/flushing (injectable)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline serum calcium; monitor for hypocalcemia
  • Assess for salmon allergy; skin test if indicated
  • Ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D supplementation
  • Teach nasal spray technique (alternate nostrils, prime pump)
  • Monitor nasal mucosa (irritation, epistaxis)
  • Assess pain relief (vertebral fracture indication)
  • Discuss long-term use risk/benefit

Client Education

  • Nasal spray: alternate nostrils each day; prime the pump before first use; report persistent nasal irritation or nosebleeds
  • Take calcium and vitamin D as recommended
  • Report numbness, tingling, or muscle twitching (low calcium)
  • Weight-bearing exercise supports bone health
  • Bedtime dosing may reduce nausea/flushing
  • Report allergic reactions (rash, swelling, difficulty breathing)
  • Discuss duration of therapy with provider (long-term risk)
  • Keep follow-up for bone density and calcium monitoring
Worked Example Raloxifene (SERM) Ch 34 — Bone Disorders · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Raloxifene (Evista)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 34 — Bone Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) — estrogen agonist on bone (and lipids), estrogen antagonist on breast and uterus
  • In bone: reduces resorption → preserves bone density
  • Lowers LDL cholesterol
  • Does NOT stimulate endometrium or breast tissue (unlike estrogen)

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention and treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis
  • Reduction of invasive breast cancer risk in high-risk postmenopausal women
  • Reduces vertebral fracture risk (less effect on hip)

Complications

  • BLACK BOX: venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE) and increased risk of fatal stroke in women with CV disease
  • Hot flashes (estrogen antagonist effect)
  • Leg cramps
  • Peripheral edema
  • Flu-like symptoms
  • Unlike estrogen: does NOT increase endometrial or breast cancer risk (may reduce breast cancer)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • History of VTE (DVT, PE, retinal vein thrombosis)
  • Pregnancy/lactation (Category X)
  • Premenopausal women
  • Prolonged immobilization (discontinue 72 hr before; thrombosis risk)
  • Hepatic impairment
  • History of stroke or high stroke risk

Interactions

  • Cholestyramine — reduces raloxifene absorption (avoid concurrent)
  • Warfarin — may decrease PT/INR (monitor)
  • Highly protein-bound drugs — potential interactions
  • Estrogen therapy — not recommended together

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Maintained or improved bone mineral density
  • Reduced vertebral fracture incidence
  • Reduced breast cancer risk (high-risk women)
  • Lower LDL cholesterol
  • No thromboembolic events

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Dose: 60 mg PO once daily
  • Take with or without food, any time of day
  • Continue calcium and vitamin D
  • Discontinue at least 72 hours before prolonged immobilization (surgery, bed rest); resume when fully mobile

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess VTE history and risk factors (contraindicated if prior VTE)
  • Educate on VTE signs (leg pain/swelling, chest pain, dyspnea)
  • Plan to hold before periods of immobilization
  • Ensure calcium and vitamin D intake
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin
  • Separate from cholestyramine
  • Verify postmenopausal status (Category X)

Client Education

  • Report signs of blood clots immediately: leg pain/swelling/warmth, chest pain, shortness of breath, sudden vision changes
  • Move around during long trips; stop the medication before prolonged bed rest or surgery (tell providers)
  • Expect possible hot flashes and leg cramps
  • Take calcium and vitamin D
  • Weight-bearing exercise; fall prevention
  • Do not take if pregnant or could become pregnant
  • Take once daily, with or without food
  • Separate from cholestyramine
  • Keep follow-up for bone density monitoring
Worked Example Ibuprofen Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ibuprofen
Review Module Chapter
Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Ibuprofen is a nonselective NSAID (COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor):

  • Inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes → ↓ prostaglandin synthesis
  • Analgesic (peripheral and central): ↓ pain
  • Anti-inflammatory: ↓ inflammation
  • Antipyretic: ↓ fever (via hypothalamic prostaglandin reduction)
  • COX-1 inhibition causes most adverse effects: gastric ulcers, ↓ platelet function, renal effects
  • Onset: 30-60 min; duration 4-6 hr

Therapeutic Use

  • Treats mild to moderate pain, fever, and inflammation by reducing prostaglandin-mediated symptoms.
  • Used long term in osteoarthritis to decrease joint pain, stiffness, and inflammatory discomfort when benefits outweigh GI, renal, bleeding, and cardiovascular risks.
  • Does not cure osteoarthritis or reverse joint damage; therapy is symptom control paired with function, activity, and safety monitoring.
  • Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate duration, with food or water to reduce GI distress.

Complications

  • Gastrointestinal effects can occur, including anorexia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn.
  • GI bleeding can occur because NSAIDs affect platelet function.
  • Nephrotoxicity can occur.
  • NSAIDs can cause CNS effects (dizziness, headache, blurred vision, and tinnitus).
  • Allergy can occur, including cross allergy with other NSAIDs (aspirin).

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to NSAIDs (cross-reactivity within class)
  • Aspirin-sensitive asthma (Samter triad: asthma + nasal polyps + NSAID sensitivity)
  • Active or history of GI bleeding, peptic ulcer disease
  • Severe heart failure, recent CABG (FDA boxed warning — ↑ MI, stroke, HF risk)
  • Severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30)
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • Pregnancy 3rd trimester (Cat D) — premature closure of fetal ductus arteriosus, fetal renal effects
  • Caution: HTN (may ↑ BP, ↓ effect of antihypertensives), elderly (↑ GI, renal, CV risk), bleeding disorders, dehydration
  • Caution: concurrent anticoagulants, corticosteroids, SSRIs

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs) → ↑ bleeding risk
  • Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) → ↑ bleeding risk
  • Other NSAIDs → additive toxicity (do not combine)
  • SSRIs/SNRIs → ↑ GI bleeding risk
  • Corticosteroids → ↑ GI ulcer/bleeding risk
  • ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics → ↓ antihypertensive effect; ↑ renal toxicity ("triple whammy" of NSAID + diuretic + ACE/ARB)
  • Lithium → ↑ lithium levels (toxicity)
  • Methotrexate → ↑ methotrexate toxicity
  • Aspirin (low-dose for CV protection) → ibuprofen can block antiplatelet effect; take aspirin ≥ 2 hr BEFORE ibuprofen, or ≥ 8 hr after
  • Alcohol → ↑ GI bleeding

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ pain to acceptable level
  • ↓ inflammation (↓ joint swelling, warmth, redness)
  • ↓ fever (return toward normal)
  • ↑ joint mobility and function (in arthritis)
  • No GI bleeding (stable Hgb, no melena/hematemesis)
  • No renal impairment (stable BUN/creatinine, normal UO)
  • BP remains controlled

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral (tablet, capsule, suspension), IV (Caldolor)
  • Adult: 200-800 mg PO q6-8h; max 3,200 mg/day (4-day OTC limit 1,200 mg/day)
  • Pediatric: 5-10 mg/kg PO q6-8h (max 40 mg/kg/day; OTC max 30 mg/kg/day)
  • Take with food, milk, or a full glass of water to ↓ GI upset
  • Do not lie down for 30 min after taking
  • For OTC use: do not exceed 10 days for pain, 3 days for fever without provider direction
  • Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration possible

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor hgb/hct and kidney function tests.
  • Assess the client for previous allergy to NSAIDs.
  • Assess the GI system, and ask about any history of GI bleed or peptic ulcer disease.
  • Advise the client to take the medication with food, milk, or an 8 oz glass of water to prevent GI distress.
  • Advise the client to tell provider about any over-the-counter medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements before taking them.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: black tarry stools, vomiting blood, severe abdominal pain, swelling of feet/face, decreased urine output, chest pain, shortness of breath, rash, unusual bleeding/bruising, ringing in ears
  • Take with food, milk, or full glass of water
  • Stay upright for 30 minutes after dose
  • Do NOT take with other NSAIDs (aspirin, naproxen, celecoxib)
  • Limit alcohol (↑ GI bleeding risk)
  • Use lowest effective dose for shortest time needed
  • Avoid in last trimester of pregnancy (premature closure of fetal ductus arteriosus)
  • Tell all providers about NSAID use before any surgery
  • If on warfarin or antiplatelet drugs: bleeding risk ↑ — monitor closely
  • Hypertension: monitor BP; ibuprofen can ↑ BP and ↓ effectiveness of antihypertensives
Worked Example Hydromorphone Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Hydromorphone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Hydromorphone is a strong opioid agonist similar to morphine but ~5-7x more potent (PO):

  • Binds primarily to mu (μ) opioid receptors
  • Produces analgesia, sedation, euphoria, respiratory depression, miosis, ↓ GI motility
  • Onset: PO 15-30 min, IV 5 min
  • Duration: 3-4 hr (IR); 12-24 hr (extended-release Exalgo)
  • Used when alternative opioid needed (allergy/intolerance to morphine, dialysis patients due to no active metabolites)
  • Reversal: naloxone

Therapeutic Use

  • Relieves moderate to severe acute or chronic pain when an opioid analgesic is indicated and non-opioid options are inadequate.
  • Used for severe postoperative, cancer-related, trauma, or palliative pain according to provider order and client response.
  • May be selected when morphine is not tolerated or when renal considerations favor hydromorphone because it lacks morphine-like active metabolites.
  • Requires close respiratory, sedation, pain, bowel, and safety monitoring because hydromorphone is much more potent than morphine.

Complications

  • Sedation
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Constipation
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Urinary retention

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to hydromorphone or opioids
  • Severe respiratory depression, acute asthma, paralytic ileus
  • Head injury with ↑ ICP
  • Suspected acute abdominal condition
  • Concurrent MAOI use
  • Caution: elderly, debilitated, hepatic/renal impairment, prostatic hyperplasia, hypothyroidism
  • Caution: history of substance use disorder
  • Pregnancy Cat C; chronic use → neonatal abstinence syndrome

Interactions

  • Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol, barbiturates, sleep aids, antihistamines, gabapentin) → additive respiratory depression — FDA black box warning
  • Other opioids → additive sedation, respiratory depression
  • MAOIs → severe and potentially fatal reactions (hypertension or hypotension, hyperpyrexia, coma); avoid within 14 days
  • SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, tramadol, St. John's wort → serotonin syndrome risk
  • Anticholinergics → ↑ constipation, urinary retention
  • Antihypertensives → additive hypotension
  • Diuretics → ↑ hypotension; opioids cause ADH release → urinary retention
  • Cimetidine → ↑ CNS effects
  • Mixed agonist-antagonists (buprenorphine, butorphanol, pentazocine) → may precipitate withdrawal; reduced analgesia
  • Naloxone — reverses effects (use for overdose)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ pain to acceptable level
  • ↑ functional ability and quality of life
  • No respiratory depression (RR ≥ 12)
  • Maintained bowel function
  • No signs of overdose (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, ↓ LOC)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral (IR and ER), IV, IM, SC, rectal
  • Adult dose:
    • PO: 2-4 mg q4-6h PRN (opioid-naive)
    • IV: 0.2-1 mg q2-3h PRN; push slowly over 2-3 min
    • ER (Exalgo): once daily — for opioid-tolerant clients only
  • NOT EQUIVALENT to morphine — much more potent (PO conversion roughly 7.5 mg PO morphine = 1.5 mg PO hydromorphone)
  • Double-check dose; medication errors are common due to potency confusion with morphine
  • Have naloxone and resuscitation equipment available
  • Monitor RR, sedation, pain

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct the client not to drive or perform other hazardous activities while using this medication.
  • Notify the provider for severe nausea or vomiting.
  • Prevent constipation by increasing intake of liquids and foods with fiber. Consider use of a stool softener or laxatives if necessary.
  • Move the client slowly from lying or sitting to standing to minimize effects of orthostatic hypotension.
  • Instruct the client to void every 4 hr. Contact the provider for manifestations of dysuria.

Client Education

  • Report: severe drowsiness, confusion, slow breathing (< 10/min), severe constipation, urinary retention, allergic reaction
  • Do NOT confuse with morphine — much more potent; double-check label every time
  • Take with or without food
  • Use stool softener and stimulant laxative as prescribed to prevent constipation
  • Increase fluid and fiber intake
  • Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants (sleep aids, benzodiazepines) — fatal respiratory depression possible
  • Avoid driving and hazardous activities
  • Do NOT crush, chew, or split extended-release tablets — overdose risk
  • Store safely (lock box if children present); do not share — controlled substance
  • Dispose of unused medication via drug take-back program
Worked Example Morphine Ch 37 — Adjuvant Medications for Pain · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Morphine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 37 — Adjuvant Medications for Pain
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Morphine is a strong opioid agonist and prototype of the class:

  • Binds primarily to mu (μ) opioid receptors in CNS and peripheral nervous system
  • Produces: analgesia, sedation, euphoria, cough suppression, decreased GI motility, miosis, respiratory depression
  • Onset: PO 30 min, IV 5-10 min; duration 3-5 hr (immediate-release)
  • Metabolized in liver, excreted in urine
  • Reversal: naloxone (Narcan) — competitive opioid antagonist

Therapeutic Use

  • Relieves moderate to severe acute or chronic pain when an opioid agonist is indicated and non-opioid options are inadequate.
  • Used for postoperative, traumatic, cancer-related, palliative, or severe persistent pain according to provider order and client response.
  • Can improve comfort, sleep, mobility, coughing, deep breathing, and participation in care when pain is limiting recovery.
  • Requires close respiratory, sedation, blood pressure, bowel, urinary, and safety monitoring because analgesia is linked to opioid adverse effects.

Complications

  • Respiratory depression is the priority risk, especially after dose increases, IV administration, or use with other CNS depressants.
  • Sedation, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, vomiting, pruritus, urinary retention, and miosis can occur.
  • Constipation is expected and persistent, so a bowel regimen is usually needed rather than waiting for symptoms.
  • Tolerance, physical dependence, misuse, and overdose are possible with ongoing therapy.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to morphine or opioids
  • Severe respiratory depression, acute asthma, paralytic ileus
  • Head injury with ↑ ICP (opioids ↑ ICP)
  • Suspected acute abdominal condition (masks symptoms)
  • Concurrent MAOIs or within 14 days
  • Caution: elderly, debilitated, hepatic/renal impairment, hypothyroidism, prostatic hyperplasia
  • Caution: history of substance use disorder
  • Pregnancy Cat C; chronic use → neonatal abstinence syndrome
  • Breastfeeding (excreted in breast milk)

Interactions

  • Benzodiazepines, alcohol, sedatives, sleep medications, and other CNS depressants increase sedation and life-threatening respiratory depression risk.
  • MAOIs or recent MAOI use can cause severe reactions and should be avoided unless specifically directed.
  • Other opioids or opioid agonist-antagonists can alter analgesia, increase adverse effects, or precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent clients.
  • Anticholinergic medications can worsen constipation and urinary retention.

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ pain to client's acceptable level (typically < 4/10 or per goal)
  • Improved ability to perform ADLs and breathing exercises
  • ↓ pain-related distress, improved sleep, restored appetite
  • No respiratory depression (RR ≥ 12, SpO₂ stable, no excessive sedation)
  • Bowel function maintained (no severe constipation/ileus)
  • No signs of overdose: pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + ↓ LOC

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral (IR, SR), IV, IM, SC, epidural, intrathecal, rectal
  • Adult dose:
    • PO: 15-30 mg q4h PRN (IR); 15-30 mg q8-12h (SR)
    • IV: 2-10 mg q3-4h PRN; slow push over 4-5 min
    • PCA: 1 mg bolus, 6-10 min lockout
  • Pediatric: weight-based, start low
  • Have naloxone and resuscitation equipment available
  • Monitor: RR (≥ 12), HR, BP, sedation level, pain
  • For SR: do NOT crush, chew, or split (overdose risk)
  • Use scheduled (not just PRN) for chronic pain

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor CBC, including platelet counts.
  • Assess for abnormal bleeding, bruising, or infection.
  • Monitor for GI manifestations, and advise the client to take the medication with food.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: severe drowsiness or unresponsiveness, slow or shallow breathing (< 10/min), severe constipation, inability to urinate, severe dizziness, hallucinations, allergic reaction, withdrawal symptoms when stopping
  • Take exactly as prescribed; do not increase dose on your own
  • Prevent constipation: take stool softener + stimulant laxative as prescribed; ↑ fluids and fiber; stay active
  • Rise slowly to prevent dizziness (orthostatic hypotension)
  • Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, sleep aids) — fatal respiratory depression possible
  • Avoid driving and operating machinery until effects are known
  • Do not crush, chew, or split extended-release tablets — overdose risk
  • Use side rails up, call light close, ask for help when getting up (fall risk)
  • Store securely in original container, out of reach of children; controlled substance — never share
  • If pregnant or planning pregnancy, tell provider — neonatal withdrawal possible
  • Have naloxone (Narcan) available at home; teach family/caregivers to use
  • For chronic pain: take on schedule, not just PRN
  • To discontinue: taper under provider direction to avoid withdrawal
  • Dispose of unused medication safely (drug take-back programs)
Worked Example Gabapentin (Anticonvulsant Adjuvant) Ch 37 — Adjuvant Medications for Pain · Adjuvants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Gabapentin (Neurontin)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 37 — Adjuvant Medications for Pain
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anticonvulsant used as an adjuvant analgesic — binds voltage-gated calcium channels (alpha-2-delta subunit), reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release
  • Modulates abnormal neuronal firing in neuropathic pain
  • Structurally related to GABA but does not act on GABA receptors

Therapeutic Use

  • Neuropathic pain (diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia)
  • Adjunct for partial seizures
  • Restless legs syndrome
  • Off-label: fibromyalgia, anxiety, hot flashes

Complications

  • Sedation, dizziness, drowsiness (most common)
  • Ataxia, peripheral edema
  • Weight gain
  • Respiratory depression when combined with opioids/CNS depressants (FDA warning)
  • Mood changes, suicidal ideation (anticonvulsant class warning)
  • Withdrawal if stopped abruptly (taper needed)
  • Misuse potential (euphoria at high doses)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Renal impairment — renally excreted; dose reduction required
  • Older adults (sedation, falls)
  • Concurrent opioids/CNS depressants (respiratory depression)
  • History of substance misuse
  • Do not stop abruptly

Interactions

  • Opioids, CNS depressants, alcohol — additive sedation and respiratory depression
  • Antacids — reduce gabapentin absorption (separate by 2 hr)
  • Other sedating drugs — additive
  • Few CYP interactions (not hepatically metabolized)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced neuropathic pain (pain scale)
  • Improved sleep and function
  • Reduced seizure frequency (seizure indication)
  • Tolerable sedation
  • No respiratory depression (if on opioids)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (capsule, tablet, solution)
  • Start low, titrate up slowly (reduce sedation/dizziness)
  • Reduce dose in renal impairment
  • Take first dose at bedtime (sedation)
  • Separate from antacids by 2 hr
  • Taper to discontinue (do not stop abruptly)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess renal function (dosing); pain level and type (neuropathic)
  • Monitor for sedation, dizziness, ataxia — fall precautions
  • Assess for respiratory depression if combined with opioids
  • Monitor mood/suicidal ideation (anticonvulsant warning)
  • Educate on slow titration and not stopping abruptly
  • Assess for edema, weight gain

Client Education

  • May take 1–2 weeks for full pain relief; take regularly as scheduled
  • Expect drowsiness/dizziness initially — use caution driving until you know the effect
  • Do NOT stop abruptly — taper to avoid withdrawal/seizures
  • Avoid alcohol and other sedatives; tell provider if also on opioids (breathing risk)
  • Separate from antacids by 2 hours
  • Report mood changes or thoughts of self-harm
  • Rise slowly; fall precautions
  • Report swelling or significant weight gain
  • Keep follow-up appointments
Worked Example Duloxetine (SNRI Adjuvant) Ch 37 — Adjuvant Medications for Pain · Adjuvants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Duloxetine (Cymbalta)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 37 — Adjuvant Medications for Pain
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) — increases serotonin and norepinephrine in descending pain pathways
  • Enhances the body’s natural pain inhibition (modulates pain signals in spinal cord)
  • Also treats depression/anxiety (dual benefit when both present)

Therapeutic Use

  • Diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain
  • Fibromyalgia
  • Chronic musculoskeletal pain (low back, osteoarthritis)
  • Major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder

Complications

  • Nausea (common, often transient), dry mouth, constipation
  • Drowsiness or insomnia, dizziness, fatigue
  • Increased blood pressure (norepinephrine effect)
  • Serotonin syndrome (with other serotonergic drugs)
  • Hepatotoxicity (avoid with alcohol/liver disease)
  • Suicidal ideation (BLACK BOX, especially < 25 yr)
  • Bleeding risk (with NSAIDs/anticoagulants)
  • Discontinuation syndrome if stopped abruptly

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent MAOIs (or within 14 days) — serotonin syndrome
  • Uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma
  • Hepatic impairment, significant alcohol use (hepatotoxicity)
  • Severe renal impairment
  • Uncontrolled hypertension
  • Bipolar disorder (screen — may trigger mania)

Interactions

  • MAOIs, other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, triptans, tramadol, linezolid) — serotonin syndrome
  • NSAIDs, anticoagulants, antiplatelets — increased bleeding
  • CYP1A2/2D6 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin) — increase duloxetine
  • Alcohol — hepatotoxicity
  • Other CNS depressants — additive

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced neuropathic/chronic pain (may take 1–4 weeks)
  • Improved mood (if depression present)
  • Improved function and sleep
  • Stable blood pressure
  • No serotonin syndrome or hepatotoxicity

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral, delayed-release capsule
  • Swallow whole — do not crush, chew, or open (sprinkling not recommended)
  • Take with or without food (consistent); food may reduce nausea
  • Once or twice daily per indication
  • Taper to discontinue (discontinuation syndrome)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and periodic BP (can increase), LFTs, pain and mood assessment
  • Screen for MAOI use and other serotonergic drugs (serotonin syndrome)
  • Monitor for serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, tachycardia)
  • Assess suicidal ideation, especially early and in young adults
  • Educate that pain/mood benefit takes weeks
  • Caution with alcohol (liver); NSAIDs/anticoagulants (bleeding)
  • Do not stop abruptly

Client Education

  • May take 1–4 weeks for full pain and mood benefit; take consistently
  • Swallow capsule whole; do not crush or chew
  • Do NOT stop abruptly — taper to avoid withdrawal symptoms (dizziness, nausea, “brain zaps”)
  • Report agitation, confusion, rapid heart rate, fever, muscle twitching (serotonin syndrome)
  • Avoid alcohol (liver injury)
  • Report worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm (especially early)
  • Report yellow skin/eyes, dark urine (liver)
  • Tell providers about all medications (interactions)
  • Rise slowly; report easy bruising/bleeding if on NSAIDs/blood thinners
Worked Example Sumatriptan Ch 38 — Miscellaneous Pain Medications · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Sumatriptan
Review Module Chapter
Ch 38 — Miscellaneous Pain Medications
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Sumatriptan is a triptan (selective 5-HT1B/1D serotonin receptor agonist) for acute migraine:

  • Causes vasoconstriction of dilated cerebral arteries (key in migraine pathophysiology)
  • Inhibits release of pro-inflammatory neuropeptides from trigeminal nerve endings
  • ↓ neurogenic inflammation around dural blood vessels
  • Onset: 10-15 min (SC), 30-60 min (oral, nasal); shorter half-life (~2 hr) → may need repeat dosing
  • Used for ACUTE attacks — NOT for prevention

Therapeutic Use

Sumatriptan is used to abort a migraine headache and associated manifestations (nausea and vomiting) after it begins by causing cranial artery vasoconstriction.

Complications

  • Chest, throat, jaw, or arm heaviness/pressure can occur; evaluate urgently for angina or coronary vasospasm if symptoms are severe or persistent.
  • Coronary vasospasm, myocardial ischemia, MI, stroke, or severe hypertension can occur, especially in clients with cardiovascular risk factors.
  • Dizziness, vertigo, flushing, tingling, weakness, and injection-site or nasal irritation can occur depending on route.
  • Serotonin syndrome risk increases with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, or other serotonergic medications; monitor for agitation, fever, tremor, clonus, and diaphoresis.
  • Medication-overuse headache can occur if used more often than prescribed or for too many headache days per month.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Cardiovascular disease: history of MI, ischemic heart disease, coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina), peripheral vascular disease
  • Cerebrovascular disease: history of stroke or TIA
  • Uncontrolled hypertension
  • Hemiplegic or basilar migraine
  • Use of another triptan or ergot within 24 hr (vasoconstriction additive)
  • Use of MAOI within 14 days (oral and nasal forms)
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • Caution: risk factors for CAD (HTN, hyperlipidemia, smoking, DM, family history, obesity, men > 40, post-menopausal women) — ECG screen if multiple risks
  • Pregnancy Cat C

Interactions

Toxicity can result if sumatriptan is given concurrently or within 2 weeks of an mAOI antidepressant. Sumatriptan should not be given concurrently with other triptan medications or within 24 hr of ergotamine or dihydroergotamine.

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of migraine within 1-2 hr (pain ↓ to mild or no pain)
  • Resolution of associated symptoms: nausea, photophobia, phonophobia
  • Return to normal function within 2-4 hr
  • No serious cardiovascular adverse events (chest pain, MI, stroke)
  • No serotonin syndrome

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral, subcutaneous, nasal spray, oral disintegrating tab
  • Adult oral: 25-100 mg PO at headache onset; may repeat after 2 hr; max 200 mg/day
  • Subcutaneous: 6 mg SC at onset; may repeat after 1 hr; max 12 mg/day
  • Nasal: 5-20 mg one nostril at onset; may repeat after 2 hr
  • Take at first sign of headache — most effective early
  • If first dose ineffective, do NOT give another dose for the SAME headache (poor responder)
  • Maximum 4 headache days per month (medication overuse headache risk)

Nursing Interventions

  • Teach clients to take sumatriptan at the first finding of migraine manifestations.
  • Teach client how to administer sumatriptan if it is prescribed intranasally or by subcutaneous injection.
  • Monitor cardiovascular risk factors and vital signs while taking this medication.
  • Advise clients to notify the provider immediately for onset of angina pain. Teach clients to distinguish transient chest or arm heaviness caused by sumatriptan from angina pain.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: chest pain or pressure, jaw/throat tightness, shortness of breath, weakness, numbness, vision changes, severe abdominal pain
  • Take at the FIRST sign of migraine for best results
  • Lie down in a dark, quiet room after taking
  • If no relief from first dose, do not take another for the same headache; call provider
  • Do NOT use more than prescribed maximum (overuse headache and CV risk)
  • Avoid other triptans or ergots within 24 hours of sumatriptan
  • Tell ALL providers about sumatriptan before any new medication
  • Keep a headache diary to identify triggers
  • If on SSRIs/SNRIs, watch for serotonin syndrome symptoms
Worked Example Lidocaine (Local Anesthetic) Ch 38 — Miscellaneous Pain Medications · Local section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Lidocaine (Xylocaine)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 38 — Miscellaneous Pain Medications
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Amide local anesthetic — blocks sodium channels in nerve membranes, preventing depolarization and nerve impulse conduction
  • Produces local loss of sensation (and motor block at higher concentrations)
  • Also a Class IB antidysrhythmic (IV) for ventricular dysrhythmias

Therapeutic Use

  • Local/regional anesthesia — infiltration, nerve block, epidural, spinal
  • Topical anesthesia (skin, mucous membranes); lidocaine patch for postherpetic neuralgia
  • Procedural anesthesia (suturing, IV insertion)
  • IV: ventricular dysrhythmias

Complications

  • Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) — from excessive dose or inadvertent IV injection
  • CNS: circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness, confusion, seizures, then CNS depression
  • Cardiac: hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest (high levels)
  • Allergic reactions (rare for amides)
  • Methemoglobinemia (high doses, topical)
  • With epinephrine: tissue ischemia if used in end-arterial areas (fingers, toes, nose, ears, penis)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to amide anesthetics
  • Heart block, severe bradycardia (IV/antidysrhythmic use)
  • Hepatic impairment (reduced metabolism — accumulation)
  • Lidocaine WITH epinephrine: avoid in end-arterial areas (fingers, toes, ears, nose, penis) — ischemia
  • Caution: older adults, debilitated, cardiac disease

Interactions

  • Other antidysrhythmics (amiodarone, beta blockers) — additive cardiac effects
  • CYP inhibitors (cimetidine) — increase lidocaine levels
  • Other local anesthetics — additive toxicity (count total dose)
  • Drugs causing methemoglobinemia — additive

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Adequate local/regional anesthesia for procedure
  • Pain relief (patch for neuropathic pain)
  • Controlled ventricular dysrhythmias (IV use)
  • No signs of systemic toxicity (LAST)
  • No tissue ischemia (with epinephrine)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: infiltration, nerve block, epidural/spinal, topical, IV (antidysrhythmic)
  • Maximum doses (do not exceed): ~4.5 mg/kg without epinephrine; ~7 mg/kg with epinephrine
  • Epinephrine prolongs effect and reduces bleeding/systemic absorption
  • Aspirate before injecting (avoid intravascular injection)
  • Use lowest effective dose; track total cumulative dose
  • Never use epinephrine-containing solutions in end-arterial areas

Nursing Interventions

  • Calculate and verify maximum safe dose by weight; track cumulative dose
  • Assess for allergy to amide anesthetics
  • Monitor for LAST (circumoral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, dizziness, seizures, arrhythmias)
  • Have resuscitation equipment and lipid emulsion (Intralipid 20%) available
  • Aspirate before injection (avoid IV)
  • Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm (IV use)
  • Verify no epinephrine in end-arterial sites
  • Cardiac monitoring for IV antidysrhythmic use

Client Education

  • The area will be numb temporarily; protect it from injury (heat, biting, pressure) until sensation returns
  • Report ringing in the ears, numbness around the mouth, metallic taste, dizziness, or confusion immediately (toxicity)
  • For dental: avoid chewing/hot foods until numbness resolves (bite injury)
  • Lidocaine patch: apply to intact skin, max wear time per directions (often 12 hr on/12 hr off); do not cut patch with metal backing
  • Report rapid heartbeat, difficulty breathing, or swelling
  • Tell providers about prior reactions to anesthetics
Worked Example Exenatide Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Exenatide
Review Module Chapter
Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Exenatide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist (incretin mimetic) for type 2 diabetes:

  • Mimics endogenous GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1): stimulates glucose-dependent insulin release from pancreatic beta cells
  • Suppresses inappropriate glucagon release
  • Slows gastric emptying → ↑ satiety, ↓ post-prandial glucose
  • Promotes weight loss (advantage over insulin/sulfonylureas)
  • Low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk (glucose-dependent action) — unless combined with insulin/sulfonylureas

Therapeutic Use

Exenatide is prescribed along with an oral antidiabetic medication (metformin or a sulfonylurea medication) for clients who have type 2 diabetes mellitus to improve diabetes control. exenatide improves insulin secretion by the pancreas, decreases secretion of glucagon, and slows gastric emptying.

Complications

  • Gi effects (nausea and vomiting)
  • Pancreatitis manifested by acute abdominal pain and possibly severe vomiting
  • Hypoglycemia, especially when taken concurrently with a sulfonylurea medication (glipizide)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Boxed warning: risk of thyroid C-cell tumors (medullary thyroid carcinoma) — avoid with personal/family history of MTC or MEN2
  • Hypersensitivity to exenatide
  • Severe gastrointestinal disease, gastroparesis
  • History of pancreatitis (caution)
  • Severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30) — exenatide contraindicated; Bydureon caution
  • Type 1 diabetes (does not replace insulin)
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis
  • Pregnancy Cat C

Interactions

  • Insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides → ↑ hypoglycemia risk (reduce insulin/sulfonylurea dose)
  • Delayed gastric emptying → may affect absorption of oral medications
  • Take oral antibiotics, contraceptives at least 1 hr BEFORE exenatide
  • Warfarin → may ↑ INR (monitor closely)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ HbA1c (target individualized, typically < 7%)
  • ↓ fasting and post-prandial glucose
  • Weight loss (often 2-5 kg)
  • ↓ insulin or sulfonylurea requirements
  • No serious adverse events: no pancreatitis, no thyroid mass, no severe hypoglycemia

Medication Administration

  • Route: subcutaneous injection only (abdomen, thigh, or upper arm)
  • Exenatide (Byetta): 5-10 mcg SC BID within 60 min BEFORE morning and evening meals
  • Exenatide ER (Bydureon): 2 mg SC once weekly
  • Rotate injection sites
  • Refrigerate; discard 30 days after first use (Byetta)
  • Do NOT give after meals
  • If a dose is missed, skip it and resume next scheduled dose (do not double up)
  • Use with diet, exercise, and other diabetes medications as prescribed

Nursing Interventions

Monitor daily blood glucose testing by the client, periodic Hba1c tests, and periodic kidney function testing. exenatide should be used cautiously in clients who have any renal impairment.

Client Education

  • Inject exenatide subcutaneously.
  • Take exenatide within 60 min before the morning and evening meal but not following the meal.
  • Withhold exenatide and notify the provider for severe abdominal pain.
  • Recognize and treat hypoglycemia.
  • Exenatide should not be given within 1 hr of oral medications, particularly antibiotics, acetaminophen, or contraceptives due to its ability to slow gastric emptying.
Worked Example Levothyroxine Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Levothyroxine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Levothyroxine is synthetic T4 (thyroxine) — replacement thyroid hormone:

  • Converted to active T3 (triiodothyronine) in peripheral tissues
  • Increases basal metabolic rate, oxygen consumption, body temperature
  • Required for normal growth, development, and metabolism
  • Long half-life (7 days) → once-daily dosing, missed doses less critical
  • Therapeutic effect assessed by TSH: target depends on age and clinical setting (typically 0.5-4.5 mIU/L)
  • Onset: 3-5 days; full effect: 4-6 weeks

Therapeutic Use

Levothyroxine replaces T4 and is used as thyroid hormone replacement therapy. Replacement of T4 also raises T3 levels, because some T4 is converted into T3.

Complications

Adverse effects are essentially the same as manifestations of hyperthyroidism: cardiac manifestations (hypertension and angina pectoris); insomnia; anxiety; weight loss; heat intolerance; increased body temperature; tremors; and menstrual irregularities.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Untreated thyrotoxicosis
  • Acute MI
  • Uncorrected adrenal insufficiency (treat adrenal first)
  • Hypersensitivity to levothyroxine
  • Caution: cardiovascular disease (start low, titrate slowly — ↑ cardiac workload)
  • Caution: elderly (↑ cardiac sensitivity, osteoporosis risk with overreplacement)
  • Caution: diabetes (may worsen control), osteoporosis
  • Pregnancy Cat A; dose typically increases during pregnancy

Interactions

  • ↓ absorption: calcium, iron, antacids (Al/Mg), sucralfate, cholestyramine, bile acid sequestrants, PPIs — separate by 4 hours
  • Soy, walnuts, high-fiber foods → ↓ absorption (consistent timing matters)
  • Espresso/coffee → can ↓ absorption (separate by 1 hour)
  • Warfarin → ↑ INR (levothyroxine ↑ catabolism of clotting factors)
  • Insulin and oral hypoglycemics → may need dose adjustment (changing metabolism)
  • Digoxin → ↓ digoxin effect
  • Estrogens, oral contraceptives → ↑ thyroid-binding globulin → may need ↑ levothyroxine dose
  • Phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin → ↑ metabolism → may need ↑ levothyroxine dose

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • TSH within target range (typically 0.5-4.5 mIU/L; tighter for pregnancy or thyroid cancer)
  • ↓ symptoms of hypothyroidism: ↓ fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, dry skin, hair loss
  • ↑ energy, ↑ mental clarity, ↑ activity tolerance
  • Normal heart rate, no chest pain
  • No signs of overreplacement (hyperthyroidism): palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, insomnia, diarrhea

Medication Administration

  • Administer orally with water on an empty stomach, ideally 30-60 min before breakfast, at the same time each day.
  • Separate calcium, iron, antacids, sucralfate, bile acid sequestrants, and similar products by at least 4 hr to protect absorption.
  • Do not switch brands or formulations without provider guidance and follow-up thyroid labs.
  • Dose adjustments are based on TSH response, usually after 4-6 weeks; older adults or clients with cardiac disease usually start at lower doses.
  • If a dose is missed, follow provider instructions; do not double doses without guidance.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor TSH and free T4 as ordered; reassess labs after dose changes because full effect can take 4-6 weeks.
  • Assess heart rate, blood pressure, chest pain, palpitations, weight, temperature intolerance, bowel pattern, energy level, and sleep changes.
  • For older adults or clients with cardiac disease, monitor closely when therapy starts or increases because thyroid replacement raises cardiac workload.
  • Screen for over-replacement: tachycardia, angina, tremor, nervousness, insomnia, heat intolerance, diarrhea, weight loss, or menstrual changes.
  • Review administration timing and interactions: give on an empty stomach with water, keep timing consistent, and separate calcium, iron, antacids, and sucralfate by at least 4 hr.
  • Teach lifelong therapy expectations and advise the client not to switch brands or stop therapy without provider guidance.

Client Education

  • Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, usually 1 hr before breakfast.
  • Thyroid replacement therapy is usually required for life
  • Monitor for adverse effects that indicate that the dosage needs to be adjusted.
Worked Example HPV Vaccine Ch 41 — Immunizations · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
HPV Vaccine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 41 — Immunizations
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

9-valent HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9) is a recombinant subunit vaccine:

  • Contains virus-like particles (VLPs) of HPV major capsid proteins (L1) from 9 HPV types
  • Stimulates humoral immune response → neutralizing antibodies against HPV
  • NOT infectious — VLPs contain no viral DNA
  • Covers HPV types: 6, 11 (cause ~90% of genital warts) and 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 (cause ~90% of HPV-related cancers)
  • Most effective when given BEFORE first sexual exposure to HPV

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention of HPV-related cancers: cervical, vulvar, vaginal, anal, oropharyngeal, penile
  • Prevention of genital warts
  • Prevention of high-grade cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal intraepithelial neoplasia
  • Routine in adolescents ages 9-26; can be used through age 45 based on shared clinical decision
  • Both males and females

Complications

  • The 9vHPV vaccine can cause redness, tenderness, and swelling at the injection site.
  • It has caused fainting in some clients shortly after the vaccine is administered.
  • Headache and mild to moderate fever are also possible adverse effects the client should monitor for.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Contraindicated with severe allergic reaction or anaphylaxis to a prior HPV vaccine dose or vaccine component, including yeast.
  • Defer vaccination during pregnancy; if pregnancy is discovered after a dose, delay remaining doses until after pregnancy.
  • Delay vaccination during moderate or severe acute illness; mild illness is not usually a reason to defer.
  • Immunocompromised clients should receive the 3-dose series and may have a reduced immune response.
  • Observe the client seated or lying for 15 min after injection because syncope can occur, especially in adolescents.

Interactions

  • Other vaccines — can be given concurrently at separate injection sites
  • Immunosuppressants → may ↓ vaccine response (still recommended)
  • Recent immunoglobulin or blood product → may interfere with response (less concern with subunit vaccines)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Completion of full vaccine series
  • No serious adverse events (anaphylaxis, severe injection reaction)
  • Continued routine cervical cancer screening (Pap/HPV testing) per age guidelines — vaccine does NOT replace screening
  • Population-level: ↓ HPV prevalence, ↓ precancerous lesions, ↓ HPV-related cancers

Medication Administration

  • Route: intramuscular (deltoid or anterolateral thigh)
  • Schedule:
    • Ages 9-14: 2 doses, 6-12 months apart
    • Ages 15-45: 3 doses at 0, 1-2 months, 6 months
    • Immunocompromised: 3 doses regardless of age
  • 0.5 mL per dose
  • Shake suspension well before drawing up
  • Do NOT mix with other vaccines in same syringe
  • Observe 15 min after injection (syncope is common in adolescents)
  • Document dose, lot number, site per immunization registry requirements
  • Provide Vaccine Information Statement (VIS)

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify age, immunization history, and any prior HPV vaccine doses
  • Screen for contraindications (anaphylaxis to prior dose or yeast)
  • Verify NOT pregnant (defer if pregnant)
  • Provide Vaccine Information Statement (VIS) and obtain consent
  • Shake the suspension well before drawing up
  • Administer 0.5 mL IM in deltoid (or anterolateral thigh in young children)
  • Observe client seated or recumbent for 15 minutes after injection — syncope is common in adolescents
  • Apply pressure to injection site; document dose, lot number, expiration, site, time
  • Schedule next dose per age-appropriate schedule (2 or 3-dose series)
  • Educate on possible side effects: injection site pain/redness/swelling, mild fever, headache, fatigue
  • Cold compress and acetaminophen for soreness
  • Provide written immunization record; update immunization registry
  • Reinforce that HPV vaccine does NOT replace cervical cancer screening — Pap/HPV testing continues per guidelines

Client Education

  • Monitor for adverse effects; the common adverse effects are mild and temporary.
  • The adolescent will require a second dose in 6 to 12 months since this one occurred before age 16. Initial administration after 16 years of age requires a three dose series.
Worked Example MMR Vaccine Ch 41 — Immunizations · Vaccines section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
MMR Vaccine (Measles, Mumps, Rubella)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 41 — Immunizations
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Live attenuated viral vaccine — contains weakened measles, mumps, and rubella viruses
  • Stimulates active immunity (antibody production and immune memory)
  • Provides long-lasting protection against all three diseases

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention of measles, mumps, and rubella
  • Routine childhood immunization: first dose 12–15 months, second dose 4–6 years
  • Susceptible adults (especially healthcare workers, those born after 1957 without immunity)
  • Rubella immunity especially important for those who may become pregnant (prevent congenital rubella syndrome)

Complications

  • Injection site soreness, redness
  • Low-grade fever (may occur 5–12 days later, as immunity develops)
  • Mild rash
  • Transient joint pain (especially rubella component, adult women)
  • Febrile seizures (rare; risk slightly higher with MMRV combination)
  • Allergic reaction (rare; gelatin, neomycin)
  • Thrombocytopenia (rare, transient)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy (live vaccine) — avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks after
  • Immunocompromised (severe immunodeficiency, high-dose steroids, chemotherapy, HIV with low CD4) — live vaccine risk
  • Severe allergic reaction to prior dose or component (gelatin, neomycin)
  • Recent blood products/immunoglobulin (may reduce response — space appropriately)
  • Moderate-severe acute illness (defer)

Interactions

  • Immunoglobulin / blood products — may blunt vaccine response; separate timing per guidelines
  • Immunosuppressants — reduce efficacy and increase risk (live vaccine)
  • Other live vaccines — give same day OR separate by ≥ 4 weeks
  • Tuberculin (PPD) test — may cause false-negative; do PPD same day or wait 4 weeks

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Development of immunity (documented vaccination; titers if needed)
  • Protection against measles, mumps, rubella
  • No serious adverse reactions
  • Completion of two-dose series

Medication Administration

  • Route: subcutaneous
  • Two-dose series (first at 12–15 months, second at 4–6 years)
  • Reconstitute per directions; use promptly; protect from light
  • Can be given with other vaccines (different sites)
  • Provide Vaccine Information Statement (VIS)

Nursing Interventions

  • Screen for contraindications: pregnancy, immunocompromise, severe allergy
  • Verify timing with blood products and other live vaccines
  • Provide VIS before administration; document
  • Administer subcutaneously; proper reconstitution/storage (cold chain)
  • Observe for immediate allergic reaction (have epinephrine available)
  • Educate on expected mild effects and delayed fever/rash
  • Counsel to avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks (rubella)

Client Education

  • Mild fever and rash may occur 5–12 days after — this is normal (immunity developing)
  • Soreness at injection site is common; use cool compress, acetaminophen for fever/discomfort
