  • Avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks after the vaccine (live virus — rubella)
  • Two doses are needed for full protection
  • Report signs of allergic reaction (difficulty breathing, swelling, hives)
  • Keep vaccination records
  • Notify provider if immunocompromised or pregnant (vaccine may be deferred)
  • Vaccines protect the individual and the community (herd immunity)
Worked Example Leuprolide Ch 42 — Chemotherapy Agents · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Leuprolide
Review Module Chapter
Ch 42 — Chemotherapy Agents
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Leuprolide is a GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) agonist:

  • Initially stimulates LH/FSH release ("flare" effect with ↑ testosterone/estrogen)
  • With continuous stimulation, down-regulates pituitary GnRH receptors → suppresses LH/FSH
  • ↓ testosterone (to castrate levels) in men; ↓ estrogen (to postmenopausal levels) in women
  • Reversible "medical castration" — hormone-sensitive cancers and conditions regress
  • Initial flare can worsen symptoms (bone pain in prostate cancer, etc.) — pretreat with antiandrogen

Therapeutic Use

  • Used as androgen-deprivation therapy for hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, including monthly IM depot therapy instead of surgical castration.
  • Continuous GnRH stimulation suppresses LH/FSH over time, lowering testosterone to slow prostate cancer growth and reduce disease manifestations.
  • May also be used for other hormone-sensitive conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and central precocious puberty when prescribed.
  • Because an initial hormone flare can worsen bone pain, urinary obstruction, or spinal cord compression risk, antiandrogen pretreatment and monitoring may be needed.

Complications

  • Hot flashes (or flashes), decreased libido, gynecomastia
  • Cardiac manifestations (dysrhythmias) and increased edema, which can lead
  • Decreased bone density, which can lead to fractures
  • Disease flare, which means manifestations of the client's prostate cancer can

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to leuprolide or other GnRH analogs
  • Pregnancy (Cat X) — fetal harm
  • Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding
  • Caution: history of QT prolongation, congenital long QT
  • Caution: history of mental health disorders
  • Caution: cardiovascular disease, diabetes (worsens with androgen deprivation)
  • Caution: existing osteoporosis (worsens with sex steroid loss)
  • Initial flare can cause: bone pain, spinal cord compression, urinary obstruction in metastatic prostate cancer (pretreat with antiandrogen)

Interactions

  • Antiandrogens (bicalutamide, flutamide) — combined to prevent flare in prostate cancer
  • QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, methadone, certain antibiotics) — additive QT risk
  • Diabetes medications — leuprolide may worsen glycemic control
  • Hormone replacement therapy → defeats the purpose
  • Drugs causing bone loss (steroids, PPIs) → additive osteoporosis risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Prostate cancer: testosterone at castrate levels (< 50 ng/dL); ↓ PSA; symptom relief
  • Endometriosis: ↓ pelvic pain, ↓ dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, ↓ lesion size on imaging
  • Fibroids: ↓ size on imaging, ↓ menorrhagia
  • Precocious puberty: regression of pubertal signs, ↓ rate of skeletal maturation
  • No flare-related complications (cord compression, bone pain crisis)
  • Bone density preserved (with concurrent therapy if appropriate)

Medication Administration

  • Routes: SC daily, monthly IM depot, 3/4/6-month depot injections, implant
  • Prostate cancer: 7.5 mg IM monthly, 22.5 mg IM q3 months, 30 mg q4 months, or 45 mg q6 months
  • Endometriosis: 3.75 mg IM monthly (max 6 months for first course)
  • Rotate injection sites (gluteal, abdomen)
  • Reconstitute according to specific product instructions
  • Administer the FULL syringe contents
  • Document next dose due date
  • Consider concurrent bone density therapy in long-term use

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor prostate-specific antigen and testosterone levels, which should both
  • Bone density testing can be needed for some clients, as well as ECG if cardia

Client Education

  • Increase calcium and vitamin D in diet.
  • Increase weight-bearing exercise to minimize bone loss.
  • Report a flare in prostate manifestations to the provider.
  • Report adverse effects (palpitations, edema, and hot flashes) to the provider.
Worked Example Vancomycin Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Vancomycin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic that:

  • Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to D-alanyl-D-alanine peptidoglycan precursors
  • Bactericidal against most gram-positive organisms, including MRSA and Clostridioides difficile (when oral)
  • Not effective against gram-negative bacteria
  • IV form = systemic infections; oral (PO) form = C. diff colitis ONLY (not absorbed systemically)
  • Renally cleared — requires dose adjustment in renal impairment

Therapeutic Use

Vancomycin is an antibiotic that kills bacteria by disrupting their cell wall. The IV form treats serious infections due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, and streptococci.

Complications

  • Infusion reactions (red man syndrome: rashes, flushing, tachycardia, and hypotension)
  • Ototoxicity (rare and reversible)
  • Renal toxicity
  • Thrombophlebitis at the IV site
  • Im and IV injection-site pain

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to vancomycin
  • Renal impairment — dose-adjust based on CrCl and serum trough levels
  • Caution: hearing loss or ototoxicity history
  • Caution: elderly, dehydration
  • Pregnancy Cat C (IV); oral form not absorbed → no fetal exposure
  • Caution in concurrent nephrotoxic or ototoxic drug use

Interactions

  • Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin) → ↑ nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) → ↑ ototoxicity
  • NSAIDs, amphotericin B, cisplatin, polymyxin B → ↑ nephrotoxicity
  • Neuromuscular blockers → ↑ neuromuscular blockade
  • Anesthetics → ↑ infusion reactions, hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection signs: ↓ fever, ↓ WBC, negative cultures
  • Trough levels within therapeutic range (10-20 mcg/mL)
  • For CDAD: ↓ diarrhea frequency, resolution of abdominal pain, normal stool form
  • No nephrotoxicity (stable BUN/creatinine, UO ≥ 30 mL/hr)
  • No ototoxicity (hearing intact, no tinnitus)
  • No infusion reactions

Medication Administration

  • IV (systemic infections): 15-20 mg/kg/dose q8-12h based on weight and renal function
  • Infuse over at least 60 minutes (longer for higher doses) — too-rapid infusion → red man/vancomycin infusion syndrome (flushing, rash, hypotension; histamine release, NOT true allergy)
  • Trough levels: 10-20 mcg/mL (15-20 for serious MRSA infections like endocarditis or pneumonia)
  • Draw trough just before the 4th dose (steady state)
  • Oral (CDAD): 125-500 mg PO QID × 10-14 days; capsules or oral solution
  • Monitor BUN, creatinine, urine output, hearing
  • Hold for unresolved red man syndrome; restart at slower rate after symptoms resolve

Nursing Interventions

  • Infuse vancomycin over at least 60 min/dose to prevent an infusion reaction.
  • Monitor the IV site for redness, pain, or other manifestations of thrombophlebitis.
  • Monitor I&O, and notify the provider for oliguria or other findings of acute renal injury.
  • Monitor for hearing loss.
  • Ask the client about allergy to antibiotics before administering the medication. Watch for allergic manifestations during and after the infusion.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: hearing changes, ringing in ears, dizziness, ↓ urine output, swelling, severe pain at IV site, rash, flushing during infusion
  • The medication will be given slowly (over an hour or more) to prevent reactions
  • Some clients experience a flushing reaction during infusion — this is not a true allergy; the rate can be adjusted
  • Lab work (drug levels, kidney function) will be checked regularly
  • For oral therapy (C. diff): complete the full course; report worsening or recurrent diarrhea
  • Maintain adequate hydration
  • Avoid taking other potentially kidney-toxic medications (NSAIDs) unless approved
Worked Example Erythromycin Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Erythromycin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic:

  • Binds to 50S ribosomal subunit → inhibits bacterial protein synthesis
  • Bacteriostatic (or bactericidal at high concentrations)
  • Spectrum: gram-positive (streptococci, staphylococci), atypicals (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia), Bordetella pertussis, some gram-negative
  • Useful in penicillin-allergic clients
  • Also stimulates motilin receptors → ↑ GI motility (gastroparesis treatment, but also major cause of GI side effects)

Therapeutic Use

Erythromycin inhibits protein synthesis in the cells of susceptible micro-organisms, usually gram-positive bacteria. Erythromycin can be either bacteriostatic or bactericidal, depending on the organism and on the medication's dosage. It also treats infections for clients who are allergic to penicillin.

Complications

  • The most common adverse effects of erythromycin are GI manifestations, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
  • Hepatotoxicity with abdominal pain, anorexia, fatigue, and possibly jaundice can occur after 1 to 2 weeks of erythromycin therapy.
  • Erythromycin can cause a prolonged QT interval on ECG, which can lead to potentially fatal tachydysrhythmias.
  • Ototoxicity can occur with high doses, especially after prolonged periods.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to erythromycin or other macrolides
  • Concurrent pimozide, cisapride, terfenadine — fatal arrhythmias (QT prolongation)
  • Concurrent simvastatin, lovastatin (high doses) — rhabdomyolysis risk
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • History of QT prolongation, torsades, hypokalemia
  • Caution: myasthenia gravis (may worsen)
  • Pregnancy Cat B (estolate form is Cat D — hepatotoxic in pregnancy; avoid)
  • Breastfeeding (small amounts in milk)

Interactions

  • Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor → ↑ levels of many drugs:
    • Warfarin → ↑ INR
    • Digoxin → ↑ digoxin levels
    • Statins (simvastatin, lovastatin) → rhabdomyolysis
    • Carbamazepine, theophylline → toxicity
    • Cyclosporine, tacrolimus → ↑ levels
    • Benzodiazepines (esp. midazolam, triazolam) → ↑ sedation
  • QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, methadone, certain antipsychotics) → torsades risk
  • Ergot alkaloids → severe vasospasm
  • Antacids → may ↓ absorption (separate)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection symptoms: ↓ fever, ↓ pain, improved appearance of infected site
  • Negative cultures (when applicable)
  • For gastroparesis: ↑ gastric emptying, ↓ nausea/early satiety
  • For acne: ↓ inflammatory lesions
  • Completion of course without relapse
  • No serious adverse events: no QT prolongation, no hepatic injury, no severe GI symptoms

Medication Administration

  • Routes: oral, IV, topical (ointment, eye), inhalation (rare)
  • Adult oral: 250-500 mg PO q6h or q12h depending on formulation
  • Take on empty stomach for best absorption (1 hr before or 2 hr after food) — though may give with food if GI upset severe
  • Take with a full glass of water
  • Swallow enteric-coated tablets whole
  • Refrigerate suspension; shake well
  • IV: dilute well; infuse slowly over ≥ 60 minutes (rapid infusion → phlebitis, hypotension, QT changes)
  • Complete the entire prescribed course

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor liver function tests for clients who take erythromycin over a period of several weeks.
  • If the client is concurrently taking warfarin or digoxin with erythromycin, carefully monitor PT and INR or digoxin levels.
  • Monitor WBC counts for effectiveness of erythromycin treatment.

Client Education

  • Take erythromycin on an empty stomach, 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals with 8 oz of water.
  • Observe for adverse effects, and call the provider for severe GI distress, manifestations of liver toxicity, and ototoxicity.
  • Take the entire course of the medication and not to stop when feeling better.
Worked Example Phenazopyridine Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Phenazopyridine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Urinary tract analgesic azo dye that acts locally on urinary tract mucosa to relieve irritation-related discomfort.
  • Provides symptomatic relief of dysuria, burning, urgency, and frequency but has no antibacterial effect.
  • Does not treat the underlying UTI, so antibiotic therapy and culture-guided follow-up remain necessary when infection is present.
  • Orange-red urine and body-fluid discoloration are expected from the dye and can interfere with color-based urine tests.

Therapeutic Use

  • Short-term relief of urinary burning, urgency, pain, and frequency while antibiotic therapy treats the infection.
  • Used as adjunct comfort therapy for cystitis or urinary tract irritation, not as standalone infection treatment.
  • Limit use to about 2 days with antibiotics so worsening infection is not masked.
  • Best paired with hydration, antibiotic adherence, and reassessment if fever, flank pain, or persistent symptoms occur.

Complications

  • Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, tears, skin, sclera (expected; harmless but stains fabrics and contact lenses)
  • GI: nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, dyspepsia (take with food)
  • Headache, dizziness, vertigo
  • Rash, pruritus (allergic reaction)
  • Hemolytic anemia in G6PD-deficient clients
  • Methemoglobinemia (rare but serious; blue-gray skin, dyspnea, headache)
  • Hepatotoxicity with prolonged use or in hepatic impairment
  • Nephrotoxicity with prolonged use, especially in renal impairment
  • Anaphylaxis (rare)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to phenazopyridine
  • Severe renal impairment (CrCl < 50)
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • G6PD deficiency (hemolytic anemia risk)
  • Caution: pregnancy Cat B; breastfeeding
  • Use limited to 2 days when combined with antibiotic (no longer needed by then)

Interactions

  • Few drug-drug interactions of significance
  • May discolor body fluids (urine, sweat, tears) → can stain clothes, soft contact lenses
  • May interfere with urine tests (color-based readings: glucose, ketones, bilirubin, urobilinogen)
  • Antacids → ↓ absorption (separate)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of burning, urgency, and frequency within 1-2 days
  • ↑ comfort during voiding
  • Antibiotic therapy continues to address infection (this is symptom relief only)
  • Resolution of UTI symptoms after antibiotic completes
  • No hemolytic anemia (CBC stable)
  • No hepatotoxicity (skin/sclera not yellowing)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Adult: 200 mg PO TID after meals
  • Pediatric (≥ 6 yr): 12 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses
  • Limit duration to 2 days when used with antibiotic for UTI
  • Take with or after food to ↓ GI upset
  • Drink plenty of fluids (≥ 8 glasses/day)
  • Stop if skin or sclera turns yellow (drug accumulation, possible hemolysis)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess pain/discomfort with urination
  • Encourage adequate fluid intake (2-3 L/day) — flushes urinary tract
  • Educate client about urine discoloration (orange-red) — harmless and expected
  • Reinforce that this drug treats SYMPTOMS only — antibiotic still needed for infection
  • Limit use to 2 days when used with antibiotic
  • Monitor for skin/sclera yellowing (hemolysis); assess CBC if indicated
  • Assess for rash, GI upset, headache
  • If still symptomatic after 2 days of antibiotic + phenazopyridine, reevaluate diagnosis

Client Education

  • Acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease are contraindications.
  • It changes urine to an orange-red color.
  • Tell clients that the urine can stain clothes.
  • Instruct clients to take it with or after meals to minimize GI discomfort.
Worked Example Isoniazid Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Isoniazid
Review Module Chapter
Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Isoniazid (INH) is a first-line antitubercular agent:

  • Inhibits synthesis of mycolic acid in the cell wall of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
  • Bactericidal against actively dividing M. tuberculosis; bacteriostatic against dormant organisms
  • Penetrates well into cerebrospinal fluid, caseous lesions, and macrophages
  • Almost always used in combination (RIPE: Rifampin, INH, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) to prevent resistance

Therapeutic Use

A client who has latent tuberculosis has been infected by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is at risk for (but has not yet developed) active tuberculosis. Some clients who have latent tuberculosis (those who are immunocompromised or who have recently immigrated to the U.S. from a country where active TB is common) can require treatment with isoniazid, with or without rifapentine, in order to prevent the onset of active TB. The client who has latent TB has a positive tuberculin test but a negative sputum culture and negative chest x-ray for TB. The client cannot infect others with tuberculosis unless the infection becomes active.

Complications

  • Paresthesias in the extremities caused by vitamin B6 deficiency
  • Hepatotoxicity
  • Hyperglycemia (if client has diabetes mellitus)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe hepatic disease, history of INH-induced hepatitis
  • Hypersensitivity to INH
  • Caution: chronic alcohol use (↑ hepatotoxicity)
  • Caution: peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine/B6 to prevent)
  • Caution: diabetes, malnutrition (↑ neuropathy risk)
  • Caution: pregnancy (Cat C; benefit usually outweighs risk for active TB)
  • Caution: HIV (may need higher doses; drug interactions)

Interactions

  • Rifampin → ↑ hepatotoxicity risk (but combination usually necessary)
  • Acetaminophen, alcohol → ↑ hepatotoxicity
  • Phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate → INH inhibits metabolism → ↑ levels of these drugs → toxicity
  • Antacids (Al-containing) → ↓ INH absorption; separate by 1-2 hr
  • Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, smoked meats) → can cause hypertensive reaction (MAO-A inhibition)
  • Disulfiram → psychosis, ataxia

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Active TB: negative sputum cultures after 2-3 months, ↓ symptoms (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss), improved chest X-ray
  • Latent TB: no progression to active disease
  • No hepatotoxicity (stable LFTs)
  • No peripheral neuropathy
  • Adherence verified (DOT or pill count)

Medication Administration

  • Administer orally or IM as prescribed; oral dosing is usually preferred for TB therapy.
  • Give on an empty stomach, 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals, for best absorption; may give with food if GI upset threatens adherence.
  • Separate aluminum-containing antacids by 1-2 hr because they can decrease isoniazid absorption.
  • Give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) as prescribed to prevent or reduce peripheral neuropathy.
  • Use directly observed therapy when ordered, and reinforce completion of the full TB regimen even when symptoms improve or latent TB feels asymptomatic.

Nursing Interventions

  • Obtain baseline liver function tests and monitor periodically or monthly during therapy, especially with alcohol use, liver disease, pregnancy, or concurrent hepatotoxic drugs.
  • Assess for hepatitis symptoms: anorexia, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dark urine, or jaundice; hold and notify the provider for concerning findings per protocol.
  • Administer pyridoxine (vitamin B6) as prescribed and monitor for peripheral neuropathy such as numbness, tingling, burning, or paresthesias.
  • Reinforce strict adherence for the full TB regimen; use directly observed therapy when ordered to reduce resistance and treatment failure.
  • Teach avoidance of alcohol and caution with acetaminophen or other hepatotoxic medications during therapy.
  • Review administration on an empty stomach when tolerated and separate aluminum-containing antacids to prevent reduced absorption.

Client Education

  • Teach the client to watch for paresthesias, and to take pyridoxine daily to reverse the effect if they occur.
  • Teach the client about indications of hepatitis (anorexia, fatigue, nausea, jaundice) and to notify the provider if these occur.
  • Teach the client to take isoniazid as prescribed, and not to stop until the entire course of treatment is completed.
  • The client who has latent tuberculosis does not feel ill. The nurse should be sure that the client understands why it is important to continue with treatment.
Worked Example Ganciclovir Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ganciclovir
Review Module Chapter
Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Ganciclovir is an antiviral nucleoside analog active against herpesviruses:

  • Phosphorylated by viral kinases (esp. CMV UL97 kinase) to active triphosphate form
  • Inhibits viral DNA polymerase → incorporates into viral DNA → halts elongation
  • Most active against cytomegalovirus (CMV); also active against HSV, VZV, EBV
  • NOT curative — suppresses viral replication; CMV may reactivate
  • Oral prodrug: valganciclovir (much higher bioavailability than oral ganciclovir)

Therapeutic Use

Ganciclovir prevents reproduction of viral dna and thus prevents viral cell replication. it is used is to prevent or treat cytomegalovirus in clients who are immunocompromised.

Complications

  • Minor discomforts (fever, headache, and nausea)
  • Suppresses the bone marrow, causing a decrease in WBcs, especially granulocytes
  • Causes thrombocytopenia frequently
  • The client should report any discomforts and be sure to report new onset of fatigue, easy bruising, or sore throat.
  • Advise the client to report manifestations of infection or bleeding, and to avoid crowds or individuals who have respiratory infections.

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe neutropenia (ANC < 500/mm³) — drug is bone marrow toxic
  • Severe thrombocytopenia (platelets < 25,000/mm³)
  • Hypersensitivity to ganciclovir or acyclovir
  • Pregnancy Cat C — teratogenic, carcinogenic, gonadotoxic in animals; use only if benefit outweighs risk
  • Caution: renal impairment — dose-adjust based on CrCl
  • Caution: severe hepatic impairment
  • Caution: history of cytopenias or bone marrow disease

Interactions

  • Zidovudine → additive bone marrow toxicity → severe neutropenia
  • Other myelosuppressive drugs (chemotherapy, trimethoprim/sulfa) → additive cytopenias
  • Nephrotoxic drugs (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B) → ↑ renal toxicity
  • Probenecid → ↑ ganciclovir levels
  • Imipenem-cilastatin → ↑ seizure risk (avoid combination)
  • Mycophenolate → ↑ levels of both drugs
  • Didanosine → ↑ didanosine levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • CMV retinitis: stabilization or improvement of retinal lesions on serial ophthalmologic exams
  • ↓ CMV viral load (PCR)
  • Resolution of CMV-associated symptoms (colitis, pneumonitis)
  • Successful prevention of CMV disease (transplant prophylaxis)
  • No significant cytopenias: ANC > 500, platelets > 25,000
  • Stable renal function

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV, intraocular implant (CMV retinitis), oral as valganciclovir
  • Induction: 5 mg/kg IV q12h × 14-21 days
  • Maintenance: 5 mg/kg IV daily or 6 mg/kg 5 days/week
  • Adjust dose for renal impairment
  • Infuse IV slowly over ≥ 1 hour (rapid infusion → toxicity)
  • Use central line if possible (extravasation causes severe tissue damage — high pH ~11)
  • Maintain hydration during infusion to prevent crystalluria
  • Wear gloves and protective equipment when handling (hazardous drug)
  • Monitor CBC: q2 weeks during induction; weekly during maintenance
  • Monitor renal function (BUN, creatinine) regularly

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor client blood counts, especially WBc, absolute neutrophil count, and thrombocyte count. expect ganciclovir therapy to be interrupted for an absolute neutrophil count less than 500/mm3 or a thrombocyte count less than 25,000/mm3.
  • Monitor blood counts.
  • Prepare to administer granulocyte colony-stimulating factors for a low absolute neutrophil count.
  • Monitor i&o, and encourage the client to increase fluid intake.
  • Avoid direct contact with the powder from oral ganciclovir or the iV solution, and wash well if contact occurs.
  • Advise clients to use a barrier contraception (condoms) during treatment and for 3 months following treatment.

Client Education

  • Report immediately: signs of infection (fever, sore throat, cough, painful urination), unusual bleeding or bruising, severe fatigue, vision changes, severe pain or burning at IV site, rash, jaundice, decreased urine output
  • You will need frequent blood tests during treatment (CBC, kidney function)
  • This medication can lower your blood counts, increasing infection and bleeding risk — avoid crowds and sick people; use a soft toothbrush; avoid contact sports
  • Use highly effective contraception during treatment AND for at least 30 days after (women) or 90 days after (men) — drug is harmful to a fetus and to sperm
  • This drug may cause infertility (men and women) — discuss preservation options before treatment if relevant
  • Stay well-hydrated unless otherwise directed
  • If CMV retinitis: keep all ophthalmology appointments — they monitor for progression
  • Wash hands thoroughly after any contact with body fluids
  • Continue maintenance therapy for full prescribed course — relapse possible if stopped early
  • Do not breastfeed while on therapy
Worked Example St. John's Wort Ch 49 — Complementary, Alternative, and Integrative Therapies · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
St. John's Wort
Review Module Chapter
Ch 49 — Complementary, Alternative, and Integrative Therapies
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) is an herbal supplement used for depression:

  • Active constituents: hyperforin and hypericin
  • Inhibits reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, GABA, glutamate (similar to multiple antidepressants)
  • Also affects MAO mildly (clinically minor)
  • Potent CYP3A4 enzyme inducer → causes many drug interactions
  • Onset: weeks for clinical effect; not standardized — preparations vary widely in potency

Therapeutic Use

  • Affects serotonin, producing antidepressant effects
  • Mild depression
  • Oral analgesic to relieve pain and inflammation
  • Applied topically to treat infection

Complications

  • Mild adverse effects, including dry mouth, lightheadedness, constipation, GI discomfort
  • Skin rash with client exposure to sunlight

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to St. John's wort
  • Severe (major) depression — efficacy unclear; risks of delaying effective treatment
  • Bipolar disorder (can trigger mania)
  • Concurrent use with prescription antidepressants — serotonin syndrome risk
  • Concurrent use with many critical medications (see Interactions) — DOZENS of significant interactions
  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding (insufficient data)
  • Surgery — discontinue at least 5 days before (anesthetic interactions)
  • Photosensitivity in fair-skinned clients

Interactions

  • Can cause serotonin syndrome when combined with other antidepressants, amphetamine, and cocaine
  • Decreases effectiveness of oral contraceptives, cyclosporine, warfarin, digoxin, calcium channel blockers, steroids, HIV protease inhibitors, and some anticancer medications

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms (questionable benefit; many studies show limited efficacy)
  • ↑ mood, ↑ energy, improved sleep
  • No serotonin syndrome
  • No suicidal ideation worsening
  • No drug interaction-related problems (contraceptive failure, transplant rejection, etc.)
  • For severe depression: assess for inadequate response — refer for evidence-based treatment

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (capsules, tablets, liquid, tea)
  • Typical dose: 300 mg PO TID (standardized to 0.3% hypericin)
  • Topical preparations available for minor wounds and inflammation
  • Effect on mood: 2-4 weeks for response
  • Quality varies — products are not FDA-regulated; choose USP-verified brands
  • Take with food to ↓ GI upset
  • If discontinuing: taper gradually if used long-term

Nursing Interventions

  • Take a thorough medication history including ALL OTC and herbal products at every visit — St. John's wort is often unreported
  • Assess depression severity — if moderate-severe, recommend evaluation for evidence-based treatment
  • Educate about the EXTENSIVE list of significant drug interactions
  • Verify: not on oral contraceptives (unintended pregnancy risk), warfarin (thrombosis), digoxin, transplant immunosuppressants, HIV medications, chemotherapy, anticonvulsants
  • Check for concurrent serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans, tramadol) — serotonin syndrome risk
  • Assess for symptoms suggestive of bipolar disorder before recommending (can trigger mania)
  • Assess for suicidal ideation, especially if used for depression
  • If client decides to start a prescription antidepressant: stop St. John's wort first; allow washout period
  • If client undergoing surgery: discontinue at least 5 days before procedure
  • Educate on photosensitivity precautions (sunscreen, protective clothing)
  • Monitor for therapeutic response and adverse effects at follow-up

Client Education

  • Report: persistent or worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, mania symptoms (decreased sleep need, racing thoughts, risky behavior), severe headache, fever with confusion (serotonin syndrome), severe sunburn
  • This is an herbal supplement, NOT FDA-regulated — preparations vary widely in potency
  • Choose USP-verified or standardized products if you decide to use
  • Inform ALL providers you are taking St. John's wort — many serious drug interactions
  • Use backup contraception if on oral contraceptives — St. John's wort can cause contraceptive failure
  • If you are on warfarin, digoxin, HIV medications, transplant medications, anti-seizure drugs, chemotherapy, or any other prescription drug — discuss with provider before continuing
  • Do NOT combine with prescription antidepressants — life-threatening serotonin syndrome
  • Stop at least 5 days before surgery
  • Use sunscreen and protective clothing — increased sun sensitivity
  • Effect on mood may take 2-4 weeks
  • For moderate to severe depression: consider evidence-based treatment rather than St. John's wort alone
  • Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Worked Example Ginkgo Biloba Ch 49 — Complementary, Alternative, and Integrative Therapies · Herbals section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ginkgo Biloba
Review Module Chapter
Ch 49 — Complementary, Alternative, and Integrative Therapies
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Herbal supplement — thought to improve blood flow and act as an antioxidant
  • Inhibits platelet aggregation (antiplatelet-like effect)
  • Promoted for cognitive and circulatory effects (evidence mixed/limited)

Therapeutic Use

  • Marketed for memory/cognitive enhancement and dementia (evidence not strongly supportive)
  • Peripheral vascular disease / intermittent claudication
  • Tinnitus, vertigo (claimed)
  • Note: a supplement, not an FDA-approved drug

Complications

  • Increased bleeding risk (antiplatelet effect) — bruising, prolonged bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage reported
  • GI upset, headache, dizziness
  • Allergic skin reactions
  • Seizures (especially with raw/unprocessed seeds — ginkgotoxin)
  • Palpitations

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Bleeding disorders
  • Concurrent anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs (additive bleeding)
  • Discontinue before surgery (~1–2 weeks; bleeding risk)
  • Seizure disorder
  • Pregnancy/lactation (avoid)

Interactions

  • Warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin, NSAIDs — increased bleeding
  • Anticonvulsants — may lower seizure threshold
  • Antidepressants (MAOIs, SSRIs) — possible interactions
  • Drugs metabolized by CYP enzymes (variable)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Self-reported symptom change (subjective; limited evidence)
  • No bleeding complications
  • No seizures or adverse effects
  • Disclosure of use to providers

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (standardized leaf extract; capsules/tablets/liquid)
  • Use standardized products; do NOT consume raw seeds (toxic)
  • Effects (if any) may take weeks
  • Not regulated for purity/potency like drugs

Nursing Interventions

  • Ask about ginkgo use; assess for bleeding risk and concurrent anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs
  • Advise discontinuation ~1–2 weeks before surgery
  • Monitor for bruising/bleeding
  • Educate that evidence for benefit is limited and products are not standardized
  • Encourage disclosure to all providers
  • Assess seizure history

Client Education

  • Tell all providers you take ginkgo, especially before surgery or if on blood thinners
  • Increases bleeding risk — report unusual bruising or bleeding; avoid combining with aspirin/NSAIDs/anticoagulants without provider guidance
  • Stop ~1–2 weeks before any surgery or dental procedure
  • Do not eat raw ginkgo seeds (can cause seizures)
  • “Natural” does not mean safe; products are not standardized
  • Discuss with your provider before starting, especially with other medications or conditions
  • Do not use to replace prescribed treatment for serious conditions
Worked Example Kava Ch 49 — Complementary, Alternative, and Integrative Therapies · Herbals section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Kava (Piper methysticum)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 49 — Complementary, Alternative, and Integrative Therapies
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Herbal supplement with anxiolytic and sedative effects (kavalactones)
  • Thought to affect GABA and limbic system activity
  • Produces calming/relaxant effects

Therapeutic Use

  • Used for anxiety, stress, and insomnia (self-treatment)
  • Marketed as a relaxant
  • A dietary supplement — not an FDA-approved anxiety treatment

Complications

  • Hepatotoxicity — severe liver damage, including liver failure (FDA warning); the major safety concern
  • Sedation, drowsiness, impaired motor function
  • With heavy/chronic use: scaly skin rash (“kava dermopathy”)
  • GI upset
  • Possible dependence/withdrawal

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Liver disease or hepatic risk (alcohol use, hepatotoxic drugs)
  • Concurrent CNS depressants/alcohol
  • Depression (may worsen)
  • Pregnancy/lactation (avoid)
  • Before driving/operating machinery (sedation)
  • Before surgery (anesthesia interaction)

Interactions

  • Alcohol and CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedatives) — additive sedation; increased hepatotoxicity with alcohol
  • Hepatotoxic drugs — additive liver injury
  • Levodopa — may reduce effect (worsen Parkinson’s)
  • Anesthetics — potentiate

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Self-reported reduction in anxiety/stress (subjective)
  • No signs of liver injury (normal LFTs)
  • No excessive sedation or impairment
  • Disclosure of use to providers

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (capsules, extracts, traditional beverage)
  • Not regulated for potency/purity
  • Avoid prolonged use (hepatotoxicity, dermopathy)
  • Do not combine with alcohol or sedatives

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess liver function and hepatic risk factors (alcohol, hepatotoxic drugs)
  • Screen for CNS depressant/alcohol use (additive sedation)
  • Assess for depression
  • Educate on hepatotoxicity warning signs
  • Advise caution with driving and before surgery
  • Encourage disclosure to providers; suggest evidence-based anxiety treatment if appropriate

Client Education

  • Report yellowing skin/eyes, dark urine, abdominal pain, or fatigue immediately (liver damage — serious risk)
  • Avoid alcohol and other sedating substances (additive sedation; liver injury)
  • Do not drive or operate machinery until you know the effect (sedation)
  • Tell all providers you take kava, especially before surgery
  • Avoid prolonged or high-dose use
  • Not recommended in pregnancy/breastfeeding or with liver disease
  • “Natural” does not mean safe; discuss anxiety with your provider for evidence-based options
  • Stop and seek care if signs of liver problems develop
Worked Example Lithium Carbonate Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Lithium Carbonate
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Mood stabilizer that alters cation (sodium) transport and modulates norepinephrine, serotonin, and dopamine activity in the CNS; exact mechanism not fully understood
  • Narrow therapeutic index — requires serum level monitoring

Therapeutic Use

  • Controls acute mania and supports long-term mood stabilization in bipolar disorder.
  • Reduces relapse risk when serum levels, renal function, thyroid function, sodium intake, and fluid intake remain stable.
  • Useful for maintenance therapy but requires ongoing monitoring because the therapeutic range is narrow and toxicity can occur with dehydration or sodium depletion.
  • Not an as-needed medication; therapeutic benefit depends on consistent dosing and scheduled serum level checks.

Complications

  • GI: nausea, diarrhea (early)
  • Fine hand tremor, polyuria, polydipsia, weight gain
  • Long-term: hypothyroidism/goiter, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal impairment
  • Toxicity (level > 1.5 mEq/L): coarse tremor, confusion, ataxia, seizures, dysrhythmias

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Renal impairment, significant cardiovascular disease
  • Dehydration or sodium depletion
  • Pregnancy (Category D) — Ebstein cardiac anomaly; breastfeeding
  • Caution with diuretics, NSAIDs, and older adults

Interactions

  • Thiazide/loop diuretics, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors → decrease excretion → ↑ lithium level/toxicity
  • ↑ sodium intake or caffeine → ↓ lithium level
  • Antipsychotics → additive CNS effects

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Stabilized mood, ↓ manic symptoms (grandiosity, pressured speech, impulsivity)
  • Therapeutic serum level 0.6–1.2 mEq/L (acute mania up to 1.5)
  • Normal thyroid and renal function maintained

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO (tablet, capsule, oral solution); give with food to reduce GI upset
  • Maintain 2–3 L fluid/day and consistent sodium intake
  • Monitor levels every few days initially, then every 1–3 months; draw trough (before AM dose)
  • Baseline and periodic renal function and TSH

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor serum lithium, renal function, and thyroid (TSH)
  • Assess for early signs of toxicity; hold and notify provider if level > 1.5 mEq/L
  • Ensure adequate hydration and steady sodium intake
  • Teach self-monitoring and adherence to lab schedule

Client Education

  • Take exactly as prescribed; do not skip or double doses
  • Maintain steady salt and fluid intake; avoid dehydration (heat, vomiting, diarrhea, strenuous exercise)
  • Report early toxicity: nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, tremor, confusion, slurred speech
  • Keep all lab appointments for level checks
  • Avoid NSAIDs and new diuretics without provider approval
  • Use reliable contraception (fetal risk)
Worked Example Insulin (Regular) Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Insulin (Regular)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Short-acting insulin that promotes cellular uptake of glucose, inhibits hepatic glucose production, and promotes glycogen, protein, and fat synthesis
  • The only insulin that can be given IV (for DKA/critical care)

Therapeutic Use

  • Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperglycemic emergencies (IV infusion)
  • Hyperkalemia (with dextrose) to shift potassium intracellularly

Complications

  • Hypoglycemia (most serious): shakiness, diaphoresis, tachycardia, confusion
  • Weight gain
  • Lipohypertrophy at repeated injection sites
  • Hypokalemia (shifts potassium into cells)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypoglycemia
  • Hypersensitivity to the formulation
  • Caution with renal/hepatic impairment (altered clearance) and during illness

Interactions

  • Beta blockers → mask signs of hypoglycemia and may prolong it
  • Alcohol, other hypoglycemics → ↑ hypoglycemia risk
  • Corticosteroids, thiazides → ↑ blood glucose (may need higher dose)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Blood glucose within target range; HbA1c trending toward goal
  • Resolution of hyperglycemia/DKA
  • No recurrent hypoglycemia

Medication Administration

  • Onset ~30 min, peak 2–3 hr, duration ~5–7 hr (SubQ)
  • Routes: SubQ (rotate sites); IV only for regular insulin
  • When mixing with NPH, draw up regular (clear) before NPH (cloudy) — “clear before cloudy”
  • Use an insulin syringe/pen; double-check dose with a second nurse (high-alert)
  • Time SubQ dose ~30 min before a meal

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor blood glucose and for signs of hypoglycemia (especially at peak)
  • Verify dose independently with a second nurse (high-alert medication)
  • Ensure the meal will be available after a meal-time dose
  • Monitor potassium; rotate injection sites

Client Education

  • Recognize and treat hypoglycemia (15 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 min)
  • Carry a fast-acting carbohydrate source at all times
  • Rotate injection sites within one region; store unopened insulin refrigerated, in-use vial at room temp ~28 days
  • Do not skip meals after dosing
  • Monitor glucose regularly and during illness
Worked Example Metformin Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Metformin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Biguanide that decreases hepatic glucose production, decreases intestinal glucose absorption, and improves insulin sensitivity (peripheral glucose uptake)
  • Does not cause hypoglycemia when used alone and does not promote weight gain

Therapeutic Use

  • First-line for type 2 diabetes mellitus
  • Polycystic ovary syndrome (off-label), prediabetes

Complications

  • GI: nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, metallic taste (often transient)
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
  • Lactic acidosis (rare but serious): malaise, myalgia, hyperventilation, somnolence

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Renal impairment (eGFR thresholds) — accumulation/lactic acidosis risk
  • Conditions causing hypoxia/lactic acidosis: HF, sepsis, shock, dehydration
  • Alcohol use disorder; hepatic impairment
  • Hold before/after iodinated contrast (acute kidney injury risk)

Interactions

  • Iodinated contrast media → ↑ risk of renal failure/lactic acidosis (hold 48 hr)
  • Alcohol → ↑ lactic acidosis risk
  • Cimetidine → ↑ metformin levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Fasting glucose and HbA1c within target
  • No hypoglycemia, stable weight
  • No signs of lactic acidosis or B12 deficiency

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO with meals to reduce GI effects
  • Immediate- and extended-release forms (do not crush ER)
  • Withhold before and 48 hr after contrast; resume after renal function confirmed
  • Monitor renal function and B12 periodically

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor renal function, glucose, HbA1c, and B12
  • Hold for contrast procedures and acute illness with hypoxia/dehydration
  • Educate on lactic acidosis warning signs
  • Assess GI tolerance

Client Education

  • Take with food; report persistent GI upset
  • Stop and report muscle pain, weakness, trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness (lactic acidosis)
  • Limit alcohol
  • Inform providers before any procedure using contrast dye
  • Continue lifestyle measures (diet, exercise)
Worked Example Heparin (Unfractionated) Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Heparin (Unfractionated)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anticoagulant that activates antithrombin III, inhibiting thrombin and factor Xa to prevent fibrin clot formation
  • Prevents new clot formation and extension of existing clots (does not dissolve clots)

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention/treatment of venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE)
  • Acute coronary syndrome, during dialysis/surgery, and to maintain line patency (low-dose flush)

Complications

  • Bleeding/hemorrhage (major risk)
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — platelet drop, paradoxical clotting (typically days 5–10)
  • Injection-site hematoma; long-term: osteoporosis

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia, history of HIT
  • Recent surgery/trauma of the eye, brain, or spinal cord; severe hypertension
  • Caution near procedures and with other anticoagulants

Interactions

  • Other anticoagulants/antiplatelets, NSAIDs, thrombolytics → ↑ bleeding
  • Avoid concurrent herbals that increase bleeding (ginkgo, garlic)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • No new clot formation; resolution of VTE signs
  • aPTT 1.5–2 times control (therapeutic) when monitored
  • Platelet count stable; no bleeding

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV (continuous infusion via pump) or SubQ — never IM (hematoma)
  • SubQ: inject into abdomen 2 in from umbilicus, 90°, do not aspirate or rub
  • Monitor aPTT/anti-Xa and adjust per protocol; double-check infusions (high-alert)
  • Antidote: protamine sulfate

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor aPTT, CBC/platelets (for HIT), and signs of bleeding
  • Verify pump settings independently (high-alert)
  • Have protamine sulfate available
  • Apply pressure to puncture sites

Client Education

  • Report bleeding: bruising, bleeding gums, blood in urine/stool, severe headache
  • Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor; avoid injury
  • Do not take NSAIDs/aspirin or new supplements without approval
  • Keep lab appointments for monitoring
Worked Example Prednisone Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Prednisone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Glucocorticoid (corticosteroid) that suppresses inflammation and the immune response by inhibiting inflammatory mediators and immune cell activity

Therapeutic Use

  • Wide range of inflammatory and autoimmune conditions: asthma/COPD exacerbations, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, IBD, allergic reactions, and adrenal insufficiency (replacement)

Complications

  • Hyperglycemia, increased infection risk (immunosuppression)
  • Osteoporosis, muscle wasting, weight gain, Cushingoid features (moon face, buffalo hump)
  • Peptic ulcers/GI bleeding, mood changes/insomnia
  • Fluid retention, hypertension, hypokalemia
  • Adrenal suppression with prolonged use

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Systemic fungal infection, live vaccines (during high-dose therapy)
  • Caution: diabetes, infection, peptic ulcer disease, osteoporosis, psychiatric illness

Interactions

  • NSAIDs → ↑ GI bleeding
  • Diuretics → ↑ potassium loss
  • Vaccines (live) → reduced response/infection risk; hypoglycemics → reduced glucose control

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced inflammation/symptoms of the treated condition
  • No infection, controlled glucose, no GI bleeding

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; give with food to reduce GI irritation, in the morning to mimic cortisol rhythm
  • Never stop abruptly after prolonged use — taper to prevent adrenal crisis
  • May need stress dosing during illness/surgery
  • Monitor glucose, electrolytes, weight, BP

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor blood glucose, electrolytes (potassium), weight, BP, and for infection
  • Assess for GI bleeding (give with food; consider GI protection)
  • Reinforce taper schedule; teach stress-dose need
  • Monitor for mood changes

Client Education

  • Do not stop suddenly — follow the taper exactly
  • Take with food in the morning
  • Report signs of infection, black/tarry stools, swelling, or marked mood changes
  • Carry medical identification; inform providers before surgery/illness (may need extra dose)
  • Monitor glucose if diabetic; ensure calcium/vitamin D and weight-bearing activity
Worked Example Haloperidol Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Haloperidol
Review Module Chapter
Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • First-generation (typical) antipsychotic that blocks dopamine (D2) receptors in the CNS, reducing positive psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, agitation)

Therapeutic Use

  • Acute and chronic schizophrenia and acute psychosis/agitation
  • Tourette syndrome; severe behavioral problems

Complications

  • Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): acute dystonia, akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia (late, may be irreversible)
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): high fever, muscle rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability
  • Anticholinergic effects, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation
  • Hyperprolactinemia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, severe CNS depression
  • Elderly with dementia-related psychosis (black box: ↑ mortality)
  • Caution: QT prolongation, cardiac disease

Interactions

  • Other CNS depressants → additive sedation
  • QT-prolonging drugs → ↑ dysrhythmia risk
  • Levodopa/dopamine agonists → reduced effect of both

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ hallucinations, delusions, agitation; improved thought organization
  • No EPS, NMS, or significant QT prolongation

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO, IM (including long-acting depot decanoate for adherence), IV (cardiac monitoring)
  • Monitor for EPS using a standardized scale (e.g., AIMS for tardive dyskinesia)
  • Baseline/periodic ECG; assess for NMS
  • Anticholinergic (benztropine) available for acute dystonia

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for EPS, NMS (vital signs, rigidity), and QT changes
  • Give anticholinergic for acute dystonia; treat NMS as emergency (stop drug, cool, dantrolene)
  • Monitor for orthostatic hypotension; rise slowly
  • Promote adherence (consider depot form)

Client Education

  • Report muscle stiffness, tremors, restlessness, or involuntary movements
  • Report high fever with muscle rigidity immediately (NMS)
  • Rise slowly to prevent dizziness; avoid alcohol
  • Use sunscreen (photosensitivity); do not stop abruptly
Worked Example Omeprazole Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Omeprazole
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Proton pump inhibitor that irreversibly blocks the gastric H+/K+-ATPase pump on parietal cells.
  • Inhibits the final step of gastric acid secretion, producing stronger and longer acid suppression than H2-receptor antagonists.
  • Lower acid exposure promotes healing of peptic ulcers and erosive esophagitis and reduces GERD symptoms.
  • Because new pumps must be made before acid secretion fully returns, dosing before meals and avoiding crushed delayed-release forms support effectiveness.

Therapeutic Use

  • GERD, peptic ulcer disease, erosive esophagitis
  • H. pylori eradication (with antibiotics), Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, NSAID ulcer prevention

Complications

  • Generally well tolerated short-term: headache, nausea, diarrhea
  • Long-term: ↓ calcium/B12/magnesium absorption (fracture risk), C. difficile infection, rebound acid hypersecretion

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: long-term use, osteoporosis risk, hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Reduces absorption of drugs needing acid (some antifungals, atazanavir)
  • Clopidogrel → omeprazole may reduce its antiplatelet activation (use alternative PPI)
  • Warfarin, phenytoin, diazepam → levels may rise

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of heartburn/epigastric pain; healed ulcer/esophagitis on follow-up
  • H. pylori eradication confirmed when treated

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, before meals (usually 30–60 min before breakfast)
  • Swallow capsules whole; do not crush delayed-release forms (may open and sprinkle per labeling)
  • Use lowest effective dose for the shortest duration
  • IV form available for inpatients

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess symptom relief and for long-term effect signs (fractures, low magnesium)
  • Reinforce taking before meals and completing H. pylori regimens
  • Review interacting medications (clopidogrel)
  • Encourage taper if discontinuing long-term therapy

Client Education

  • Take before eating; swallow whole
  • For long-term use, report muscle cramps/spasms (low magnesium) and discuss bone health
  • Report persistent diarrhea (possible C. difficile)
  • Do not stop abruptly after long-term use (rebound acid); combine with lifestyle measures
Worked Example Lisinopril Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Lisinopril
Review Module Chapter
Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • ACE inhibitor — blocks conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II → vasodilation, ↓ aldosterone (↓ sodium/water retention), and ↓ blood pressure and afterload

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypertension
  • Heart failure and post-myocardial infarction
  • Diabetic nephropathy (renal protection)

Complications

  • Persistent dry cough (from bradykinin)
  • First-dose hypotension, dizziness
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Angioedema (rare, life-threatening — face/lip/tongue swelling)
  • Acute kidney injury

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy (Category D) — fetal injury
  • History of angioedema
  • Bilateral renal artery stenosis
  • Caution: renal impairment, hyperkalemia, volume depletion

Interactions

  • Potassium-sparing diuretics / potassium supplements / salt substitutes → hyperkalemia
  • NSAIDs → ↓ antihypertensive effect and ↑ renal risk
  • Lithium → ↑ lithium level
  • Other antihypertensives/diuretics → ↑ hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Blood pressure within target
  • Improved heart failure symptoms
  • No cough or angioedema; stable potassium and renal function

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO
  • First dose may cause hypotension — monitor closely
  • Monitor BP, potassium, and renal function (BUN/creatinine)
  • Full effect on HF develops over weeks

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor BP, potassium, and renal function
  • Assess for cough and angioedema
  • Implement first-dose hypotension precautions
  • Hold and notify for significant hypotension or rising potassium/creatinine

Client Education

  • Report swelling of face, lips, or tongue immediately (angioedema)
  • Report a persistent dry cough (may switch to an ARB)
  • Rise slowly to prevent dizziness
  • Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes
  • Do not use if pregnant; do not stop abruptly
Worked Example Metoprolol Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Metoprolol
Review Module Chapter
Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Cardioselective beta-1 blocker that slows heart rate, decreases myocardial contractility, and lowers blood pressure.
  • Reduces myocardial oxygen demand, helping control angina and protect the heart after myocardial infarction.
  • Decreases renin release from the kidney, contributing to antihypertensive effects.
  • Can still affect beta-2 receptors at higher doses, so monitor for bronchospasm in asthma/COPD and for masked hypoglycemia in diabetes.

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypertension, angina
  • Heart failure (extended-release succinate) and post-myocardial infarction
  • Certain dysrhythmias (rate control)

Complications

  • Bradycardia, hypotension, dizziness, fatigue
  • Can mask signs of hypoglycemia
  • Bronchospasm (use caution in asthma)
  • Depression, erectile dysfunction

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe bradycardia, second/third-degree heart block
  • Decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic shock
  • Caution: asthma/COPD, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease

Interactions

  • Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) → bradycardia/heart block
  • Other antihypertensives → ↑ hypotension
  • Insulin/oral hypoglycemics → masks hypoglycemia

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Heart rate and BP within target
  • ↓ angina episodes; improved HF/post-MI outcomes

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO (IR tartrate, ER succinate for HF), IV for acute settings
  • Check apical pulse (1 full minute) and BP before each dose
  • Hold and notify provider for HR < 60/min or SBP < 90 mmHg (per parameters)
  • Do not stop abruptly — taper to avoid rebound

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor apical pulse and BP before dosing; hold per parameters
  • Assess for worsening heart failure (weight, edema, dyspnea)
  • Educate on not stopping abruptly
  • Monitor glucose in clients with diabetes

Client Education

  • Check pulse; report HR < 60, dizziness, weight gain, edema, or shortness of breath
  • Do not stop suddenly (rebound angina, hypertension, MI risk)
  • Diabetics: monitor glucose closely (drug masks hypoglycemia)
  • Rise slowly to prevent dizziness
Worked Example Amlodipine Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Amlodipine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker — blocks calcium entry into vascular smooth muscle → arterial vasodilation → ↓ blood pressure; also dilates coronary arteries

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypertension
  • Chronic stable and variant (Prinzmetal/vasospastic) angina

Complications

  • Peripheral edema (ankles/feet), flushing, headache
  • Dizziness, reflex tachycardia
  • Gingival hyperplasia (long-term)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe hypotension
  • Caution: severe aortic stenosis, heart failure, hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Grapefruit juice → ↑ amlodipine level
  • Other antihypertensives → ↑ hypotension
  • Simvastatin → ↑ statin level (myopathy risk)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • BP at target
  • ↓ angina frequency
  • No significant peripheral edema

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO once daily, with or without food
  • Titrate gradually; monitor BP and peripheral edema
  • Long half-life — steady-state effect over days

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor BP, heart rate (reflex tachycardia), and peripheral edema
  • Daily weights if edema present
  • Assess oral health (gingival hyperplasia)

Client Education

  • Report swelling of ankles/feet, severe dizziness, or palpitations
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Rise slowly; maintain good oral hygiene/dental visits
  • Do not stop abruptly
Worked Example Losartan Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Losartan
Review Module Chapter
Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) — blocks angiotensin II at AT1 receptors → vasodilation and ↓ aldosterone → ↓ blood pressure. Does not raise bradykinin, so no cough

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypertension; heart failure
  • Diabetic nephropathy
  • Alternative for clients who cannot tolerate the ACE inhibitor cough

Complications

  • Hypotension, dizziness
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Angioedema (rare)
  • Acute kidney injury

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy — fetal injury
  • Bilateral renal artery stenosis
  • Caution: renal impairment, hyperkalemia, volume depletion

Interactions

  • Potassium-sparing diuretics/potassium supplements/salt substitutes → hyperkalemia
  • NSAIDs → ↓ effect and ↑ renal risk
  • Lithium → ↑ lithium level

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • BP within target
  • No cough (unlike ACE inhibitors)
  • Stable potassium and renal function

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, with or without food
  • Monitor BP, potassium, and renal function
  • Full antihypertensive effect over 3–6 weeks

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor BP, potassium, renal function
  • Assess for angioedema
  • First-dose hypotension precautions, especially if volume-depleted

Client Education

  • Report facial/lip swelling or marked dizziness
  • Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes
  • Do not use if pregnant
  • Rise slowly; do not stop abruptly
Worked Example Prazosin (Alpha-Adrenergic Blocker) Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure · Sympatholytics section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Prazosin (Minipress)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist — blocks alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation (arterial and venous) → reduced BP
  • Also relaxes smooth muscle in bladder neck and prostate
  • Reduces peripheral vascular resistance

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypertension (not first-line; usually add-on)
  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — improves urinary flow
  • PTSD-associated nightmares (off-label; well-supported)
  • Raynaud’s phenomenon, pheochromocytoma (perioperative)

Complications

  • First-dose orthostatic hypotension / syncope — pronounced drop in BP with first dose or dose increases; can cause fainting
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, headache
  • Reflex tachycardia, palpitations
  • Nasal congestion (alpha blockade)
  • Fluid retention/edema (may need diuretic)
  • Priapism (rare)
  • Fatigue, drowsiness
  • Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (cataract surgery)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to prazosin or other quinazolines
  • History of orthostatic hypotension / syncope
  • Older adults — fall risk (Beers Criteria caution)
  • Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — severe hypotension
  • Planned cataract surgery (floppy iris syndrome — inform ophthalmologist)
  • Pregnancy and lactation — limited data

Interactions

  • PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) — additive hypotension (severe)
  • Other antihypertensives, diuretics — additive hypotension
  • Beta blockers — enhanced first-dose hypotension
  • NSAIDs — reduce antihypertensive effect
  • Alcohol — additive hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • BP reduction to target
  • Improved urinary symptoms (BPH): stream, frequency, urgency
  • Reduced nightmares (PTSD use)
  • No syncope or significant orthostatic symptoms
  • Tolerable side effects

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Start LOW: 1 mg PO at BEDTIME (first-dose effect) — titrate slowly; usual 6–15 mg/day in divided doses
  • PTSD nightmares: start 1 mg at bedtime; titrate up
  • Take first dose at bedtime to minimize syncope risk
  • Take with or without food (consistent)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and ongoing BP (sitting and standing) — assess orthostatic changes
  • Administer first dose at bedtime; have client stay in bed and rise slowly
  • Fall precautions, especially first 24 hours and after dose changes
  • Educate about first-dose phenomenon
  • Monitor for edema (may need diuretic)
  • Assess urinary symptoms if BPH indication
  • Inform of cataract surgery interaction (notify ophthalmologist)
  • Screen for PDE5 inhibitor use

Client Education

  • Take the FIRST dose at bedtime — may cause dizziness or fainting
  • Rise slowly from sitting/lying, especially when starting or increasing dose
  • If you feel dizzy, sit or lie down immediately
  • Do not drive after first dose until you know how it affects you
  • Avoid alcohol (worsens hypotension)
  • Do not combine with erectile dysfunction drugs (sildenafil) without provider approval — dangerous BP drop
  • Continue medication even if feeling well; do not stop abruptly
  • Report fainting, persistent dizziness, prolonged erection (emergency), or swelling
  • If having cataract surgery, tell your eye surgeon you take this medication
  • For BPH: may take a few weeks for urinary improvement
Worked Example Enoxaparin Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Enoxaparin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) — preferentially inhibits factor Xa (via antithrombin) to prevent clot formation; more predictable effect than unfractionated heparin

Therapeutic Use

  • VTE prophylaxis (post-surgery, immobility) and treatment of DVT/PE
  • Acute coronary syndrome

Complications

  • Bleeding, injection-site bruising/hematoma
  • Thrombocytopenia (HIT — less common than with UFH)
  • Rarely osteoporosis with long-term use

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active bleeding, history of HIT
  • Hypersensitivity to heparin/pork products
  • Caution: renal impairment (accumulation), recent surgery, spinal/epidural procedures

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, thrombolytics → ↑ bleeding
  • Bleeding-promoting herbals (ginkgo, garlic)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • No new clot formation; resolution of VTE
  • No bleeding; routine aPTT not required (anti-Xa level if monitored)

Medication Administration

  • Route: SubQ only (alternate sides of the abdomen)
  • Do not expel the air bubble in the prefilled syringe; do not aspirate or rub the site
  • No routine coagulation monitoring needed
  • Antidote: protamine sulfate (partial reversal)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for bleeding, CBC/platelets, and renal function
  • Use correct SubQ technique; rotate sites
  • Have protamine sulfate available
  • Hold before spinal/epidural procedures per protocol

Client Education

  • Report bleeding/bruising, blood in urine or stool, severe headache
  • Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor
  • Learn proper self-injection technique; rotate sites
  • Avoid NSAIDs/aspirin and new supplements without approval
Worked Example Ondansetron Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ondansetron
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist — blocks serotonin centrally (chemoreceptor trigger zone) and peripherally (vagal/GI) to prevent nausea and vomiting

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevents and treats nausea and vomiting related to chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and postoperative recovery.
  • Often given before emetogenic chemotherapy or near the end of surgery to prevent symptoms before they begin.
  • Helps maintain hydration, nutrition, medication tolerance, and comfort when vomiting risk is high.
  • Use with QT-risk screening and electrolyte monitoring when clients have cardiac risk factors or other QT-prolonging medications.

Complications

  • Headache, constipation, dizziness
  • QT prolongation (dysrhythmia risk)
  • Rarely serotonin syndrome (with serotonergic drugs)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Congenital long QT syndrome
  • Concurrent apomorphine
  • Caution: other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte imbalances (low K/Mg)

Interactions

  • Other QT-prolonging drugs → ↑ dysrhythmia risk
  • Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs) → serotonin syndrome
  • Apomorphine → severe hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Absence or reduction of nausea/vomiting
  • Maintained hydration and nutrition

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO (tablet, orally disintegrating tablet), IV (give slowly/diluted), IM
  • Give before emetogenic chemotherapy or at the end of surgery
  • Monitor ECG/electrolytes in at-risk clients

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess nausea/vomiting and hydration status
  • Monitor ECG and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) in at-risk clients
  • Administer prophylactically before chemotherapy
  • Manage constipation

Client Education

  • Report palpitations, chest pain, or fainting
  • Prevent constipation with fluids and fiber
  • ODT: let it dissolve on the tongue
  • Take before situations likely to cause nausea
Worked Example Naloxone Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Naloxone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Pure opioid antagonist — competitively blocks opioid receptors, rapidly reversing opioid effects including respiratory depression, sedation, and analgesia

Therapeutic Use

  • Opioid overdose / reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression
  • Reversal of excessive opioid sedation

Complications

  • Acute opioid withdrawal in dependent clients (pain, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea/vomiting)
  • Resedation when it wears off (short duration)
  • Rarely pulmonary edema, dysrhythmias

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution in opioid-dependent clients (precipitates withdrawal) and cardiovascular disease

Interactions

  • Reverses all opioid effects (including analgesia)
  • Reversal of buprenorphine may be incomplete (high receptor affinity)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Restored adequate respiratory rate and depth
  • Improved level of consciousness and oxygenation
  • Reversal of overdose without precipitating severe complications

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV (fastest), IM, SubQ, intranasal
  • Titrate to restore effective respirations
  • Short half-life → repeat dosing and continuous monitoring often required (may outlast naloxone)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor respiratory rate/depth, LOC, and oxygen saturation continuously
  • Be prepared to give repeat doses (drug duration shorter than many opioids)
  • Monitor for opioid withdrawal and resedation
  • Ensure airway support available

Client Education

  • Caregivers: recognize overdose (slow/absent breathing, unresponsive, pinpoint pupils) and give intranasal naloxone
  • Call emergency services and stay with the person
  • Expect possible withdrawal/agitation after reversal
  • Watch for return of symptoms (resedation) — repeat dose may be needed
Worked Example Buspirone Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Buspirone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Atypical anxiolytic that acts mainly as a partial serotonin 5-HT1A agonist.
  • Reduces chronic anxiety without the rapid sedation, muscle relaxation, dependence, or withdrawal risk associated with benzodiazepines.
  • Has delayed onset because therapeutic effect develops gradually over weeks, so it is not useful for acute panic relief.
  • Does not significantly depress respirations or potentiate alcohol in the same way as benzodiazepines, but serotonergic interactions still matter.

Therapeutic Use

  • Generalized anxiety disorder (long-term management)
  • Adjunct for depression

Complications

  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, headache, nausea
  • Restlessness (uncommon)
  • No significant sedation or abuse potential

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent MAOIs (hypertensive crisis)
  • Caution: hepatic/renal impairment

Interactions

  • MAOIs → hypertensive crisis
  • Grapefruit juice → ↑ buspirone level
  • Other serotonergic drugs → serotonin syndrome

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced generalized anxiety symptoms after consistent scheduled use for about 3-6 weeks.
  • Improved daily functioning, concentration, sleep quality, and ability to use nonpharmacologic coping strategies.
  • No need for rescue benzodiazepine escalation and no evidence of hypertensive crisis or serotonin syndrome.
  • Client verbalizes that buspirone is scheduled maintenance therapy, not a PRN medication.

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, taken consistently (with or without food, but be consistent)
  • Not for PRN use — full effect takes weeks
  • Avoid grapefruit juice

Nursing Interventions

  • Reinforce that relief is delayed (weeks), not immediate
  • Assess anxiety symptoms; encourage adherence
  • Review for MAOI/serotonergic interactions

Client Education

  • Take regularly as scheduled, not as needed
  • Full effect takes 3–4 weeks — continue even without immediate relief
  • No dependence or sedation, but avoid grapefruit juice
  • Report persistent dizziness
Worked Example Alprazolam Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Alprazolam
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Benzodiazepine that enhances GABA-A receptor activity, increasing inhibitory signaling in the CNS.
  • Produces rapid anxiolytic, sedative, muscle-relaxant, and anticonvulsant effects, which explains both benefit and safety risk.
  • Can cause CNS and respiratory depression, especially with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives.
  • Tolerance, physical dependence, rebound anxiety, and withdrawal seizures can occur with ongoing use or abrupt discontinuation.

Therapeutic Use

  • Short-term relief of acute anxiety symptoms and panic disorder manifestations while longer-term therapies are started or adjusted.
  • Used when rapid symptom control is needed, but limited by sedation, fall risk, dependence, and withdrawal concerns.
  • Not preferred for chronic long-term management when safer maintenance options such as SSRIs/SNRIs, buspirone, or therapy are appropriate.
  • Requires careful screening for substance use disorder, respiratory disease, older-adult fall risk, and concurrent CNS depressants.

Complications

  • Sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia
  • Tolerance and physical dependence
  • Respiratory depression (with other CNS depressants)
  • Paradoxical excitation (older adults); anterograde amnesia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Sleep apnea, severe respiratory disease, acute narrow-angle glaucoma
  • Pregnancy; substance use disorder history
  • Caution: older adults (Beers — falls)

Interactions

  • Alcohol, opioids, other CNS depressants → additive respiratory depression
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (grapefruit, azoles) → ↑ levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ anxiety/panic symptoms; client able to function
  • No oversedation or respiratory depression

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; Schedule IV controlled substance
  • Short-term use; taper to discontinue (never stop abruptly)
  • Antidote for overdose: flumazenil (use cautiously)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for sedation, respiratory status, and fall risk
  • Assess for dependence; reinforce taper
  • Screen for concurrent CNS depressants/alcohol

Client Education

  • Avoid alcohol and other sedatives
  • Do not stop abruptly (withdrawal/seizures) — taper with provider
  • Risk of dependence; use lowest dose for shortest time
  • Avoid driving until response known; rise slowly
Worked Example Fluoxetine Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Fluoxetine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor that blocks presynaptic serotonin reuptake, increasing serotonin availability in the CNS.
  • Improves depressive, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, panic, bulimia, and PMDD symptoms gradually over several weeks.
  • Long half-life lowers discontinuation symptoms compared with shorter-acting SSRIs, but it also extends interaction washout needs.
  • Can contribute to serotonin syndrome, bleeding risk, hyponatremia, early activation/anxiety, and suicidality monitoring needs in clients under 25.

Therapeutic Use

  • Major depressive disorder, OCD, panic disorder, bulimia, PMDD
  • Often first-line; long half-life

Complications

  • GI upset, headache, insomnia or somnolence
  • Sexual dysfunction, weight changes
  • Serotonin syndrome (with other serotonergics)
  • Hyponatremia; ↑ bleeding risk; early ↑ anxiety

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent MAOIs (or within 14 days; 5 weeks after fluoxetine)
  • Black box: increased suicidality in clients < 25 years
  • Caution: bipolar disorder (mania), bleeding risk

Interactions

  • MAOIs, triptans, tramadol, St. John’s wort → serotonin syndrome
  • NSAIDs/anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding
  • Inhibits CYP enzymes → ↑ levels of some drugs

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ depressive/target symptoms over 4–6 weeks
  • No serotonin syndrome or worsening suicidality

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, usually in the morning (may cause insomnia)
  • Effect takes 4–6 weeks; taper to discontinue (long half-life reduces discontinuation effects)
  • Observe 14-day washout to/from MAOIs (5 weeks after fluoxetine)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess suicide risk, especially early and in young clients
  • Monitor mood, for serotonin syndrome, and bleeding
  • Reinforce delayed onset and adherence

Client Education

  • Full effect takes 4–6 weeks — continue even if not improved yet
  • Report worsening mood or suicidal thoughts immediately
  • Report agitation, fever, tremor, sweating (serotonin syndrome)
  • Do not stop abruptly; avoid alcohol; report unusual bleeding
Worked Example Amitriptyline Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Amitriptyline
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Tricyclic antidepressant that blocks norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake, increasing both neurotransmitters in the CNS.
  • Also blocks muscarinic, histamine, and alpha-adrenergic receptors, causing anticholinergic effects, sedation, and orthostatic hypotension.
  • Used less often as a first-line antidepressant because overdose can cause serious cardiotoxicity and dysrhythmias.
