  • Low-dose use for neuropathic pain or migraine prevention still requires attention to anticholinergic burden, falls, and cardiac risk.

Therapeutic Use

  • Depression (second-line)
  • Neuropathic pain and migraine prophylaxis (low dose)

Complications

  • Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision)
  • Orthostatic hypotension, sedation, weight gain
  • Cardiotoxic in overdose (wide QRS, dysrhythmias) — narrow margin
  • Lowered seizure threshold

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Recent MI, dysrhythmias
  • Concurrent MAOIs
  • Beers — avoid in older adults
  • Black box: suicidality in clients < 25; caution glaucoma, BPH

Interactions

  • MAOIs → hypertensive crisis/serotonin syndrome
  • Other anticholinergics → additive effects
  • CNS depressants → sedation; antihypertensives → ↑ hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ depressive symptoms or neuropathic pain over weeks
  • No cardiac toxicity or excessive anticholinergic effects

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, often at bedtime (sedation)
  • Effect takes several weeks; lower doses for pain than depression
  • Taper to discontinue; overdose is a medical emergency (cardiac monitoring)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess suicide risk and cardiac status (ECG baseline in at-risk)
  • Monitor for anticholinergic effects and orthostatic hypotension
  • Manage constipation/dry mouth

Client Education

  • Full effect takes weeks
  • Rise slowly (orthostatic hypotension); relieve dry mouth with sugar-free gum
  • Report difficulty urinating, irregular heartbeat, or worsening mood
  • Do not stop abruptly; keep out of reach (overdose danger)
Worked Example Clozapine Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Clozapine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Second-generation antipsychotic that blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors to reduce psychotic symptoms.
  • Has relatively weak D2 blockade compared with many antipsychotics, which contributes to lower extrapyramidal symptom risk but does not remove seizure or metabolic risk.
  • Used when schizophrenia is treatment-resistant and can reduce recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia.
  • Because it can cause severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis, therapy is linked to REMS enrollment and scheduled ANC monitoring.

Therapeutic Use

  • Treatment-resistant schizophrenia
  • Reduction of recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia

Complications

  • Agranulocytosis (life-threatening — requires ANC monitoring)
  • Seizures (dose-related)
  • Metabolic syndrome (weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia)
  • Myocarditis, severe constipation/ileus, orthostatic hypotension, sedation, hypersalivation

Contraindications/Precautions

  • History of clozapine-induced agranulocytosis
  • Severe neutropenia (low ANC)
  • Caution: cardiac disease, seizure disorder, diabetes

Interactions

  • Other myelosuppressive drugs → ↑ agranulocytosis risk
  • CNS depressants → sedation
  • Smoking → ↓ clozapine level (changes in smoking alter levels)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ psychotic symptoms when other agents failed
  • ANC within safe range; no metabolic or cardiac complications

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; requires enrollment in a REMS program with scheduled ANC monitoring
  • Dispensed only when ANC is acceptable; titrate slowly
  • Monitor weight, glucose, lipids, and for myocarditis early in therapy

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor ANC/WBC on the required schedule; hold for low ANC
  • Assess for fever/sore throat (infection), seizures, constipation, cardiac symptoms
  • Monitor metabolic parameters

Client Education

  • Report fever, sore throat, or signs of infection immediately
  • Keep all blood-draw appointments (mandatory)
  • Report chest pain, palpitations, severe constipation, or seizures
  • Rise slowly; tell provider about smoking changes
Worked Example Levodopa/Carbidopa Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Levodopa/Carbidopa
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antiparkinson agent — levodopa converts to dopamine in the brain (replacing deficient dopamine); carbidopa prevents peripheral breakdown so more levodopa reaches the CNS and reduces peripheral side effects

Therapeutic Use

  • Reduces core Parkinson disease motor symptoms: bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, and impaired mobility.
  • Improves ability to perform activities of daily living when dopamine replacement is timed consistently.
  • Carbidopa allows more levodopa to reach the brain and reduces peripheral nausea and cardiovascular effects.
  • Long-term therapy can lead to dyskinesias and wearing-off/on-off fluctuations that require provider dose adjustment.

Complications

  • Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness
  • Dyskinesias and ‘wearing-off’/‘on-off’ fluctuations
  • Hallucinations, confusion; darkened sweat/urine (harmless)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Concurrent nonselective MAOIs (hypertensive crisis)
  • Narrow-angle glaucoma; caution: psychiatric illness, cardiac disease, melanoma history

Interactions

  • High-protein meals and vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) → ↓ levodopa effect
  • Nonselective MAOIs → hypertensive crisis
  • Antipsychotics (dopamine blockers) → ↓ effect

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved mobility — ↓ tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia
  • Manageable motor fluctuations

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; take consistently; separate from high-protein meals
  • Effect may take weeks; do not stop abruptly (risk of NMS-like crisis)
  • Monitor for orthostatic hypotension and dyskinesias

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess motor function and for ‘wearing-off’
  • Monitor BP (orthostasis) and for hallucinations/confusion
  • Educate on protein/B6 timing

Client Education

  • Take consistently; space from high-protein meals; avoid B6 supplements unless approved
  • Sweat/urine may darken (harmless)
  • Rise slowly; report uncontrolled movements, hallucinations, or marked symptom fluctuations
  • Do not stop abruptly
Worked Example Donepezil Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Donepezil
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Cholinesterase inhibitor that prevents acetylcholine breakdown, increasing acetylcholine availability in the CNS.
  • Supports cholinergic signaling involved in memory, cognition, and functional ability in Alzheimer disease.
  • Does not cure dementia or stop disease progression, but can slow cognitive and functional decline for some clients.
  • Cholinergic effects explain major monitoring needs: GI upset, weight loss, bradycardia, syncope, sleep disturbance, and cholinergic excess.

Therapeutic Use

  • Management of mild, moderate, or severe Alzheimer disease symptoms.
  • Used to slow cognitive and functional decline, support daily functioning, and delay symptom worsening when tolerated.
  • Benefit is measured by stabilization or slower decline rather than reversal of dementia.
  • Requires caregiver involvement for adherence, safety monitoring, realistic expectations, and reporting bradycardia or GI intolerance.

Complications

  • GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia/weight loss
  • Bradycardia, dizziness, insomnia (vivid dreams)
  • Cholinergic effects; excess → cholinergic crisis

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: bradycardia/heart block, peptic ulcer disease, asthma/COPD, seizures

Interactions

  • Anticholinergic drugs → ↓ effect
  • NSAIDs → ↑ GI bleeding risk
  • Beta blockers → additive bradycardia

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Stabilized or slower decline in memory, cognition, behavior, and activities of daily living compared with baseline.
  • Caregiver reports improved or maintained participation in routine tasks and no rapid functional deterioration.
  • Tolerable GI effects, stable weight, and no clinically significant bradycardia, syncope, or cholinergic toxicity.
  • Client and caregiver understand the medication slows symptoms but does not cure Alzheimer disease.

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, usually at bedtime
  • Titrate gradually; take consistently
  • Monitor heart rate, weight, and GI tolerance

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor heart rate (bradycardia), weight, and GI effects
  • Assess cognition/function over time
  • Educate family on realistic expectations (slows, not cures)

Client Education

  • Give at bedtime; report persistent GI upset, fainting, or slow heart rate
  • Effect is to slow decline, not reverse the disease
  • Report changes in alertness; ensure safety/supervision
  • Do not combine with anticholinergic OTC drugs without approval
Worked Example Fluticasone (Inhaled) Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Fluticasone (Inhaled)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Glucocorticoid anti-inflammatory medication that decreases inflammatory mediator release in the airway or nasal mucosa.
  • Reduces edema, mucus production, and airway hyperresponsiveness, making it useful for long-term control rather than acute rescue.
  • Inhaled forms help prevent asthma symptoms and exacerbations; intranasal forms reduce rhinitis inflammation over days to weeks.
  • Local steroid effects explain the need for scheduled use, spacer technique when appropriate, and mouth rinsing to prevent oral candidiasis.

Therapeutic Use

  • Long-term control/prevention of asthma (not for acute attacks)
  • Maintenance therapy in COPD (combination products)

Complications

  • Oral candidiasis (thrush) and hoarseness
  • Throat irritation, cough
  • Systemic effects rare at inhaled doses (high-dose/long-term: bone loss, slowed growth in children)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Acute asthma attack/status asthmaticus (not a rescue drug)
  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: active oral/respiratory infection

Interactions

  • Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir, ketoconazole) → ↑ systemic corticosteroid effect
  • Minimal interactions at inhaled doses

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ frequency/severity of asthma symptoms and exacerbations
  • Improved peak flow; reduced rescue-inhaler use

Medication Administration

  • Route: inhaled (MDI or DPI); use a spacer with MDI
  • Take on a scheduled basis (not PRN); effect builds over time
  • Rinse mouth after each use; if used with a bronchodilator, give the bronchodilator first

Nursing Interventions

  • Reinforce daily/scheduled use and correct inhaler technique
  • Teach mouth rinsing and spacer use to prevent thrush
  • Assess for oral candidiasis; monitor growth in children

Client Education

  • This is a controller, not a rescue inhaler — use a SABA for acute attacks
  • Use every day even when feeling well
  • Rinse mouth after use; report white patches in the mouth
  • Use a spacer; carry a rescue inhaler separately
Worked Example Montelukast Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Montelukast
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Leukotriene receptor antagonist that blocks leukotriene-mediated airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, edema, and mucus production.
  • Provides oral long-term asthma control and allergic rhinitis symptom reduction but does not reverse acute bronchospasm.
  • Can help prevent exercise-induced bronchoconstriction when taken according to the prescribed timing.
  • Because serious mood or behavior changes can occur, symptom control must be balanced with neuropsychiatric monitoring and teaching.

Therapeutic Use

  • Long-term asthma control/prophylaxis (including exercise-induced)
  • Allergic rhinitis

Complications

  • Headache, GI upset
  • Neuropsychiatric effects (mood/behavior changes, depression, sleep disturbances) — black box
  • Not effective for acute bronchospasm

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Acute asthma attack
  • Caution: history of psychiatric illness

Interactions

  • Phenobarbital, rifampin → ↓ montelukast level
  • Generally few significant interactions

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ asthma symptoms and exacerbations
  • Reduced rescue-inhaler use; controlled allergic rhinitis

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, usually once daily in the evening
  • For exercise-induced asthma, take at least 2 hr before exercise (per regimen)
  • Not for acute attacks; chewable/granule forms for children

Nursing Interventions

  • Reinforce scheduled use (not for acute attacks)
  • Monitor for mood/behavior changes and educate family to report them
  • Assess asthma control

Client Education

  • Take daily as prescribed, even when well
  • Report mood changes, agitation, depression, or unusual behavior
  • Keep a rescue inhaler for acute symptoms
  • Do not use to treat an asthma attack
Worked Example Diphenhydramine Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Diphenhydramine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • First-generation H1 antihistamine that competitively blocks histamine at H1 receptors.
  • Reduces allergic symptoms such as rhinorrhea, itching, urticaria, and sneezing, and is used as an adjunct after epinephrine in anaphylaxis care.
  • Crosses the blood-brain barrier, producing sedation and making it useful for selected motion sickness, insomnia, or extrapyramidal symptom situations.
  • Strong anticholinergic activity explains dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, confusion, and fall risk, especially in older adults.

Therapeutic Use

  • Allergic rhinitis, urticaria, and allergic reactions/anaphylaxis adjunct
  • Motion sickness, insomnia, and as an antiemetic; mild parkinsonism/EPS

Complications

  • Sedation, drowsiness
  • Anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention
  • Dizziness, paradoxical excitation in children; confusion/falls in older adults

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Acute narrow-angle glaucoma, BPH/urinary retention
  • Newborns/breastfeeding
  • Beers — avoid in older adults (anticholinergic, falls)

Interactions

  • Alcohol and other CNS depressants → additive sedation
  • Other anticholinergics → additive effects
  • MAOIs → intensified anticholinergic effects

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of allergic symptoms or target symptom (sleep, nausea, dystonia)
  • No excessive sedation or anticholinergic toxicity

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO, IM, IV
  • Caution with driving/sedation; give with food if GI upset
  • Use cautiously and at lower doses in older adults

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor sedation, fall risk, and anticholinergic effects
  • Caution in older adults and those with glaucoma/BPH
  • Assess effectiveness for the intended use

Client Education

  • Causes drowsiness — avoid driving/hazardous tasks and alcohol
  • Relieve dry mouth with sugar-free gum; increase fluids/fiber for constipation
  • Report difficulty urinating or confusion
  • Use cautiously in older adults
Worked Example Loratadine (Claritin) Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Loratadine (Claritin)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Second-generation H1 antihistamine — selectively blocks peripheral H1 receptors
  • Minimal CNS penetration (does NOT cross BBB significantly) → non-sedating at recommended doses
  • Minimal anticholinergic effects (vs first-gen like diphenhydramine)
  • OTC and prescription availability
  • Onset 1–3 hr; duration 24 hr

Therapeutic Use

  • Allergic rhinitis (seasonal and perennial)
  • Chronic idiopathic urticaria (hives)
  • Allergic conjunctivitis
  • Mild allergic reactions
  • Preferred in older adults due to less sedation and fewer anticholinergic effects

Complications

  • Mild headache, dry mouth, fatigue (usually well tolerated)
  • Minimal sedation at standard doses (slight increase at high doses)
  • Tachycardia, palpitations (rare)
  • Hepatotoxicity (rare; monitor LFTs if pre-existing hepatic disease)
  • QT prolongation at very high doses (much less than older antihistamines like terfenadine)
  • GI upset

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to loratadine
  • Hepatic impairment — dose reduction
  • Renal impairment — dose adjustment
  • Pregnancy — Category B (no evidence of harm; preferred antihistamine in pregnancy along with cetirizine)
  • Lactation — small amounts in breast milk; generally considered safe
  • Children < 2 yr (separate dosing for ages 2–5)

Interactions

  • Most clinically significant interactions minimal at standard doses
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, ritonavir) — mild increase in loratadine levels
  • Concurrent use with first-gen antihistamines — additive (but redundant)
  • Alcohol — minimal interaction (much less than diphenhydramine)
  • Antihistamines + decongestant combination products: monitor BP

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of allergy symptoms: less sneezing, rhinorrhea, itchy/watery eyes, nasal congestion
  • Resolution of urticaria (hives)
  • No undue sedation or impairment
  • Improved quality of life during allergy season
  • Tolerable side effect profile

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet, ODT, syrup)
  • Adult/> 6 yr dose: 10 mg PO once daily
  • Children 2–5 yr: 5 mg PO once daily
  • Hepatic/severe renal impairment: every other day
  • Take with or without food (food slightly delays absorption but not extent)
  • ODT (RediTabs): place on tongue; will dissolve quickly

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess allergy symptoms, severity, triggers
  • Verify diagnosis is consistent with histamine-mediated symptoms
  • Educate about non-pharmacologic strategies: allergen avoidance, nasal saline, environmental control
  • For severe allergies: ensure client has epinephrine auto-injector available
  • Consider intranasal corticosteroids (more effective for chronic allergic rhinitis)
  • Monitor for response after 1–2 weeks; if inadequate, consider alternative or add-on

Client Education

  • Take once daily at the same time
  • Less drowsiness than first-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine) — generally safe for driving
  • May take a few days to reach full effect
  • Combine with allergen avoidance, nasal saline, and HEPA filters
  • For seasonal allergies: start BEFORE peak season (1–2 weeks)
  • Drink adequate fluids if dry mouth
  • Carry epinephrine auto-injector if known severe allergies (anaphylaxis)
  • OTC: choose loratadine OR cetirizine OR fexofenadine; not multiple antihistamines at once
  • Pregnancy/lactation: loratadine is among the preferred antihistamines — discuss with provider
Worked Example Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Alpha-1 adrenergic agonist — vasoconstricts mucosal blood vessels in nasal passages
  • Reduces nasal edema and congestion
  • Also has some beta-adrenergic activity (cardiac, bronchodilatory)
  • Behind-the-counter (BTC) in US — restricted purchase due to methamphetamine precursor status (Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act)
  • Onset 30 min; duration 4–6 hr (IR); 12 hr (ER)

Therapeutic Use

  • Nasal congestion from allergic rhinitis
  • Sinusitis with congestion
  • Common cold / upper respiratory infection
  • Eustachian tube congestion (ear)
  • Adjunct in allergic rhinitis combined with antihistamine

Complications

  • Hypertension — vasoconstriction; especially risky in HTN clients
  • Tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias
  • CNS stimulation: nervousness, insomnia, anxiety, tremor, headache
  • Dry mouth
  • Urinary retention — especially BPH
  • Rebound congestion with prolonged use (less than topical decongestants)
  • Rare: stroke, MI, hypertensive crisis (with MAOI or in vulnerable clients)
  • Hallucinations, paranoia at high doses

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe hypertension or coronary artery disease
  • Hyperthyroidism, diabetes (caution — can affect BP and glucose)
  • Closed-angle glaucoma
  • BPH or urinary retention
  • Concurrent or recent (14 days) MAOI use — hypertensive crisis
  • Pregnancy — avoid in 1st trimester (some risk of birth defects)
  • Lactation — may decrease milk supply
  • Children < 4 yr — avoid (overdose risk; OTC cough/cold meds not recommended)

Interactions

  • MAOIs (within 14 days) — hypertensive crisis (CONTRAINDICATED)
  • Other sympathomimetics (stimulants, ADHD meds) — additive cardiovascular effects
  • Beta blockers — unopposed alpha effects can cause hypertension
  • TCAs — potentiate cardiovascular effects
  • Methyldopa, reserpine — decreased antihypertensive effect
  • Caffeine — additive stimulant effects (avoid in product combinations)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of nasal congestion
  • Improved breathing through nose
  • Stable blood pressure and heart rate
  • No insomnia, anxiety, or jitteriness
  • Resolution of symptoms within expected timeframe (typically 7–10 days for acute)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet, ER tablet, liquid)
  • Adult dose: 60 mg PO every 4–6 hr (IR); 120 mg every 12 hr (12-hr ER); 240 mg once daily (24-hr ER); max 240 mg/day
  • Take last dose several hours before bedtime to avoid insomnia
  • Take with or without food
  • BTC: must show ID; sales limits per federal law
  • Children: dose by age per product (avoid in < 4 yr)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline BP, HR, history of CV disease, urinary symptoms, mental health
  • Verify no MAOI use in past 14 days
  • Check medication list for sympathomimetics, stimulants, beta blockers, TCAs
  • Monitor BP especially in older adults and HTN clients
  • Assess insomnia, anxiety, palpitations at follow-up
  • Educate about combination products (cold/sinus formulations often contain pseudoephedrine + others)
  • Document BTC purchase per state requirements

Client Education

  • Take in morning/early afternoon; avoid evening (insomnia)
  • Stay hydrated (vasoconstriction can dry mucous membranes)
  • Limit to a few days for self-treatment; longer use should be discussed with provider
  • Do NOT combine with other decongestants or stimulants
  • Avoid if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, BPH, or hyperthyroidism (consult provider)
  • Do NOT take if you have used an MAOI in the last 2 weeks
  • Report: chest pain, palpitations, severe headache, vision changes (signs of hypertensive event)
  • Discontinue and seek care if symptoms worsen or last > 7 days
  • Pregnancy: discuss with provider before use, especially 1st trimester
  • BTC restrictions: show ID at pharmacy; tracked purchase
  • Use saline nasal sprays as alternative or adjunct (no systemic effects)
Worked Example Spironolactone Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Spironolactone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Potassium-sparing diuretic (aldosterone antagonist) — blocks aldosterone in the distal nephron → excretes sodium/water while retaining potassium

Therapeutic Use

  • Heart failure, hypertension, edema
  • Hyperaldosteronism, ascites (cirrhosis); off-label for acne/hirsutism

Complications

  • Hyperkalemia (most serious)
  • Gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities (endocrine effects)
  • Dizziness, GI upset

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hyperkalemia, severe renal impairment, Addison disease
  • Concurrent potassium supplements/salt substitutes
  • Caution: diabetes, other potassium-raising drugs

Interactions

  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium supplements, salt substitutes → hyperkalemia
  • NSAIDs → ↓ effect and ↑ renal risk
  • Lithium → ↑ lithium level

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ edema, controlled BP, improved HF symptoms
  • Potassium within normal range

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, with food; give in the morning to limit nocturia
  • Monitor potassium and renal function
  • Effect on potassium is the key monitoring point

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor potassium and renal function; report K > 5.0
  • Assess edema, daily weights, BP
  • Educate to avoid potassium supplements/salt substitutes

Client Education

  • Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes, and high-potassium foods in excess
  • Report muscle weakness, palpitations (hyperkalemia)
  • Gynecomastia/menstrual changes are possible — discuss with provider
  • Take in the morning; rise slowly
Worked Example Hydrochlorothiazide Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Hydrochlorothiazide
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Thiazide diuretic that blocks sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule.
  • Promotes excretion of sodium and water to lower blood volume and blood pressure.
  • Increases potassium loss, which drives monitoring for hypokalemia, dysrhythmias, and digoxin toxicity risk.
  • Increases calcium reabsorption, which can help reduce calcium stone recurrence but may contribute to hypercalcemia in at-risk clients.

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypertension (first-line)
  • Mild edema/heart failure; reduces calcium-based kidney stones

Complications

  • Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, dehydration
  • Hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia (gout), hyperlipidemia, hypercalcemia
  • Orthostatic hypotension; photosensitivity; sulfa cross-sensitivity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Anuria, severe renal impairment (ineffective)
  • Sulfonamide allergy (cross-sensitivity)
  • Caution: gout, diabetes, electrolyte imbalance

Interactions

  • Digoxin → hypokalemia ↑ digoxin toxicity
  • Lithium → ↑ lithium level
  • NSAIDs → ↓ effect; antihypertensives → ↑ hypotension

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • BP at target; ↓ edema
  • Electrolytes (especially potassium) within normal limits

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, in the morning (avoid nocturia)
  • Monitor electrolytes, glucose, uric acid, and renal function
  • Less effective in significant renal impairment (use a loop diuretic)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor potassium/sodium, glucose, uric acid, and BP
  • Encourage potassium-rich foods; daily weights
  • Assess for orthostatic hypotension/fall risk

Client Education

  • Take in the morning; rise slowly
  • Eat potassium-rich foods (bananas, oranges) unless told otherwise
  • Use sunscreen (photosensitivity); report muscle cramps/weakness
  • Diabetics: monitor glucose; report gout symptoms
Worked Example Mannitol (Osmotic Diuretic) Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Mannitol (Osmitrol)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Osmotic diuretic — freely filtered at glomerulus but not reabsorbed; increases osmolarity of filtrate → draws water into the tubule → diuresis
  • Also increases plasma osmolarity → pulls fluid from tissues (brain, eye) into vascular space
  • Onset 1–3 hr (diuresis); 15 min for reducing ICP

Therapeutic Use

  • Increased intracranial pressure (ICP) — reduces cerebral edema
  • Increased intraocular pressure (IOP) — acute glaucoma
  • Acute kidney injury prevention — maintains urine flow (oliguria from low perfusion)
  • Promote excretion of toxins (rhabdomyolysis, certain overdoses)

Complications

  • Fluid and electrolyte imbalances — dehydration, hypo/hypernatremia, hypokalemia
  • Pulmonary edema / fluid overload — initial intravascular volume expansion (DANGEROUS in heart failure)
  • Rebound increased ICP if mannitol crosses damaged BBB
  • Headache, nausea, vomiting
  • Crystallization of solution at low temperatures (must use filter needle/in-line filter)
  • Acute kidney injury at high cumulative doses
  • Hypotension from rapid diuresis

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Anuria (no urine output) — cannot excrete; causes fluid overload
  • Severe heart failure / pulmonary edema — volume expansion worsens
  • Severe dehydration
  • Active intracranial bleeding (except during craniotomy)
  • Severe renal impairment without proven response
  • Hypersensitivity to mannitol

Interactions

  • Other diuretics — additive electrolyte depletion
  • Nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs) — increased renal injury risk
  • Digoxin — hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk
  • Lithium — increased renal clearance → reduced lithium levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Increased urine output
  • Reduced ICP (improved neuro status, ICP monitor reading)
  • Reduced IOP
  • Maintained urine flow in AKI prevention
  • Stable or improved electrolytes and fluid balance
  • No signs of fluid overload

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV ONLY
  • ICP dose: 0.25–1 g/kg IV over 30–60 min
  • USE AN IN-LINE FILTER — mannitol can crystallize
  • If crystals present: warm the solution (warm water bath), then re-inspect before use
  • Test dose for oliguria (assess for response before full dosing)
  • Continuous monitoring during administration
  • Indwelling catheter for accurate output measurement

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline: renal function, electrolytes, vital signs, neuro status, weight, I&O
  • Use in-line filter; inspect for crystals before administration
  • Insert indwelling catheter; monitor hourly urine output
  • Monitor for fluid overload: lung sounds, JVD, edema, SpO2 (especially first hour)
  • Frequent electrolyte and serum osmolality monitoring
  • Neuro checks for ICP indication (LOC, pupils, GCS)
  • Strict I&O and daily weights
  • Have emergency equipment ready (pulmonary edema risk)

Client Education

  • (Often given in acute/critical settings; education to family) Mannitol reduces brain or eye swelling and increases urine output
  • Frequent monitoring of urine output, labs, and vital signs is necessary
  • Indwelling catheter is needed to measure response accurately
  • Report headache, nausea, shortness of breath, swelling, or chest tightness
  • Expect frequent neuro checks (for brain swelling indication)
  • Position: head of bed elevated 30 degrees for ICP management
Worked Example Amiodarone Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Amiodarone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Class III antidysrhythmic that blocks potassium channels, prolonging repolarization and the refractory period to stabilize rhythm.
  • Also has sodium-channel-blocking, beta-blocking, and calcium-channel-blocking effects, which contribute to broad antidysrhythmic activity.
  • Has a very long half-life, so therapeutic effects, interactions, and toxicity can persist for weeks after discontinuation.
  • Can affect pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic, ocular, skin, and cardiac function, requiring baseline and periodic monitoring.

Therapeutic Use

  • Treats life-threatening ventricular dysrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation when clinically indicated.
  • Used for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter when benefits outweigh pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic, and proarrhythmic risks.
  • May be given IV for acute dysrhythmia management or orally for maintenance therapy with continuous ECG and toxicity monitoring as appropriate.
  • Often reserved for serious or refractory rhythm problems because of its long half-life and multi-organ adverse-effect profile.

Complications

  • Pulmonary toxicity/fibrosis (cough, dyspnea)
  • Thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyper-), hepatotoxicity
  • Bradycardia, hypotension, QT prolongation, proarrhythmia
  • Blue-gray skin discoloration, corneal deposits, photosensitivity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe bradycardia, heart block (without pacemaker)
  • Iodine hypersensitivity (contains iodine)
  • Caution: thyroid, hepatic, and pulmonary disease

Interactions

  • Digoxin and warfarin → amiodarone ↑ their levels (reduce doses)
  • Other QT-prolonging drugs → ↑ dysrhythmia risk
  • Grapefruit juice → ↑ amiodarone level

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Controlled/converted dysrhythmia; stable rhythm
  • No pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic, or cardiac toxicity

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO and IV (IV via central line/filter when prolonged; continuous monitoring)
  • Baseline and periodic chest X-ray/PFTs, TFTs, LFTs, ECG, eye exams
  • Long half-life — effects persist for weeks after stopping

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor ECG, BP, heart rate, and for pulmonary/thyroid/hepatic toxicity
  • Reduce digoxin/warfarin doses and monitor levels/INR
  • Assess for vision changes and skin discoloration

Client Education

  • Report cough, shortness of breath (lung toxicity), or fatigue/weight changes (thyroid)
  • Use sunscreen; expect possible blue-gray skin tint
  • Get regular eye exams and labs; avoid grapefruit juice
  • Report palpitations or fainting
Worked Example Adenosine (Adenocard) Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm · Classes section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Adenosine (Adenocard)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Endogenous nucleoside antidysrhythmic — slows conduction through the AV node
  • Briefly interrupts AV nodal reentry pathways → terminates SVT
  • Causes transient asystole (brief pause) — this is EXPECTED as the heart “resets”
  • Extremely short half-life: ~10 seconds — must be given by rapid IV push followed by immediate flush

Therapeutic Use

  • Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT/SVT) — first-line conversion to sinus rhythm
  • Diagnostic aid in differentiating wide-complex tachycardias
  • Pharmacologic stress testing (vasodilation)
  • NOT effective for atrial fibrillation/flutter or ventricular tachycardia

Complications

  • Transient asystole / brief pause (several seconds) — expected; alarming but self-limiting
  • Sense of impending doom, chest pressure, flushing, dyspnea — very brief (seconds), due to short half-life
  • Facial flushing
  • Bronchospasm (caution in asthma/COPD)
  • Transient dysrhythmias during conversion (PVCs, bradycardia)
  • Headache, dizziness

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Second- or third-degree AV block (without pacemaker)
  • Sick sinus syndrome (without pacemaker)
  • Severe asthma/bronchospastic disease (caution — bronchospasm risk)
  • Known hypersensitivity
  • Atrial fibrillation/flutter (not effective; may worsen)
  • Caution with carbamazepine (heart block potentiation)

Interactions

  • Methylxanthines (caffeine, theophylline) — ANTAGONIZE adenosine; may need higher dose
  • Dipyridamole — POTENTIATES adenosine; reduce dose
  • Carbamazepine — increased heart block risk
  • Nicotine — may potentiate

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Conversion of SVT to normal sinus rhythm
  • Resolution of tachycardia symptoms (palpitations, dyspnea)
  • Brief pause/asystole followed by return of normal rhythm on monitor
  • Stable hemodynamics after conversion

Medication Administration

  • Route: rapid IV push ONLY
  • Dose: 6 mg rapid IV push over 1–2 seconds; if no conversion in 1–2 min, give 12 mg; may repeat 12 mg once
  • IMMEDIATELY follow with 20 mL rapid saline flush and elevate the extremity (drug has ~10 sec half-life)
  • Use the IV port CLOSEST to the patient (proximal)
  • Use a stopcock or two-syringe technique for rapid drug-then-flush
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring with rhythm strip/print during administration
  • Have emergency/resuscitation equipment available

Nursing Interventions

  • Continuous cardiac monitoring; PRINT a rhythm strip during administration to document conversion
  • Establish proximal large-bore IV; prepare flush in advance
  • Warn the client about brief but intense sensations (chest pressure, flushing, feeling of doom, brief pause) lasting only seconds
  • Have resuscitation equipment and ACLS readily available
  • Use rapid push + immediate flush technique (two-syringe or stopcock)
  • Monitor for bronchospasm in respiratory disease
  • Assess for caffeine/theophylline (may reduce effect) or dipyridamole (potentiates)
  • Reassess rhythm and vital signs after administration

Client Education

  • (Acute/emergency setting) This medication will quickly slow your heart to reset the rhythm
  • You may briefly feel chest pressure, flushing, shortness of breath, or a feeling of doom — these last only a few seconds and are expected
  • You will be on a heart monitor throughout
  • Report if symptoms persist beyond a few seconds
  • After conversion, follow-up may include evaluation for the cause of the rapid rhythm
  • Discuss avoiding triggers (excess caffeine, stimulants) for future SVT prevention
Worked Example Famotidine Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Famotidine
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Histamine H2-receptor antagonist that blocks histamine stimulation of gastric parietal cells.
  • Reduces basal, nocturnal, and meal-stimulated gastric acid secretion, helping ulcer and reflux symptoms improve.
  • Less acid allows gastric and duodenal mucosa to heal and supports stress-ulcer prophylaxis when indicated.
  • Has fewer CYP450 drug interactions than cimetidine, but renal dosing and confusion monitoring matter in older adults or renal impairment.

Therapeutic Use

  • GERD, peptic ulcer disease, heartburn
  • Stress ulcer prophylaxis; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

Complications

  • Generally well tolerated: headache, dizziness, constipation/diarrhea
  • Confusion in older adults or with renal impairment (high doses)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: renal impairment (dose reduction), older adults

Interactions

  • Reduces absorption of drugs needing an acidic environment (some antifungals)
  • Fewer interactions than cimetidine (which inhibits CYP450)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of heartburn/epigastric pain; ulcer healing
  • Reduced GI bleeding risk in prophylaxis

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO and IV
  • May take without regard to meals; can be taken before meals to prevent symptoms
  • Reduce dose in renal impairment

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess symptom relief; monitor renal function and mental status in older adults
  • Separate from acid-dependent drugs
  • Reinforce lifestyle measures for GERD

Client Education

  • Take as directed; may use before meals to prevent heartburn
  • Report black/tarry stools or persistent pain
  • Avoid smoking, alcohol, and trigger foods
  • Report confusion (older adults) or no improvement
Worked Example Sucralfate (Carafate) Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · Mucosal protectants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Sucralfate (Carafate)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Mucosal protectant — in acidic environment, forms a thick, sticky, protective barrier (paste) that adheres to ulcerated/eroded tissue
  • Protects the ulcer from acid, pepsin, and bile
  • Acts locally; minimal systemic absorption
  • Does NOT reduce acid secretion (different from PPIs/H2 blockers)

Therapeutic Use

  • Duodenal and gastric ulcers — treatment and maintenance
  • Stress ulcer prophylaxis
  • Mucositis/stomatitis (oral form)
  • GERD-related esophagitis (adjunct)

Complications

  • Constipation (most common)
  • Dry mouth, nausea
  • Aluminum toxicity in renal impairment (contains aluminum)
  • Bezoar formation (rare)
  • Reduced absorption of many other medications (binds them)
  • Hypophosphatemia (binds phosphate)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to sucralfate
  • Chronic renal failure / dialysis (aluminum accumulation)
  • Diabetic gastroparesis (bezoar risk)
  • Dysphagia (aspiration risk with tablets)
  • Caution with concurrent medications (timing)

Interactions

  • Binds and reduces absorption of MANY drugs: fluoroquinolones, digoxin, phenytoin, levothyroxine, warfarin, tetracyclines
  • Separate other medications by ≥ 2 hours
  • Antacids — reduce sucralfate effectiveness (needs acid to activate); separate by 30 min
  • May reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Ulcer healing (symptom relief, endoscopic confirmation)
  • Reduced epigastric pain
  • No GI bleeding (black stools, hematemesis)
  • No constipation or other intolerable effects
  • No interference with other medication effectiveness (proper timing)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet or suspension)
  • Dose: 1 g PO four times daily
  • Take on an EMPTY stomach — 1 hour before meals and at bedtime
  • Separate other medications by ≥ 2 hours
  • If also on antacids: give antacids 30 min before or after sucralfate (not together)
  • Shake suspension well

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess renal function (aluminum accumulation risk)
  • Carefully time other medications (≥ 2 hr separation) — review full med list
  • Monitor for constipation; implement prevention (fluids, fiber)
  • Assess for ongoing GI bleeding (stool color, Hgb)
  • Educate on empty-stomach timing
  • Monitor phosphate in long-term/renal patients
  • Assess swallowing ability if using tablets

Client Education

  • Take on an empty stomach — 1 hour before meals and at bedtime
  • Take other medications at least 2 hours apart from sucralfate
  • Increase fluids and fiber to prevent constipation
  • Do not take antacids within 30 minutes of sucralfate
  • Complete the full course even if feeling better
  • Report black/tarry stools, worsening pain, or no improvement
  • Avoid smoking, alcohol, NSAIDs, and trigger foods (worsen ulcers)
  • Shake liquid form well before use
Worked Example Bupropion Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Bupropion
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Atypical antidepressant that inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake with little direct serotonergic activity.
  • Can improve depressive symptoms and aid smoking cessation through dopaminergic and noradrenergic effects.
  • Less likely than SSRIs to cause sexual dysfunction or weight gain, but can cause insomnia, agitation, hypertension, and weight loss.
  • Lowers the seizure threshold in a dose-related manner, making seizure disorder, eating disorders, and abrupt alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal major safety concerns.

Therapeutic Use

  • Major depressive disorder, seasonal affective disorder
  • Smoking cessation (sustained-release form)
  • Often chosen to avoid SSRI sexual dysfunction/weight gain

Complications

  • Lowers seizure threshold (dose-related)
  • Insomnia, agitation, headache, dry mouth, weight loss
  • Hypertension; no sexual dysfunction (advantage)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Seizure disorder; eating disorders (bulimia/anorexia)
  • Abrupt alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal
  • Concurrent MAOIs; caution: head injury

Interactions

  • MAOIs → hypertensive crisis
  • Drugs that lower seizure threshold → ↑ seizure risk
  • Alcohol → ↑ seizure risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ depressive symptoms over weeks
  • Smoking cessation achieved; no seizures

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO; do not exceed recommended dose (seizure risk)
  • Give doses spaced apart; avoid bedtime dosing (insomnia)
  • For smoking cessation, start while still smoking; set a quit date ~1–2 weeks in

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess suicide risk and for seizures
  • Monitor BP, sleep, and weight
  • Reinforce not exceeding the dose; screen for eating disorder history

Client Education

  • Take as prescribed; do not double doses (seizure risk)
  • Avoid alcohol; take earlier in the day to limit insomnia
  • Report mood worsening or any seizure
  • For quitting smoking, continue smoking until the quit date as directed
Worked Example Phenelzine (MAOI) Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · MAOIs section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Phenelzine (Nardil)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) — non-selective, irreversibly inhibits MAO-A and MAO-B enzymes
  • Prevents breakdown of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine → increased synaptic levels
  • Tyramine (from food) is normally broken down by MAO in the GI tract — MAOI blocks this, allowing tyramine accumulation → hypertensive crisis

Therapeutic Use

  • Treatment-resistant depression (third- or fourth-line; rarely first-line due to dietary/drug restrictions)
  • Atypical depression (mood reactivity, hypersomnia, weight gain, sensitivity to rejection)
  • Panic disorder, social phobia
  • Selegiline (selective MAO-B inhibitor) used for Parkinson’s disease

Complications

  • Hypertensive crisis — from tyramine-rich foods or sympathomimetic drugs (severe headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, blurred vision, chest pain, sweating, intracranial hemorrhage, death)
  • Serotonin syndrome — with serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, tramadol, triptans, meperidine, dextromethorphan, St. John’s wort)
  • Orthostatic hypotension (paradoxical — common at therapeutic doses)
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Weight gain, insomnia, peripheral edema
  • Suicidality (FDA black box warning, especially < 25 yr)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pheochromocytoma, severe cardiovascular disease, hepatic/renal impairment
  • Recent stroke or CHF
  • Concurrent serotonergic medications (require 2-week washout; 5 weeks for fluoxetine)
  • Sympathomimetic exposure (OTC cold meds, recreational stimulants)
  • Pregnancy — avoid; lactation — avoid
  • Inability to follow strict tyramine-restricted diet

Interactions

  • Tyramine-rich foods: aged cheeses, cured/smoked meats, fermented foods (sauerkraut, soy sauce, miso), red wine, draft/tap beer, fava beans, overripe bananas, smoked fish
  • Serotonergic drugs (any) → serotonin syndrome
  • Sympathomimetics (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, dopamine, epinephrine) → hypertensive crisis
  • Meperidine → severe reactions (fatal); use fentanyl or morphine instead
  • Alcohol — avoid (some beers/wines contain tyramine)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Improved mood, sleep, appetite, and energy within 2–4 weeks
  • PHQ-9 score reduction
  • Absence of hypertensive crisis or serotonin syndrome events
  • Adherence to dietary restrictions (key indicator of successful management)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Adult dose: 15 mg PO TID, titrate to 60–90 mg/day
  • Take with food to reduce GI upset
  • Therapeutic effect: 2–4 weeks
  • Effects PERSIST 2 weeks after discontinuation (irreversible MAOI) — dietary and drug restrictions continue 2 weeks after stopping

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify dietary restrictions are understood BEFORE starting
  • Comprehensive medication reconciliation including OTC and herbal — no serotonergic or sympathomimetic agents
  • Monitor BP at baseline and regularly
  • Provide written list of foods and drugs to avoid
  • Assess suicide risk at every visit
  • Monitor for hypertensive crisis: severe headache, chest pain — emergency BP-lowering with phentolamine if confirmed
  • Have phentolamine available in inpatient settings

Client Education

  • Strict tyramine-restricted diet — continue 2 weeks AFTER discontinuation
  • Avoid: aged cheeses, cured meats, fermented foods, red wine, tap beer, soy sauce, fava beans, overripe bananas
  • Notify all healthcare providers and pharmacists about MAOI use
  • Avoid all OTC cold/cough/allergy/decongestant medications (consult pharmacist for safe alternatives like saline spray, antihistamines may be OK)
  • Carry MAOI alert card or wear medical alert ID
  • Report immediately: severe headache, chest pain, palpitations, neck stiffness, vision changes (signs of hypertensive crisis — emergency)
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic dizziness
  • Do not abruptly discontinue — taper
Worked Example Valproic Acid Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Valproic Acid
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Mood stabilizer and antiepileptic that increases CNS GABA activity and stabilizes neuronal firing.
  • Also affects sodium and calcium channel activity, helping reduce abnormal repetitive neuronal discharge.
  • Provides antimanic, antiseizure, and migraine-prophylaxis effects depending on the prescribed indication.
  • Requires serum level, liver function, platelet, pregnancy-risk, and pancreatitis monitoring because toxicity can be serious.

Therapeutic Use

  • Bipolar disorder (acute mania, maintenance)
  • Seizure disorders; migraine prophylaxis

Complications

  • GI upset, sedation, tremor, weight gain
  • Hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis
  • Thrombocytopenia; teratogenic (neural tube defects)
  • Hyperammonemia

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hepatic disease
  • Pregnancy (neural tube defects)
  • Urea cycle disorders; caution: bleeding/platelet issues

Interactions

  • Other hepatotoxic drugs → ↑ liver injury
  • Aspirin → ↑ free valproate level
  • Lamotrigine → ↑ rash risk; warfarin → ↑ bleeding

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Stabilized mood / seizure control
  • Therapeutic level 50–125 mcg/mL; normal LFTs and platelets

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO (do not crush ER); give with food to reduce GI upset
  • Monitor serum levels, LFTs, platelets, and ammonia
  • Baseline and periodic labs; pregnancy screening

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor LFTs, platelets, drug levels, and for pancreatitis (abdominal pain, vomiting)
  • Assess for bruising/bleeding and sedation
  • Educate on teratogenic risk and contraception

Client Education

  • Report abdominal pain, vomiting, yellowing of skin/eyes (liver/pancreas)
  • Report unusual bruising or bleeding
  • Use reliable contraception; do not stop abruptly
  • Take with food; keep all lab appointments
Worked Example Disulfiram Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Disulfiram
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Alcohol deterrent — inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase so that drinking alcohol causes a buildup of acetaldehyde, producing a highly unpleasant reaction

Therapeutic Use

  • Used to maintain abstinence in alcohol use disorder by creating a strong aversion to drinking alcohol.
  • Appropriate only for clients who understand the reaction risk, are alcohol-free before starting, and are engaged in counseling or recovery support.
  • Not used to treat acute alcohol withdrawal; benzodiazepines and supportive care address withdrawal safety.
  • Clients must avoid alcohol-containing beverages, medicines, mouthwash, sauces, and topical products because reactions can occur during therapy and for up to 2 weeks after stopping.

Complications

  • If alcohol is consumed: flushing, throbbing headache, nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension, dyspnea (can be severe)
  • Drowsiness, metallic/garlic taste; rare hepatotoxicity, neuropathy

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Recent alcohol intake (within 12 hr); use of alcohol-containing products
  • Severe cardiac disease, psychosis
  • Pregnancy; concurrent metronidazole

Interactions

  • Any alcohol (including OTC cough syrups, mouthwash, aftershave, sauces) → disulfiram-alcohol reaction
  • Metronidazole → psychosis/confusion
  • Warfarin, phenytoin → ↑ levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Maintained sobriety; client engaged in a recovery program
  • No accidental disulfiram-alcohol reactions

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO once daily
  • Start only after ≥ 12 hr alcohol-free
  • Effects (with alcohol) can occur up to 2 weeks after stopping the drug
  • Most effective combined with counseling and support

Nursing Interventions

  • Confirm the client understands the reaction and is motivated/abstinent
  • Teach avoidance of all hidden alcohol sources
  • Monitor LFTs; reinforce support program participation

Client Education

  • Avoid ALL alcohol — including mouthwash, cough syrup, vinegar, aftershave, hand sanitizer
  • A reaction can occur up to 2 weeks after the last dose
  • Wear medical identification
  • Take daily as part of a recovery plan; report yellowing skin or numbness/tingling
Worked Example Naltrexone Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Naltrexone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Opioid receptor antagonist that blocks opioid effects at receptor sites, reducing reward and reinforcement from opioids and alcohol.
  • Reduces alcohol craving and relapse risk without causing a disulfiram-like reaction if alcohol is consumed.
  • Blocks opioid analgesics and can precipitate withdrawal if opioids are still present, so opioid-free status must be verified before treatment.
  • Hepatic metabolism and possible hepatotoxicity make liver history, LFTs, and other hepatotoxic medications important safety checks.

Therapeutic Use

  • Maintenance treatment for alcohol use disorder to reduce cravings and support abstinence or reduced relapse risk.
  • Used for opioid use disorder relapse prevention after detoxification, once the client is opioid-free.
  • Available as daily oral therapy or monthly IM extended-release injection to support adherence.
  • Not an acute overdose reversal medication and not a withdrawal treatment; combine with counseling, recovery planning, and monitoring.

Complications

  • Nausea, headache, dizziness, fatigue
  • Hepatotoxicity (high doses)
  • Precipitates withdrawal if opioids are present; loss of opioid tolerance → overdose risk if relapse

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Current opioid use / acute opioid withdrawal (must be opioid-free ~7–10 days)
  • Acute hepatitis or liver failure
  • Caution: hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Opioids → blocked analgesia and precipitated withdrawal
  • Other hepatotoxic drugs → ↑ liver injury

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ cravings; maintained abstinence
  • Engagement in recovery program; normal LFTs

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO daily or monthly IM depot (extended-release) for adherence
  • Confirm opioid-free status before starting
  • Monitor LFTs; combine with counseling/support

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify no recent opioid use before initiating
  • Monitor liver function and for withdrawal
  • Educate on reduced opioid tolerance and overdose risk if relapse
  • Promote adherence (consider IM form)

Client Education

  • Must be opioid-free before starting (avoids withdrawal)
  • If you relapse, your tolerance is lower — overdose risk is high
  • Carry medical identification (opioid analgesics will be blocked)
  • Report yellowing skin, dark urine, or abdominal pain; continue counseling
Worked Example Naloxone (Narcan) Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · Opioid section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Naloxone (Narcan, Evzio)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Pure opioid receptor antagonist — competitively binds to mu, kappa, delta opioid receptors
  • Rapidly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression, sedation, and analgesia
  • Onset: 1–3 min IV/IM/IN; duration 30–90 min (often SHORTER than the opioid causing overdose — redose required)

Therapeutic Use

  • Opioid overdose — reversal of respiratory depression (FIRST-LINE emergency)
  • Suspected opioid overdose in unresponsive client
  • Iatrogenic opioid overdose (post-op, PCA error)
  • Reversal of opioid sedation when needed (e.g., for procedure completion)
  • Available OTC for layperson use to reverse community overdose

Complications

  • Precipitated opioid withdrawal — in opioid-dependent clients: agitation, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, severe pain
  • Acute pain return in clients with chronic opioid pain management
  • Rare: pulmonary edema, ventricular arrhythmias (especially with rapid reversal in cardiac clients)
  • RE-NARCOTIZATION — opioid effects can return when naloxone wears off; client may relapse into respiratory depression

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to naloxone
  • Caution in opioid-dependent clients (precipitates withdrawal)
  • Caution in chronic pain clients (reverses analgesia)
  • Pregnancy: use if benefits outweigh risks (will precipitate withdrawal in fetus of opioid-dependent mother)
  • Cardiac disease — rapid reversal may cause hemodynamic stress

Interactions

  • All opioids — reverses effects (morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, methadone, heroin)
  • Buprenorphine — may require higher dose due to high-affinity binding
  • Mixed agonist-antagonists (pentazocine, butorphanol) — partial reversal
  • No significant CYP450 interactions; no clinically significant drug interactions otherwise

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Return of spontaneous breathing (RR ≥ 12)
  • Increased responsiveness, arousal
  • Reversal of pinpoint pupils
  • Sustained reversal — no relapse into respiratory depression
  • Continued monitoring for at least 2–4 hours after the longest-acting opioid effect would normally last

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV (preferred in healthcare), IM, SC, intranasal (community use), sublingual
  • Adult initial dose: 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/SC; repeat every 2–3 min as needed (max 10 mg if no response — reconsider diagnosis)
  • Intranasal (Narcan): 4 mg (one spray) per nostril; alternate nostrils for repeat doses every 2–3 min
  • Pediatric: 0.1 mg/kg IV/IM; up to adult dose
  • IV infusion may be needed for long-acting opioids (methadone, sustained-release formulations)
  • Stable at room temperature; protect from light

Nursing Interventions

  • Activate emergency response immediately for suspected overdose
  • Position: lateral recovery position to prevent aspiration
  • Establish airway, provide bag-valve-mask ventilation if needed
  • Administer naloxone per protocol; redose every 2–3 min until response or max
  • Monitor closely for at least 2–4 hours — opioid effect may outlast naloxone (re-narcotization)
  • For long-acting opioids (methadone, ER formulations): admit and consider naloxone IV infusion
  • Anticipate withdrawal in dependent clients: have IV access, antiemetics, anxiolytics ready
  • Connect to substance use treatment after stabilization

Client Education

  • For families/contacts of opioid users: obtain and learn to use naloxone (OTC in most states)
  • Recognize overdose: slow/no breathing, blue/gray skin, unresponsive, pinpoint pupils
  • Call 911 IMMEDIATELY after administering naloxone — effect is temporary
  • Roll person to side after dosing (recovery position)
  • Be prepared for the person to be confused/upset on waking
  • Multiple doses may be needed for synthetic opioids (fentanyl)
  • Naloxone is safe even if opioid use is uncertain — can’t hurt; can save a life
  • Good Samaritan laws protect those who call for help
  • Discuss with provider: substance use treatment options after this crisis
Worked Example Buprenorphine / Suboxone Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · Opioid section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Buprenorphine (Subutex) / Buprenorphine-Naloxone (Suboxone)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Partial mu-opioid receptor agonist — relieves cravings and prevents withdrawal without producing the full opioid “high”
  • Ceiling effect — respiratory depression plateaus at higher doses, making it safer than methadone
  • Suboxone combines buprenorphine + naloxone — naloxone is inactive sublingually but causes withdrawal if injected (anti-diversion)

Therapeutic Use

  • Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) — induction, stabilization, and maintenance
  • Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) in office-based settings
  • Withdrawal management (less intense than going cold-turkey)
  • Chronic pain (less common indication)

Complications

  • Precipitated withdrawal — if started before opioid has cleared (must wait until client is in mild-moderate withdrawal: COWS ≥ 8)
  • Respiratory depression (lower risk than full agonists due to ceiling effect; combine with benzos → danger)
  • Dependence (physical dependence develops; tapering required to stop)
  • QT prolongation (high doses, especially methadone interaction)
  • Constipation (typical opioid effect)
  • Hepatotoxicity (rare; monitor LFTs)
  • Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) in pregnancy — less severe than methadone NAS

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to buprenorphine or naloxone
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • Concurrent use of full opioid agonists (may precipitate withdrawal OR additive sedation)
  • Concurrent benzodiazepines/alcohol (risk of fatal respiratory depression)
  • Pregnancy: buprenorphine alone (Subutex) preferred over Suboxone in pregnancy
  • Mental health crisis without close monitoring

Interactions

  • CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol, sedatives) — fatal respiratory depression risk
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir, clarithromycin) — raise buprenorphine levels
  • CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) — lower levels; may precipitate withdrawal
  • Other opioids — partial agonism can displace full agonists and cause withdrawal
  • Naltrexone — will precipitate severe withdrawal

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced cravings and use of illicit opioids
  • Improved functional status (work, relationships, self-care)
  • Negative urine drug screens for illicit opioids
  • Stable dose without diversion or misuse
  • Engagement in counseling and recovery support
  • Reduced overdose risk in OUD population

Medication Administration

  • Routes: sublingual (tablets, films), subdermal implant (Probuphine 6-month), monthly SC injection (Sublocade)
  • Induction: wait until COWS ≥ 8 (mild-moderate withdrawal) before first dose to avoid precipitated withdrawal; start 2–4 mg; titrate to 8–16 mg day 1
  • Maintenance: 8–24 mg sublingually once daily (typical 16 mg)
  • SL administration: place under tongue; let dissolve completely; do not chew or swallow whole; no eating/drinking for 5–10 min after
  • Schedule III — restricted prescribing; requires DEA X-waiver (recently broadened access)

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify withdrawal severity (COWS scale) before induction
  • Baseline: LFTs, HIV, hepatitis screen, pregnancy test (in childbearing age)
  • Observed dosing during induction; titrate based on COWS reduction
  • Naloxone available for emergency reversal (high dose may be needed due to high affinity)
  • Monitor for signs of diversion (asking for early refills, multiple prescribers)
  • Coordinate counseling and behavioral therapy (MAT is more than just medication)
  • Educate family on signs of overdose and naloxone use

Client Education

  • Take sublingually exactly as prescribed; do not swallow, chew, or snort/inject (precipitates withdrawal)
  • Allow tablet/film to dissolve completely; no eating/drinking for 5–10 min
  • Do NOT combine with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives (fatal)
  • Do not stop abruptly — taper with provider to prevent withdrawal
  • Continue counseling/support groups — MAT works best with behavioral treatment
  • Naloxone access: keep available for emergency overdose reversal
  • Carry medication ID card; inform all providers about MAT
  • Pregnancy: discuss with provider; Subutex preferred
  • Recovery is a process; relapse does not mean failure; reach out for help
Worked Example Metoclopramide Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Metoclopramide
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Dopamine D2 receptor antagonist that acts in the chemoreceptor trigger zone to reduce nausea and vomiting.
  • Increases upper GI motility by enhancing gastric emptying and intestinal transit and by increasing lower esophageal sphincter tone.
  • At higher doses, also has serotonin-receptor activity that contributes to antiemetic effects.
  • Dopamine blockade explains major safety risks, including extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

Therapeutic Use

  • Gastroparesis (especially diabetic), GERD
  • Nausea/vomiting (chemotherapy, postoperative)

Complications

  • Extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia (black box — limit to ≤ 12 weeks)
  • Sedation, restlessness, diarrhea
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • GI obstruction, perforation, or hemorrhage
  • Pheochromocytoma, seizure disorder
  • Parkinson disease; caution: older adults, depression

Interactions

  • Other dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) → ↑ EPS
  • CNS depressants/alcohol → ↑ sedation
  • Affects absorption/timing of other oral drugs

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ nausea/vomiting; improved gastric emptying (less bloating, early satiety)
  • No EPS or tardive dyskinesia

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO (before meals and at bedtime), IV, IM
  • Limit duration to ≤ 12 weeks (tardive dyskinesia risk)
  • Give 30 min before meals for gastroparesis

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for EPS/tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements)
  • Limit treatment duration; monitor for sedation
  • Give before meals; assess GI symptom relief

Client Education

  • Take before meals as directed; limit to prescribed duration
  • Report involuntary movements (face, tongue, limbs) immediately
  • Avoid alcohol; report restlessness or muscle stiffness
  • May cause drowsiness — use caution driving
Worked Example Loperamide (Imodium) Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Loperamide (Imodium)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antidiarrheal — opioid receptor agonist acting locally on intestinal mu-receptors
  • Slows intestinal motility → increases transit time → more water/electrolyte reabsorption → firmer stools
  • Does NOT cross blood-brain barrier at normal doses (no central opioid/analgesic effects)
  • Reduces stool frequency and volume

Therapeutic Use

  • Acute nonspecific diarrhea
  • Chronic diarrhea (IBS-D, IBD — with caution)
  • Reduce ostomy output
  • Traveler’s diarrhea (with caution)

Complications

  • Constipation (most common)
  • Toxic megacolon — in infectious/inflammatory colitis (C. diff, ulcerative colitis); slowing motility traps toxins/bacteria
  • Cardiac arrhythmias / QT prolongation at high (abuse) doses — FDA warning; torsades, cardiac arrest
  • Abdominal cramping, bloating, nausea
  • Dizziness, drowsiness
  • Paralytic ileus

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Bloody diarrhea or high fever (suspected invasive bacterial infection — do not slow clearance)
  • C. difficile or pseudomembranous colitis (toxic megacolon risk)
  • Acute ulcerative colitis flare (toxic megacolon)
  • Children < 2 years
  • Known QT prolongation
  • Do not use for abuse/euphoria (cardiotoxic at high doses)

Interactions

  • CYP3A4/CYP2C8 inhibitors (ritonavir, gemfibrozil, ketoconazole) — increase loperamide levels
  • P-glycoprotein inhibitors (quinidine) — may allow CNS penetration (opioid effects)
  • QT-prolonging drugs — additive arrhythmia risk
  • Other CNS depressants — additive drowsiness (high doses)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced stool frequency and improved consistency
  • Resolution of diarrhea
  • Maintained hydration and electrolyte balance
  • No constipation, ileus, or toxic megacolon
  • No cardiac effects (used appropriately)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (capsule, tablet, liquid)
  • Adult: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool; max 8 mg/day OTC (16 mg/day Rx)
  • Do not exceed recommended dose (cardiac risk)
  • Take with adequate fluids
  • OTC available; counsel on appropriate use

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess cause of diarrhea — do NOT use if infectious (bloody stool, fever) or C. diff suspected
  • Monitor stool frequency, consistency, hydration, electrolytes
  • Assess for abdominal distension (ileus, megacolon)
  • Monitor for cardiac effects if high doses suspected
  • Educate on max dose (cardiotoxicity with overuse/abuse)
  • Encourage oral rehydration
  • Reassess if diarrhea persists > 48 hr (needs evaluation)

Client Education

  • Take as directed; do NOT exceed the maximum dose — high doses can cause serious heart rhythm problems
  • Do NOT use if you have bloody stools or high fever — see a provider
  • Stay hydrated; use oral rehydration solutions
  • Stop and seek care if diarrhea lasts more than 48 hours, abdominal swelling, or no improvement
  • Report severe constipation or abdominal distension
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Keep out of reach of children
  • This medication treats symptoms, not the cause — persistent diarrhea needs evaluation
Worked Example Ferrous Sulfate Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ferrous Sulfate
Review Module Chapter
Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Oral iron supplement that provides elemental iron required for hemoglobin, myoglobin, and normal oxygen transport.
  • Restores the iron substrate bone marrow needs for erythropoiesis, increasing reticulocyte response before hemoglobin fully rises.
  • Absorption improves in an acidic environment and with vitamin C, but decreases with antacids, PPIs, calcium, dairy, tea, and coffee.
  • Dark stools and GI upset are expected effects, while overdose is dangerous enough that child-safe storage is essential.

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevents or treats iron-deficiency anemia caused by inadequate intake, chronic blood loss, pregnancy needs, or other provider-identified deficiency states.
  • Used when iron studies and blood counts support iron replacement, with expected improvement in fatigue, pallor, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and reticulocytes.
  • Therapy often continues after blood counts improve to replete iron stores, so clients should not stop early without provider direction.
  • Administration teaching focuses on absorption timing, vitamin C pairing, constipation management, dark stools, and separation from interacting medications.

Complications

  • GI: constipation, nausea, epigastric pain, dark/black stools (harmless)
  • Teeth staining (liquid forms)
  • Overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hemochromatosis/iron overload, hemolytic anemia
  • Peptic ulcer disease, ulcerative colitis (caution)

Interactions

  • Antacids, PPIs, dairy, calcium, tea/coffee → ↓ iron absorption
  • Vitamin C → ↑ absorption
  • Reduces absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↑ hemoglobin, hematocrit, and reticulocytes; ↑ energy
  • Resolution of anemia symptoms

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, ideally on an empty stomach (take with food if GI upset)
  • Take with vitamin C / orange juice to enhance absorption
  • Use a straw for liquid forms; separate from antacids/dairy/other drugs by ≥ 2 hr

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess hemoglobin/hematocrit response
  • Manage constipation (fluids, fiber)
  • Store safely away from children (overdose risk)

Client Education

  • Take on an empty stomach with vitamin C; expect dark stools (normal)
  • Increase fluids and fiber to prevent constipation
  • Keep away from children (poisoning danger)
  • Separate from antacids, dairy, and tea/coffee by 1–2 hr
Worked Example Potassium Chloride Supplement Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals · Minerals section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Potassium Chloride (KCl)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Electrolyte supplement — replaces potassium, essential for cardiac rhythm, neuromuscular function, and acid-base balance
  • Potassium is the major intracellular cation
  • Normal serum: 3.5–5.0 mEq/L
  • HIGH-ALERT MEDICATION (ISMP)

Therapeutic Use

  • Hypokalemia — from diuretics (loop/thiazide), GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea), DKA treatment
  • Prevention of hypokalemia in at-risk clients
  • Maintenance with potassium-wasting medications

Complications

  • Hyperkalemia — peaked T-waves, widened QRS, bradycardia, cardiac arrest (especially if given too fast/too much or renal impairment)
  • GI irritation — nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, GI ulceration/bleeding (oral)
  • IV: phlebitis, pain at site; FATAL ARRHYTHMIA if given IV push
  • Cardiac arrhythmias

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hyperkalemia (existing)
  • Severe renal impairment / oliguria (cannot excrete)
  • Concurrent potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs (hyperkalemia risk)
  • Addison’s disease
  • Severe dehydration
  • GI obstruction or delayed transit (oral — ulceration)

Interactions

  • Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone), ACE inhibitors, ARBs — additive hyperkalemia
  • NSAIDs — reduce potassium excretion
  • Salt substitutes (contain potassium) — additive
  • Digoxin — both hypo- and hyperkalemia affect digoxin toxicity

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Serum potassium returns to normal (3.5–5.0 mEq/L)
  • Resolution of hypokalemia symptoms (weakness, arrhythmias, cramps)
  • Normal EKG
  • No hyperkalemia
  • No GI ulceration (oral) or phlebitis (IV)

Medication Administration

  • Oral: take WITH food and a full glass of water; do not crush ER tablets; dilute liquid/effervescent forms
  • IV: NEVER give IV push or bolus — FATAL. Always DILUTE and give as slow infusion
  • IV rate: generally ≤ 10 mEq/hr on a general floor (higher only in ICU with continuous cardiac monitoring)
  • Maximum concentration limits per policy; use infusion pump
  • NEVER concentrated KCl on floor stock (removed for safety)
  • Central line for higher concentrations (peripheral causes phlebitis)
  • High-alert: independent double-check

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify adequate urine output / renal function BEFORE administering (must be able to excrete)
  • Baseline and follow-up serum potassium, renal function, EKG
  • IV: always dilute; use pump; cardiac monitoring for higher rates; never push
  • Assess IV site for phlebitis; central line for high concentration
  • Oral: give with food/water; sit upright; don’t crush ER forms
  • Monitor for hyperkalemia: peaked T-waves, weakness, paresthesias, arrhythmias
  • High-alert medication: independent double-check; verify concentration and rate
  • Review concurrent medications (K-sparing diuretics, ACE/ARB)

Client Education

  • Take oral potassium WITH food and a full glass of water to prevent stomach upset
  • Do not crush or chew extended-release tablets; swallow whole
  • Report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, black stools (GI irritation)
  • Report muscle weakness, irregular heartbeat, tingling (potassium imbalance)
  • Do not use salt substitutes (high in potassium) without provider approval
  • Keep all lab appointments (potassium monitoring)
  • Eat potassium-rich foods if recommended (bananas, oranges, potatoes)
  • Tell provider about all medications (some raise potassium)
  • Keep out of reach of children
Worked Example Folic Acid (Vitamin B9) Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals · Vitamins section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Folic Acid (Vitamin B9)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 30 — Vitamins and Minerals
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Water-soluble B vitamin — essential for DNA synthesis, RBC formation, and cell division
  • Required for normal erythropoiesis (prevents megaloblastic anemia)
  • Critical for fetal neural tube development

Therapeutic Use

  • Prevention of neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly) — before conception and during pregnancy
  • Folate-deficiency (megaloblastic) anemia
  • Malabsorption states, alcoholism, pregnancy/lactation
  • Counteract folate-depleting drugs (methotrexate rescue [leucovorin], phenytoin, sulfasalazine)

Complications

  • Generally very safe (water-soluble; excess excreted)
  • CAN MASK vitamin B12 deficiency — corrects the anemia but allows neurologic damage of B12 deficiency to progress undetected
  • Rare: allergic reactions, GI upset, altered sleep, irritability (high doses)
  • May reduce phenytoin levels (lowered seizure threshold)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Undiagnosed anemia — must rule out/co-treat B12 deficiency first (folate alone masks B12 deficiency)
  • Pernicious anemia (give with B12)
  • Generally safe in pregnancy (recommended)

Interactions

  • Phenytoin — folic acid may decrease phenytoin levels (seizure risk); phenytoin lowers folate
  • Methotrexate — folate antagonist (leucovorin is the reduced form used as rescue)
  • Sulfasalazine, trimethoprim — reduce folate
  • Oral contraceptives — may lower folate

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Correction of megaloblastic anemia (Hgb, MCV normalize; reticulocytosis)
  • Adequate serum folate levels
  • Prevention of neural tube defects (pregnancy)
  • No masked B12 deficiency (B12 checked/co-treated)

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (also IM/IV/SC for severe deficiency or malabsorption)
  • Prevention in pregnancy: 400–800 mcg/day; start before conception, continue 1st trimester
  • High-risk (prior NTD pregnancy): 4 mg/day
  • Deficiency treatment: 1 mg/day
  • Take with or without food

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for B12 deficiency BEFORE/with folate treatment in anemia (folate masks B12)
  • Baseline CBC, folate level, B12 level
  • Monitor hematologic response (reticulocytes, Hgb, MCV)
  • Counsel women of childbearing age on preconception folate
  • Monitor phenytoin levels if co-prescribed
  • Dietary counseling: leafy greens, citrus, legumes, fortified grains

Client Education

  • Women of childbearing age: take folic acid daily — neural tube forms in the first weeks, often before pregnancy is known
  • Take before conception and through early pregnancy
  • Folate-rich foods: dark leafy greens, citrus fruits, beans, fortified cereals/grains
