  • If treating anemia, B12 deficiency must also be checked (folate alone can hide it)
  • Take as directed; safe vitamin but follow dosing
  • If on phenytoin, keep seizure follow-up (interaction)
  • Generally well-tolerated; report unusual symptoms
Worked Example Acetaminophen Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Acetaminophen
Review Module Chapter
Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Non-opioid analgesic/antipyretic — reduces pain and fever primarily through central inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis. Little anti-inflammatory effect

Therapeutic Use

  • Mild-to-moderate pain and fever
  • Preferred when NSAIDs are contraindicated (no GI/bleeding effects)

Complications

  • Well tolerated at therapeutic doses
  • Hepatotoxicity with overdose or chronic high intake (especially with alcohol) — leading cause of acute liver failure

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe hepatic impairment/active liver disease
  • Chronic high alcohol use (caution)
  • Hypersensitivity

Interactions

  • Alcohol and other hepatotoxic drugs → ↑ liver injury
  • Warfarin → ↑ INR with high/prolonged doses

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of pain; reduced fever
  • No signs of liver injury

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO, rectal, IV
  • Maximum ~4 g/day for healthy adults (lower with liver disease/alcohol)
  • Beware hidden acetaminophen in many combination OTC/cold products
  • Antidote for overdose: acetylcysteine

Nursing Interventions

  • Total all acetaminophen sources to avoid exceeding the daily max
  • Monitor liver function in at-risk clients
  • Recognize overdose; have acetylcysteine available

Client Education

  • Do not exceed the maximum daily dose; check all OTC/combination products for acetaminophen
  • Limit or avoid alcohol
  • Report nausea, abdominal pain, or yellowing of skin/eyes
  • Keep out of reach of children
Worked Example Alteplase Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Alteplase
Review Module Chapter
Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Thrombolytic tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) that binds fibrin in a clot and converts plasminogen to plasmin.
  • Plasmin breaks down fibrin strands, dissolving an existing thrombus and helping restore perfusion to ischemic tissue.
  • Used within strict time windows for selected ischemic stroke, STEMI, massive pulmonary embolism, or catheter occlusion protocols.
  • Does not prevent new clot formation; bleeding risk remains the major safety concern during and after therapy.

Therapeutic Use

  • Acute ischemic stroke, STEMI, and massive pulmonary embolism
  • Clearing occluded central venous catheters (low dose)

Complications

  • Serious bleeding/hemorrhage (including intracranial) — primary risk
  • Reperfusion dysrhythmias; hypotension; angioedema

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active internal bleeding, recent intracranial hemorrhage/surgery/trauma, history of hemorrhagic stroke
  • Severe uncontrolled hypertension, known bleeding disorder
  • Narrow time window from symptom onset

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants such as heparin, warfarin, and direct oral anticoagulants increase major bleeding risk and require strict protocol review before therapy.
  • Antiplatelet medications such as aspirin, clopidogrel, and GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors increase bleeding risk when used near alteplase therapy.
  • NSAIDs and other medications or supplements that impair hemostasis can increase bleeding risk.
  • Recent invasive procedures, punctures, surgery, trauma, or uncontrolled hypertension amplify hemorrhage risk and must be screened before administration.

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Restored perfusion (e.g., neurologic improvement in stroke, reperfusion in MI)
  • No major bleeding

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV per strict protocol; give within the approved time window from symptom onset
  • Obtain baseline coagulation studies; avoid unnecessary punctures/invasive procedures
  • Continuous neuro and bleeding assessment; have it ready as a high-alert drug

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for bleeding (neuro checks, puncture sites, GI/GU), vital signs, and dysrhythmias
  • Minimize invasive procedures; apply prolonged pressure to sites
  • Verify eligibility/time window and absence of contraindications

Client Education

  • Report any bleeding, severe headache, or weakness immediately
  • Understand the need for close monitoring during/after infusion
  • Avoid activities risking injury during the bleeding-risk period
Worked Example Warfarin (Coumadin) Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation · Warfarin section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Warfarin (Coumadin)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 25 — Medications Affecting Coagulation
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant — inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → reduces synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and proteins C and S
  • Delayed onset (full effect 3–5 days; existing factors must deplete)
  • Narrow therapeutic index — requires INR monitoring
  • Often bridged with heparin/LMWH initially (until INR therapeutic)

Therapeutic Use

  • Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention (especially mechanical valves)
  • Venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE) treatment and prevention
  • Mechanical heart valves (DOACs not used here — warfarin required)
  • Post-MI in select cases
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome

Complications

  • Bleeding/hemorrhage (BLACK BOX) — major risk; GI bleed, intracranial hemorrhage, hematuria, epistaxis
  • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis (early; protein C depletion before factor depletion)
  • Purple toe syndrome
  • Teratogenic (Category X) — fetal warfarin syndrome; use heparin/LMWH in pregnancy
  • Numerous drug and food interactions affecting INR

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy — teratogenic (use heparin/LMWH instead)
  • Active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia
  • Recent or planned surgery/invasive procedures
  • Severe hepatic disease (impaired factor synthesis)
  • Uncontrolled hypertension
  • History of warfarin-induced skin necrosis
  • Inability to monitor INR or adhere to monitoring
  • Fall risk (caution in older adults)

Interactions

  • INCREASE INR / bleeding risk: amiodarone, fluconazole/azoles, metronidazole, SSRIs, NSAIDs, aspirin, many antibiotics, acetaminophen (high dose), cranberry juice, alcohol (acute)
  • DECREASE INR / clot risk: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, high vitamin K foods (leafy greens — keep CONSISTENT, not avoided), St. John’s wort, chronic alcohol
  • CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genetic variants affect dosing
  • Always review interactions before starting any new medication

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • INR within target range: 2–3 for most indications; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valves
  • Prevention of thromboembolic events (no stroke, DVT, PE)
  • No bleeding complications
  • Stable, consistent INR over time
  • Adherence to monitoring schedule

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (also IV in hospital)
  • Individualized dose based on INR (typical 2–10 mg/day)
  • Take at the same time each day, usually evening
  • Antidote: vitamin K (phytonadione) for elevated INR/bleeding; fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) for major bleeding
  • Bridge with heparin/LMWH until INR therapeutic (overlap 4–5 days)
  • INR monitoring: frequent initially, then every 2–4 weeks when stable

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and ongoing INR/PT; CBC; assess bleeding risk
  • Monitor for bleeding: gums, urine, stool (guaiac), bruising, neuro changes (intracranial)
  • Have vitamin K available as antidote
  • Comprehensive medication AND diet review (interactions)
  • Bleeding precautions: soft toothbrush, electric razor, fall prevention
  • Educate on consistent vitamin K intake (don’t eliminate greens — keep steady)
  • Pregnancy screening in childbearing age (teratogenic)
  • Coordinate INR monitoring and follow-up; consider anticoagulation clinic

Client Education

  • Take exactly as prescribed at the same time daily; never double up for a missed dose
  • Regular INR blood tests are essential — keep all appointments
  • Keep vitamin K intake CONSISTENT (don’t suddenly increase or eliminate leafy greens, broccoli, etc.)
  • Report bleeding: gums, nosebleeds, blood in urine/stool, excessive bruising, severe headache
  • Use soft toothbrush, electric razor; avoid injury-prone activities
  • Tell ALL providers and dentists you take warfarin; check before any new medication (including OTC and herbal)
  • Avoid alcohol excess; avoid cranberry juice and St. John’s wort
  • Carry medical alert ID
  • Do NOT take if pregnant or planning pregnancy — tell provider immediately
  • Limit aspirin/NSAIDs unless directed
Worked Example Methotrexate Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Methotrexate
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) / antimetabolite — inhibits folic acid metabolism and rapidly dividing cells, suppressing inflammation and immune response

Therapeutic Use

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (first-line DMARD), psoriasis
  • Certain cancers (higher doses)

Complications

  • Bone marrow suppression (infection, bleeding, anemia)
  • Hepatotoxicity and pulmonary toxicity
  • GI ulceration/stomatitis, nausea
  • Highly teratogenic; nephrotoxicity (high dose)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding
  • Liver disease, alcohol use disorder, significant blood dyscrasias
  • Active infection; caution: renal impairment

Interactions

  • NSAIDs and salicylates → ↑ methotrexate toxicity
  • Other hepatotoxic/nephrotoxic drugs → ↑ toxicity
  • Live vaccines → infection risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ joint inflammation/pain and slowed joint damage (RA)
  • Normal CBC, LFTs; no infection or pulmonary symptoms

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO, SubQ, IM (RA dosing is usually once weekly — not daily)
  • Folic acid supplementation reduces toxicity
  • Monitor CBC, LFTs, and renal function; leucovorin rescue for high-dose/overdose

Nursing Interventions

  • Confirm weekly (not daily) dosing for RA — a common, dangerous error
  • Monitor CBC, LFTs, renal function, and for infection/bleeding/cough
  • Ensure folic acid; verify contraception

Client Education

  • Take once weekly as prescribed (never daily) for arthritis
  • Avoid alcohol and NSAIDs/aspirin unless approved; take folic acid as directed
  • Report fever, sore throat, mouth sores, unusual bleeding, cough, or yellowing skin
  • Use reliable contraception (do not become pregnant)
Worked Example Allopurinol Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Allopurinol
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Xanthine oxidase inhibitor that blocks conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid.
  • Lowers serum urate over time, helping prevent urate crystal deposition, recurrent gout attacks, and uric acid kidney stones.
  • Used for chronic urate control rather than immediate analgesia, so it does not relieve an acute gout attack by itself.
  • Starting therapy can trigger a gout flare as urate shifts, and rash can signal severe hypersensitivity that requires urgent reporting.

Therapeutic Use

  • Chronic gout (prevention — not for acute attacks)
  • Hyperuricemia from chemotherapy/tumor lysis; recurrent uric acid stones

Complications

  • Hypersensitivity/severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) — stop if rash
  • GI upset, drowsiness
  • May trigger an acute gout flare when starting

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity/prior severe reaction
  • Caution: renal impairment (dose reduction)

Interactions

  • Azathioprine, mercaptopurine → toxic accumulation (reduce their dose)
  • Warfarin → ↑ effect
  • Ampicillin → ↑ rash; thiazides → ↑ allopurinol level

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • ↓ serum uric acid; fewer gout attacks over time
  • No severe skin reaction

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, after meals to reduce GI upset
  • Not for acute attacks — continue during a flare if already taking it
  • Increase fluids; titrate to target urate; reduce dose in renal impairment

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor serum uric acid, renal/liver function, and for rash
  • Encourage fluids (2–3 L/day)
  • Explain it prevents (not treats) acute attacks

Client Education

  • Stop and report any rash immediately (serious reaction risk)
  • Take after meals; drink plenty of fluids
  • Continue daily even when feeling well; it won’t relieve an acute attack
  • Limit alcohol and purine-rich foods
Worked Example Colchicine (Acute Gout) Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · Gout/SLE section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Colchicine (Colcrys)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anti-inflammatory (not a uric acid drug) — inhibits microtubule polymerization, disrupting neutrophil migration and activation
  • Reduces the inflammatory response to urate crystals in joints
  • Does NOT lower uric acid levels (different from allopurinol)
  • Most effective when started early in an acute attack

Therapeutic Use

  • Acute gout flares — relieve pain/inflammation
  • Gout flare prophylaxis when starting urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol can trigger flares initially)
  • Familial Mediterranean fever
  • Pericarditis (off-label)

Complications

  • GI toxicity (most common, dose-limiting) — nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain (early sign of toxicity)
  • Bone marrow suppression (high/toxic doses) — agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia
  • Myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (especially with statins, renal impairment)
  • Narrow therapeutic index — overdose can be fatal
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Hepatotoxicity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Severe renal or hepatic impairment (dose adjust; combination renal+hepatic = avoid)
  • Concurrent strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors (in renal/hepatic impairment — fatal toxicity)
  • Blood dyscrasias
  • Older adults (toxicity risk)
  • Pregnancy — weigh risk

Interactions

  • Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, ketoconazole, ritonavir) — increase colchicine to toxic/fatal levels
  • P-glycoprotein inhibitors (cyclosporine, verapamil) — increase levels
  • Statins, fibrates — additive myopathy/rhabdomyolysis
  • Grapefruit juice — increases levels
  • Avoid combinations in renal/hepatic impairment

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of acute gout pain and inflammation (usually within 24–48 hr)
  • Reduced joint swelling, redness, warmth
  • Prevention of flares during urate-lowering initiation
  • No GI toxicity, myopathy, or marrow suppression

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral
  • Acute gout: 1.2 mg at first sign, then 0.6 mg 1 hr later (max 1.8 mg over 1 hr per attack)
  • Prophylaxis: 0.6 mg once or twice daily
  • Reduce dose in renal/hepatic impairment and with interacting drugs
  • Start as EARLY as possible in a flare for best effect
  • Take with food to reduce GI upset

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess renal and hepatic function (dose adjustment)
  • Review for CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors and statins (toxicity)
  • Monitor for GI symptoms — first sign of toxicity; hold and notify if severe diarrhea/vomiting
  • Periodic CBC (marrow suppression with chronic use)
  • Assess for muscle pain/weakness (myopathy)
  • Educate on early use in flares and max dosing limits
  • Distinguish from urate-lowering therapy (colchicine does not lower uric acid)

Client Education

  • Take at the FIRST sign of a gout attack for best results
  • Do NOT exceed the prescribed dose — overdose can be dangerous
  • Stop and call your provider for severe diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain (early toxicity signs)
  • Report muscle pain, weakness, numbness/tingling, unusual bleeding or infection
  • Take with food
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Tell providers about all medications (serious interactions, especially certain antibiotics and statins)
  • This relieves the attack but does NOT lower uric acid — continue any urate-lowering medication separately
  • Limit alcohol and purine-rich foods
Worked Example Aspirin Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Aspirin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • NSAID/salicylate — irreversibly inhibits COX enzymes, reducing prostaglandins (anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic) and thromboxane (antiplatelet)

Therapeutic Use

  • Pain, fever, inflammation
  • Low-dose: prevention of MI/stroke (antiplatelet)

Complications

  • GI bleeding/ulceration, dyspepsia
  • Salicism/toxicity (tinnitus, hyperventilation) at high doses
  • Bleeding (prolonged); Reye syndrome in children/teens with viral illness

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Children/adolescents with viral illness (Reye syndrome)
  • Active GI bleeding/peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders
  • Third-trimester pregnancy; aspirin/NSAID allergy

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants, other NSAIDs, alcohol → ↑ bleeding
  • Ibuprofen → may blunt aspirin’s cardioprotective effect
  • ↑ effect of some hypoglycemics; ↓ effect of some antihypertensives

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Relief of pain/fever/inflammation
  • Cardioprotection (no MI/stroke) for low-dose preventive use; no bleeding

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO with food/full glass of water (enteric-coated to reduce GI effects)
  • Stop ~1 week before surgery (per provider) due to bleeding
  • Avoid in children with fever/viral illness

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for GI bleeding (black/tarry stools), bleeding, and tinnitus (toxicity)
  • Give with food; assess for allergy/asthma sensitivity
  • Hold before procedures per orders

Client Education

  • Take with food; report black/tarry stools, ringing in the ears, or unusual bleeding
  • Do not give to children/teens with fever or viral illness
  • Avoid alcohol and other NSAIDs; tell providers before surgery/dental work
  • Low-dose daily aspirin only if prescribed
Worked Example Fentanyl Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Fentanyl
Review Module Chapter
Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Potent opioid agonist that binds primarily to mu opioid receptors in the CNS to alter pain perception and response.
  • Produces strong analgesia and sedation but also depresses the respiratory center, making respiratory assessment the priority safety monitor.
  • Has rapid onset with IV/transmucosal forms; transdermal delivery provides sustained analgesia for chronic opioid-tolerant clients.
  • High lipid solubility and potency increase overdose risk, especially with heat exposure to patches, opioid-naive clients, or concurrent CNS depressants.

Therapeutic Use

  • Severe pain (surgical, procedural, breakthrough cancer pain)
  • Anesthesia adjunct; transdermal patch for chronic, opioid-tolerant pain

Complications

  • Respiratory depression (most serious), sedation
  • Constipation, nausea, urinary retention, hypotension, bradycardia
  • Chest wall rigidity (rapid IV); high overdose/diversion risk

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Opioid-naïve clients (transdermal/long-acting forms)
  • Severe respiratory depression, acute/severe asthma
  • Paralytic ileus; caution: head injury, hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol) → additive respiratory depression
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors → ↑ fentanyl level
  • Serotonergic drugs → serotonin syndrome

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Adequate pain relief with maintained respirations
  • No oversedation or respiratory compromise

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IV, transdermal patch, transmucosal; Schedule II controlled substance
  • Transdermal patch: apply to clean dry skin, rotate sites; full effect ~24 hr; avoid heat (↑ absorption)
  • Monitor respirations closely; naloxone available; dispose of patches carefully

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor respiratory rate/depth, sedation, and oxygenation
  • Keep naloxone available; assess pain
  • Educate on patch use, heat avoidance, and safe disposal; prevent/manage constipation

Client Education

  • Apply patch to clean, dry, intact skin; rotate sites; avoid heat sources (heating pads, hot baths)
  • Do not cut patches; fold used patches and dispose safely away from children/pets
  • Report slow/shallow breathing or extreme drowsiness
  • Avoid alcohol/sedatives; use a bowel regimen for constipation
Worked Example Morphine Sulfate Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Morphine Sulfate
Review Module Chapter
Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Pure opioid agonist — binds mu (and kappa) receptors in CNS
  • Alters perception of and response to pain; produces analgesia, sedation, euphoria
  • Also causes respiratory depression, miosis, decreased GI motility, venodilation
  • Prototype opioid; high-alert medication

Therapeutic Use

  • Moderate to severe acute pain (postoperative, trauma, MI)
  • Chronic severe pain (cancer)
  • Acute pulmonary edema / acute MI — reduces preload, anxiety, dyspnea
  • Sedation/comfort in palliative care

Complications

  • Respiratory depression (most serious — dose-dependent; potentiated by other CNS depressants)
  • Sedation, CNS depression
  • Constipation (does not develop tolerance; needs bowel regimen)
  • Hypotension, orthostasis (venodilation)
  • Nausea, vomiting; urinary retention
  • Miosis (pinpoint pupils)
  • Pruritus, histamine release
  • Physical dependence, tolerance, addiction potential

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Respiratory depression/insufficiency; severe asthma; paralytic ileus
  • Increased ICP / head injury (masks signs; CO2 retention)
  • Severe hypotension, shock
  • Concurrent CNS depressants, benzodiazepines (BLACK BOX — fatal respiratory depression)
  • Hepatic/renal impairment (accumulation of active metabolite)
  • Older adults; opioid-naive (lower doses)

Interactions

  • CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol, sedatives) — additive respiratory depression (BLACK BOX)
  • MAOIs — severe reactions
  • Other opioids — additive
  • Anticholinergics — worsen constipation/urinary retention
  • Serotonergic drugs — serotonin syndrome risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Pain reduced to acceptable level (pain scale)
  • Improved function and comfort
  • Adequate respiratory rate (≥ 12/min) and oxygenation
  • Reduced dyspnea (pulmonary edema/MI)
  • Manageable side effects; bowel regimen effective

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO (IR/ER), IV, IM, SC, epidural/intrathecal, rectal; PCA pump common
  • IV: dilute and give slowly; never crush ER tablets
  • Antidote: naloxone (have available)
  • Assess pain and respiratory rate before and after
  • High-alert: independent double-check for IV/PCA
  • Individualize dose; lower in opioid-naive, older adults, renal/hepatic impairment

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess respiratory rate, depth, and sedation level before and after — hold and notify if RR < 12/min or excessive sedation
  • Monitor pain (scale), BP (orthostasis), bowel function, urinary output
  • Have naloxone and resuscitation equipment available
  • Use sedation scale (e.g., POSS) for opioid-induced sedation
  • Initiate prophylactic bowel regimen (stimulant laxative +/- stool softener)
  • Fall precautions; rise slowly
  • Screen for concurrent CNS depressants/benzodiazepines
  • PCA: educate client (only client presses button); monitor

Client Education

  • Take as prescribed; report inadequate pain control rather than self-increasing
  • Do NOT combine with alcohol, sedatives, or benzodiazepines (dangerous breathing slowdown)
  • Report slow/shallow breathing, extreme drowsiness, confusion
  • Use a bowel regimen (fluids, fiber, stimulant laxative) — constipation is expected and persistent
  • Rise slowly (dizziness/orthostasis); fall precautions
  • Do not crush/chew extended-release forms
  • Do not drive until you know how it affects you
  • Store securely away from others (misuse risk); dispose of unused properly
  • Naloxone may be prescribed for emergencies — teach family use
  • Physical dependence can develop; do not stop abruptly (taper)
Worked Example Glipizide Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Glipizide
Review Module Chapter
Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Sulfonylurea oral hypoglycemic that stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin.
  • Requires functioning beta cells, so it is used for type 2 diabetes and not for type 1 diabetes or DKA.
  • Lowers blood glucose independent of meal intake once active, which explains the major risk for hypoglycemia if meals are skipped.
  • Can cause weight gain and may interact with alcohol, beta blockers, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and thiazides.

Therapeutic Use

  • Improves glycemic control in type 2 diabetes when nutrition, activity, and first-line therapy such as metformin are insufficient or not tolerated.
  • Used with meal planning, glucose monitoring, exercise, and HbA1c follow-up rather than as a substitute for lifestyle measures.
  • Best suited for clients who can eat reliably and recognize/treat hypoglycemia.
  • Not appropriate for type 1 diabetes, DKA, or situations where severe renal/hepatic impairment makes hypoglycemia risk unacceptable.

Complications

  • Hypoglycemia (main risk, especially with missed meals)
  • Weight gain, GI upset
  • Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Type 1 diabetes/DKA
  • Severe renal or hepatic impairment
  • Sulfonamide allergy (caution); caution: older adults

Interactions

  • Alcohol → disulfiram-like reaction and hypoglycemia
  • Beta blockers → mask hypoglycemia
  • NSAIDs, sulfonamides → ↑ hypoglycemia; corticosteroids/thiazides → ↑ glucose

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Fasting glucose and HbA1c within target
  • No severe hypoglycemia

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, ~30 min before a meal (immediate-release)
  • Ensure the client will eat to avoid hypoglycemia
  • Monitor glucose, HbA1c

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor blood glucose and for hypoglycemia
  • Ensure meals are eaten; educate on hypoglycemia management
  • Review alcohol interaction

Client Education

  • Take before a meal and do not skip meals (hypoglycemia)
  • Recognize/treat hypoglycemia (15 g fast carb); carry a source
  • Avoid alcohol (flushing/illness, low glucose)
  • Monitor glucose; continue diet and exercise
Worked Example Methimazole Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Methimazole
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antithyroid medication that inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking iodine organification and coupling reactions needed to make thyroid hormone.
  • Lowers new T3 and T4 synthesis over time but does not immediately remove hormone already stored in the thyroid gland.
  • Gradually reduces hyperthyroid manifestations such as palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, weight loss, and anxiety as hormone levels normalize.
  • Can cause serious agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity, making fever, sore throat, mouth sores, jaundice, and dark urine urgent reportable findings.

Therapeutic Use

  • Hyperthyroidism / Graves disease
  • Preparation for thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine therapy

Complications

  • Agranulocytosis (sore throat, fever — life-threatening)
  • Hepatotoxicity; rash, arthralgia
  • Hypothyroidism if over-treated; teratogenic (1st trimester)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • First trimester of pregnancy (PTU preferred then)
  • Hypersensitivity, prior agranulocytosis/severe liver injury
  • Breastfeeding (caution)

Interactions

  • Anticoagulants → effect altered as thyroid status changes
  • Digoxin, beta blockers → dose needs change as metabolism normalizes

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Normalized thyroid levels (↓ T3/T4, normalizing TSH)
  • ↓ symptoms (palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss); no agranulocytosis/hepatotoxicity

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO, taken consistently (effect over several weeks)
  • Monitor CBC and LFTs; monitor thyroid function
  • Do not stop abruptly without provider guidance

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor for infection (CBC), liver function, and thyroid levels
  • Assess for resolution of hyperthyroid symptoms and signs of hypothyroidism
  • Educate on reporting sore throat/fever immediately

Client Education

  • Report sore throat, fever, or mouth sores immediately (low white cells)
  • Report yellowing skin, dark urine, or fatigue (liver)
  • Take consistently; effects take weeks; keep lab appointments
  • Avoid pregnancy in the first trimester on this drug — discuss options
Worked Example Penicillin G Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Penicillin G
Review Module Chapter
Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Beta-lactam penicillin antibiotic that weakens the bacterial cell wall by blocking cross-linking during wall synthesis.
  • Cell-wall weakening causes osmotic instability and bacterial cell lysis, so penicillin G is bactericidal against susceptible organisms.
  • Because human cells do not have cell walls, the major nursing concern is hypersensitivity rather than direct host-cell wall toxicity.
  • Activity is strongest against susceptible gram-positive organisms and selected pathogens such as Treponema pallidum.

Therapeutic Use

  • Treats susceptible gram-positive infections such as streptococcal pneumonia, endocarditis, and pharyngitis when the organism is sensitive.
  • Used for selected meningococcal infections and remains a key medication for syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum.
  • May be used for endocarditis prophylaxis before dental or other procedures in clients who meet risk criteria.
  • Effectiveness depends on allergy screening, appropriate culture/sensitivity guidance, around-the-clock dosing, and completion of the full course.

Complications

  • Allergic reactions — including anaphylaxis (most serious)
  • GI upset, diarrhea; rash
  • Superinfection (e.g., C. difficile); high IV doses → electrolyte issues

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Penicillin or cephalosporin hypersensitivity (cross-sensitivity possible)
  • Caution: renal impairment (dose adjust)

Interactions

  • Probenecid → ↑ penicillin level (delays excretion)
  • Aminoglycosides → inactivation if mixed in same line
  • May reduce effectiveness of oral contraceptives

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection (↓ fever/WBC, negative cultures)
  • No allergic reaction or superinfection

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IM, IV (penicillin G); obtain allergy history before first dose
  • Observe ~30 min after administration for allergic reaction; keep emergency equipment available
  • Give around the clock to maintain levels; complete the full course

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for penicillin/cephalosporin allergy before administering
  • Monitor for anaphylaxis (have epinephrine ready); assess for superinfection/C. difficile
  • Monitor renal function with high doses

Client Education

  • Report rash, itching, swelling, or difficulty breathing immediately (allergy)
  • Complete the entire course even if feeling better
  • Report severe/watery diarrhea (C. difficile)
  • Use a backup contraceptive method if applicable
Worked Example Ceftriaxone Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ceftriaxone
Review Module Chapter
Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Third-generation cephalosporin beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis and produces bactericidal cell lysis.
  • Has broader gram-negative coverage than earlier cephalosporins and better ability to reach cerebrospinal fluid, supporting use in serious infections.
  • Greater beta-lactamase resistance across later cephalosporin generations helps preserve activity against selected resistant organisms.
  • Like other cephalosporins, therapeutic benefit must be balanced with allergy screening, C. difficile risk, and calcium-solution compatibility precautions.

Therapeutic Use

  • Treats serious susceptible infections including meningitis, pneumonia, sepsis, gonorrhea, and other invasive infections when coverage is appropriate.
  • Useful when a parenteral third-generation cephalosporin is needed for broad gram-negative coverage and CNS penetration.
  • May be included in surgical prophylaxis or empiric therapy according to local protocol and culture results.
  • In neonates, avoid calcium-containing IV solutions because ceftriaxone-calcium precipitation can be fatal.

Complications

  • Allergic reactions (cross-sensitivity with penicillins)
  • GI upset, diarrhea; C. difficile superinfection
  • Biliary sludging; disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Cephalosporin/penicillin hypersensitivity
  • Neonates — do not combine with calcium-containing IV solutions (precipitation)
  • Caution: renal/hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Alcohol → disulfiram-like reaction
  • Calcium-containing IV solutions (neonates) → fatal precipitates
  • Anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection (↓ fever/WBC, negative cultures)
  • No allergic reaction or C. difficile infection

Medication Administration

  • Routes: IM, IV; assess penicillin/cephalosporin allergy first
  • Do not mix with calcium-containing solutions in neonates
  • Complete full course; monitor injection site

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for beta-lactam allergy and cross-sensitivity
  • Monitor for anaphylaxis, C. difficile diarrhea, and bleeding
  • Avoid calcium co-administration in neonates

Client Education

  • Avoid alcohol during and a few days after therapy
  • Report rash/swelling/breathing trouble or severe diarrhea
  • Complete the full course
  • Report unusual bleeding/bruising
Worked Example Amoxicillin/Clavulanate (Augmentin) Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall · Penicillins section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Amoxicillin/Clavulanate (Augmentin)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Aminopenicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor
  • Amoxicillin: inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis (bactericidal)
  • Clavulanate: inhibits beta-lactamase enzymes that would otherwise inactivate amoxicillin → extends spectrum to beta-lactamase-producing organisms
  • Broader spectrum than amoxicillin alone

Therapeutic Use

  • Otitis media, sinusitis
  • Respiratory infections (community-acquired pneumonia, bronchitis)
  • Skin/soft tissue infections, animal/human bites
  • Urinary tract infections
  • Beta-lactamase-producing organisms (H. influenzae, some E. coli, S. aureus)

Complications

  • GI effects — diarrhea (more than amoxicillin alone, due to clavulanate), nausea, vomiting
  • Allergic reactions (penicillin class) — rash to anaphylaxis
  • C. difficile superinfection / antibiotic-associated diarrhea
  • Candidiasis (oral/vaginal)
  • Hepatotoxicity (rare; clavulanate-associated)
  • Rash with mononucleosis (do not use if mono suspected)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Penicillin allergy
  • History of amoxicillin/clavulanate-associated hepatic dysfunction
  • Mononucleosis (high rash incidence)
  • Renal impairment (dose adjust)
  • Caution with cephalosporin allergy (possible cross-reactivity)

Interactions

  • Probenecid — increases amoxicillin levels (delays excretion)
  • Oral contraceptives — possible reduced efficacy (use backup)
  • Warfarin — may increase INR (monitor)
  • Allopurinol — increased rash risk
  • Methotrexate — increased toxicity

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection (decreased fever, WBC, symptoms)
  • Negative follow-up cultures if applicable
  • No allergic reaction
  • No C. difficile or significant superinfection
  • Completion of full course

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablet, ER, chewable, suspension)
  • Take at the START of a meal to reduce GI upset and improve clavulanate absorption
  • Do not substitute two lower-dose tablets for one higher-dose (clavulanate content differs)
  • Shake suspension; refrigerate; discard after 10 days
  • Space doses evenly; complete full course

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess penicillin/cephalosporin allergy before first dose
  • Obtain cultures before starting if ordered
  • Monitor for allergic reaction (have epinephrine available); observe after first dose
  • Monitor for diarrhea / C. difficile
  • Assess renal function (dosing)
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin
  • Educate on taking with food and completing course

Client Education

  • Take at the start of a meal to reduce stomach upset
  • Complete the entire course even if feeling better
  • Report rash, swelling, difficulty breathing (allergy) immediately
  • Report severe or watery/bloody diarrhea (C. difficile)
  • Use backup contraception if on oral contraceptives
  • Take doses evenly spaced
  • Shake liquid; keep refrigerated; discard leftover suspension after 10 days
  • Report yellowing skin/eyes (rare liver effect)
  • Do not share or save antibiotics
Worked Example Doxycycline Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Doxycycline
Review Module Chapter
Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Tetracycline antibiotic that binds the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibits protein synthesis.
  • The effect is primarily bacteriostatic, slowing bacterial growth so host defenses and the full treatment course can clear infection.
  • Broad-spectrum activity supports use across selected respiratory, reproductive, rickettsial, Lyme, acne, anthrax, and H. pylori-related regimens.
  • Chelation with calcium, iron, magnesium, and antacids blocks absorption, so administration timing directly affects effectiveness.

Therapeutic Use

  • Treats acne and selected respiratory or reproductive tract infections, including chlamydia and mycoplasma pneumonia when indicated.
  • Used for rickettsial infections such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever and for Lyme disease when benefits outweigh age-related concerns.
  • May be used for anthrax, H. pylori regimens, and malaria prophylaxis depending on the clinical indication.
  • Teaching must connect the use to safety: avoid pregnancy and routine use in children under 8 years, separate from minerals/dairy, and protect from sun exposure.

Complications

  • Photosensitivity, GI upset/esophagitis
  • Tooth discoloration and inhibited bone growth in children < 8 yr and fetus
  • Superinfection (candidiasis, C. difficile); hepatotoxicity (rare)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Pregnancy/breastfeeding and children < 8 years
  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Antacids, dairy, iron, calcium → ↓ absorption (chelation)
  • Warfarin → ↑ effect; may ↓ oral contraceptive effectiveness
  • Isotretinoin → ↑ intracranial pressure

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection
  • No photosensitivity injury or superinfection

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO with a full glass of water, sitting upright (avoid esophageal irritation)
  • Separate from antacids/dairy/iron by ≥ 2 hr
  • Complete the full course; can take with food if GI upset

Nursing Interventions

  • Educate on photosensitivity and chelation interactions
  • Monitor for superinfection and GI/esophageal effects
  • Avoid use in pregnancy and young children

Client Education

  • Use sunscreen and protective clothing (severe sunburn risk)
  • Take with water, stay upright ~30 min; separate from dairy/antacids/iron
  • Complete the full course; use backup contraception
  • Not for use in pregnancy or children under 8
Worked Example Azithromycin Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Azithromycin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Macrolide antibiotic that binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibits protein synthesis.
  • Primarily bacteriostatic, limiting bacterial growth in susceptible respiratory, skin, otitis, and sexually transmitted infections.
  • Often serves as an alternative for clients with penicillin allergy when the organism and infection type are appropriate.
  • Long tissue persistence supports short-course regimens, while QT prolongation, liver effects, and warfarin monitoring remain nursing priorities.

Therapeutic Use

  • Respiratory infections, otitis media, skin infections
  • Chlamydia and other STIs; atypical pneumonia

Complications

  • GI: nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain
  • QT prolongation (dysrhythmia risk)
  • Hepatotoxicity (rare); superinfection

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to macrolides
  • History of cholestatic jaundice with prior use
  • Caution: QT prolongation, hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Other QT-prolonging drugs → ↑ dysrhythmia risk
  • Warfarin → ↑ effect
  • Antacids (aluminum/magnesium) → ↓ peak absorption (separate dosing)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection
  • No cardiac dysrhythmia or significant GI/hepatic effects

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO (often a short course, e.g., higher first dose then lower); IV available
  • Separate from aluminum/magnesium antacids
  • Complete the prescribed course (long half-life allows short regimens)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess cardiac history/QT risk and concurrent QT drugs
  • Monitor for GI effects and superinfection
  • Reinforce completing the course

Client Education

  • Report palpitations or fainting (heart rhythm)
  • Take as directed; separate from antacids
  • Complete the full course even if symptoms improve
  • Report severe diarrhea or yellowing of skin/eyes
Worked Example Gentamicin (Aminoglycoside) Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Gentamicin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Aminoglycoside antibiotic — binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis (bactericidal)
  • Concentration-dependent killing with post-antibiotic effect
  • Primarily effective against aerobic gram-negative bacteria
  • Narrow therapeutic index — requires serum level monitoring

Therapeutic Use

  • Serious gram-negative infections (Pseudomonas, E. coli, Klebsiella)
  • Sepsis, complicated UTIs, intra-abdominal infections
  • Synergy with beta-lactams for gram-positive endocarditis
  • Often empiric in serious infections pending cultures

Complications

  • Nephrotoxicity (often reversible) — rising creatinine, decreased urine output
  • Ototoxicity (often irreversible) — cochlear (hearing loss, tinnitus) and vestibular (vertigo, ataxia) damage
  • Neuromuscular blockade (rare; respiratory depression, especially with anesthetics/NM blockers)
  • Hypersensitivity reactions
  • Toxicity risk increases with high troughs, prolonged therapy, dehydration

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to aminoglycosides
  • Renal impairment (dose adjust; high toxicity risk)
  • Pre-existing hearing loss / vestibular disease
  • Myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular blockade)
  • Older adults; dehydration
  • Pregnancy (fetal ototoxicity)
  • Concurrent nephrotoxic/ototoxic drugs

Interactions

  • Other nephrotoxic drugs (vancomycin, amphotericin B, NSAIDs, contrast) — additive nephrotoxicity
  • Other ototoxic drugs (loop diuretics) — additive ototoxicity
  • Neuromuscular blockers / anesthetics — enhanced neuromuscular blockade
  • Beta-lactams — synergy (but do not mix in same IV — inactivation)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection (fever, WBC, cultures)
  • Therapeutic peak (efficacy) and acceptable trough (safety) levels
  • Stable renal function
  • No hearing/vestibular changes
  • Completion of therapy without toxicity

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV (most common), IM; topical/ophthalmic forms
  • Once-daily (extended-interval) or divided dosing per protocol
  • Peak level: drawn ~30 min after IV infusion completes
  • Trough level: drawn just before the next dose
  • Adjust dose to levels and renal function
  • Do not mix with beta-lactams in the same line (inactivation)
  • Ensure adequate hydration

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor peak and trough levels; draw at correct times
  • Baseline and ongoing renal function (BUN/creatinine), urine output; daily weights, I&O
  • Assess for ototoxicity — hearing changes, tinnitus, vertigo, balance (report immediately)
  • Ensure hydration; avoid concurrent nephro/ototoxic drugs when possible
  • Obtain cultures before first dose
  • Administer over recommended time; do not co-infuse with penicillins
  • Monitor for neuromuscular effects (respiratory) if on NM blockers

Client Education

  • Report any hearing changes, ringing in the ears, dizziness, or balance problems immediately (ototoxicity — may be permanent)
  • Report decreased urination or swelling (kidney effects)
  • Drink adequate fluids
  • Regular blood draws are needed to monitor drug levels and kidney function
  • Report any new medications (interaction risk)
  • Complete the full course
  • This is used for serious infections and requires close monitoring
Worked Example Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole
Review Module Chapter
Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Combination antibiotic that blocks two sequential steps of bacterial folic acid synthesis.
  • Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, and trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.
  • The dual blockade is synergistic and can be bactericidal against susceptible organisms.
  • Because folate-related and sulfonamide effects can affect blood cells, skin, kidneys, potassium, and pregnancy safety, monitor for rash, blood dyscrasias, renal injury, and hyperkalemia.

Therapeutic Use

  • Urinary tract infections, otitis media
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (treatment/prophylaxis), some MRSA skin infections

Complications

  • Allergic/skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  • Hyperkalemia, crystalluria/renal injury
  • Photosensitivity, GI upset, blood dyscrasias
  • Kernicterus risk in neonates

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Sulfonamide allergy; pregnancy (near term)/breastfeeding, infants < 2 months
  • Megaloblastic anemia (folate deficiency)
  • Significant renal/hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Warfarin → ↑ bleeding
  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics → ↑ hyperkalemia
  • Oral hypoglycemics → ↑ hypoglycemia; methotrexate → ↑ toxicity

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of UTI/infection (↓ symptoms, negative culture)
  • No allergic reaction, renal injury, or hyperkalemia

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO (IV available); take with a full glass of water and increase fluids (prevent crystalluria)
  • Assess sulfa allergy before starting; complete full course
  • Monitor renal function, potassium, and CBC

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for sulfa allergy; monitor for rash (stop if rash appears)
  • Encourage fluids; monitor potassium, renal function, and CBC
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin

Client Education

  • Drink plenty of fluids; report any rash immediately (serious skin reaction)
  • Use sunscreen (photosensitivity)
  • Complete the full course; report sore throat/fever/bleeding (blood effects)
  • Report decreased urination or palpitations
Worked Example Nitrofurantoin Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Nitrofurantoin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Urinary antiseptic that damages bacterial DNA after activation inside susceptible bacteria.
  • Concentrates in the urine, producing a local antibacterial effect in the bladder rather than reliable systemic tissue levels.
  • Because tissue penetration is limited, it is appropriate for lower UTI cystitis but not for pyelonephritis or systemic infection.
  • Food or milk improves tolerance and absorption, while poor renal function can reduce urinary concentration and increase toxicity risk.

Therapeutic Use

  • Treats acute uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection caused by susceptible organisms.
  • May be used for prophylaxis of recurrent lower UTIs when long-term risk and monitoring are appropriate.
  • Not appropriate for upper UTI, pyelonephritis, or systemic infection because it concentrates mainly in urine.
  • Safety teaching should include taking with food, completing the course, reporting cough/dyspnea/fever, and expecting harmless dark yellow or brown urine.

Complications

  • GI upset (take with food)
  • Harmless brown/dark urine discoloration
  • Pulmonary reactions (acute and chronic), peripheral neuropathy (long-term)
  • Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Significant renal impairment (ineffective and toxic)
  • Pregnancy at term, infants < 1 month
  • G6PD deficiency (caution)

Interactions

  • Antacids (magnesium) → ↓ absorption
  • Probenecid → ↓ urinary excretion (less effective)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of UTI symptoms; negative urine culture
  • No pulmonary or neurologic complications

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO with food (↑ absorption, ↓ GI upset)
  • Maintain adequate urine output; complete full course
  • Not for upper UTI/pyelonephritis or poor renal function

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor renal function and for pulmonary symptoms (cough, dyspnea)
  • Educate on harmless urine discoloration
  • Assess for neuropathy with long-term use

Client Education

  • Take with food; expect brown/dark urine (normal)
  • Report cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath (lung reaction)
  • Report numbness/tingling (nerve effect) with long-term use
  • Complete the full course
Worked Example Ciprofloxacin (Fluoroquinolone) Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections · Urinary section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Ciprofloxacin (Cipro)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Fluoroquinolone antibiotic — inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication (bactericidal)
  • Broad spectrum, especially gram-negative
  • Good tissue penetration

Therapeutic Use

  • Complicated UTIs, pyelonephritis
  • Respiratory, GI, bone/joint, intra-abdominal infections
  • Anthrax (post-exposure)
  • Reserved for serious infections due to safety profile (not first-line for uncomplicated UTI)

Complications

  • BLACK BOX: tendon rupture/tendinitis (especially Achilles; higher risk older adults, steroid use, transplant)
  • BLACK BOX: peripheral neuropathy (can be permanent)
  • BLACK BOX: CNS effects (confusion, seizures, hallucinations); avoid in myasthenia gravis (exacerbation)
  • QT prolongation → dysrhythmias
  • Aortic aneurysm/dissection risk
  • Dysglycemia (hypo/hyperglycemia)
  • Photosensitivity; GI upset; C. difficile

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to fluoroquinolones
  • Myasthenia gravis (may worsen)
  • History of tendon disorders with fluoroquinolones
  • QT prolongation / concurrent QT drugs
  • Children/adolescents and pregnancy (cartilage effects — use only if no alternative)
  • Aortic aneurysm risk (older adults, hypertension)
  • Caution with diabetes (dysglycemia)

Interactions

  • Antacids, dairy, iron, calcium, magnesium, sucralfate — chelate ciprofloxacin, reducing absorption (separate by 2–6 hr)
  • Warfarin — increased INR/bleeding
  • Theophylline — increased levels/toxicity
  • Tizanidine — contraindicated
  • QT-prolonging drugs — additive
  • NSAIDs — increased CNS/seizure risk
  • Caffeine — increased effect

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection (symptoms, cultures, WBC)
  • No tendon, neuropathy, or CNS adverse effects
  • No cardiac dysrhythmia
  • Stable glucose
  • Completion of course

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral, IV
  • Take with plenty of fluids
  • Separate from antacids, dairy, iron, calcium, magnesium, sucralfate by 2–6 hours
  • Do not crush ER tablets
  • Complete full course; space doses evenly

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess for tendon pain/swelling; stop and report tendon pain (rupture risk)
  • Monitor for neuropathy (numbness, tingling), CNS effects (confusion, seizures)
  • Baseline/monitor QT if at risk; review QT-prolonging drugs
  • Monitor glucose in diabetics
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin
  • Educate on drug/food separation (chelation)
  • Avoid in myasthenia gravis; caution in older adults
  • Ensure hydration; assess for C. difficile

Client Education

  • Stop the drug and report tendon pain, swelling, or inability to move a joint (Achilles tendon rupture risk); avoid strenuous exercise during therapy
  • Report numbness/tingling (nerve damage — can be permanent)
  • Report confusion, hallucinations, mood changes, or seizures
  • Separate from antacids, dairy, calcium, iron, and supplements by 2–6 hours
  • Drink plenty of fluids; avoid excess caffeine
  • Use sunscreen (photosensitivity)
  • Report palpitations or fainting (heart rhythm)
  • Diabetics: monitor blood sugar (can rise or fall)
  • Report severe diarrhea (C. difficile)
  • Complete the full course
Worked Example Rifampin Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Rifampin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Bactericidal antitubercular antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA synthesis by blocking RNA polymerase.
  • Used as part of multidrug TB therapy because combination treatment limits resistance during the long treatment course.
  • Potent hepatic enzyme induction lowers levels of many medications, including oral contraceptives, warfarin, antiretrovirals, and methadone.
  • Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears is expected, but hepatotoxicity and adherence problems require close monitoring.

Therapeutic Use

  • Tuberculosis (always in combination to prevent resistance)
  • Meningococcal and certain other exposures (prophylaxis)

Complications

  • Harmless red-orange discoloration of body fluids (urine, sweat, tears — stains contacts)
  • Hepatotoxicity
  • GI upset, flu-like syndrome
  • Potent enzyme inducer → reduces many drug levels

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Active liver disease
  • Caution: alcohol use, hepatic impairment

Interactions

  • Strong CYP inducer → ↓ effectiveness of oral contraceptives, warfarin, many antiretrovirals, and others
  • Other hepatotoxic drugs/alcohol → ↑ liver injury

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Negative sputum cultures over time; clinical improvement
  • Normal LFTs; adherence to multidrug regimen

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO on an empty stomach (1 hr before or 2 hr after meals)
  • Always part of combination therapy; emphasize long-term adherence (months)
  • Monitor LFTs; review interacting medications

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor liver function and adherence; assess for hepatotoxicity
  • Educate on red-orange fluids and drug interactions
  • Stress completing the full multi-month regimen (resistance/relapse risk)

Client Education

  • Expect red-orange urine, sweat, and tears (harmless; may permanently stain soft contact lenses)
  • Use a non-hormonal backup contraceptive (reduces birth control effectiveness)
  • Take on an empty stomach; report yellowing skin, dark urine, or fatigue
  • Take all TB medications for the full course (do not stop early)
Worked Example Amphotericin B Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Amphotericin B
Review Module Chapter
Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antifungal that binds ergosterol in fungal cell membranes.
  • Creates pores that increase membrane permeability, causing leakage of intracellular contents and fungal cell death.
  • Human renal tubular cells can also be injured, explaining the major nephrotoxicity and electrolyte-wasting risks.
  • Lipid formulations reduce but do not eliminate nephrotoxicity, so renal function, potassium, magnesium, CBC, and infusion reactions still require monitoring.

Therapeutic Use

  • Treats serious, invasive, or life-threatening systemic fungal infections when potent IV antifungal therapy is required.
  • Used for infections such as cryptococcal meningitis, aspergillosis, severe candidiasis, and other systemic mycoses per provider/infectious-disease guidance.
  • Often reserved for severe disease because infusion reactions, nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and anemia are common safety concerns.
  • Requires infusion-center or inpatient-style monitoring with premedication, hydration, renal/electrolyte labs, and follow-up cultures or symptom response.

Complications

  • Infusion reactions (fever, chills/rigors, ‘shake and bake’)
  • Nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting), hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia
  • Phlebitis at IV site; anemia, hepatotoxicity

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: renal impairment, electrolyte imbalance

Interactions

  • Other nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, cyclosporine) → ↑ renal injury
  • Corticosteroids/diuretics → ↑ potassium loss
  • Digoxin → toxicity if hypokalemic

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of fungal infection
  • Stable renal function and electrolytes; tolerable infusions

Medication Administration

  • Route: IV slowly; premedicate (antipyretics, antihistamines, sometimes meperidine for rigors) to reduce infusion reactions
  • Lipid formulations reduce nephrotoxicity; ensure hydration
  • Monitor renal function, electrolytes (K, Mg), CBC, and LFTs

Nursing Interventions

  • Premedicate and monitor closely during infusion (vital signs, rigors)
  • Monitor renal function and electrolytes; replace potassium/magnesium as ordered
  • Ensure adequate hydration; rotate IV sites

Client Education

  • Expect possible chills/fever during infusion (treated with premedication)
  • Therapy is given IV, often over weeks
  • Report decreased urination, muscle weakness/cramps, or unusual fatigue
  • Keep all lab and infusion appointments
Worked Example Metronidazole (Flagyl) Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections · Fungal/Parasitic section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Metronidazole (Flagyl)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antiprotozoal and antibacterial — disrupts DNA in anaerobic organisms and protozoa (bactericidal/amebicidal)
  • Active against anaerobes and certain parasites

Therapeutic Use

  • Protozoal infections: trichomoniasis, giardiasis, amebiasis
  • Anaerobic bacterial infections: intra-abdominal, pelvic, abscesses
  • Bacterial vaginosis
  • C. difficile colitis (alternative)
  • H. pylori (combination therapy)

Complications

  • Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — severe flushing, nausea, vomiting, palpitations, headache
  • Metallic taste (common)
  • Nausea, anorexia, GI upset
  • Darkened/reddish-brown urine (harmless)
  • Peripheral neuropathy (prolonged use)
  • CNS: headache, dizziness; rarely seizures
  • Candidiasis superinfection

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Alcohol use (and for 48–72 hr after) — disulfiram reaction
  • First trimester of pregnancy (avoid for trichomoniasis)
  • Hepatic impairment (dose adjust)
  • Blood dyscrasias; CNS/seizure disorders
  • Caution: peripheral neuropathy history

Interactions

  • Alcohol (including hidden sources: mouthwash, cough syrup, sauces) — disulfiram reaction
  • Warfarin — increased INR/bleeding
  • Lithium — increased levels/toxicity
  • Phenytoin, phenobarbital — altered metabolism
  • Disulfiram — psychosis (avoid concurrent)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of infection (symptoms, cultures, microscopy)
  • No disulfiram reaction (alcohol avoided)
  • No peripheral neuropathy
  • Treatment of partner (trichomoniasis) to prevent reinfection
  • Completion of course

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral, IV, topical/vaginal
  • Take with food to reduce GI upset
  • Complete full course; space doses
  • Trichomoniasis: treat sexual partners simultaneously

Nursing Interventions

  • Strongly counsel to avoid ALL alcohol during and for 48–72 hr after (including hidden sources)
  • Assess for peripheral neuropathy (prolonged use)
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin; lithium levels if applicable
  • Educate that urine may darken (harmless)
  • Treat partners for trichomoniasis
  • Assess for candidiasis superinfection
  • Monitor hepatic function if impaired

Client Education

  • Do NOT drink alcohol during treatment and for at least 48–72 hours after — causes severe flushing, vomiting, palpitations (disulfiram reaction)
  • Avoid hidden alcohol: mouthwash, cough syrups, some sauces, OTC liquids
  • A metallic taste is common; urine may turn dark/reddish-brown (harmless)
  • Take with food
  • Report numbness/tingling (nerve effect)
  • Complete the full course
  • For trichomoniasis/STIs: partner(s) must also be treated; avoid intercourse until both treated
  • Report severe diarrhea (C. difficile possible)
Worked Example Fluconazole (Azole Antifungal) Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections · Fungal/Parasitic section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Fluconazole (Diflucan)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Azole antifungal — inhibits fungal cytochrome P450 (ergosterol synthesis), disrupting the fungal cell membrane (fungistatic)
  • Good oral bioavailability and CNS penetration

Therapeutic Use

  • Candidiasis — oropharyngeal (thrush), esophageal, vaginal, systemic
  • Cryptococcal meningitis (including maintenance in HIV)
  • Antifungal prophylaxis in immunocompromised
  • Single-dose for uncomplicated vaginal candidiasis

Complications

  • Hepatotoxicity — monitor LFTs (especially prolonged/high dose)
  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea
  • Headache, dizziness
  • QT prolongation → dysrhythmias
  • Rash; rarely Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  • Numerous drug interactions (CYP inhibition)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to azoles
  • Concurrent QT-prolonging drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 (e.g., some antiarrhythmics) — contraindicated
  • Hepatic impairment
  • Pregnancy (high-dose teratogenic; avoid except single low-dose may be considered)
  • Renal impairment (dose adjust)

Interactions

  • Potent CYP inhibitor — raises levels of many drugs:
  • Warfarin (increased INR), phenytoin, sulfonylureas (hypoglycemia), statins (myopathy), certain benzodiazepines
  • QT-prolonging drugs — additive (amiodarone, some antipsychotics)
  • Rifampin — decreases fluconazole levels
  • Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) — increased levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Resolution of fungal infection (thrush clears, symptoms resolve)
  • Negative cultures (systemic infection)
  • Normal LFTs
  • No QT prolongation or serious rash
  • No interaction-related toxicity

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral, IV (well-absorbed orally)
  • Vaginal candidiasis: single 150 mg oral dose
  • Other infections: loading dose then daily; duration varies
  • Take with or without food
  • Adjust dose in renal impairment

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline and periodic LFTs; assess for hepatotoxicity
  • Comprehensive medication review (extensive CYP interactions)
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin; glucose if on sulfonylureas
  • Assess QT risk / concurrent QT drugs
  • Assess infection response
  • Monitor for rash (discontinue if severe)
  • Pregnancy screening (teratogenic at high doses)

Client Education

  • Take as directed; complete the full course (single dose for simple vaginal yeast)
  • Report yellowing skin/eyes, dark urine, persistent nausea, or abdominal pain (liver)
  • Report palpitations or fainting (heart rhythm)
  • Tell all providers you take this — many drug interactions
  • Report rash, especially blistering or peeling (stop and seek care)
  • Inform provider if pregnant or could become pregnant
  • For recurrent yeast infections, follow up for evaluation
Worked Example Acyclovir Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Acyclovir
Review Module Chapter
Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Antiviral medication that inhibits viral DNA synthesis after activation in herpes-infected cells.
  • Suppresses replication of herpes simplex and varicella-zoster viruses, which helps lesions heal faster and decreases viral shedding.
  • Does not eradicate dormant virus, so recurrent outbreaks can still occur and suppressive therapy may be needed for frequent recurrences.
  • Crystalluria and nephrotoxicity are more likely with rapid IV infusion, dehydration, or renal impairment, making hydration and slow infusion essential.

Therapeutic Use

  • Herpes simplex (genital, oral), varicella-zoster (shingles, chickenpox)
  • Suppression of recurrent herpes outbreaks

Complications

  • Nephrotoxicity (crystalluria), especially IV/dehydration
  • Phlebitis at IV site; GI upset, headache
  • Neurotoxicity (high doses/renal impairment)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: renal impairment, dehydration

Interactions

  • Other nephrotoxic drugs → ↑ renal injury
  • Probenecid → ↑ acyclovir level

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Faster lesion healing; reduced pain and viral shedding
  • Fewer recurrences (suppressive therapy); stable renal function

Medication Administration

  • Routes: PO, IV, topical; maintain adequate hydration (prevent crystalluria), especially IV
  • Start early in an outbreak for best effect; complete the course
  • Reduce dose in renal impairment; infuse IV slowly

Nursing Interventions

  • Ensure good hydration; monitor renal function (BUN/creatinine, urine output)
  • Educate that it controls but does not cure herpes
  • Monitor IV site for phlebitis

Client Education

  • Drink plenty of fluids during therapy
  • Start at the first sign of an outbreak; complete the full course
  • It controls outbreaks but does not cure the virus; it can still transmit — use precautions
  • Report decreased urination or confusion
Worked Example Oseltamivir Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Oseltamivir
Review Module Chapter
Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Neuraminidase inhibitor that blocks release of new influenza virus particles from infected respiratory cells.
  • Limits spread of influenza A and B within the respiratory tract when started early in the illness.
  • Does not replace annual influenza vaccination and is most effective for treatment when begun within 48 hours of symptom onset.
  • Renal dosing and monitoring for nausea, vomiting, and rare neuropsychiatric changes support safe use.

Therapeutic Use

  • Treats influenza A and B when started as early as possible, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset.
  • May be used for post-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk clients or outbreak settings according to provider order and protocol.
  • Can reduce symptom duration and severity but does not cure instantly or replace infection-control measures.
  • Clients should complete the prescribed course, take with food if GI upset occurs, and continue prevention measures such as vaccination, hand hygiene, and staying home while contagious.

Complications

  • Nausea and vomiting (most common)
  • Headache
  • Rare neuropsychiatric events (confusion, abnormal behavior), especially in children/adolescents

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Caution: renal impairment (dose adjust)

Interactions

  • Few significant drug interactions
  • Live attenuated influenza vaccine — avoid around antiviral use

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Shorter duration/severity of flu symptoms when started early
  • Prevention of influenza in exposed clients

Medication Administration

  • Route: PO (capsule or suspension), with food to reduce GI upset
  • Start within 48 hr of symptom onset for treatment benefit
  • Complete the full course; reduce dose in renal impairment

Nursing Interventions

  • Emphasize early initiation (within 48 hr)
  • Monitor for GI tolerance and, in youth, neuropsychiatric/behavioral changes
  • Reinforce it complements—not replaces—annual vaccination

Client Education

  • Start within 48 hours of symptoms; take with food; complete the full course
  • Watch children/teens for confusion or unusual behavior and report it
  • Continue good hygiene and infection precautions
  • It is not a substitute for the yearly flu vaccine
Worked Example Zidovudine (NRTI) Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS · HIV section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Zidovudine (AZT, Retrovir)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) — inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase, blocking viral DNA synthesis
  • Suppresses viral replication (does not cure)
  • Used as part of combination ART

Therapeutic Use

  • HIV infection (component of HAART)
  • Prevention of perinatal (mother-to-child) transmission — during pregnancy, labor, and to the newborn
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (component)

Complications

  • Bone marrow suppression (BLACK BOX) — anemia, neutropenia (hallmark of zidovudine)
  • Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (BLACK BOX, NRTI class) — potentially fatal
  • Myopathy (prolonged use)
  • Headache, nausea, fatigue, insomnia
  • Hyperpigmentation of nails
  • Lipodystrophy

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity
  • Pre-existing bone marrow suppression (severe anemia/neutropenia)
  • Hepatic impairment (lactic acidosis risk)
  • Renal impairment (dose adjust)
  • Obesity, female sex (higher lactic acidosis risk)

Interactions

  • Bone marrow suppressants (ganciclovir, chemotherapy, other myelosuppressives) — additive
  • Stavudine — antagonistic (do not combine)
  • Drugs affecting hepatic/renal clearance
  • Probenecid — increases zidovudine levels

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Decreased viral load (ideally undetectable)
  • Maintained/improved CD4 count
  • Prevention of perinatal transmission (negative infant testing)
  • Stable blood counts (no severe anemia/neutropenia)
  • No lactic acidosis

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (capsule, tablet, syrup), IV
  • Take as part of combination ART, on schedule
  • Perinatal: oral during pregnancy, IV during labor, oral syrup to newborn
  • Adjust dose in renal impairment
  • Take with or without food (consistent)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor CBC for anemia and neutropenia (bone marrow suppression)
  • Monitor for lactic acidosis (nausea, abdominal pain, fatigue, rapid breathing) and hepatomegaly — check LFTs
  • Assess CD4 and viral load response
  • Review for myelosuppressive drug interactions
  • Intensive adherence counseling (resistance)
  • Perinatal: coordinate maternal and neonatal dosing
  • Monitor renal function

Client Education

  • Strict adherence is essential — take every dose on time; do not stop (resistance)
  • Report unusual fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath (anemia), or fever/infection signs (low white cells)
  • Report nausea, abdominal pain, unusual fatigue, rapid breathing (lactic acidosis — emergency)
  • Regular blood tests are needed (CBC, CD4, viral load)
  • This controls but does not cure HIV; continue prevention measures
  • Tell providers about all medications
  • Pregnancy: this medication helps protect the baby from HIV; follow the full regimen
  • Report side effects rather than stopping on your own
Worked Example Lamotrigine (Lamictal) Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · Anticonvulsants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Lamotrigine (Lamictal)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anticonvulsant / mood stabilizer — inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels in neurons; stabilizes neuronal membranes
  • Decreases glutamate release
  • Better tolerated than lithium for many clients; particularly effective for bipolar depression (not acute mania)

Therapeutic Use

  • Bipolar I disorder maintenance — especially preventing depressive episodes
  • Partial-onset seizures (adjunct or monotherapy)
  • Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (epilepsy)
  • Not effective for acute mania; not first-line for acute bipolar depression but excellent maintenance agent

Complications

  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) — BLACK BOX WARNING; potentially fatal; risk highest in first 8 weeks; higher with rapid titration or concurrent valproate
  • Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) — multi-organ involvement; can be fatal
  • Aseptic meningitis (rare)
  • CNS: dizziness, headache, diplopia, ataxia, somnolence (typically dose-related)
  • GI upset, blurred vision
  • Pregnancy: limited risk data, generally lower teratogenic risk than valproate

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Prior hypersensitivity to lamotrigine
  • History of rash with other antiepileptics — cross-reactivity risk
  • Hepatic impairment — dose adjustment
  • Pediatrics < 2 yr (efficacy/safety not established)
  • Concurrent valproic acid — doubles lamotrigine levels; reduce lamotrigine dose by half
  • Concurrent enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) — reduce lamotrigine levels; may need higher dose

Interactions

  • Valproic acid — INHIBITS lamotrigine metabolism → doubles lamotrigine level; use HALF the usual lamotrigine dose
  • Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampin — INDUCE lamotrigine metabolism → reduce lamotrigine level; may need higher dose
  • Oral contraceptives — can decrease lamotrigine levels; may need higher dose during active OCP weeks
  • No significant CYP450 interactions otherwise

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduced frequency and severity of bipolar depressive episodes
  • Improved mood stability with maintenance dose
  • Seizure-free or reduced seizure frequency (for epilepsy)
  • No serious rash or hypersensitivity reactions
  • Tolerable side effect profile

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablets, chewable, ODT, XR)
  • SLOW TITRATION IS MANDATORY — 25 mg PO daily × 2 weeks, then 50 mg daily × 2 weeks, then increase by 50 mg every 1–2 weeks; target maintenance 200–400 mg/day
  • If concurrent valproate: half the dose at each titration step
  • If missed for > 5 days, MUST RESTART TITRATION from beginning
  • Take with or without food
  • Available immediate-release and extended-release

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline labs: LFTs, CBC
  • Assess and DOCUMENT any rash IMMEDIATELY — even minor rash may herald SJS; discontinue if rash develops
  • Educate on slow titration schedule; provide written titration calendar
  • Monitor mood and seizure activity
  • Assess for signs of hypersensitivity: fever, lymphadenopathy, multi-organ symptoms
  • Reinforce that missed doses for > 5 days require restart from beginning (call provider)
  • Monitor for OCP interaction in clients of childbearing age

Client Education

  • STOP and notify provider IMMEDIATELY if any rash develops — especially with fever or mucous membrane involvement (eyes, mouth, genitals)
  • Follow titration schedule EXACTLY — do not increase faster (rash risk)
  • If you miss doses for more than 5 days, call provider before restarting — you will need to restart titration
  • Do NOT abruptly discontinue (seizure risk if used for epilepsy)
  • May cause dizziness or blurred vision — avoid driving until response known
  • Birth control may be less effective — discuss alternatives with provider
  • Report sore throat, fever, mouth sores, swelling — signs of hypersensitivity
Worked Example Carbamazepine (Tegretol) Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · Anticonvulsants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Carbamazepine (Tegretol)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Anticonvulsant / mood stabilizer — blocks voltage-gated sodium channels; reduces high-frequency repetitive neuronal firing
  • Decreases neurotransmitter release
  • Potent CYP3A4 INDUCER — including auto-induction (induces its own metabolism in first weeks)

Therapeutic Use

  • Bipolar I disorder — acute mania, mixed episodes, and maintenance
  • Partial and tonic-clonic seizures
  • Trigeminal neuralgia — first-line
  • Diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia (off-label)

Complications

  • Bone marrow suppression (BLACK BOX) — aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis; CBC monitoring
  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN (BLACK BOX) — especially in clients with HLA-B*1502 (mostly Asian ancestry) — screen before starting
  • Hyponatremia / SIADH — common (~5%); monitor sodium
  • Hepatotoxicity — transient mild elevation common; severe hepatitis rare
  • Hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS) — multi-organ; can be fatal
  • CNS: drowsiness, dizziness, diplopia, ataxia, blurred vision (especially early)
  • GI: nausea, vomiting
  • Teratogenic — neural tube defects, craniofacial defects (Category D)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • History of bone marrow suppression
  • Prior hypersensitivity to TCAs (structural similarity)
  • Within 14 days of an MAOI
