  • HLA-B*1502 positive (genetic test before prescribing in Asian populations)
  • Pregnancy — avoid; if essential, ensure adequate folate supplementation
  • Hepatic impairment, atrioventricular block, porphyria

Interactions

  • Carbamazepine INDUCES CYP3A4 — reduces levels of: oral contraceptives, warfarin, doxycycline, theophylline, methadone, lamotrigine, valproate, statins, HIV antiretrovirals
  • Auto-induction — carbamazepine’s OWN level drops over first 2–4 weeks; may need dose increase
  • Grapefruit juice — INHIBITS metabolism; can elevate levels to toxic range
  • Erythromycin, clarithromycin, fluoxetine, fluconazole — increase carbamazepine levels → toxicity
  • Concurrent MAOIs — contraindicated (hypertensive crisis)

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Therapeutic serum level: 4–12 mcg/mL
  • Improved mood stability; reduced manic episodes
  • Seizure control
  • Pain relief in trigeminal neuralgia
  • Stable CBC, LFTs, sodium
  • No serious rash or hypersensitivity

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablets, chewables, suspension, XR)
  • Start 200 mg PO BID; titrate weekly; target 400–1,600 mg/day in divided doses
  • Take with food (reduces GI upset and improves absorption)
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • XR tablets must be swallowed whole (do not crush)
  • Serum level monitoring at steady state (~5 days after each change)

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline labs: CBC, LFTs, BUN/Cr, sodium, pregnancy test, HLA-B*1502 in Asian clients
  • Monitor CBC every 1–3 months initially; sodium periodically
  • Carbamazepine levels at trough; therapeutic 4–12 mcg/mL
  • Assess for rash at every contact — discontinue if SJS/TEN suspected
  • Monitor for signs of bone marrow suppression: fatigue, infection, bruising, bleeding
  • Comprehensive medication reconciliation due to CYP3A4 induction
  • Counsel on alternative contraception (OCPs ineffective)
  • Avoid abrupt discontinuation (seizure risk)

Client Education

  • Report any rash, fever, sore throat, mouth sores, unusual bleeding, or fatigue IMMEDIATELY
  • Use barrier contraception (carbamazepine reduces OCP effectiveness)
  • Avoid pregnancy — teratogenic; use reliable contraception; if pregnancy planned, discuss with provider
  • AVOID grapefruit juice — increases drug levels and toxicity risk
  • Take with food
  • Do NOT abruptly stop — seizure risk
  • Notify all providers and pharmacists of carbamazepine use (many drug interactions)
  • Keep follow-up appointments for blood level monitoring
  • Report dizziness, drowsiness, or vision changes — especially in first weeks
Worked Example Risperidone (Risperdal) Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · Second-generation section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Risperidone (Risperdal)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic
  • Blocks dopamine D2 receptors AND serotonin 5-HT2A receptors
  • 5-HT2A blockade reduces EPS risk and improves negative symptoms
  • More EPS risk than other atypicals; less than typical antipsychotics

Therapeutic Use

  • Schizophrenia (positive AND negative symptoms)
  • Bipolar I disorder — acute mania, mixed episodes, maintenance
  • Irritability in autism spectrum disorder (FDA-approved for children ≥ 5)
  • Off-label: behavioral disturbances in dementia (BLACK BOX — increased mortality in older adults)

Complications

  • EPS — dose-related; more common than other atypicals (especially > 6 mg/day)
  • Hyperprolactinemia — gynecomastia, galactorrhea, menstrual irregularities, sexual dysfunction; MORE pronounced than other atypicals
  • Metabolic syndrome — weight gain, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia (less than olanzapine/clozapine but still significant)
  • Orthostatic hypotension — especially during titration
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — rare but life-threatening
  • Sedation, dizziness, headache
  • QT prolongation
  • Increased mortality in older adults with dementia (BLACK BOX)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to risperidone or paliperidone (active metabolite)
  • Older adults with dementia-related psychosis — black box warning
  • History of NMS, tardive dyskinesia
  • Cardiovascular disease, history of seizures
  • Diabetes, dyslipidemia (caution; monitor metabolic parameters)
  • Pregnancy — risk of withdrawal/EPS in neonate
  • Renal or hepatic impairment — dose adjustment

Interactions

  • CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine) — increase risperidone levels
  • CYP3A4 inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin) — decrease levels
  • CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines) — additive sedation
  • Levodopa, dopamine agonists — antagonistic effects (worsen psychosis vs improve parkinsonism)
  • QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, ondansetron, fluoroquinolones) — additive QT risk

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Reduction in positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking)
  • Improvement in negative symptoms (affect, motivation, social engagement)
  • Improved functioning and adherence
  • Stable mood (bipolar use)
  • Reduced irritability (autism)
  • Tolerable side-effect profile; minimal EPS; stable metabolic parameters

Medication Administration

  • Route: oral (tablets, ODT, oral solution); long-acting IM injection (Risperdal Consta — every 2 weeks)
  • Schizophrenia: start 2 mg PO daily; target 4–6 mg/day; max effective < 6 mg/day (above increases EPS)
  • Bipolar mania: 2–6 mg/day
  • Autism: weight-based dosing for children
  • Take with or without food (consistent)
  • Long-acting IM: requires 3-week overlap with oral until levels established

Nursing Interventions

  • Baseline: BMI/weight, BP, fasting glucose, lipid panel, EKG (if cardiac risk), AIMS for movement
  • Monitor metabolic parameters at 4 weeks, 12 weeks, then quarterly
  • Monitor for EPS (especially first weeks); use AIMS scale
  • Assess for NMS: fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability — emergency
  • Monitor prolactin levels if symptomatic (gynecomastia, galactorrhea, menstrual changes)
  • Monitor orthostatic BP during titration; advise slow position changes
  • Suicide risk assessment
  • Encourage exercise, healthy diet to mitigate weight gain

Client Education

  • Therapeutic effect develops over weeks; continue even if not feeling improvement immediately
  • Take consistently; do not stop abruptly (relapse risk)
  • Report movement abnormalities (tremor, rigidity, restlessness, tongue movements)
  • Report fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion — emergency (NMS)
  • Report breast enlargement, milk production, menstrual changes
  • Weight monitoring; diet and exercise are important to counter metabolic effects
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic dizziness
  • Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants
  • Use sunscreen (photosensitivity)
  • Pregnancy planning: discuss with provider

Worked Example Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction
Review Module Chapter
Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction

Description of Skill

A structured medication-safety process that uses the rights of medication administration, two client identifiers, allergy checks, order verification, barcoding when available, and immediate documentation to reduce preventable medication errors.

Indications

  • Every medication administration encounter
  • Medication reconciliation, order clarification, preparation, administration, and response monitoring
  • High-risk moments such as admission, transfer, discharge, verbal/telephone orders, pediatric dosing, and high-alert medications

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Medication is given to the correct client, at the correct dose, route, time, and for the correct reason
  • Allergies, labs, vital signs, and clinical appropriateness are checked before administration
  • Medication response and adverse effects are monitored and documented
  • Medication errors or near misses are reported according to facility policy
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Verify order, allergy history, medication reconciliation, relevant labs/vitals, two identifiers, and the three label checks before administration. Clarify incomplete, illegible, unsafe, or unexpected orders before giving the medication.

Intra: Use barcode medication administration when available, communicate the medication purpose to the client, administer by the ordered route, and do not leave medications unattended. Stay with the client until oral medications are swallowed when required by policy or clinical risk.

Post: Document immediately after administration, monitor therapeutic and adverse effects, and report/refuse/hold doses according to policy when concerns occur.

Client Education

  • Keep an updated list of prescription, OTC, herbal, and supplement products.
  • Ask about the name, purpose, dose, schedule, and major adverse effects of each medication.
  • Do not stop, share, double, or restart medications without provider/pharmacist guidance.

Potential Complications

  • Wrong client, medication, dose, route, time, documentation, indication, or monitoring response
  • Allergic reaction, toxicity, therapeutic failure, or preventable adverse drug event
  • Sound-alike/look-alike confusion, calculation error, transcription error, or missed allergy/lab contraindication

Nursing Interventions

  • Use two identifiers and the medication rights for every administration.
  • Complete the three label checks and compare the MAR/order with the medication label.
  • Assess required client data before administration and response after administration.
  • Escalate unsafe orders, adverse effects, refusals, and medication errors per facility policy.
Worked Example Six (or Eight) Rights of Medication Administration Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction · Rights section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Six (or Eight) Rights of Medication Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction

Description of Skill

A bedside safety framework used before each medication dose. The core rights are right client, medication, dose, route, time, and documentation; expanded rights include reason/indication, response/evaluation, education, assessment, and the client right to refuse.

Indications

  • Before every medication administration
  • During medication preparation, bedside verification, and documentation
  • When a dose, route, time, or client identity is unclear or high risk

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • All required medication rights are verified before the medication reaches the client
  • Two client identifiers are used; room number is not used as an identifier
  • Medication label is checked when removing, preparing, and at bedside
  • Client response is evaluated and documented after administration
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Review order, allergies, indication, relevant labs/vitals, client identifiers, and medication label before preparation. Perform the first and second label checks while removing and preparing the medication.

Intra: At bedside, verify two identifiers, complete the third label check, confirm route/time/dose, explain the medication, and honor the client right to refuse.

Post: Document after administration, evaluate therapeutic response and adverse effects, and document teaching, refusal, hold parameters, or provider notification.

Client Education

  • Tell the client the medication name, purpose, and major effects before administration when appropriate.
  • Teach the client to ask questions if a medication looks different or unexpected.
  • Explain that refusal is allowed, but the nurse will review risks and notify the provider when needed.

Potential Complications

  • Medication error or adverse drug event if one right is skipped
  • Wrong-client administration when two identifiers are not used
  • Legal/ethical risk from documenting before administration or ignoring refusal

Nursing Interventions

  • Use two identifiers and all medication rights at the bedside.
  • Check the label three times and compare against the MAR/order.
  • Do not administer unclear or unsafe orders until clarified.
  • Document administration, response, teaching, and any refusal or hold.
Worked Example High-Alert Medications (ISMP) Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction · Error Prevention section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
High-Alert Medication Safeguards
Review Module Chapter
Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction

Description of Skill

Use of additional safeguards for medications that can cause significant harm when used in error, including insulin, heparin, opioids, chemotherapy, concentrated electrolytes, neuromuscular blockers, and other drugs identified by policy or ISMP.

Indications

  • Administration of high-alert medications or high-risk concentrations
  • Dose calculation, titration, infusion-pump programming, or route changes for high-alert drugs
  • Pediatric, critical-care, oncology, perioperative, and emergency medication workflows

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • High-alert medication is independently verified when policy requires it
  • Dose, concentration, route, rate, pump settings, client data, and antidote/rescue plan are confirmed
  • Client is monitored for expected therapeutic and adverse effects
  • No preventable harm occurs from high-alert medication use
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Verify order, indication, dose limits, allergies, weight, renal/hepatic function, labs, and required independent double-check. Use standardized concentrations, order sets, smart pumps, and barcode scanning when available.

Intra: Administer through the correct route and device; confirm pump programming, concentration, tubing, and patient connection before starting. Avoid interruptions and stop if any discrepancy appears.

Post: Monitor response and adverse effects closely; document required checks, dose/rate changes, and handoff details.

Client Education

  • Explain why extra checks are used and that they are a safety step.
  • Teach major warning symptoms specific to the drug class, such as bleeding with anticoagulants or hypoglycemia with insulin.
  • Tell the client not to adjust high-alert medications without provider guidance.

Potential Complications

  • Severe bleeding, hypoglycemia, respiratory depression, dysrhythmia, tissue injury, paralysis without ventilation, or death
  • Sentinel event from skipped double-check, wrong concentration, or wrong pump programming
  • Delayed rescue if antidote or emergency equipment is unavailable

Nursing Interventions

  • Follow facility high-alert policy exactly.
  • Use independent double-checks for required medications and rate changes.
  • Keep rescue medications/equipment available when indicated.
  • Document verification, administration, monitoring, and client response.
Worked Example Controlled Substances and DEA Schedules Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction · Controlled section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Controlled Substance Handling and Documentation
Review Module Chapter
Ch 2 — Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction

Description of Skill

Safe handling, administration, wasting, documentation, and security of medications regulated because of abuse, dependence, or diversion potential. Nursing responsibilities include locked storage, accurate counts, witnessed waste, and prompt discrepancy reporting.

Indications

  • Administration of opioids, benzodiazepines, stimulants, ketamine, codeine combinations, and other scheduled medications
  • Removal, administration, partial-dose waste, end-of-shift count, or discrepancy resolution
  • Pain management and sedation workflows requiring controlled medication accountability

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Controlled substance count remains accurate and discrepancies are resolved promptly
  • Dose administered and waste are documented according to policy
  • Client receives appropriate pain/anxiety/sedation relief while safety is monitored
  • Diversion risk is reduced through secure handling and witnessed waste
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Verify order, schedule restrictions, allergy history, pain/sedation assessment, respiratory status, and secure medication access. Remove only the ordered dose and prepare witnessed waste if a partial dose is required.

Intra: Administer to the correct client, reassess pain/sedation/respiratory status, and never leave controlled substances unattended.

Post: Document administration, response, unused amount, witnessed waste, and any discrepancy immediately according to policy.

Client Education

  • Teach safe home storage in a locked location and never sharing prescribed controlled substances.
  • Review major adverse effects such as sedation, constipation, respiratory depression, and fall risk.
  • Explain safe disposal through take-back programs or facility-approved methods.

Potential Complications

  • Diversion, count discrepancy, impaired practice concern, or legal/professional consequences
  • Oversedation, respiratory depression, constipation, falls, dependence, or withdrawal
  • Inadequate pain control if fear of regulation prevents appropriate administration

Nursing Interventions

  • Follow controlled-substance storage, count, administration, and waste policy.
  • Use witnessed waste for partial doses.
  • Monitor therapeutic response and adverse effects.
  • Report discrepancies immediately and document objectively.
Worked Example Dosage Calculation Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Dosage Calculation
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation

Description of Skill

Calculating a medication dose or volume using the prescribed dose, available concentration, client weight when applicable, and the ordered route/frequency. The skill prevents decimal, unit, and concentration errors before administration.

Indications

  • Available dose differs from prescribed dose
  • Weight-based, renal/hepatic-adjusted, infusion-rate, or pediatric medication calculations
  • High-alert drugs requiring independent dose verification

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Correct dose and volume are prepared and administered
  • Calculation and dose range are verified before administration
  • No decimal, unit-conversion, or concentration error reaches the client
  • Client response is therapeutic without preventable toxicity
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Confirm the order, client weight in kg when needed, available concentration, safe-dose range, relevant labs, and required double-check.

Intra: Use a calculator or standard method, avoid trailing zeros, use leading zeros, and measure with the correct device.

Post: Document exact dose/volume/rate given and monitor therapeutic response and adverse effects.

Client Education

  • Use the measuring device supplied for liquid medications, not household spoons.
  • Do not estimate children's doses; verify weight-based dosing with a pharmacist or provider.
  • Ask before doubling a missed dose or changing medication amounts.

Potential Complications

  • Tenfold decimal error, mg/mcg or kg/lb mix-up, wrong concentration, overdose, underdose, or toxicity
  • Subtherapeutic treatment from underdosing
  • High-alert medication harm from unverified calculation

Nursing Interventions

  • Set up calculations consistently and check unit cancellation.
  • Verify safe dose ranges for pediatric and high-alert medications.
  • Use independent double-checks when required.
  • Hold the medication and clarify when a dose appears unsafe.
Worked Example IV Drip Rate Calculation (gtt/min) Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation · Formulas section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
IV Drip Rate Calculation (gtt/min)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation

Description of Skill

Calculating gravity infusion flow in drops per minute when an infusion pump is unavailable or when verifying pump accuracy. Formula: (volume in mL / time in min) × drop factor = gtt/min.

Indications

  • Gravity IV infusion without a pump
  • Backup when a pump malfunctions or is unavailable
  • Manual verification of ordered infusion rate

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Infusion completes within the ordered timeframe
  • Client maintains stable vital signs and fluid balance
  • IV site remains patent and free of infiltration or phlebitis
  • Therapeutic goal of fluid or medication is achieved
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Verify solution, volume, time, indication, tubing drop factor, client fluid status, and IV site patency.

Intra: Calculate gtt/min, adjust roller clamp, count drops for 15 or 30 seconds, and recheck after position changes.

Post: Document start time, rate, volume infused, IV site condition, and client response.

Client Education

  • Tell the client to report swelling, pain, burning, leaking, shortness of breath, or pump/flow concerns.
  • Explain that arm position can change a gravity drip rate.
  • Ask for help before ambulating with IV tubing or pole.

Potential Complications

  • Fluid overload or subtherapeutic delivery from incorrect rate
  • Infiltration, phlebitis, infection, or air in tubing
  • Dextrose interruption or medication underdelivery if infusion ends early or runs slow

Nursing Interventions

  • Use the correct tubing drop factor and round to whole drops.
  • Reassess gravity rates frequently because flow can drift.
  • Monitor IV site, vital signs, intake/output, and expected bag volume.
  • Escalate abnormal response or site complications promptly.
Worked Example Weight-Based Pediatric Dosing & Safe Dose Range Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation · Pediatric section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Weight-Based Pediatric Dosing
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation

Description of Skill

Calculating and verifying pediatric medication doses using the child's current weight in kilograms and a published safe dose range expressed as mg/kg/dose or mg/kg/day. The skill includes converting pounds to kilograms when needed, calculating the ordered dose against the minimum and maximum safe range, checking concentration/volume, and holding out-of-range or unclear orders for clarification before administration.

Indications

  • All pediatric medication doses
  • Weight-based medications in any age group
  • High-alert pediatric doses requiring independent verification

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Ordered dose falls within the recommended safe range for the child's current kg weight
  • Therapeutic response occurs without preventable adverse effects
  • Family demonstrates correct measuring and dosing technique for home medications
  • Unsafe doses are held and clarified before administration
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Obtain current weight in kg, verify dose range in a current reference, calculate minimum/maximum dose, and compare the order to the safe range.

Intra: Administer only if within range; hold and contact provider if outside range. Use oral syringes or precise syringes for small volumes.

Post: Document dose, weight used, route, response, and teaching; reassess therapeutic and adverse effects.

Client Education

  • Use an oral syringe rather than teaspoons or tablespoons.
  • Do not estimate pediatric doses or use adult dosing logic.
  • Call pharmacist/provider before giving a dose that seems different, unclear, or outside instructions.

Potential Complications

  • Overdose, underdose, toxicity, therapeutic failure, or 10-fold decimal error
  • Wrong-concentration liquid medication errors
  • Caregiver measurement error at home

Nursing Interventions

  • Use kg only and reweigh when weight is outdated or inconsistent.
  • Calculate safe dose range before administration.
  • Independently double-check high-alert pediatric doses.
  • Hold and clarify out-of-range doses.
Worked Example Independent Double-Check (High-Alert Medications) Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation · Safety section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Independent Double-Check
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Dosage Calculation

Description of Skill

A safety process in which two licensed clinicians separately verify a high-risk medication, calculation, concentration, route, and pump setting before comparing results. The check must be independent to reduce confirmation bias.

Indications

  • High-alert medications such as insulin, heparin, chemotherapy, PCA/opioid infusions, pediatric doses, and concentrated electrolytes
  • Initiation or rate change of a high-risk infusion
  • Institutional policy requiring two-clinician verification

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Two clinicians independently reach the same correct result before administration
  • Discrepancies are resolved before the medication reaches the client
  • Pump programming, dose, route, concentration, and client data are accurate
  • High-alert medication harm is prevented
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Gather order, MAR, medication label, concentration, weight, labs, pump settings, and policy requirements.

Intra: Each clinician calculates/verifies independently before discussion; compare results and stop for any mismatch.

Post: Document the independent check, monitor response, and repeat verification for required rate/dose changes.

Client Education

  • Explain to the client/family that a second check is an added safety step.
  • Encourage questions if a medication or pump process seems unexpected.
  • Teach warning signs related to the specific high-alert medication.

Potential Complications

  • Confirmation bias, skipped verification, or shared wrong assumption leading to overdose/underdose
  • Insulin, heparin, chemotherapy, opioid, or electrolyte error with severe harm
  • Diffusion of responsibility if neither checker fully verifies the order

Nursing Interventions

  • Perform the check independently, not by verbal agreement.
  • Verify order, client, dose, concentration, route, rate, pump, and line.
  • Resolve discrepancies before administration.
  • Document according to facility policy.
Worked Example Intravenous Therapy Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Intravenous Therapy
Review Module Chapter
Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy

Description of Skill

Administration of fluids, medications, blood products, or nutrition through peripheral or central venous access to provide rapid onset, precise dose control, hydration, or continuous infusion.

Indications

  • NPO status, dehydration, electrolyte replacement, resuscitation, blood products, TPN, IV medications, contrast, or continuous infusions
  • Need for rapid medication effect or inability to use the oral route
  • Long-term, vesicant, or hypertonic therapy requiring central access

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Correct fluid, medication, and rate are delivered
  • Therapeutic response is achieved and fluid balance remains appropriate
  • IV site remains patent, intact, and free of complications
  • Catheter is removed safely when no longer needed
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Verify order, allergies, compatibility, concentration, client fluid status, vein/site selection, catheter gauge, and aseptic setup.

Intra: Insert/access using appropriate technique, secure/label dressing, maintain closed system, monitor rate and site, and use pump or manual drip checks as ordered.

Post: Document site, catheter, rate, solution/medication, response, and complications; remove catheter using policy when therapy ends.

Client Education

  • Report pain, burning, swelling, redness, warmth, coolness, leaking, fever/chills, chest pain, or shortness of breath.
  • Avoid pulling, wetting, or kinking tubing/dressing.
  • Ask for help when ambulating with IV equipment.

Potential Complications

  • Infiltration, extravasation, phlebitis, infection, fluid overload, air embolism, or catheter dislodgement
  • Wrong fluid, medication, rate, or compatibility issue
  • Skin injury or bloodstream infection from poor site care

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess IV site and infusion at required intervals.
  • Maintain aseptic technique and a closed system.
  • Verify fluid/medication compatibility and ordered rate.
  • Stop infusion and intervene promptly for site or systemic complications.
Worked Example IV Fluid Tonicity (Isotonic / Hypotonic / Hypertonic) Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy · Solutions section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
IV Fluid Tonicity Selection and Monitoring
Review Module Chapter
Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy

Description of Skill

Selection and monitoring of IV fluids based on tonicity relative to plasma: isotonic fluids stay primarily intravascular, hypotonic fluids shift water into cells, and hypertonic fluids pull water from cells into the intravascular space.

Indications

  • Fluid resuscitation, maintenance fluids, dehydration, sodium/osmolality problems, cerebral edema, or parenteral nutrition
  • Need to match fluid choice to clinical status, labs, and provider order
  • Monitoring clients at risk for fluid overload, cerebral edema, or electrolyte shift

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Ordered fluid matches indication and client condition
  • Fluid balance, vital signs, lung sounds, neurologic status, and labs remain within expected range
  • No cerebral edema, osmotic injury, phlebitis, or fluid overload occurs
  • Therapeutic hydration/electrolyte goal is achieved
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Review fluid order, indication, serum sodium/osmolality, renal/cardiac status, neurologic risk, and line access requirements.

Intra: Administer at ordered rate, monitor site and systemic response, and use central access for high-osmolar solutions when required.

Post: Trend intake/output, daily weight, lung sounds, edema, neurologic status, and labs; report rapid sodium/fluid shifts.

Client Education

  • Explain why a specific IV fluid is ordered and why rates should not be changed by the client.
  • Teach signs to report: shortness of breath, swelling, headache, confusion, IV site pain, or burning.
  • Reinforce asking staff before disconnecting or adjusting IV tubing.

Potential Complications

  • Fluid overload, electrolyte shift, cerebral edema, osmotic demyelination, phlebitis, or tissue injury
  • Wrong fluid choice for increased ICP, burns/trauma, hyperkalemia, heart failure, or renal disease
  • Peripheral vein irritation from hypertonic solutions

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify solution tonicity and client-specific contraindications.
  • Monitor labs, neuro status, lungs, edema, I/O, weight, and IV site.
  • Use pump/rate safeguards and appropriate line access.
  • Report unexpected symptoms or lab shifts promptly.
Worked Example Central Venous Access Device (CVAD/PICC) Management Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy · Access section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
CVAD/PICC Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy

Description of Skill

Care and maintenance of central venous access devices whose catheter tip terminates in a central vein, used for vesicants, hypertonic solutions, TPN, long-term therapy, frequent blood draws, or poor peripheral access.

Indications

  • Caustic/vesicant medications, TPN, vasopressors, chemotherapy, or hypertonic fluids
  • Long-term IV therapy, poor peripheral access, hemodynamic monitoring, or frequent blood draws
  • Need for multiple simultaneous infusions

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Catheter remains patent and correctly positioned
  • No CLABSI, occlusion, dislodgement, thrombosis, pneumothorax, or air embolism occurs
  • Therapy is delivered safely through appropriate central access
  • Removal occurs without bleeding or retained catheter fragment
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Verify order/indication, consent when applicable, coagulation status, allergies, insertion type, and whether tip placement has been confirmed before first use.

Intra: Use sterile/aseptic technique, scrub the hub, maintain occlusive dressing, flush per policy, clamp/secure line, and assess site/patency daily.

Post: Document dressing/site status, line use, flushes, complications, and removal details; use supine/Trendelenburg and occlusive dressing for removal per policy.

Client Education

  • Keep dressing clean, dry, and intact.
  • Report fever, chills, redness, drainage, swelling, shortness of breath, chest pain, or line leakage.
  • Do not pull on the line; follow home flushing/dressing instructions if discharged with a CVAD.

Potential Complications

  • CLABSI, occlusion, migration, dislodgement, thrombosis, pneumothorax, air embolism, bleeding, or pinch-off syndrome
  • Using the line before tip placement is verified
  • Breaks in sterile technique or hub scrubbing

Nursing Interventions

  • Confirm placement before first use when required.
  • Scrub the hub before access and maintain sterile dressing changes.
  • Assess site, patency, and systemic infection signs.
  • Clamp, flush, secure, and remove according to device and facility policy.
Worked Example Infiltration vs Extravasation Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy · Complications section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Infiltration and Extravasation Recognition/Response
Review Module Chapter
Ch 4 — Intravenous Therapy

Description of Skill

Assessment and urgent response to leakage of IV fluid or medication into surrounding tissue. Infiltration involves non-vesicant fluid; extravasation involves a vesicant and can cause tissue necrosis.

Indications

  • Any IV site with pain, swelling, coolness, blanching, leaking, slowed flow, loss of blood return, or burning
  • Peripheral administration of vesicants or irritants
  • Clients unable to report pain due to age, sedation, anesthesia, or altered cognition

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Infiltration or extravasation is recognized early and infusion is stopped promptly
  • Appropriate protocol is followed for non-vesicant vs vesicant exposure
  • Tissue injury is minimized and therapy is restarted safely at another site
  • Assessment, treatment, and notifications are documented
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre: Know whether the infusing medication is vesicant, irritant, or non-vesicant; select the safest vein/access and verify blood return when required.

Intra: Assess site frequently for pain, swelling, temperature/color change, leakage, and flow changes; stop immediately when infiltration/extravasation is suspected.

Post: For infiltration, remove catheter and elevate/apply compress per solution. For extravasation, leave catheter initially, aspirate drug, administer antidote per protocol, notify provider, photograph/document, and consult as needed.

Client Education

  • Report burning, pain, swelling, tightness, coolness, leaking, or slowed infusion immediately.
  • Do not ignore mild discomfort during vesicant infusions.
  • Protect the affected extremity and follow compress/elevation instructions after an event.

Potential Complications

  • Tissue necrosis, nerve injury, compartment syndrome, scarring, delayed therapy, surgical debridement, grafting, or amputation
  • Legal risk if vesicant protocol is delayed or documentation is incomplete
  • Recurrence if a high-risk peripheral site is reused

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess IV sites at required intervals and more often for vesicants.
  • Stop infusion immediately for suspected infiltration/extravasation.
  • Differentiate non-vesicant from vesicant response.
  • Document site appearance, size, drug/fluid, actions, provider notification, and client response.
Worked Example Eye Drop Administration Technique Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Ophthalmic Medication Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders

Description of Skill

Proper administration of ophthalmic medications (eye drops and ointments) ensures therapeutic effect, minimizes systemic absorption, prevents contamination, and avoids ocular injury.

Eye drops achieve immediate effect; ointments have longer contact time but blur vision (typically used at bedtime). Key techniques: punctal occlusion (reduces systemic absorption), spacing multiple drops (≥ 5 min), and avoiding tip contact with the eye (contamination).

Indications

  • Glaucoma management (chronic IOP control)
  • Eye infections (bacterial conjunctivitis, keratitis)
  • Ocular inflammation (allergic conjunctivitis, uveitis)
  • Pre- and post-operative eye care (cataract, retinal surgery)
  • Diagnostic procedures (mydriatics, anesthetics)
  • Dry eye / lubrication

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Medication reaches target eye without contamination of dropper tip
  • Client tolerates instillation without injury
  • Therapeutic effect achieved (e.g., IOP reduction, infection resolution, allergic symptom relief)
  • Minimal systemic side effects (punctal occlusion effective)
  • Client/family demonstrate correct technique for home use
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify order: medication name, concentration, eye (OD = right, OS = left, OU = both), dose, frequency
  • Two patient identifiers, check allergies
  • Gather supplies: bottle/tube, tissues, gloves
  • Assess eyes: discharge, redness, swelling, vision; cleanse with sterile saline if discharge present (inner-to-outer canthus, separate gauze each eye)
  • Position client supine or seated with head tilted back

Intra (administration):

  1. Hand hygiene; don gloves
  2. Have client look upward
  3. Gently pull down lower lid to create conjunctival sac (“pocket”)
  4. Hold dropper 1–2 cm above the eye (do NOT touch eye or eyelid — contamination)
  5. Instill the prescribed number of drops into the conjunctival sac (NOT directly on cornea)
  6. Have client close eye gently (do not squeeze tight); blot excess with tissue
  7. Apply punctal occlusion (press inner canthus) for 1–2 min — reduces systemic absorption and prolongs ocular contact
  8. For ointment: same lower-lid technique; squeeze ribbon 1/4–1/2 inch into sac, twist tube to detach; instruct gentle blinking
  9. Multiple drops: wait ≥ 5 minutes between
  10. Drops before ointments (ointments hold contact time)

Post:

  • Document medication, dose, eye, time, response
  • Assess for adverse effects: stinging, redness, blurred vision (expected initially), systemic effects
  • Reinforce client/family education

Client Education

  • Wash hands before and after administration and avoid touching the dropper or ointment tip to the eye, eyelid, lashes, or any surface.
  • Use the ordered eye exactly as prescribed; wait at least 5 minutes between different drops and apply ointment last when both are ordered.
  • Close the eye gently and use punctal occlusion when instructed to reduce systemic absorption.
  • Report eye pain, worsening redness, vision changes, drainage, or signs of infection.

Potential Complications

  • Contamination of dropper tip → ocular infection (touching eye/eyelid)
  • Systemic absorption → significant effects (especially beta blockers → bradycardia, bronchospasm; if punctal occlusion not used)
  • Corneal abrasion from improper technique (touching eye with dropper)
  • Sub-therapeutic dose if drop missed eye, wiped immediately, or eye blinked excessively
  • Drug interaction if multiple drops too close together (washout effect)
  • Adverse drug reactions: hypersensitivity, stinging, burning, blurred vision
  • Cross-contamination between eyes if dropper used on both without cleaning

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify the correct medication, concentration, dose, frequency, and ordered eye before administration.
  • Use hand hygiene, gloves, aseptic technique, and avoid contaminating the dropper or ointment tip.
  • Instill medication into the conjunctival sac, use punctal occlusion when appropriate, and space multiple eye medications.
  • Assess therapeutic response, ocular irritation, vision changes, and adverse or systemic effects.
Worked Example Sublingual Nitroglycerin Administration Ch 22 — Angina · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Sublingual Nitroglycerin Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 22 — Angina

Description of Skill

Administration of sublingual nitroglycerin (SL NTG) for acute angina — a fast-acting vasodilator that relieves anginal chest pain by reducing preload (venodilation) and improving coronary perfusion.

The 3-dose protocol and recognizing when to activate emergency response are critical patient-safety skills. Onset is 1–3 minutes; tablet should produce a tingling/fizzing sensation under the tongue (indicates potency).

Indications

  • Acute anginal chest pain (stable angina)
  • Prophylaxis before known triggers (exertion, emotional stress, cold, sexual activity)
  • Acute coronary syndrome management (in monitored settings)
  • Acute hypertensive episodes with chest pain (clinical settings)

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Chest pain relieved (ideally within 5 min of first dose for stable angina)
  • Stable hemodynamics; no symptomatic hypotension
  • Client/family demonstrate correct self-administration technique and 3-dose protocol
  • Client knows when to call 911
  • Appropriate escalation to emergency care if unrelieved
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Assess chest pain (PQRST: provocation, quality, radiation, severity, timing)
  • Obtain baseline vital signs — check BP (hold if SBP < 90 mmHg); heart rate
  • 12-lead EKG if in clinical setting
  • Verify NO PDE5 inhibitor use (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil within 24–48 hr) — fatal hypotension risk
  • Confirm tablet potency: should be stored in original dark glass bottle, replaced every 6 months

Intra (3-dose protocol):

  1. Have client sit or lie down (prevents falls from hypotension)
  2. Place ONE tablet under the tongue; do not swallow; let dissolve
  3. Client should feel tingling/fizzing (indicates potency)
  4. Wait 5 minutes; reassess pain and BP
  5. If pain unrelieved after FIRST dose — call 911 / activate EMS (current AHA guidance), then may give up to 2 more doses 5 min apart (max 3 doses total)
  6. Recheck BP before each subsequent dose (hold if SBP < 90)
  7. Monitor continuously for hypotension

Post:

  • Document pain relief, number of doses, vital signs response, EKG changes
  • Reassess and continue monitoring
  • If relieved: identify trigger; reinforce teaching
  • If unrelieved: prepare for ACS workup (troponin, continued monitoring, possible PCI)
  • Wear gloves if applying topical/paste forms (absorption through skin)

Client Education

  • Sit or lie down before taking sublingual nitroglycerin because dizziness or hypotension can occur.
  • Place the tablet under the tongue and let it dissolve; do not chew, crush, or swallow it.
  • Call emergency services if chest pain is not relieved after the first dose or as directed by the provider.
  • Avoid phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and keep tablets in the original dark container, replacing them when expired.

Potential Complications

  • Hypotension — can cause dizziness, syncope, falls; worse if volume-depleted or with other vasodilators
  • Severe/fatal hypotension with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — absolute contraindication
  • Reflex tachycardia
  • Headache (very common — from vasodilation; treat with acetaminophen)
  • Tolerance with continuous use (need nitrate-free interval for long-acting forms)
  • Flushing, dizziness
  • Masking an MI — delaying emergency care if relying solely on NTG for unrelieved pain
  • Loss of potency if improperly stored (no tingling = possibly expired/inactive)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess chest pain, blood pressure, medication history, and contraindicated phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use before administration.
  • Keep the client seated or lying down and administer the medication sublingually without swallowing or chewing.
  • Monitor pain relief, blood pressure, dizziness, headache, and need for emergency escalation.
  • Document dose timing, client response, teaching, and provider or emergency notification when indicated.
Worked Example Vaccine Administration & Schedule Ch 41 — Immunizations · Vaccines section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Vaccine Administration & Schedule
Review Module Chapter
Ch 41 — Immunizations

Description of Skill

Safe administration of vaccines per the recommended immunization schedule, including correct route/site, proper spacing, cold-chain maintenance, screening, documentation, and adverse-event monitoring.

Key safety: correct route (some vaccines are SC, others IM), age-appropriate site/needle, providing the Vaccine Information Statement (VIS), and maintaining the cold chain (vaccine potency depends on proper storage).

Indications

  • Routine immunization per CDC/ACIP schedule (infants, children, adolescents, adults)
  • Catch-up immunization
  • Travel and occupational requirements
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (some vaccines)
  • High-risk groups (e.g., influenza, pneumococcal in older adults)

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Vaccine administered safely by correct route/site
  • No immediate adverse reaction
  • Accurate, complete documentation
  • Client/family understand expected effects and follow-up doses
  • Immunization schedule kept up to date
  • Cold chain maintained (vaccine potency preserved)
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Screen for contraindications/precautions (allergy, immunocompromise, pregnancy for live vaccines, current illness)
  • Verify which vaccines are due (review record/schedule)
  • Check vaccine storage and expiration (cold chain intact)
  • Provide the current Vaccine Information Statement (VIS); answer questions; obtain consent
  • Verify route for each vaccine

Intra:

  • Routes/sites: IM (vastus lateralis for infants; deltoid for older children/adults); SC (some, e.g., MMR, varicella); intranasal/oral for select
  • Age-appropriate needle length/gauge
  • Multiple vaccines: separate sites (label/document each site); ≥ 1 inch apart in same limb
  • Use comfort measures (positioning, distraction; topical anesthetic if appropriate)
  • Never mix vaccines in one syringe unless specifically licensed as a combination

Post:

  • Observe for immediate reactions ~15 minutes (anaphylaxis); have epinephrine available
  • Document: vaccine, dose, route, site, lot number, manufacturer, expiration, VIS date given, administering nurse
  • Update immunization record; schedule next doses
  • Educate on expected effects and when to report
  • Report adverse events to VAERS as indicated

Client Education

  • Keep a personal immunization record and bring it to health visits.
  • Expect mild soreness, redness, low-grade fever, or fatigue after many vaccines; use comfort measures as instructed.
  • Report severe allergic reaction symptoms, high fever, or unusual neurologic symptoms immediately.
  • Return for all doses in a vaccine series and follow the recommended schedule for age and risk factors.

Potential Complications

  • Anaphylaxis (rare; the reason for post-vaccination observation)
  • Local reactions (pain, redness, swelling)
  • Systemic: fever, malaise, rash
  • Vasovagal syncope (especially adolescents) — have patient seated/lying
  • Wrong route → reduced efficacy or increased local reaction
  • Cold-chain breach → ineffective vaccine
  • Wrong vaccine/dose/spacing → need for revaccination
  • Administration to contraindicated patient (e.g., live vaccine to immunocompromised)

Nursing Interventions

  • Screen for allergies, contraindications, precautions, pregnancy status when relevant, and previous vaccine reactions.
  • Verify vaccine, route, site, dose, expiration, storage requirements, and current schedule recommendations.
  • Administer with appropriate technique and observe for immediate hypersensitivity or syncope when indicated.
  • Document vaccine name, lot number, site, route, date, and required education materials according to policy.
Worked Example Chemotherapy Safe Handling & Administration Ch 42 — Chemotherapy Agents · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Chemotherapy Safe Handling & Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 42 — Chemotherapy Agents

Description of Skill

Safe handling and administration of hazardous antineoplastic (chemotherapy) drugs, which pose risks to healthcare workers through skin contact, inhalation, and exposure to patient body fluids.

Requires specialized training/certification, personal protective equipment (PPE), closed-system transfer devices, and spill management. Many agents are vesicants (cause tissue necrosis if extravasated).

Indications

  • Administration of chemotherapy (IV, oral, intrathecal, etc.)
  • Handling, preparing, or disposing of hazardous drugs
  • Managing patient body fluids during/after chemo (excreted for ~48 hr)
  • Cleaning chemotherapy spills

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Chemotherapy administered safely and accurately
  • No healthcare worker exposure
  • No extravasation or unmanaged infusion reaction
  • Proper disposal and body-fluid precautions maintained
  • Patient/family understand home safety precautions
  • Accurate documentation
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Only specially trained/certified personnel prepare and administer
  • Verify orders (often requires independent double-check by two chemo-certified nurses: drug, dose, route, rate, patient)
  • Confirm labs (CBC, renal/hepatic function) acceptable
  • Verify informed consent
  • Don PPE: chemo-rated gloves (double), impermeable gown, eye/face protection as indicated
  • Prepare in a biological safety cabinet (pharmacy); use closed-system transfer devices
  • Ensure patent IV; central line preferred for vesicants

Intra:

  • Verify blood return before and during vesicant administration
  • Monitor IV site continuously for extravasation (vesicants)
  • Administer at prescribed rate; monitor for hypersensitivity/infusion reactions
  • Use luer-lock connections; avoid aerosolization

Post:

  • Dispose of all materials in designated hazardous (chemo) waste containers
  • Handle body fluids with PPE for ~48 hr (drug excreted); double-flush toilet per policy
  • Document administration, site, patient response
  • Spill management: use a chemotherapy spill kit; restrict area; don PPE; contain and clean per protocol; report
  • Monitor for delayed toxicities

Client Education

  • Report fever, signs of infection, unusual bleeding, severe nausea/vomiting, mouth sores, or new pain promptly.
  • Notify the nurse immediately for burning, pain, swelling, redness, or leaking at the IV site during chemotherapy.
  • Follow home precautions for oral chemotherapy, body fluids, and contaminated linens or supplies as instructed.
  • Keep laboratory and treatment appointments and avoid pregnancy exposure precautions as directed by the oncology team.

Potential Complications

  • Occupational exposure (carcinogenic/teratogenic risk to staff)
  • Extravasation of vesicants → severe tissue necrosis
  • Hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis and infusion reactions
  • Medication errors (high-alert; wrong dose/route — intrathecal errors can be fatal)
  • Spill contamination
  • Patient toxicities: myelosuppression, mucositis, nausea, organ toxicity

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify protocol, dose, route, body-surface-area calculation, labs, consent, and required independent checks before administration.
  • Use chemotherapy precautions, required PPE, correct tubing, and vesicant safeguards throughout handling and administration.
  • Monitor for hypersensitivity, extravasation, myelosuppression, nausea/vomiting, mucositis, and organ toxicity.
  • Dispose of contaminated supplies correctly and document administration, site status, response, and teaching.
Worked Example Inhaler & Spacer Administration Technique Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · Antiinflammatory section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Inhaler / Spacer / Nebulizer Use
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders

Description of Skill

Proper technique for inhaled medications via metered-dose inhalers (MDIs), dry powder inhalers (DPIs), soft mist inhalers (SMIs), and nebulizers. Up to 50–70% of clients use inhalers incorrectly — impacting drug delivery and disease control.

Choice depends on client’s coordination, age, severity, and inspiratory effort.

Indications

  • Asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis
  • Croup, RSV (nebulizers in pediatrics)
  • Pulmonary hypertension (some agents)
  • Acute pulmonary edema (some nebulized agents)

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Client demonstrates correct technique on return-demonstration
  • Improvement in pulmonary symptoms (decreased wheeze, dyspnea)
  • Improvement in peak flow or FEV1
  • Reduced need for rescue inhaler
  • No oral side effects (thrush, hoarseness) from ICS — indicates good rinse habit
  • Adherence to controller medications evident in refill patterns
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify order: medication, dose, device, frequency
  • Assess client’s ability to coordinate inhalation with actuation (determines need for spacer)
  • Inspect device: full canister, mouthpiece clean, expiration date
  • Position client upright (sitting or high Fowler’s)

Intra (MDI without spacer):

  1. Shake the inhaler
  2. Prime if first use or unused ≥ 2 weeks
  3. Exhale completely
  4. Hold mouthpiece 1–2 inches from open mouth OR seal lips around mouthpiece (per device instructions)
  5. Begin SLOW deep inhalation; press canister at start of inhalation
  6. Continue inhaling deeply for 3–5 sec
  7. Hold breath for 10 seconds (or as long as comfortable)
  8. Exhale slowly through pursed lips
  9. Wait 30–60 sec between puffs of same medication; 1–5 min between different medications

MDI WITH spacer (preferred for most clients):

  1. Shake inhaler; attach to spacer
  2. Exhale completely; seal lips around spacer mouthpiece
  3. Press canister ONE time; breathe in slowly and deeply
  4. Hold breath 10 sec
  5. Exhale; wait 30–60 sec; repeat for additional puffs

DPI (e.g., Diskus, Flexhaler):

  1. Load the dose per device-specific instructions
  2. Exhale FULLY away from device (moisture deactivates)
  3. Seal lips; inhale RAPIDLY and deeply (different from MDI)
  4. Hold breath 10 sec
  5. Exhale slowly away from device

Nebulizer:

  1. Assemble per kit instructions; add medication to chamber
  2. Connect to oxygen source (6–8 L/min) or compressor
  3. Client sits upright; uses mouthpiece (preferred) or mask
  4. Slow normal breaths with occasional deep breaths
  5. Treatment continues 8–15 min until medication is fully nebulized

Post:

  • RINSE MOUTH with water after inhaled corticosteroids (prevents oral candidiasis and dysphonia)
  • Clean mouthpiece weekly with warm water; allow to air-dry
  • Track doses remaining (some devices have counters)
  • Document medication, dose, response, peak flow if applicable
  • Reassess technique at every visit (≥ 70% have errors)

Client Education

  • Use inhalers in the prescribed order and technique; shake and prime the device when required.
  • Exhale fully, inhale slowly and deeply through the device or spacer, and hold the breath for about 10 seconds when able.
  • Rinse the mouth after inhaled corticosteroids to reduce oral candidiasis risk.
  • Clean the spacer/nebulizer as instructed and seek care if rescue inhaler use increases or symptoms worsen.

Potential Complications

  • Sub-therapeutic delivery from poor technique (~50–70% of clients)
  • Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) and dysphonia from ICS without rinsing
  • Systemic absorption with high-dose ICS: adrenal suppression, growth suppression in children, cataracts/glaucoma, osteoporosis
  • Paradoxical bronchospasm (rare; with first dose or new device)
  • Tachycardia, tremor from SABAs (especially with overuse)
  • Pneumonia risk with high-dose ICS in COPD (numerically increased)
  • Device-specific issues: empty canister not detected (older devices), DPI moisture damage
  • Confusion between rescue and controller inhaler → missed control, overuse of rescue

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess respiratory status, prescribed device, spacer need, medication order, and the client's current technique.
  • Demonstrate and coach correct inhaler, spacer, or nebulizer use with return demonstration.
  • Monitor symptom relief, breath sounds, oxygenation, adverse effects, and frequency of rescue medication use.
  • Reinforce cleaning, mouth rinsing after corticosteroids, trigger control, and when to seek urgent care.
Worked Example Blood Transfusion Administration Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products · Administration section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Skill Name
Blood Transfusion Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products

Description of Skill

Safe administration of blood and blood products (packed RBCs, platelets, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate) requiring strict verification, monitoring, and reaction recognition.

Critical safety elements: two-licensed-person verification, Y-tubing with 0.9% normal saline ONLY (no dextrose — hemolysis; no LR — clotting), blood filter, and the 4-hour maximum infusion time per unit.

Indications

  • Symptomatic anemia, acute blood loss, hemorrhage
  • Packed RBCs: low hemoglobin with symptoms (often Hgb < 7–8 g/dL)
  • Platelets: thrombocytopenia with bleeding or very low counts
  • Fresh frozen plasma: coagulation factor deficiency, warfarin reversal
  • Cryoprecipitate: fibrinogen deficiency, DIC

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Transfusion completed without adverse reaction
  • Improvement in target parameter (increased Hgb/Hct, platelet count, coagulation)
  • Resolution of symptoms (reduced fatigue, dyspnea; controlled bleeding)
  • Stable vital signs throughout
  • Client understands signs to report post-transfusion
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify provider order; confirm informed consent
  • Verify type and crossmatch completed
  • Ensure large-bore IV (18–20 gauge) patent
  • Obtain baseline vital signs (temp, HR, BP, RR, SpO2) — if febrile, notify provider before starting
  • Gather Y-tubing with in-line filter and 0.9% normal saline ONLY
  • TWO licensed personnel verify at bedside: client name/DOB (two identifiers), blood type and Rh, unit number, expiration, crossmatch compatibility, product appearance
  • Have emergency equipment available

Intra:

  • Start SLOWLY (~2 mL/min / 25–50 mL over first 15 min) — stay with client the first 15 minutes (most reactions occur early)
  • Recheck vital signs at 15 min, then per policy (often every 30–60 min) and at completion
  • If no reaction after 15 min, increase to ordered rate
  • Complete infusion within 4 hours (bacterial growth risk)
  • Use only NS to prime/flush; never add medications to blood
  • Monitor continuously for reaction signs

Post:

  • Final set of vital signs
  • Document: product, volume, time, vital signs, client response
  • Dispose of bag/tubing per policy; some retained if reaction suspected
  • Continue monitoring for delayed reactions

Client Education

  • Report chills, fever, itching, rash, back or chest pain, shortness of breath, anxiety, dark urine, or feeling unwell during or after transfusion.
  • Expect frequent vital sign checks and remain available for close monitoring during the first part of the transfusion.
  • Do not adjust tubing or leave the area without assistance while connected to the transfusion.
  • Report delayed fever, jaundice, dark urine, or unexpected fatigue after discharge or later in the admission.

Potential Complications

  • Acute hemolytic reaction (ABO incompatibility) — most dangerous; fever, chills, flank/back pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, DIC
  • Febrile non-hemolytic reaction — most common; fever, chills (from donor WBCs)
  • Allergic reaction — urticaria, itching; anaphylaxis (severe)
  • TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) — dyspnea, crackles, hypertension, JVD (too fast/too much)
  • TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) — acute respiratory distress; leading cause of transfusion death
  • Bacterial contamination/sepsis — high fever, hypotension, shock
  • Delayed hemolytic reaction (days later); iron overload (chronic); disease transmission (rare)

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify prescription, consent, blood type/crossmatch, client identity, product, expiration, and compatibility with another licensed nurse per policy.
  • Use appropriate IV access and tubing, obtain baseline vital signs, and start the transfusion slowly while closely monitoring the client.
  • Stop the transfusion and maintain IV access with normal saline if reaction symptoms occur; notify provider and blood bank per protocol.
  • Document verification, start/stop times, vital signs, volume infused, client response, teaching, and any reaction management.

Worked Example Individual Considerations of Medication Administration Ch 6 — Individual Considerations of Medication Administration · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Individual Considerations of Medication Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 6 — Individual Considerations of Medication Administration

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Individual client factors affecting medication administration, dosing, and response:

  • Age: neonates, infants, children, older adults — altered pharmacokinetics
  • Body weight and BMI: weight-based dosing; obesity affects drug distribution
  • Pregnancy and lactation: drug crosses placenta, enters breast milk; pregnancy categories
  • Renal function: dose adjustments based on CrCl/eGFR for renally cleared drugs
  • Hepatic function: dose adjustments for hepatically metabolized drugs
  • Genetic variations (pharmacogenomics): CYP2D6, CYP2C19, HLA-B variants affect metabolism and adverse reactions
  • Race, ethnicity, cultural beliefs: variable responses (ACE inhibitor sensitivity in Black clients); beliefs about medication use
  • Health literacy and language: ability to understand and adhere to regimen
  • Comorbidities, polypharmacy

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Pediatric considerations:
    • Immature liver/kidney function — slower metabolism and excretion
    • ↑ body water, ↓ body fat → altered distribution of water-soluble drugs
    • Lower albumin → ↑ free drug levels
    • Immature blood-brain barrier in neonates → ↑ CNS drug penetration
    • Doses always weight-based or BSA-based
  • Older adult considerations:
    • ↓ renal clearance (even with normal serum creatinine — use eGFR)
    • ↓ hepatic blood flow and metabolism
    • ↑ body fat, ↓ lean mass → altered distribution
    • ↓ total body water
    • ↓ plasma protein → ↑ free drug
    • ↑ sensitivity to CNS drugs, anticholinergics, opioids
    • Polypharmacy → ↑ interaction and adverse effect risk
    • Beers Criteria identifies potentially inappropriate medications
  • Pregnancy/lactation:
    • ↑ blood volume, ↑ renal clearance, ↑ hepatic metabolism
    • Drugs may cross placenta — teratogenicity (categorical risk)
    • Drugs in breast milk — infant exposure
  • Renal impairment: ↓ clearance → drug accumulation and toxicity for renally cleared drugs (digoxin, vancomycin, gabapentin, lithium, metformin)
  • Hepatic impairment: ↓ first-pass metabolism, ↓ albumin → ↑ levels of hepatically cleared drugs

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Use medication reconciliation at every transition of care and routine visit.
  • Promote one prescriber/pharmacy when possible to reduce interaction and duplication risk.
  • Screen renal/hepatic function, pregnancy/lactation status, allergies, health literacy, culture, and ability to self-administer.
  • Use individualized teaching, teach-back, large print, interpreter services, and caregiver support as needed.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Infants, children, older adults, pregnancy, and lactation.
  • Renal impairment, hepatic impairment, low albumin, dehydration, and low or high body weight.
  • Polypharmacy, high-alert medications, OTC/herbal use, substance use, and multiple prescribers.
  • Low health literacy, language barriers, cognitive impairment, vision changes, poor dexterity, cost barriers, and cultural/religious concerns.
  • Pharmacogenomic variants affecting medication metabolism or hypersensitivity risk.

Expected Findings

  • Comprehensive medication history identifying ALL medications including OTC, supplements, herbals
  • Documented allergies and adverse drug reactions (with type of reaction)
  • Current weight (in kg) and recent labs (BUN, creatinine, GFR, LFTs, albumin)
  • Pregnancy status (if applicable)
  • Genetic testing results (when available — e.g., for warfarin, clopidogrel, abacavir)
  • Cultural and religious beliefs that may affect medication use (porcine products, alcohol-containing medications)
  • Assessment of cognition, vision, dexterity affecting self-administration
  • Identified barriers to adherence: cost, transportation, complexity of regimen

Laboratory Tests

  • Current weight in kg for weight-based dosing.
  • BUN, creatinine, and eGFR/CrCl for renally cleared medications.
  • Liver function tests, bilirubin, and albumin for hepatic metabolism/protein binding concerns.
  • Pregnancy test when clinically indicated before teratogenic or pregnancy-sensitive medications.
  • Therapeutic drug levels for narrow-therapeutic-index medications.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Medication reconciliation comparing prescriptions, OTC products, herbals, supplements, and recent changes.
  • Allergy/adverse-reaction history with reaction type and severity.
  • Swallowing, cognition, vision, hearing, dexterity, and caregiver-support assessment.
  • Beers Criteria or facility geriatric medication screen for older adults.
  • Pharmacogenomic testing when ordered for medications with known genotype-related risk.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Use kg-only weights, renal/hepatic dose adjustment, and independent checks for high-alert medications.
  • Clarify unsafe orders, duplicate therapies, allergy conflicts, and unexpected doses before administration.
  • Avoid crushing extended-release, enteric-coated, or hazardous medications unless pharmacy confirms it is safe.
  • Use fall precautions and close monitoring when medications increase sedation, orthostasis, or anticholinergic effects.

Complications

  • Medication toxicity from reduced renal/hepatic clearance or altered distribution.
  • Adverse drug reactions, allergic reactions, drug-drug interactions, and therapeutic failure.
  • Falls, confusion, oversedation, bleeding, hypoglycemia, or other high-alert medication harm.
  • Nonadherence related to cost, complex regimens, low literacy, cultural concerns, or access barriers.
  • Fetal/infant exposure during pregnancy or lactation when risks are not recognized.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

  • Conduct medication reconciliation and compare all products with current prescriptions.
  • Verify age, weight, renal/hepatic function, allergies, pregnancy/lactation status, and relevant labs before administration.
  • Identify potentially inappropriate medications, duplicate therapy, interactions, and high-alert safeguards.
  • Use individualized administration aids, caregiver support, and adherence strategies.
  • Communicate concerns to provider/pharmacist and document teaching and response.

Medications

  • Adjust renally cleared or hepatically metabolized medications as prescribed.
  • Use extra caution with opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, anticoagulants, insulin, digoxin, lithium, and other narrow-therapeutic-index medications.
  • Review OTC, herbal, and supplement products for interactions.
  • Screen pregnancy/lactation safety and avoid known teratogens unless benefits clearly outweigh risks.

Client Education

  • Tailor education to client's literacy level and cultural background
  • Use teach-back method to verify understanding
  • Provide written materials in client's preferred language
  • Include caregivers in education for pediatric or cognitively impaired clients
  • Address common myths and concerns
  • For older adults: large-print labels, pill organizers, medication review at each visit
  • Discuss any cost concerns; explore generic substitution, patient assistance programs
  • Coordinate with social work, pharmacy for complex needs
  • For pregnant/breastfeeding clients: discuss benefits and risks of each medication
  • Encourage use of one pharmacy for interaction screening
  • Emphasize importance of consistent provider communication about all substances taken

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Medication reconciliation and deprescribing review when medication burden is high.
  • Use pill organizers, calendars, simplified schedules, large-print labels, or assistive devices when appropriate.
  • Arrange interpreter-supported education and culturally respectful medication planning.
  • Coordinate home health, pharmacy packaging, or social-work support for complex regimens.

Interprofessional Care

  • Provider adjusts therapy based on age, labs, pregnancy/lactation, adverse effects, and goals of care.
  • Pharmacist reviews interactions, dosing, therapeutic drug monitoring, and administration concerns.
  • Genetic counselor or specialist supports pharmacogenomic risk interpretation when ordered.
  • Social worker/case manager assists with cost, transportation, access, and adherence barriers.
  • Caregivers help with administration when cognition, vision, dexterity, or age limits self-management.
Worked Example Bipolar Disorders Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Bipolar Disorders
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Bipolar Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Bipolar Disorders — mood disorders characterized by episodes of mania (or hypomania) alternating with depressive episodes:

  • Bipolar I: ≥ 1 manic episode (with or without depression); often severe with psychotic features
  • Bipolar II: hypomanic episodes + depressive episodes; no full manic episode
  • Cyclothymic disorder: chronic (≥ 2 yr) hypomanic and depressive symptoms not meeting full criteria
  • Rapid cycling: ≥ 4 mood episodes in 12 months
  • Mixed features: depressive + manic symptoms concurrently — high suicide risk

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Multifactorial: genetic, neurochemical, and environmental factors
  • Genetics: strong heritability; first-degree relatives have ~10x risk
  • Neurotransmitter dysregulation: serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, glutamate, GABA
  • Structural brain changes: prefrontal cortex, amygdala, hippocampus alterations on imaging
  • Circadian rhythm disruption — sleep changes both precipitate and reflect mood episodes
  • Triggers: sleep deprivation, antidepressants without mood stabilizer, substance use, major life events, postpartum period, seasonal changes
  • Onset typically late adolescence to mid-20s; chronic, episodic course

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Maintain regular sleep, meals, activity, and medication routines.
  • Avoid alcohol, stimulants, and recreational substances that can destabilize mood.
  • Use relapse-prevention planning: recognize early sleep changes, increased energy, impulsivity, depression, or suicidal thoughts.
  • Promote follow-up care, psychotherapy, support systems, and crisis/safety planning.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Family history of bipolar disorder, early adult onset, and recurrent mood episodes.
  • Sleep deprivation, postpartum period, major stress, seasonal changes, and substance use.
  • Antidepressant use without a mood stabilizer can precipitate mania in susceptible clients.
  • Medication nonadherence, dehydration or sodium changes with lithium, and poor follow-up.
  • Mixed features, psychosis, prior suicide attempt, and comorbid substance use increase safety risk.

Expected Findings

Manic episode (must last ≥ 1 week or require hospitalization):

  • Elevated, expansive, or irritable mood
  • Increased goal-directed activity or energy
  • ↓ need for sleep (feels rested after 2-3 hr)
  • Pressured speech, flight of ideas, racing thoughts
  • Grandiosity, inflated self-esteem
  • Distractibility
  • Risk-taking: excessive spending, sexual indiscretions, reckless driving, business ventures
  • Psychotic features possible (delusions, hallucinations)

Hypomanic episode: similar but ≥ 4 days, no marked impairment, no psychosis

Depressive episode: same criteria as MDD

  • Persistent sadness, anhedonia, fatigue
  • Sleep and appetite disturbances
  • Concentration impairment
  • Hopelessness, worthlessness, suicidal ideation

Laboratory Tests

  • Lithium level, renal function, thyroid function, electrolytes, and pregnancy test when lithium is used.
  • Valproate level, liver function tests, CBC/platelets, and pregnancy test when valproate is used.
  • Carbamazepine level, CBC, liver function tests, and sodium when carbamazepine is used.
  • Weight/BMI, fasting glucose/A1c, and lipids for atypical antipsychotics.
  • Toxicology screen when substance use may contribute to mood symptoms.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Mental status examination and mood-episode assessment using DSM criteria.
  • Suicide, homicide, psychosis, impulsivity, and ability-to-care-for-self assessment.
  • Medication history, adherence review, and trigger review including sleep and substance use.
  • Standardized mood screening tools when used by the setting.
  • Assessment for medical or substance-induced causes of mood symptoms.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Institute suicide precautions and close observation when risk is present.
  • Provide a low-stimulation environment during acute mania and set clear, consistent limits.
  • Monitor hydration, sodium intake, lithium toxicity symptoms, and medication adverse effects.
  • Reduce access to means of self-harm and involve support persons when appropriate.

Complications

  • Suicide, self-injury, risky behavior, financial/sexual/legal consequences, or impaired judgment during mania.
  • Psychosis, severe agitation, exhaustion, dehydration, or inability to meet basic needs.
  • Lithium toxicity, renal/thyroid effects, valproate hepatotoxicity, carbamazepine blood dyscrasias, or antipsychotic metabolic/EPS effects.
  • Relapse from nonadherence, substance use, antidepressant monotherapy, or disrupted sleep.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

  • Assess mood, sleep, energy, judgment, psychosis, safety, medication adherence, and substance use.
  • During mania, reduce stimulation, set limits, offer high-calorie finger foods, and protect sleep/rest.
  • Monitor lithium/anticonvulsant/antipsychotic adverse effects and required labs.
  • Hold lithium and notify provider for toxicity signs such as vomiting, diarrhea, ataxia, coarse tremor, confusion, or severe sedation.
  • Support safety planning, relapse-prevention teaching, and follow-up care.

Medications

  • Mood stabilizers: lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine depending on episode pattern and client factors.
  • Atypical antipsychotics can treat acute mania, psychosis, and maintenance needs.
  • Benzodiazepines may be used short term for severe agitation or insomnia.
  • Avoid antidepressant monotherapy because it can precipitate mania or rapid cycling.
  • Monitor medication-specific labs, pregnancy risks, toxicity, and adherence.

Client Education

  • Maintain 2–3 L fluid intake daily
  • Maintain consistent sodium intake
  • When vomiting/diarrhea/fever/heavy sweating: hold lithium and notify provider
  • AVOID NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors
  • Carry a medical alert
  • Schedule routine lithium levels and follow up

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Psychotherapy, psychoeducation, family-focused therapy, CBT, and interpersonal/social rhythm therapy.
  • Hospitalization for severe mania, psychosis, suicidal risk, or inability to maintain safety.
  • ECT may be considered for severe depression, catatonia, psychosis, or urgent symptoms when medication response is inadequate.
  • Relapse-prevention plans, sleep-rhythm stabilization, and substance-use treatment when indicated.

Interprofessional Care

  • Psychiatric provider manages diagnosis, mood-stabilizing medications, and acute safety needs.
  • Therapist supports coping skills, relapse prevention, and family education.
  • Pharmacist reviews interactions, lithium/anticonvulsant monitoring, and adverse effect prevention.
  • Social worker/case manager supports access to care, crisis resources, insurance, housing, and follow-up.
  • Family/support persons help monitor early relapse signs and medication adherence when appropriate.
Worked Example Psychotic Disorders Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Psychotic Disorders
Review Module Chapter
Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Psychotic Disorders — characterized by loss of contact with reality:

  • Schizophrenia: chronic psychotic disorder with positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms ≥ 6 months
  • Schizophreniform disorder: schizophrenia-like symptoms 1-6 months
  • Brief psychotic disorder: < 1 month, often stress-related
  • Schizoaffective disorder: psychotic + mood disorder features
  • Delusional disorder: persistent non-bizarre delusions; otherwise functional
  • Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder
  • Onset typically late teens to early 30s; earlier and more severe in men

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Multifactorial: genetic predisposition + environmental triggers
  • Strong genetic component: 50% concordance in identical twins; multiple genes implicated
  • Neurochemical:
    • Dopamine hyperactivity in mesolimbic pathway → positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions)
    • Dopamine hypoactivity in mesocortical pathway → negative symptoms and cognitive impairment
    • Glutamate, serotonin, and GABA also involved
  • Structural brain changes: enlarged ventricles, reduced gray matter, reduced hippocampal volume
  • Neurodevelopmental hypothesis: early disruptions in brain development with manifestation in adolescence/young adulthood
  • Environmental factors: prenatal infection or malnutrition, perinatal complications, childhood trauma, cannabis use (esp. heavy, early-life)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote consistent antipsychotic adherence and early reporting of relapse warning signs.
  • Avoid cannabis, stimulants, alcohol misuse, and sleep deprivation that can worsen psychosis.
  • Encourage structured routine, stress reduction, social support, and follow-up mental health care.
  • Support nutrition, activity, metabolic monitoring, and smoking-cessation resources when appropriate.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Family history of psychotic disorder and adolescent/young adult onset.
  • Prenatal/perinatal complications, childhood trauma, and high-stress environments.
  • Cannabis or stimulant use, especially early and heavy use.
  • Medication nonadherence, poor insight, homelessness, isolation, and limited support.
  • History of suicide attempt, command hallucinations, severe depression, or substance use increases safety risk.

Expected Findings

Positive symptoms (excesses):
