  • Hallucinations — auditory most common (voices), also visual, tactile, olfactory, gustatory
  • Delusions — fixed false beliefs (persecutory, grandiose, referential, religious, somatic)
  • Disorganized speech — loose associations, tangentiality, neologisms, word salad
  • Disorganized or catatonic behavior

Negative symptoms (deficits):

  • Affective flattening — diminished emotional expression
  • Alogia — poverty of speech
  • Avolition — lack of motivation
  • Anhedonia — inability to experience pleasure
  • Asociality — lack of interest in social interactions

Cognitive symptoms: impaired attention, working memory, executive function

Functional decline in work, school, relationships, self-care

Laboratory Tests

  • CBC/ANC for clozapine therapy and when infection or blood dyscrasia is a concern.
  • Fasting glucose/A1c, lipids, weight/BMI, and waist circumference for metabolic monitoring.
  • Liver and renal function as indicated for medication selection and safety.
  • Pregnancy test when clinically indicated before medication changes.
  • Toxicology screen when substance-induced psychosis is possible.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Mental status examination assessing hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, negative symptoms, cognition, insight, and judgment.
  • Suicide, violence, command hallucination, self-care, and safety assessment.
  • DSM-based diagnostic evaluation and review of duration, functional decline, mood symptoms, and substance/medical causes.
  • AIMS or other movement-disorder screening for antipsychotic adverse effects.
  • Medication adherence and relapse-pattern review.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Assess command hallucinations, suicidal/homicidal ideation, paranoia, agitation, and ability to meet basic needs.
  • Use a calm, low-stimulation environment and clear, simple communication.
  • Do not argue with delusions; acknowledge the client's feelings while presenting reality-based support.
  • Monitor for antipsychotic adverse effects including EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS, metabolic syndrome, and clozapine agranulocytosis.

Complications

  • Suicide, self-neglect, victimization, homelessness, social isolation, and impaired functioning.
  • Relapse, hospitalization, or unsafe behavior related to untreated psychosis or nonadherence.
  • Extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, QT prolongation, and sedation.
  • Clozapine-associated agranulocytosis, myocarditis, seizures, or severe constipation.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

  • Assess hallucinations, delusions, thought process, mood, cognition, insight, judgment, self-care, and safety risk.
  • Use therapeutic communication, short concrete statements, and reality-based support without arguing about delusions.
  • Maintain safety, reduce stimulation, and monitor for suicide risk or command hallucinations.
  • Monitor medication adherence and adverse effects including EPS, metabolic changes, NMS, and clozapine warning signs.
  • Support coping strategies, relapse-prevention planning, and follow-up care.

Medications

  • First-generation antipsychotics treat positive symptoms but carry higher EPS/tardive dyskinesia risk.
  • Second-generation antipsychotics treat positive symptoms and some negative symptoms but require metabolic monitoring.
  • Clozapine can be used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and requires ANC monitoring.
  • Long-acting injectable antipsychotics can support adherence when appropriate.
  • Anticholinergic or other medications may be prescribed for EPS management.

Client Education

  • This is a chronic, treatable condition — long-term management is essential
  • Take antipsychotic medications consistently as prescribed — even when feeling well
  • Non-adherence is the primary cause of relapse
  • Long-acting injectable antipsychotics may improve adherence (every 2-4 weeks or longer)
  • Recognize early warning signs of relapse (sleep changes, social withdrawal, suspicious thoughts) and have a plan
  • Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs (especially cannabis, methamphetamine — can precipitate psychosis)
  • Build daily routine and structure
  • Engage in supported employment, vocational rehabilitation, social skills training
  • Family education and involvement essential — psychoeducation reduces expressed emotion and relapse
  • Address metabolic side effects of antipsychotics: diet, exercise, regular monitoring
  • Avoid stigma — psychotic disorders are medical illnesses, not personal failings
  • Crisis plan: warning signs, who to contact, safe environment
  • Suicide risk is elevated; address openly; connect with mental health resources
  • Smoking cessation: many clients smoke heavily; affects antipsychotic levels and overall health

Therapeutic Procedures

  • CBT for psychosis, social-skills training, family psychoeducation, and supported employment/education.
  • Hospitalization or crisis stabilization for danger to self/others, severe psychosis, or inability to care for self.
  • ECT may be used for catatonia or severe treatment-resistant symptoms in selected cases.
  • Community mental health follow-up, case management, and relapse-prevention planning.

Interprofessional Care

  • Psychiatric provider manages diagnosis, medication selection, safety, and treatment response.
  • Therapist supports coping skills, reality testing, family education, and relapse prevention.
  • Pharmacist reviews antipsychotic adverse effects, interactions, long-acting injectable schedules, and clozapine monitoring.
  • Social worker/case manager supports housing, benefits, follow-up appointments, crisis resources, and adherence barriers.
  • Primary care monitors metabolic and cardiovascular health affected by antipsychotic therapy.
Worked Example ADHD in Children and Adolescents Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 11 — Medications for Children and Adolescents

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) — neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interfere with functioning across multiple settings (school, home, work).

  • DSM-5 requires: ≥ 6 symptoms in children (≥ 5 in adolescents/adults) of inattention OR hyperactivity-impulsivity, present < 12 yr, in ≥ 2 settings, for > 6 months
  • Three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, combined
  • Prevalence ~5–10% in children; persists into adulthood in ~50–65%
  • Boys diagnosed more often; girls often missed (more inattentive presentation)
  • Common comorbidities: learning disabilities, anxiety, depression, ODD, conduct disorder, tic disorders

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Dopamine and norepinephrine dysregulation in prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia — impaired executive function
  • Underactivation of prefrontal cortex → poor attention regulation, working memory, impulse control
  • Altered reward processing → preference for immediate over delayed rewards
  • Genetic component — heritability 70–80%
  • Environmental contributors: prenatal alcohol/tobacco/lead exposure, prematurity, low birth weight, head injury
  • NOT caused by: bad parenting, too much sugar, video games, or food dyes (myths)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote structured routines, consistent expectations, balanced meals, regular sleep/wake times, exercise, planners, alarms, and checklists.
  • Collaborate with school supports such as 504 plan, IEP, preferred seating, written instructions, extended time, and frequent breaks.
  • Teach medication adherence and morning dosing for stimulants when prescribed, while reinforcing that behavioral strategies remain important.
  • Screen and address comorbid learning disabilities, anxiety, depression, ODD, conduct disorder, tic disorders, and adolescent diversion/misuse risk.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess family history/genetic predisposition and symptoms beginning before age 12 in at least two settings.
  • Review environmental contributors such as prenatal alcohol/tobacco/lead exposure, prematurity, low birth weight, and head injury.
  • Screen for common comorbidities including learning disabilities, anxiety, depression, ODD, conduct disorder, and tic disorders.
  • Assess cardiovascular history, appetite/growth concerns, sleep pattern, substance-use/diversion risk, and school/home functioning before and during medication therapy.

Expected Findings

Inattention symptoms:

  • Difficulty sustaining attention; easily distracted
  • Careless mistakes; trouble following instructions
  • Difficulty organizing tasks; loses things; avoids tasks requiring sustained effort
  • Forgetfulness in daily activities

Hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms:

  • Fidgeting, leaving seat, running/climbing inappropriately
  • Unable to play quietly; “driven by a motor”; excessive talking
  • Blurts out answers; difficulty waiting turn; interrupts others

Assessment tools:

  • Vanderbilt ADHD Rating Scale (parents and teachers)
  • Conners Rating Scales
  • NICHQ assessment
  • School observation, academic records, family history

Laboratory Tests

  • No routine laboratory test diagnoses ADHD; diagnosis is clinical and functional across settings.
  • Monitor growth parameters, appetite/weight, BP, pulse, and sleep as medication-safety indicators rather than diagnostic labs.
  • Use additional labs only when ordered to evaluate alternate causes of attention symptoms or medication-safety concerns.
  • Trend adverse-effect findings and school/home reports with medication response to guide therapy adjustment.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use DSM-5 criteria: persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity for more than 6 months, onset before age 12, and impairment in at least two settings.
  • Use parent/teacher rating scales such as Vanderbilt, Conners, or NICHQ to document symptoms and impairment.
  • Review school observation, academic records, family history, and behavior across home and school.
  • Assess for anxiety, depression, learning disorders, sleep problems, substance use, and other conditions that can mimic or worsen ADHD.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Stimulant safety: monitor BP, pulse, appetite, sleep, mood changes, growth concerns, and cardiovascular symptoms.
  • Atomoxetine safety: monitor for suicidal ideation and delayed onset over weeks.
  • Diversion/misuse: teach secure storage and avoid sharing stimulants, especially with adolescents.
  • Functional safety: coordinate with caregivers/school when impulsivity or inattention creates injury, academic, or social risk.

Complications

  • Untreated ADHD can impair academic performance, organization, relationships, self-esteem, and safety due to impulsivity/inattention.
  • Comorbid anxiety, depression, learning disorders, ODD, conduct disorder, tic disorders, and substance-use risk can worsen outcomes.
  • Stimulants can cause appetite suppression, sleep disturbance, growth concerns, cardiovascular symptoms, and mood changes.
  • Medication diversion, missed follow-up, or inconsistent routines can reduce treatment benefit.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Treatment plan: multimodal — pharmacotherapy + behavioral interventions + school accommodations

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Stimulants (first-line): methylphenidate, amphetamines — 70–80% response rate
  • Non-stimulants: atomoxetine (SNRI), guanfacine ER, clonidine ER — for those who don’t tolerate stimulants or have tic disorder/substance abuse concerns
  • Bupropion (off-label) — especially for comorbid depression

Behavioral interventions:

  • Parent training in behavior management
  • Behavior modification at home and school
  • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (older children, adolescents)
  • Structured routines, consistent expectations

School accommodations:

  • 504 plan or IEP
  • Preferred seating, extended time, frequent breaks
  • Written instructions, organizational support

Medications

  • Stimulants (first-line): methylphenidate, amphetamines — 70–80% response rate
  • Non-stimulants: atomoxetine (SNRI), guanfacine ER, clonidine ER — for those who don’t tolerate stimulants or have tic disorder/substance abuse concerns
  • Bupropion (off-label) — especially for comorbid depression

Behavioral interventions:

  • Parent training in behavior management
  • Behavior modification at home and school
  • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (older children, adolescents)
  • Structured routines, consistent expectations

School accommodations:

  • 504 plan or IEP
  • Preferred seating, extended time, frequent breaks
  • Written instructions, organizational support

Client Education

  • ADHD is a medical condition — not laziness or poor parenting
  • Medication helps regulate brain function but is not a cure; behavioral strategies remain important
  • Stimulants: report cardiovascular symptoms, mood changes, growth concerns; take in the morning; balanced meals important
  • Non-stimulants: longer onset (weeks); monitor for suicidal ideation in atomoxetine
  • Set up routines: consistent sleep/wake times, balanced meals, exercise
  • Use planners, alarms, checklists, organizers
  • Collaborate with school: share rating scale results, accommodations
  • Address co-occurring conditions (anxiety, learning disabilities)
  • Adolescents: avoid stimulant diversion/misuse; substance abuse risk is real
  • Long-term outlook: many do well with treatment; ADHD often persists but symptoms can be managed

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Behavioral therapy, parent training in behavior management, and school-based behavior plans are core interventions with medication.
  • School accommodations can include 504 plan/IEP, preferred seating, written instructions, organizational supports, extended time, and breaks.
  • CBT can help older children/adolescents with planning, organization, and coping skills.
  • Medication monitoring visits should review symptom ratings, growth/appetite, BP/pulse, sleep, mood, and school/home reports.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with prescriber, pharmacist, parents/caregivers, teachers, school nurse, counselor, and psychologist/behavioral therapist.
  • Use school-based teams for rating scales, 504/IEP supports, accommodations, and progress tracking.
  • Refer to behavioral health for comorbid anxiety/depression, tic disorder, conduct concerns, substance-use/diversion risk, or suicidal ideation.
  • Communicate medication response, side effects, growth/BP/pulse trends, adherence barriers, and school/home functioning.
Worked Example Glaucoma Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders · Glaucoma meds section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Glaucoma
Review Module Chapter
Ch 14 — Eye and Ear Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Glaucoma — a group of progressive eye diseases characterized by optic nerve damage, typically associated with elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), leading to irreversible vision loss starting peripheral and progressing centrally.

Two main types:

  • Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG) — most common (90%); painless, gradual peripheral vision loss; often asymptomatic until late; bilateral
  • Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma — medical emergency; sudden severe eye pain, headache, nausea, halos around lights, fixed mid-dilated pupil; can cause blindness within hours if untreated

Normal IOP: 10–21 mmHg. Glaucoma diagnosis based on optic nerve appearance, visual field testing, and IOP — not IOP alone (normal-tension glaucoma exists).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • POAG: resistance to aqueous humor outflow through trabecular meshwork → gradual IOP elevation → optic nerve damage
  • Angle-closure: peripheral iris blocks trabecular meshwork (narrow anterior chamber angle) → sudden, severe IOP rise
  • Elevated IOP compresses optic nerve fibers and blood vessels → ischemia → cell death
  • Optic disc cupping develops; nerve fibers lost progressively
  • Risk factors: age > 60, African or Asian ancestry, family history, diabetes, high myopia, prolonged corticosteroid use, eye trauma

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote routine eye exams for at-risk clients, especially older adults and clients with family history, diabetes, high myopia, prolonged corticosteroid use, or eye trauma.
  • Teach lifelong adherence with prescribed eye drops even when vision feels normal because glaucoma can be asymptomatic until late.
  • Reinforce proper eye-drop technique, punctal occlusion, spacing multiple drops by at least 5 min, and bringing all eye medications to follow-up visits.
  • Teach family screening and immediate reporting of sudden eye pain, halos, severe headache, nausea, or vision change.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Age >60 years, family history, African or Asian ancestry, diabetes, high myopia, eye trauma, and prolonged corticosteroid use increase glaucoma risk.
  • Narrow anterior chamber angle increases risk for acute angle-closure glaucoma.
  • Medication history matters: anticholinergics, some antihistamines, and sympathomimetics can precipitate angle-closure in susceptible clients.
  • Assess adherence barriers because missed eye-drop therapy can allow IOP to rise without obvious early symptoms.

Expected Findings

POAG (chronic):

  • Often asymptomatic in early stages
  • Gradual loss of peripheral vision (“tunnel vision” in late stage)
  • Mild eye discomfort, frequent prescription changes
  • IOP > 21 mmHg (often)
  • Optic disc cupping on fundoscopy
  • Visual field defects on perimetry

Angle-closure (acute — emergency):

  • Sudden severe eye pain, headache
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Blurred vision, halos around lights
  • Fixed mid-dilated pupil; eye feels hard on palpation
  • Conjunctival injection (red eye)
  • IOP often > 40 mmHg

Laboratory Tests

  • No routine laboratory test diagnoses glaucoma; diagnosis and monitoring are primarily ophthalmic.
  • If systemic acetazolamide or mannitol is used, monitor renal function and electrolytes as ordered because these agents affect fluid/electrolyte balance.
  • For clients with diabetes, trend glucose control as part of overall risk management and medication-safety review.
  • Report abnormal medication-safety labs or dehydration findings that could increase systemic therapy risk.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Measure intraocular pressure; normal IOP is about 10-21 mmHg, but glaucoma diagnosis is not based on IOP alone.
  • Assess optic nerve appearance for optic disc cupping and progressive nerve damage.
  • Use visual field testing/perimetry to detect peripheral field loss and progression.
  • Evaluate for acute angle-closure findings: fixed mid-dilated pupil, hard eye, halos, severe pain, nausea/vomiting, and markedly elevated IOP.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Acute angle-closure warning: sudden severe eye pain, vision changes, halos, severe headache, nausea, or vomiting needs immediate ophthalmology/emergency care because blindness can occur rapidly.
  • Eye-drop safety: teach correct instillation and punctal occlusion, especially with timolol, to reduce systemic absorption.
  • Medication precautions: monitor pulse and respiratory symptoms with timolol; use asthma/COPD/diabetes caution; teach latanoprost eye-color/eyelash changes and acetazolamide sulfonamide-allergy caution.
  • Vision safety: reinforce fall prevention and home safety for peripheral vision loss.

Complications

  • Progressive optic nerve damage with permanent peripheral vision loss that can advance to central vision loss or blindness.
  • Acute angle-closure glaucoma can cause rapid, irreversible blindness if IOP is not lowered quickly.
  • Medication-related harm includes timolol-related bradycardia or bronchospasm, latanoprost-related iris/eyelash changes, and acetazolamide sulfonamide-type hypersensitivity concern.
  • Peripheral vision loss increases fall and injury risk.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

POAG treatment:

  • Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost, bimatoprost) — FIRST-LINE
  • Beta blockers (timolol) — second-line; systemic absorption can cause bradycardia, bronchospasm
  • Alpha agonists (brimonidine), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide), miotics (pilocarpine)
  • Laser trabeculoplasty if drops insufficient
  • Surgical: trabeculectomy, drainage devices

Angle-closure (EMERGENCY):

  • Immediate ophthalmology consult
  • IV mannitol (osmotic), IV acetazolamide (CAI) to rapidly lower IOP
  • Topical miotics (pilocarpine) once IOP lowered
  • Topical beta blocker, alpha agonist
  • Definitive: laser peripheral iridotomy

Nursing care:

  • Routine eye exams for at-risk populations (annual after age 40, more frequent if positive family history)
  • Teach eye drop technique and adherence
  • Avoid medications that can trigger angle-closure (anticholinergics, some antihistamines, sympathomimetics) in susceptible clients
  • Falls prevention for peripheral vision loss

Medications

  • Timolol (beta blocker): decreases aqueous humor production to lower IOP; apply punctal occlusion for 30-60 sec, monitor pulse, and use caution with asthma/COPD or diabetes due to systemic bradycardia/bronchospasm risk.
  • Brimonidine (alpha2 agonist): decreases aqueous humor production and increases outflow; used as a first-line option for primary open-angle glaucoma; can cause stinging and dry mouth.
  • Latanoprost (prostaglandin analog): increases aqueous humor outflow; teach possible permanent brown iris pigmentation and eyelash growth, and to report eye changes.
  • Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor): reduces aqueous humor production through diuresis; use sulfonamide-allergy caution.
  • Mannitol and pilocarpine: mannitol rapidly lowers IOP in acute angle-closure glaucoma; pilocarpine constricts the pupil to improve outflow.

Client Education

  • Vision loss from glaucoma is permanent — goal is to PREVENT further loss
  • Medications must be taken EXACTLY as prescribed, lifelong
  • Do not stop drops even if vision feels normal (asymptomatic disease)
  • Schedule regular eye exams: IOP measurement, visual fields, optic nerve imaging
  • Learn proper instillation technique with punctal occlusion
  • Multiple drops: space by ≥ 5 minutes
  • Family members should be screened (genetic component)
  • Seek immediate care for sudden eye pain, vision changes, halos, severe headache, nausea (signs of angle-closure)
  • Avoid activities that increase IOP excessively: heavy lifting, prolonged head-down position; specific activity restrictions depend on type and severity
  • Inform all providers of glaucoma diagnosis (drug list checks)
  • Vision aids and home modifications for safety

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Laser trabeculoplasty: may be used when drops are insufficient for open-angle glaucoma.
  • Trabeculectomy or drainage devices: surgical options for inadequate IOP control despite medication/laser therapy.
  • Laser peripheral iridotomy: definitive procedure for angle-closure glaucoma after urgent IOP-lowering measures.
  • Prepare the client for ophthalmology-directed procedures, reinforce medication continuation as ordered, and monitor/report post-procedure pain, vision change, or rising IOP symptoms.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate urgently with ophthalmology for acute angle-closure symptoms and for laser or surgical management when medication is insufficient.
  • Work with the pharmacist to review glaucoma-drop technique, duplicate therapy, contraindications, systemic absorption risk, and sulfonamide-allergy caution with acetazolamide.
  • Involve vision services, low-vision resources, and fall-prevention support when peripheral vision loss affects safety.
  • Communicate IOP trends, visual-field changes, adherence barriers, and adverse effects across the care team.
Worked Example Insomnia Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Insomnia
Review Module Chapter
Ch 16 — Sedative-Hypnotics

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Insomnia — difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, or non-restorative sleep that causes daytime impairment, despite adequate sleep opportunity.

  • DSM-5 requires: dissatisfaction with sleep quality/quantity + ≥ 1 of (difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, early morning awakening); ≥ 3 nights/week for ≥ 3 months; significant impairment
  • Acute: < 3 months (often triggered by stress)
  • Chronic: ≥ 3 months
  • Comorbid: with another medical or psychiatric condition (most common)
  • Prevalence: ~10–30% chronic; higher in women, older adults, shift workers

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Hyperarousal model: physiologic (elevated HR, cortisol), cognitive (rumination), and emotional (anxiety) hyperarousal
  • Dysregulation of sleep-wake cycle (suprachiasmatic nucleus)
  • Altered neurotransmitter balance: reduced GABA, elevated orexin/CRH
  • Conditioned arousal — bedroom becomes associated with wakefulness
  • Genetic predisposition — heritability 30–40%
  • Triggers: stress, life events, medical conditions, medications, environment

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Maintain a consistent bedtime and wake time, including weekends, and protect a dark, cool, quiet sleep environment.
  • Limit caffeine after noon, avoid alcohol as a sleep aid, stop screens 30–60 min before bed, and keep naps shorter than 30 min before 3 PM.
  • Use CBT-I strategies first when available: stimulus control, sleep restriction, relaxation, cognitive restructuring, and sleep hygiene.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Stress, life events, shift work, poor sleep habits, and environmental disruption can trigger acute or chronic insomnia.
  • Comorbid depression, anxiety, pain, GERD, sleep apnea, and periodic limb movement disorder can sustain sleep disruption.
  • Older adults and clients using CNS depressants, anticholinergic OTC sleep aids, caffeine, alcohol, or interacting medications need focused safety review.

Expected Findings

Nighttime symptoms:

  • Prolonged sleep latency (> 30 min to fall asleep)
  • Frequent awakenings; difficulty returning to sleep
  • Early morning awakening (cannot return to sleep)
  • Reduced total sleep time
  • Non-restorative sleep

Daytime impairment:

  • Fatigue, sleepiness
  • Concentration and memory problems
  • Mood disturbance (irritability, depression, anxiety)
  • Reduced motivation, productivity
  • Increased errors, accidents
  • Social/occupational impairment

Assessment tools:

  • Sleep diary (gold standard for outpatient assessment, 2 weeks)
  • Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) — standardized scale
  • Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index
  • Polysomnography (only if suspect other sleep disorder — apnea, periodic limb movements)

Laboratory Tests

  • Insomnia is diagnosed clinically; no routine lab test confirms the disorder.
  • Review targeted laboratory results only when symptoms suggest a contributing condition or when medication safety requires renal or hepatic review.
  • Trend findings with sleep diary data and daytime impairment rather than treating an isolated lab value as diagnostic for insomnia.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use a 2-week sleep diary as the practical outpatient baseline for sleep latency, awakenings, wake time, naps, and triggers.
  • Use standardized tools such as the Insomnia Severity Index or Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index to track severity and response.
  • Reserve polysomnography for suspected sleep apnea, periodic limb movements, or another sleep disorder rather than routine uncomplicated insomnia.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Keep hypnotics short term when prescribed and monitor for next-day sedation, impaired driving, falls, confusion, tolerance, and dependence.
  • Avoid benzodiazepines and diphenhydramine in older adults when possible because of fall risk, cognitive effects, and anticholinergic burden.
  • Teach clients to avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants with sleep medications and to report complex sleep behaviors or severe mood changes promptly.

Complications

  • Daytime fatigue, impaired concentration, mood disturbance, reduced productivity, errors, accidents, and social or occupational impairment.
  • Worsening depression, anxiety, pain, GERD, sleep apnea, or other comorbid conditions when the underlying driver is missed.
  • Medication-related harm, including falls, oversedation, rebound insomnia, tolerance, dependence, and unsafe OTC antihistamine use.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

FIRST-LINE: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) — more effective long-term than medications. Components: sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relaxation, sleep hygiene.

Pharmacotherapy (short-term, when CBT-I inaccessible or inadequate):

  • Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone, zaleplon) — preferred over benzodiazepines
  • Benzodiazepines (temazepam, triazolam) — high addiction risk; avoid in older adults
  • Melatonin agonist (ramelteon) — non-controlled; preferred when worry about dependence
  • Orexin receptor antagonists (suvorexant, lemborexant) — newer; for chronic insomnia
  • Sedating antidepressants (trazodone, doxepin low-dose, mirtazapine) — off-label; useful if comorbid depression
  • Antihistamines (diphenhydramine) — OTC; AVOID in older adults (anticholinergic burden, Beers list)
  • Melatonin (OTC) — mild effect; safe for short-term

Sleep hygiene principles:

  • Consistent bedtime and wake time (including weekends)
  • Dark, cool, quiet bedroom
  • No electronic screens 30–60 min before bed
  • No caffeine after noon; limit alcohol (disrupts sleep)
  • Regular exercise (not late evening)
  • Bedroom for sleep only (not work, TV, eating)
  • If unable to sleep in 20 min: get up, do quiet activity, return when sleepy

Medications

  • Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone, zaleplon) — preferred over benzodiazepines
  • Benzodiazepines (temazepam, triazolam) — high addiction risk; avoid in older adults
  • Melatonin agonist (ramelteon) — non-controlled; preferred when worry about dependence
  • Orexin receptor antagonists (suvorexant, lemborexant) — newer; for chronic insomnia
  • Sedating antidepressants (trazodone, doxepin low-dose, mirtazapine) — off-label; useful if comorbid depression
  • Antihistamines (diphenhydramine) — OTC; AVOID in older adults (anticholinergic burden, Beers list)
  • Melatonin (OTC) — mild effect; safe for short-term

Sleep hygiene principles:

  • Consistent bedtime and wake time (including weekends)
  • Dark, cool, quiet bedroom
  • No electronic screens 30–60 min before bed
  • No caffeine after noon; limit alcohol (disrupts sleep)
  • Regular exercise (not late evening)
  • Bedroom for sleep only (not work, TV, eating)
  • If unable to sleep in 20 min: get up, do quiet activity, return when sleepy

Client Education

  • Sleep is a learned behavior; sleep hygiene matters
  • CBT-I is highly effective and durable — consider before medications
  • If medications used: short-term only (weeks, not months)
  • Avoid alcohol as sleep aid — worsens sleep architecture
  • Caffeine half-life is 6–8 hours — limit after noon
  • Address underlying causes: depression, anxiety, pain, GERD, sleep apnea
  • Older adults: most sleep aids are riskier; consider behavioral interventions, melatonin, ramelteon
  • Track sleep with a diary or app to identify patterns
  • Manage stress with relaxation techniques, mindfulness, exercise
  • Naps should be < 30 min and before 3 PM
  • Light exposure in morning helps regulate circadian rhythm
  • Seek evaluation for snoring/gasping (sleep apnea) or leg movements (PLMD)

Therapeutic Procedures

  • CBT-I is first-line and includes stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring, relaxation, and sleep hygiene coaching.
  • Use polysomnography only when assessment suggests sleep apnea, periodic limb movements, or another sleep disorder requiring specialist evaluation.
  • Prepare the client for behavioral therapy follow-up and reinforce sleep diary tracking between visits.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the prescriber and pharmacist to choose the safest short-term medication plan and check CNS depressant, alcohol, and OTC interactions.
  • Refer to CBT-I, behavioral health, or counseling when anxiety, depression, stress, or maladaptive sleep beliefs are sustaining insomnia.
  • Involve a sleep specialist when snoring, gasping, periodic limb movements, refractory insomnia, or diagnostic uncertainty is present.
Worked Example Angina Pectoris Ch 22 — Angina · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Angina Pectoris
Review Module Chapter
Ch 22 — Angina

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Angina Pectoris — chest pain or discomfort resulting from myocardial ischemia (oxygen demand exceeds supply), usually due to coronary artery disease.

Types:

  • Stable (exertional) angina: predictable; triggered by exertion/stress; relieved by rest or nitroglycerin; < 15 min
  • Unstable angina: new, worsening, or at rest; medical emergency; part of acute coronary syndrome (ACS); NOT relieved predictably
  • Variant (Prinzmetal) angina: coronary vasospasm; often at rest, cyclical; responds to calcium channel blockers

Unstable angina vs MI: angina has no/minimal troponin elevation; MI has myocardial necrosis (elevated troponin).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Atherosclerosis narrows coronary arteries → reduced blood flow
  • When myocardial oxygen demand (exertion, stress, tachycardia) exceeds supply → ischemia → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid → pain
  • Stable: fixed plaque; ischemia only with increased demand
  • Unstable: plaque rupture → partial thrombus → ischemia at rest (impending MI)
  • Variant: coronary artery spasm (may have minimal atherosclerosis)
  • Risk factors: smoking, HTN, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, obesity, family history, sedentary lifestyle

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Reduce myocardial oxygen demand and ASCVD risk through smoking cessation, heart-healthy diet, regular activity as tolerated, weight management, stress reduction, and cardiac rehabilitation.
  • Control hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia and reinforce adherence with antiplatelet, cholesterol-lowering, ACE-inhibitor, and antianginal therapy when prescribed.
  • Teach the client to carry nitroglycerin, store it correctly, and use it before known triggers when prescribed.
  • Reinforce emergency action for new, worsening, rest, prolonged, or unrelieved chest pain.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess CAD risk factors: smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, family history, and older age.
  • Identify demand triggers such as exertion, emotional stress, tachycardia, cold exposure, and sexual activity.
  • Screen for variant-angina pattern at rest and for unstable-angina symptoms that are new, worsening, or not predictably relieved.
  • Review medication history for nitrate interactions, especially PDE5 inhibitors, and ranolazine interaction risks.

Expected Findings

Symptoms:

  • Substernal chest pain/pressure (“squeezing,” “tightness,” “elephant on chest”)
  • Radiation to left arm, jaw, neck, back, shoulder
  • Dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea
  • Anxiety, sense of doom
  • Atypical presentations (women, older adults, diabetics): fatigue, indigestion, jaw/back pain, dyspnea without chest pain

Diagnostic:

  • 12-lead EKG: ST depression or T-wave inversion (ischemia); transient ST elevation (variant)
  • Cardiac biomarkers (troponin) — to differentiate from MI
  • Stress testing (exercise or pharmacologic)
  • Coronary angiography (definitive for CAD extent)
  • Lipid panel, fasting glucose, CBC

Laboratory Tests

  • Use cardiac biomarkers, especially troponin, to help distinguish angina from myocardial infarction during new or worsening symptoms.
  • Monitor lipid panel and fasting glucose because hyperlipidemia and diabetes are major modifiable CAD risks.
  • Review CBC and other ordered labs when evaluating chest pain, oxygen delivery, or medication safety.
  • For ranolazine, monitor electrolytes such as potassium when clinically indicated because hypokalemia increases dysrhythmia/QT risk.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Obtain a 12-lead ECG during symptoms; ischemia can show ST depression, T-wave inversion, or transient ST elevation with variant angina.
  • Use exercise or pharmacologic stress testing to evaluate inducible ischemia when ordered.
  • Coronary angiography can define CAD extent and guide revascularization decisions.
  • Monitor ECG with ranolazine therapy when QT prolongation risk is present or suspected.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Unrelieved angina: if pain is not relieved after the first sublingual nitroglycerin dose or is new/worsening, activate emergency response because ACS/MI must be ruled out.
  • Nitrate safety: monitor for headache, dizziness from hypotension, and rebound tachycardia; teach the client not to use sustained-release oral nitroglycerin to abort an acute attack.
  • Ranolazine safety: monitor ECG for QT prolongation/torsades risk and BP; avoid use with prolonged QT, hepatic impairment, ventricular dysrhythmias, hypokalemia, or QT-prolonging drugs.
  • Interaction safety: avoid PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates and review interacting drugs such as verapamil, digoxin, and simvastatin when ranolazine is used.

Complications

  • Untreated or worsening myocardial ischemia can progress to acute coronary syndrome, myocardial infarction, dysrhythmia, heart failure, or death.
  • Nitroglycerin can cause headache, hypotension-related dizziness, and rebound tachycardia; persistent effects should be reported for dose or regimen review.
  • Ranolazine can prolong QT and increase risk for torsades de pointes; report palpitations, chest pain, or dyspnea.
  • Poor adherence to antiplatelet, lipid-lowering, ACE-inhibitor, or antianginal therapy can increase MI and mortality risk in chronic stable angina.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Acute angina episode:

  • Stop activity, rest, sit or lie down
  • Administer sublingual nitroglycerin (up to 3 doses, 5 min apart)
  • Oxygen if hypoxic (SpO2 < 90%)
  • 12-lead EKG; assess pain (PQRST); vital signs
  • If pain unrelieved after first NTG or new/worsening: call 911 / activate emergency response (possible ACS)
  • Aspirin (chewed) for suspected ACS

Chronic pharmacotherapy:

  • Nitrates (nitroglycerin) — acute relief and prophylaxis (long-acting)
  • Beta blockers — reduce HR and contractility → reduced O2 demand (first-line chronic)
  • Calcium channel blockers — vasodilation; first-line for variant angina
  • Ranolazine — chronic stable angina (adjunct)
  • Antiplatelet (aspirin, clopidogrel) — prevent thrombosis
  • Statins — plaque stabilization, lipid lowering
  • ACE inhibitors if HTN/diabetes/HF

Revascularization: PCI (stent) or CABG for significant CAD.

Medications

  • Organic nitrates: relieve or prevent angina by improving myocardial oxygen supply/demand; sublingual nitroglycerin treats an acute attack, while oral sustained-release and transdermal forms are for prevention.
  • Beta blockers and calcium channel blockers: reduce myocardial oxygen demand for long-term angina control.
  • Ranolazine: used for chronic stable angina with amlodipine, a beta blocker, or an organic nitrate; monitor ECG for QT prolongation/torsades risk and monitor BP.
  • Chronic stable angina adjuncts: antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel), a cholesterol-lowering agent, and an ACE inhibitor help reduce MI and death risk.
  • Safety: avoid ranolazine with prolonged QT, hepatic impairment, ventricular dysrhythmias, hypokalemia, or other QT-prolonging drugs; teach to report palpitations, chest pain, or dyspnea.

Client Education

  • Recognize angina vs emergency: stable pattern relieved by rest/NTG is expected; new, worsening, prolonged, or rest pain = call 911
  • Sublingual NTG protocol: 1 tablet under tongue; if no relief in 5 min, call 911, may take up to 3 doses 5 min apart
  • Carry NTG at all times; store in original dark glass container; replace every 6 months
  • Take NTG prophylactically before known triggers (exertion, sex, cold exposure)
  • Lifestyle: smoking cessation, heart-healthy diet, regular exercise (as tolerated), weight management, stress reduction
  • Control comorbidities: HTN, diabetes, hyperlipidemia
  • Take aspirin and statins as prescribed
  • Recognize MI symptoms; act FAST
  • Cardiac rehabilitation participation
  • Avoid PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) with nitrates (fatal hypotension)

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Acute evaluation: obtain/prepare for 12-lead ECG and cardiac biomarker testing when symptoms are new, worsening, or unrelieved by nitroglycerin.
  • Coronary angiography: may be used to define CAD extent when stress testing or symptoms indicate significant disease.
  • Revascularization: PCI with stent placement or CABG can be used for significant CAD when medication therapy is insufficient or disease severity warrants it.
  • Reinforce cardiac rehabilitation and risk-factor modification after revascularization or ACS evaluation.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider/cardiology team for acute chest pain evaluation, medication adjustment, stress testing, angiography, PCI, CABG, or cardiac rehabilitation.
  • Work with the pharmacist to verify nitrate form/use, screen PDE5 inhibitor and ranolazine interactions, and review antiplatelet/statin/ACE-inhibitor therapy.
  • Involve dietitian, diabetes educator, smoking-cessation resources, and cardiac rehabilitation for risk-factor reduction.
  • Communicate pain pattern, nitroglycerin response, ECG/lab findings, BP/HR trends, and adverse effects promptly.
Worked Example Hyperlipidemia / Dyslipidemia Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Hyperlipidemia / Dyslipidemia
Review Module Chapter
Ch 24 — Antilipemic Agents

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Hyperlipidemia / Dyslipidemia — abnormal levels of lipids (cholesterol, triglycerides) in the blood, a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

Lipid components:

  • LDL (“bad”): primary target; optimal < 100 mg/dL (< 70 for high risk)
  • HDL (“good”): protective; desirable ≥ 60 mg/dL; low < 40 (men) / < 50 (women)
  • Triglycerides: normal < 150 mg/dL; very high > 500 (pancreatitis risk)
  • Total cholesterol: desirable < 200 mg/dL

Often asymptomatic; detected on screening lipid panel. May be primary (genetic, e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia) or secondary (diet, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, medications).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Elevated LDL deposits cholesterol in arterial walls → atherosclerotic plaque formation
  • Plaque narrows arteries → reduced perfusion (CAD, PAD, cerebrovascular disease)
  • Plaque rupture → thrombosis → MI, stroke
  • Low HDL reduces reverse cholesterol transport (removal from tissues)
  • High triglycerides contribute to atherogenesis; very high levels → pancreatitis
  • Genetic factors (LDL receptor defects), diet (saturated/trans fats), obesity, sedentary lifestyle, diabetes, metabolic syndrome

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote therapeutic lifestyle changes: heart-healthy diet, reduced saturated/trans fats, increased fiber, fruits/vegetables/whole grains/fish, regular aerobic exercise, weight management, and smoking cessation.
  • Reinforce that hyperlipidemia is often asymptomatic, so medication adherence and lab follow-up prevent future ASCVD events.
  • Limit alcohol when triglycerides are elevated and manage related conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, hypothyroidism, and metabolic syndrome.
  • Encourage family screening when early, severe, or familial hypercholesterolemia features are present.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess dietary saturated/trans fat intake, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, smoking, hypertension, and alcohol use.
  • Screen for primary/genetic causes such as familial hypercholesterolemia, especially with very high LDL or premature ASCVD/family history.
  • Assess secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, liver/renal disease, and medications that worsen lipid levels.
  • Use ASCVD risk factors and 10-year risk estimation to guide intensity of therapy and follow-up teaching.

Expected Findings

Usually asymptomatic. With severe or familial forms:

  • Xanthomas — lipid deposits in skin/tendons
  • Xanthelasma — yellow plaques on eyelids
  • Corneal arcus — gray ring around cornea (premature in young = familial)

Signs of complications:

  • Angina, MI (CAD)
  • Claudication (PAD)
  • TIA/stroke symptoms
  • Acute pancreatitis (very high triglycerides)

Diagnostic:

  • Fasting lipid panel (9–12 hr fast): total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides
  • ASCVD risk calculator (10-year risk)
  • Secondary cause workup: glucose/A1c, TSH, liver/renal function
  • Consider coronary artery calcium score for risk refinement

Laboratory Tests

  • Obtain a fasting lipid panel when ordered: total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides.
  • Check baseline and periodic liver function and kidney function for medication safety, especially with statins, ezetimibe combinations, fibrates, and PCSK9 therapy plans.
  • Monitor glucose/A1c and TSH when evaluating secondary causes or metabolic risk.
  • Repeat lipids after starting or changing therapy and periodically thereafter to evaluate response and adherence.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use ASCVD risk calculation and clinical history to stratify cardiovascular risk and guide therapy intensity.
  • Coronary artery calcium scoring may refine risk when ordered, especially when treatment decisions are uncertain.
  • Assess for physical signs of severe/familial disease such as xanthomas, xanthelasma, and premature corneal arcus.
  • Evaluate complication symptoms such as angina, claudication, TIA/stroke findings, or pancreatitis symptoms when triglycerides are very high.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Asymptomatic condition: reinforce adherence and lab follow-up because clients might not feel abnormal lipid levels or early ASCVD risk.
  • Statin/myopathy warning: report muscle pain, tenderness, weakness, or dark urine; monitor liver function and teach liver-injury symptoms such as jaundice or persistent fatigue.
  • Combination risk: fibrates combined with statins increase myopathy risk; ezetimibe with statins increases liver dysfunction/myopathy monitoring needs.
  • Absorption and GI safety: separate bile-acid sequestrants from other medications and manage constipation with fiber/fluids if not restricted.

Complications

  • Uncontrolled dyslipidemia contributes to atherosclerotic disease, including CAD/angina/MI, PAD with claudication, TIA/stroke, and high-triglyceride pancreatitis.
  • Familial or severe hyperlipidemia can present with xanthomas, xanthelasma, or premature corneal arcus.
  • Medication complications include statin-associated myopathy/rhabdomyolysis, hepatotoxicity, fibrate-associated myopathy risk, bile-acid sequestrant constipation, and absorption interference.
  • Missed monitoring can delay recognition of inadequate lipid response or medication toxicity.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Statin therapy (first-line) based on ASCVD risk:

  • High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg): clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥ 190, diabetes 40–75 yr with high risk, 10-yr risk ≥ 20%
  • Moderate-intensity statin: diabetes, intermediate risk

Add-on / alternative agents:

  • Ezetimibe — add if LDL goal not met on max statin
  • PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) — injectable; for familial or refractory
  • Bile-acid sequestrants (cholestyramine)
  • Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) — primarily for high triglycerides
  • Omega-3 fatty acids / icosapent ethyl — high triglycerides
  • Niacin — less used now (flushing, limited benefit)

Nursing care:

  • Lipid panel monitoring (baseline, 4–12 weeks after starting/changing, then periodically)
  • LFT monitoring with statins
  • Assess for muscle symptoms (statin myopathy)
  • Reinforce lifestyle interventions
  • Medication adherence support (asymptomatic condition)

Medications

  • Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors): primary class for LDL reduction; monitor liver function and muscle symptoms according to the therapy plan.
  • Ezetimibe: decreases cholesterol absorption in the small intestine and is often combined with a statin; take 2 hr before or 4 hr after bile-acid sequestrants.
  • Bile-acid sequestrants (colesevelam, colestipol): decrease LDL; can cause constipation and interfere with other medication absorption, so separate dosing.
  • Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate): primarily lower triglycerides; increased myopathy risk when combined with statins.
  • PCSK9 inhibitors: injectable agents used when LDL remains uncontrolled on statins or with familial hypercholesterolemia.
  • Monitoring: obtain baseline and periodic total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, liver function, and kidney function while continuing diet, activity, and weight-control measures.

Client Education

  • Therapeutic lifestyle changes are foundational: heart-healthy diet (reduce saturated/trans fats, increase fiber, fruits, vegetables, whole grains, fish)
  • Regular aerobic exercise (150 min/week)
  • Weight management; smoking cessation; limit alcohol
  • Take statins as prescribed (usually evening — cholesterol synthesis peaks at night; though atorvastatin/rosuvastatin can be any time)
  • Report muscle pain, tenderness, weakness, or dark urine (statin myopathy/rhabdomyolysis)
  • Report yellowing skin/eyes, persistent fatigue (liver)
  • Avoid grapefruit juice with some statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin)
  • This is a long-term condition; medication usually continued indefinitely
  • Keep lab appointments (lipids, liver function)
  • Manage related conditions: diabetes, hypertension, obesity
  • Family screening for familial hypercholesterolemia if early/severe

Therapeutic Procedures

  • No routine therapeutic procedure treats hyperlipidemia itself in this Pharm-focused card; management centers on lifestyle change plus lipid-lowering medication.
  • Coronary artery calcium scoring may be used for ASCVD risk refinement, but it is diagnostic/risk stratification rather than treatment.
  • If complications occur, prepare the client for condition-specific treatment pathways such as CAD, PAD, stroke/TIA, or pancreatitis management.
  • Use follow-up visits and lipid panels to adjust therapy intensity and reinforce long-term adherence.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider and pharmacist for statin intensity, add-on therapy, interaction review, myopathy/hepatotoxicity monitoring, and adherence barriers.
  • Refer to a dietitian for lipid-lowering diet, weight management, diabetes-friendly planning, and triglyceride/alcohol counseling.
  • Involve cardiology or lipid specialist for familial hypercholesterolemia, refractory LDL elevation, PCSK9 therapy, or ASCVD complications.
  • Communicate lipid trends, liver/kidney results, muscle symptoms, adherence issues, and ASCVD-risk changes to the care team.
Worked Example Anemia Ch 26 — Growth Factors · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Anemia
Review Module Chapter
Ch 26 — Growth Factors

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Anemia — a reduction in red blood cell mass, hemoglobin, or hematocrit below normal, resulting in decreased oxygen-carrying capacity.

Common types:

  • Iron-deficiency anemia (most common): microcytic, hypochromic; from blood loss, poor intake, malabsorption
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency / pernicious anemia: macrocytic; impaired absorption (lack of intrinsic factor) → neurologic symptoms
  • Folate deficiency: macrocytic; poor intake, alcoholism, pregnancy
  • Anemia of chronic disease: inflammation, CKD (reduced erythropoietin)
  • Hemolytic anemia: increased RBC destruction
  • Aplastic anemia: bone marrow failure

Normal Hgb: ~12–16 g/dL (women), ~14–18 (men).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Three mechanisms: decreased production, increased destruction, or blood loss
  • Iron deficiency: insufficient iron for hemoglobin synthesis → small, pale RBCs
  • B12/folate deficiency: impaired DNA synthesis → large, immature RBCs (megaloblasts)
  • Pernicious anemia: autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor → B12 not absorbed in terminal ileum
  • CKD: reduced erythropoietin production by kidneys → reduced RBC production
  • Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity → tissue hypoxia → compensatory tachycardia, increased respiratory rate

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote nutrition matched to anemia type: iron-rich foods, vitamin C with iron, B12 sources, folate-rich foods, and avoidance of absorption blockers around oral iron.
  • Teach safe iron storage away from children and expected dark stools/constipation with oral iron.
  • Encourage follow-up labs to confirm response and identify ongoing blood loss, deficiency, CKD anemia, or marrow-suppression patterns.
  • Use energy conservation, activity pacing, and fall precautions while symptomatic anemia improves.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess for blood loss sources such as GI bleeding, GU bleeding, heavy menses, surgery, trauma, or occult blood loss.
  • Review diet, malabsorption history, pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, chronic inflammatory disease, chemotherapy, and marrow-suppressing medications.
  • Screen for B12 deficiency risk, including pernicious anemia, vegan diet without supplementation, gastric surgery, or neurologic symptoms.
  • Assess baseline cardiovascular/pulmonary disease because anemia-related tissue hypoxia can worsen chest pain, dyspnea, or tachycardia.

Expected Findings

General anemia symptoms (from tissue hypoxia):

  • Fatigue, weakness, lethargy
  • Pallor (skin, conjunctiva, nail beds)
  • Dyspnea on exertion, tachycardia, palpitations
  • Dizziness, headache, cold intolerance
  • Tachypnea

Type-specific:

  • Iron deficiency: spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), pica, glossitis, cheilosis
  • B12 deficiency: neurologic symptoms — paresthesias, ataxia, impaired proprioception, cognitive changes; beefy red tongue
  • Hemolytic: jaundice, splenomegaly

Diagnostic:

  • CBC: Hgb, Hct, RBC indices (MCV distinguishes micro/normo/macrocytic)
  • Iron studies: ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation
  • B12 and folate levels; reticulocyte count
  • Peripheral smear; Schilling test (historical) for pernicious anemia
  • Stool occult blood (GI loss)

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor CBC values including Hgb, Hct, RBC indices/MCV, and platelet/WBC trends when growth factors are used.
  • Use iron studies such as ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, and transferrin saturation to evaluate iron deficiency and therapy response.
  • Check B12, folate, reticulocyte count, and peripheral smear when differentiating anemia type.
  • For epoetin alfa/ESA therapy, monitor Hgb/Hct at least twice weekly and iron levels before and during therapy; for leukopoietic agents, monitor CBC twice weekly.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use stool occult blood testing and GI/GU evaluation when blood loss is suspected.
  • Review peripheral smear and reticulocyte response to help distinguish production problem, deficiency, or hemolysis.
  • Investigate type-specific clues such as neurologic findings in B12 deficiency or jaundice/splenomegaly in hemolytic anemia.
  • Evaluate transfusion need and monitor response when severe or symptomatic anemia requires packed RBCs.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Tissue-hypoxia safety: monitor fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia, chest pain, dizziness, and activity intolerance; use fall precautions and oxygen if symptomatic hypoxia is present.
  • ESA safety: monitor BP and Hgb/Hct at least twice weekly; report chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, or unilateral weakness due to thrombotic-event risk.
  • Leukopoietic safety: monitor CBC twice weekly and reduce/interrupt therapy for excessive ANC, WBC, or platelet response per provider parameters.
  • Administration safety: keep epoetin/filgrastim-type products refrigerated, avoid shaking/freezing, and note sargramostim is contraindicated with yeast allergy.

Complications

  • Untreated anemia can worsen tissue hypoxia, causing fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia, palpitations, dizziness, falls, and chest pain in vulnerable clients.
  • Severe anemia can require packed RBC transfusion and close monitoring for transfusion reactions when ordered.
  • Epoetin alfa/ESA therapy can cause hypertension and thrombotic events such as MI or stroke.
  • Leukopoietic agents can cause bone pain, diarrhea, weakness, rash, malaise, leukocytosis, and thrombocytosis.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Treatment by type:

  • Iron deficiency: oral iron (ferrous sulfate) — take on empty stomach with vitamin C; IV iron if intolerant/malabsorption; treat underlying cause (find blood loss source)
  • B12 deficiency / pernicious: B12 injections (IM) or high-dose oral; lifelong for pernicious anemia
  • Folate deficiency: folic acid supplementation; dietary improvement
  • CKD anemia: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin) + iron
  • Severe: packed RBC transfusion

Nursing care:

  • Monitor CBC, iron studies, reticulocyte response
  • Energy conservation; activity pacing; rest periods
  • Fall precautions (dizziness)
  • Oxygen if symptomatic hypoxia
  • Dietary counseling (iron-rich foods, B12 sources, folate)
  • Assess for bleeding source (GI, GU, menstrual)
  • Safe transfusion administration if ordered

Medications

  • Epoetin alfa / erythropoietic stimulating agents: stimulate RBC production, especially for chronic kidney disease-related anemia; monitor Hgb/Hct at least twice weekly and iron levels before and during therapy.
  • Major ESA risks: hypertension and thrombotic events such as MI or stroke; monitor BP and report chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, or unilateral weakness.
  • Filgrastim/pegfilgrastim and sargramostim: increase WBC/neutrophil production for neutropenia, post-chemotherapy recovery, or marrow recovery; effectiveness includes absence of infection and expected WBC/differential response.
  • Leukopoietic adverse effects: bone pain, diarrhea, weakness, rash, and malaise; acetaminophen can be used for bone pain if prescribed.
  • Safety monitoring: CBC twice weekly; reduce or interrupt leukopoietic therapy for ANC >=20,000, WBC >=50,000, or platelets >=500,000/mm3; sargramostim is contraindicated with yeast allergy.

Client Education

  • Oral iron: take on empty stomach (1 hr before/2 hr after meals) with vitamin C (orange juice) for absorption; take with food if GI upset (reduces absorption but improves tolerance)
  • Iron causes dark/black stools (harmless) and constipation (increase fiber/fluids)
  • Use a straw for liquid iron (stains teeth); rinse mouth
  • Separate iron from antacids, dairy, tea, coffee (reduce absorption)
  • Pernicious anemia: B12 injections are LIFELONG — cannot be cured by diet alone
  • Iron-rich foods: red meat, beans, fortified cereals, leafy greens
  • B12 sources: meat, fish, dairy, eggs, fortified foods
  • Folate: leafy greens, citrus, legumes, fortified grains
  • Energy conservation; pace activities; rest as needed
  • Report worsening fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain, or bleeding
  • Keep lab appointments to monitor response
  • Take iron away from children (overdose dangerous)

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Packed RBC transfusion: used for severe or symptomatic anemia when ordered; verify blood product, monitor vital signs, and stop/report suspected transfusion reaction.
  • Cause-directed therapy: investigate and treat blood loss sources, nutritional deficiency, CKD anemia, or marrow suppression based on labs and provider evaluation.
  • Growth-factor therapy: epoetin alfa and leukopoietic agents are medication-centered treatments that require scheduled lab monitoring rather than a procedure.
  • Support activity pacing, fall precautions, and dietary teaching while response to therapy is monitored.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider, pharmacist, and lab team for anemia typing, iron/B12/folate replacement, ESA or growth-factor dosing, and CBC monitoring.
  • Involve nephrology for CKD-related anemia and oncology/hematology for chemotherapy-related cytopenias, marrow disorders, or complex growth-factor use.
  • Consult dietitian for iron, B12, folate, renal-diet, or pregnancy-related nutrition planning.
  • Communicate symptomatic hypoxia, bleeding signs, transfusion reactions, BP changes on ESA therapy, thrombotic symptoms, and abnormal CBC trends promptly.
Worked Example Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract · Men’s health section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 31 — Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) — non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland, common in aging men, causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) from urethral compression.

  • Very common: ~50% of men by age 60, ~90% by age 85
  • Not cancer and does not increase prostate cancer risk (but symptoms overlap — must evaluate)
  • Symptoms range from mild to severe urinary obstruction
  • Can lead to complications: urinary retention, UTIs, bladder stones, renal damage

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Age-related hormonal changes (dihydrotestosterone, DHT) stimulate prostate cell proliferation
  • Prostate gland enlarges, compressing the urethra
  • Static component: physical enlargement of glandular tissue
  • Dynamic component: increased smooth muscle tone (alpha-1 receptors) in prostate and bladder neck
  • Urethral compression → obstruction → bladder must work harder → bladder muscle hypertrophy, then decompensation
  • Incomplete emptying → residual urine → UTIs, stones, eventually retention

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Use timed voiding, double voiding, and evening fluid limits to reduce lower urinary tract symptoms and nocturia.
  • Limit caffeine and alcohol, which can worsen urinary frequency and urgency.
  • Review OTC labels and avoid antihistamines, decongestants, and anticholinergics unless cleared because they can worsen urinary retention.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Advanced age and DHT-related prostate cell proliferation increase prostate size and urethral compression.
  • Urinary obstruction, incomplete bladder emptying, and residual urine increase risk for UTIs, bladder stones, and retention.
  • Medications with anticholinergic or sympathomimetic effects can worsen hesitancy, weak stream, and retention.

Expected Findings

Obstructive symptoms (voiding):

  • Weak/intermittent urine stream
  • Hesitancy (difficulty starting)
  • Straining to void
  • Incomplete emptying; post-void dribbling

Irritative symptoms (storage):

  • Frequency, urgency
  • Nocturia
  • Urge incontinence

Diagnostic:

  • Digital rectal exam (DRE): smooth, enlarged, firm prostate
  • AUA/IPSS symptom score
  • PSA (rule out cancer; BPH can mildly elevate)
  • Urinalysis (rule out infection/hematuria)
  • Post-void residual; uroflowmetry
  • Renal function if obstruction suspected

Laboratory Tests

  • Use PSA as ordered to support prostate evaluation, remembering 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors can lower PSA values.
  • Use urinalysis or urine culture when dysuria, fever, hematuria, or infection symptoms accompany lower urinary tract symptoms.
  • Monitor renal function when obstruction, retention, hydronephrosis, or renal compromise is suspected.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Assess symptom severity with lower urinary tract symptom history and tools such as the International Prostate Symptom Score when used by the provider.
  • Expect digital rectal examination and prostate evaluation to help distinguish BPH from other causes of urinary symptoms.
  • Use bladder scan or postvoid residual testing when incomplete emptying or urinary retention is suspected.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Treat inability to urinate as urgent acute urinary retention requiring prompt evaluation.
  • Monitor alpha-1 blockers for orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, and fall risk; teach slow position changes.
  • Teach that 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors take months to work, can cause sexual adverse effects, lower PSA, and should not be handled as crushed or broken tablets by pregnant clients.

Complications

  • Acute urinary retention, recurrent UTIs, bladder stones, hematuria, bladder decompensation, and renal damage from prolonged obstruction.
  • Falls or syncope from alpha-1 blocker orthostatic hypotension.
  • Delayed cancer evaluation if overlapping symptoms or PSA changes are not reported and followed.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin) — relax smooth muscle; rapid symptom relief; orthostatic hypotension
  • 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) — shrink prostate over months; lower PSA; sexual side effects; teratogenic (pregnant women avoid handling)
  • Combination therapy (alpha blocker + 5-ARI) for larger prostates
  • PDE5 inhibitors (tadalafil) — for BPH + ED
  • Anticholinergics — cautiously for storage symptoms (retention risk)

Procedural/surgical: TURP (transurethral resection), laser therapy, prostatic urethral lift, for refractory cases.

Nursing care:

  • Assess urinary symptoms, post-void residual, signs of retention
  • Monitor for acute urinary retention (emergency — catheterization)
  • Monitor BP (alpha blockers); fall precautions
  • Post-TURP care: continuous bladder irrigation, monitor for hemorrhage, TURP syndrome
  • Distinguish from prostate cancer (PSA, DRE)

Medications

  • Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin) — relax smooth muscle; rapid symptom relief; orthostatic hypotension
  • 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) — shrink prostate over months; lower PSA; sexual side effects; teratogenic (pregnant women avoid handling)
  • Combination therapy (alpha blocker + 5-ARI) for larger prostates
  • PDE5 inhibitors (tadalafil) — for BPH + ED
  • Anticholinergics — cautiously for storage symptoms (retention risk)

Procedural/surgical: TURP (transurethral resection), laser therapy, prostatic urethral lift, for refractory cases.

Client Education

  • BPH is benign (not cancer) but needs management to prevent complications
  • Alpha blockers: rise slowly (orthostatic hypotension); inform eye surgeon (cataract/floppy iris); symptom relief is quick
  • 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: take months to work; sexual side effects; lower PSA (tell providers); pregnant women should not handle crushed/broken tablets (teratogenic)
  • Avoid medications that worsen retention: antihistamines, decongestants, anticholinergics (read OTC labels)
  • Lifestyle: limit fluids in evening, limit caffeine/alcohol, double voiding, timed voiding
  • Seek emergency care if unable to urinate (acute retention)
  • Report fever, dysuria (UTI), blood in urine
  • Keep prostate cancer screening per provider
  • Do not stop medications without provider guidance

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Use catheterization for acute retention or severe obstruction as ordered.
  • Escalate refractory or complicated symptoms to urologic procedures such as TURP, laser therapy, or prostatic urethral lift.
  • Prepare the client for post-procedure monitoring of urine output, bleeding, infection symptoms, and symptom relief.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with urology for persistent symptoms, retention, hematuria, recurrent infection, stones, or procedure evaluation.
  • Work with the pharmacist to screen OTC products, alpha-blocker hypotension risk, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor counseling, and tadalafil interactions.
  • Communicate PSA trends, postvoid residual findings, renal function concerns, and adherence barriers to the prescribing provider.
Worked Example Osteoporosis Ch 34 — Bone Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Osteoporosis
Review Module Chapter
Ch 34 — Bone Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Osteoporosis — a systemic skeletal disorder characterized by low bone mass and deterioration of bone tissue, leading to increased bone fragility and fracture risk.

  • “Silent disease” — often asymptomatic until fracture
  • Most common in postmenopausal women and older adults
  • T-score (DEXA): normal ≥ -1.0; osteopenia -1.0 to -2.5; osteoporosis ≤ -2.5
  • Common fracture sites: vertebrae (compression), hip, wrist (Colles)

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Imbalance between bone resorption (osteoclasts) and bone formation (osteoblasts) — resorption exceeds formation
  • Estrogen deficiency (menopause) accelerates bone loss (estrogen normally restrains osteoclasts)
  • Aging → reduced osteoblast activity, calcium/vitamin D deficiency, reduced absorption
  • Secondary causes: corticosteroids (steroid-induced), hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, immobility, malabsorption
  • Risk factors: female, advanced age, postmenopausal, low body weight, smoking, excess alcohol, sedentary, family history, white/Asian ethnicity, low calcium/vitamin D, certain medications (steroids, PPIs, some anticonvulsants)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote adequate calcium and vitamin D intake, weight-bearing/resistance exercise, smoking cessation, and limited alcohol or caffeine.
  • Teach fall prevention: remove clutter and rugs, improve lighting, use grab bars and non-slip footwear, and maintain vision checks.
  • Reinforce long-term adherence because osteoporosis is often silent until fracture occurs.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Postmenopausal estrogen loss, advanced age, female sex, low body weight, family history, white or Asian ethnicity, and sedentary lifestyle increase risk.
  • Low calcium or vitamin D, smoking, excess alcohol, immobility, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, and corticosteroid therapy contribute to bone loss.
  • Certain medications such as corticosteroids, PPIs, and some anticonvulsants can increase fracture risk.

Expected Findings

  • Often asymptomatic until fracture
  • Fragility fractures (from minimal trauma) — vertebral, hip, wrist
  • Loss of height (vertebral compression)
  • Kyphosis (“dowager’s hump”)
  • Back pain (acute with vertebral fracture)
  • Reduced mobility, fear of falling

Diagnostic:

  • DEXA scan (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) — gold standard; T-score
  • FRAX tool (10-year fracture risk)
  • Labs: calcium, vitamin D, phosphate, PTH, TSH (secondary causes)
  • X-rays (fractures; less sensitive for density)

Laboratory Tests

  • Review calcium and vitamin D status when replacement therapy, deficiency, or hypocalcemia risk is a concern.
  • Monitor renal function before bisphosphonate or denosumab therapy as ordered.
  • Use thyroid, parathyroid, or other targeted labs when secondary osteoporosis is suspected.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use DEXA scan results to classify normal bone density, osteopenia, or osteoporosis by T-score.
  • Assess fracture risk with clinical history and tools such as FRAX when used by the provider.
  • Use imaging for suspected vertebral compression, hip, wrist, or other fragility fractures.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Teach exact bisphosphonate administration: take in the morning with plain water on an empty stomach, remain upright 30–60 min, and delay food or other medications.
  • Monitor for esophageal irritation, severe bone/jaw pain, dental problems, hypocalcemia symptoms, and new back pain or height loss.
  • Prioritize fall prevention and fracture precautions for older adults and clients with prior fragility fracture.

Complications

  • Hip, wrist, and vertebral compression fractures, height loss, chronic pain, reduced mobility, and loss of independence.
  • Bisphosphonate-related esophageal irritation or rare osteonecrosis of the jaw, especially without dental screening or correct administration.
  • Hypocalcemia or rebound fracture risk if injectable therapy is missed or stopped without follow-up planning.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid) — FIRST-LINE; inhibit bone resorption
  • Calcium and vitamin D supplementation (foundation)
  • SERMs (raloxifene) — postmenopausal women
  • Calcitonin — second-line; vertebral fracture pain
  • Denosumab (RANKL inhibitor) — injectable
  • Anabolic agents (teriparatide, romosozumab) — severe/high-risk; build bone
  • Hormone therapy (select cases)

Nursing care:

  • Fall prevention (home safety, lighting, remove hazards, assistive devices)
  • Promote weight-bearing and resistance exercise
  • Dietary counseling (calcium, vitamin D)
  • Educate on proper bisphosphonate administration
  • Pain management for fractures
  • Address modifiable risk factors

Medications

  • Bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid) — FIRST-LINE; inhibit bone resorption
  • Calcium and vitamin D supplementation (foundation)
  • SERMs (raloxifene) — postmenopausal women
  • Calcitonin — second-line; vertebral fracture pain
  • Denosumab (RANKL inhibitor) — injectable
  • Anabolic agents (teriparatide, romosozumab) — severe/high-risk; build bone
  • Hormone therapy (select cases)

Client Education

  • Bisphosphonate administration is critical: take in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water; remain upright (sitting/standing) for 30–60 minutes; wait 30–60 min before food/other meds (esophageal irritation risk)
  • Adequate calcium (1,000–1,200 mg/day) and vitamin D (800–1,000 IU/day) — diet and supplements
  • Weight-bearing and resistance exercise (walking, light weights) builds/maintains bone
  • Fall prevention: remove rugs/clutter, good lighting, grab bars, non-slip footwear, vision checks
  • Stop smoking; limit alcohol and caffeine
  • Get adequate sun exposure (vitamin D)
  • Dental exam before bisphosphonates (osteonecrosis of jaw risk); tell dentist
  • Report new back pain, height loss, or fractures
  • Keep DEXA follow-up appointments
  • This is often silent — adherence prevents fractures

Therapeutic Procedures

  • DEXA monitoring supports diagnosis and treatment response over time.
  • Physical therapy, balance training, assistive devices, and home safety modification reduce fall and fracture risk.
  • Orthopedic or specialty procedures may be needed after hip, wrist, or vertebral fracture.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the prescriber and pharmacist for bisphosphonate, denosumab, SERM, calcitonin, anabolic, calcium, and vitamin D therapy education.
  • Involve physical therapy or occupational therapy for strength, balance, assistive devices, and home fall-risk reduction.
  • Encourage dental care before or during antiresorptive therapy and specialty follow-up for severe osteoporosis or fractures.
Worked Example Migraine Headache Ch 38 — Miscellaneous Pain Medications · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Migraine Headache
Review Module Chapter
Ch 38 — Miscellaneous Pain Medications

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Migraine — a primary headache disorder characterized by recurrent moderate-to-severe headaches, often unilateral and pulsating, with associated symptoms.

  • Migraine without aura (most common)
  • Migraine with aura — preceded by reversible neurologic symptoms (visual, sensory)
  • More common in women; often familial
  • Can be episodic or chronic (≥ 15 headache days/month)
  • Significant disability and quality-of-life impact

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Complex neurovascular disorder involving the trigeminovascular system
  • Cortical spreading depression (wave of neuronal activity) → aura
  • Activation of trigeminal nerve → release of vasoactive peptides (CGRP — calcitonin gene-related peptide) → neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, pain
  • Serotonin (5-HT) dysregulation (basis for triptan therapy)
  • Triggers: stress, hormonal changes (menstruation), certain foods (tyramine, MSG, alcohol), sleep changes, sensory stimuli, weather, fasting

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Use a headache diary to identify personal triggers, frequency, severity, medication use, and response to therapy.
  • Promote regular sleep, meals, hydration, exercise, stress management, and avoidance of individual triggers such as tyramine-containing foods, MSG, alcohol, fasting, sensory stimuli, or weather changes when identified.
  • Teach early use of abortive medication at the first migraine manifestations and daily adherence with preventive medication when prescribed.
  • Prevent medication-overuse headache by limiting acute medications according to the therapy plan and reporting increasing use.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess sex, family history, hormonal/menstrual pattern, stress, sleep changes, fasting, sensory stimuli, weather changes, and food/alcohol triggers.
  • Review cardiovascular history before triptan or ergot therapy because these agents cause vasoconstriction.
  • Screen pregnancy status before ergotamine and review SSRI/SNRI/MAOI or other serotonergic therapy for interaction risk.
  • Assess headache frequency and disability to determine need for preventive therapy such as propranolol, topiramate, or CGRP-directed options.

Expected Findings

Phases (not all present):

  • Prodrome (hours-days before): mood changes, food cravings, fatigue, yawning
  • Aura (if present, ~20–60 min): visual (flashing lights, scotomas, zigzag lines), sensory (tingling), rarely speech
  • Headache: unilateral, pulsating/throbbing, moderate-severe, worse with activity; lasts 4–72 hr
  • Postdrome: fatigue, difficulty concentrating

Associated symptoms:

  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Photophobia and phonophobia (light/sound sensitivity)
  • Desire to lie in a dark, quiet room

Diagnostic: clinical (history, symptom pattern); neuroimaging only to rule out secondary causes if red flags.

Laboratory Tests

  • No routine laboratory test diagnoses migraine; diagnosis is primarily clinical based on pattern and history.
  • Use medication-safety labs only when required by the prescribed regimen or comorbid condition.
  • For preventive or interacting therapies, review renal/hepatic function, pregnancy testing, or other ordered monitoring when clinically indicated.
  • Escalate abnormal findings that suggest secondary headache, medication toxicity, dehydration from vomiting, or treatment contraindication.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Diagnose migraine clinically by recurrent headache pattern, associated nausea/vomiting, photophobia/phonophobia, aura pattern, and trigger history.
  • Use neurologic assessment and red-flag screening for new severe worst headache, neurologic change, or major change in headache pattern.
  • Neuroimaging is not routine for typical migraine but may be ordered to rule out secondary causes when red flags are present.
  • Review headache diary data to differentiate episodic vs chronic migraine and guide abortive/preventive therapy.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Triptan safety: assess cardiovascular risk factors and vital signs; teach the client to report angina pain and distinguish transient chest/arm heaviness from possible angina.
  • Interaction safety: do not use sumatriptan with or within 2 weeks of an MAOI, with another triptan, or within 24 hr of ergotamine/dihydroergotamine.
