  • Ergotamine safety: stop and notify the provider for positive pregnancy test, numbness/tingling in fingers or toes, or unexplained muscle pain because these can indicate serious adverse effects/ergotism.
  • Red flags: report new severe “worst headache,” neurologic changes, or a major change in headache pattern.

Complications

  • Frequent or uncontrolled migraine can cause severe disability, nausea/vomiting, dehydration risk, and missed school/work or usual activities.
  • Medication-overuse headache can occur when acute medications are used too often.
  • Sumatriptan can cause chest/arm heaviness, coronary vasospasm/angina, dizziness, and vertigo.
  • Ergotamine complications include pregnancy risk and ergotism findings such as numbness/tingling in extremities or unexplained muscle pain.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Abortive (acute) therapy:

  • Triptans (sumatriptan) — 5-HT agonists; first-line for moderate-severe; take at onset; vasoconstriction (CV contraindications)
  • NSAIDs / acetaminophen — mild-moderate
  • Ergot alkaloids (dihydroergotamine) — alternative
  • CGRP antagonists / gepants (rimegepant, ubrogepant) — newer abortive
  • Antiemetics (metoclopramide) for nausea
  • Avoid medication overuse (rebound headache)

Preventive (prophylactic) therapy (frequent/severe):

  • Beta blockers (propranolol), topiramate, valproate
  • TCAs (amitriptyline)
  • CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab) — injectable prophylaxis
  • Botox (chronic migraine)

Nursing care: identify/avoid triggers, headache diary, dark quiet environment during attacks, early treatment, monitor medication overuse.

Medications

  • Triptans (sumatriptan): abort migraine and associated nausea/vomiting after onset by causing cranial artery vasoconstriction; teach to take at the first migraine manifestations.
  • Sumatriptan safety: monitor cardiovascular risk factors and vital signs; teach the client to report angina pain and to distinguish transient chest/arm heaviness from angina.
  • Interactions: do not use sumatriptan concurrently or within 2 weeks of an MAOI, with other triptans, or within 24 hr of ergotamine or dihydroergotamine.
  • Ergotamine: abortive therapy used at migraine onset, not prophylaxis; stop and notify the provider for positive pregnancy test, numbness/tingling in fingers or toes, or unexplained muscle pain due to ergotism risk.
  • Prophylaxis: propranolol and topiramate are used for prevention; report heart block before propranolol therapy.
  • Newer prevention options: CGRP inhibitors such as erenumab and fremanezumab are migraine-prevention agents.

Client Education

  • Take abortive medication (triptan) at the FIRST sign of migraine — more effective early
  • Keep a headache diary to identify triggers and patterns
  • Identify and avoid personal triggers (specific foods, stress, sleep disruption, skipped meals)
  • Rest in a dark, quiet room during attacks
  • Avoid medication overuse (> 2–3 days/week of acute meds → rebound/medication-overuse headache)
  • Triptans: do NOT use with ergots or within 24 hr; CV risk — report chest tightness; serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs/SNRIs
  • Take preventive medication daily as prescribed (even when headache-free)
  • Maintain regular sleep, meals, hydration, exercise, stress management
  • Report new severe (“worst”) headache, neurologic changes, or change in pattern (rule out other causes)
  • Limit caffeine and alcohol if triggers

Therapeutic Procedures

  • No routine therapeutic procedure is the focus of this Pharm chapter for migraine; treatment is primarily abortive medication at onset plus preventive medication for frequent/severe attacks.
  • During an acute migraine, support nonprocedural comfort measures such as resting in a dark, quiet room, hydration as tolerated, and nausea management.
  • For chronic migraine, specialist-directed options such as Botox may be considered only when ordered; continue headache diary review and trigger management.
  • Escalate for diagnostic evaluation rather than routine migraine treatment if red-flag symptoms or a changed headache pattern appear.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider, pharmacist, and neurology/headache specialist for abortive therapy, preventive therapy, interaction screening, and cardiovascular/ergot pregnancy precautions.
  • Involve behavioral health, sleep support, or stress-management resources when triggers or comorbid anxiety/depression worsen migraines.
  • Use dietitian support when food triggers, hydration, fasting, or weight-management issues contribute to headaches.
  • Communicate headache frequency, acute-medication use, red-flag symptoms, chest/arm symptoms with triptans, and adverse effects from ergot or preventive therapy.
Worked Example Hypertension Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Hypertension
Review Module Chapter
Ch 20 — Medications Affecting Blood Pressure

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Hypertension (HTN) — persistent elevation of arterial blood pressure; a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, kidney disease, and death.

ACC/AHA (2017) classification:

  • Normal: < 120/80 mmHg
  • Elevated: 120–129/< 80
  • Stage 1: 130–139 OR 80–89
  • Stage 2: ≥ 140 OR ≥ 90
  • Hypertensive crisis: > 180 AND/OR > 120 (emergency if target-organ damage)
  • Primary (essential) HTN: ~90–95%; no single identifiable cause
  • Secondary HTN: identifiable cause (renal disease, endocrine disorders, medications, OSA)
  • Often asymptomatic — the “silent killer”

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • BP = Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance — HTN results from increase in either
  • RAAS overactivity: excess angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) and aldosterone (Na/water retention)
  • Sympathetic nervous system overactivity: increased HR, contractility, vasoconstriction
  • Endothelial dysfunction: reduced nitric oxide; impaired vasodilation
  • Vascular remodeling: arterial wall thickening → increased resistance
  • Sodium and water retention → increased blood volume
  • Risk factors: age, obesity, high sodium intake, sedentary lifestyle, alcohol, smoking, family history, diabetes, African ancestry, chronic stress

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote DASH-style eating, sodium restriction, regular aerobic activity, weight loss when indicated, smoking cessation, alcohol limitation, stress management, and adequate sleep.
  • Teach that hypertension is often asymptomatic, so medication adherence and follow-up are necessary even when the client feels well.
  • Encourage home BP monitoring with a log brought to visits and reinforce correct cuff size/positioning.
  • Prevent target-organ damage by managing diabetes, hyperlipidemia, CKD risk, and sleep apnea screening when indicated.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess age, obesity, high sodium intake, sedentary lifestyle, alcohol use, smoking, family history, diabetes, chronic stress, and African ancestry.
  • Screen for secondary causes when HTN is young-onset, severe, resistant, or abrupt, including renal disease, endocrine disorders, OSA, and medication causes.
  • Review OTC/herbal and prescription agents that can raise BP or interact with antihypertensives.
  • Assess adherence barriers because asymptomatic disease commonly leads to missed therapy.

Expected Findings

Often asymptomatic. When symptomatic or with target-organ damage:

  • Headache (especially morning, occipital)
  • Dizziness, blurred vision
  • Epistaxis
  • Fatigue

Target-organ damage findings:

  • Cardiac: LVH, heart failure, angina, prior MI
  • Cerebrovascular: TIA, stroke, cognitive impairment
  • Renal: elevated creatinine, proteinuria, CKD
  • Retinal: retinopathy (AV nicking, hemorrhages, papilledema)
  • Peripheral: PAD, bruits

Diagnostic:

  • Accurate BP measurement (proper cuff, seated, rested) on ≥ 2 occasions
  • Ambulatory or home BP monitoring (rule out white-coat HTN)
  • Labs: electrolytes, BUN/Cr, glucose, lipids, urinalysis
  • EKG (LVH); consider echo
  • Secondary workup if young, severe, or resistant

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose, lipid panel, and urinalysis to assess target-organ risk and secondary contributors.
  • Trend potassium and renal function with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aldosterone antagonists, and diuretics.
  • Evaluate glucose and lipids because diabetes and dyslipidemia greatly increase cardiovascular risk.
  • Report renal function decline, hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, or proteinuria because therapy may need adjustment.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Confirm HTN with accurate BP measurement on at least two occasions using proper cuff size, seated rest, and correct positioning.
  • Use home or ambulatory BP monitoring to rule out white-coat hypertension and evaluate control.
  • Assess EKG for LVH, dysrhythmias, or ischemic changes; echocardiogram may be used when structural disease is suspected.
  • Evaluate for target-organ damage such as retinopathy, CKD/proteinuria, PAD/bruits, TIA/stroke symptoms, angina, or heart failure findings.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Hypertensive crisis: BP >180 and/or >120 with chest pain, dyspnea, neurologic change, vision change, or renal findings requires urgent/emergency evaluation.
  • Orthostatic risk: assess dizziness/falls, especially in older adults and clients taking alpha blockers or multiple agents.
  • Medication safety: do not stop beta blockers or clonidine abruptly; avoid combining ACE inhibitor plus ARB due to hyperkalemia/renal injury risk.
  • ACE/ARB safety: monitor renal function and potassium; report facial/lip swelling, severe cough, or signs of angioedema.

Complications

  • Uncontrolled HTN can cause stroke/TIA, MI/angina, LVH, heart failure, CKD, retinopathy, PAD, cognitive impairment, and death.
  • Hypertensive emergency can produce acute target-organ damage requiring rapid evaluation and controlled BP reduction.
  • Therapy complications include orthostatic hypotension, electrolyte imbalance, renal injury, hyperkalemia, and rebound hypertension if certain drugs are stopped abruptly.
  • Poor adherence can allow silent progression of organ damage before symptoms appear.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (first-line classes):

  • Thiazide diuretics (HCTZ, chlorthalidone)
  • ACE inhibitors (lisinopril) or ARBs (losartan)
  • Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine)
  • Initial choice varies: ACE/ARB or CCB often preferred; thiazide or CCB first-line in Black clients (per guidelines); ACE/ARB preferred in diabetes/CKD (renal protection)
  • Stage 2 or BP > 20/10 above goal: start with 2 agents
  • Add-ons: beta blockers (if compelling indication like CAD/HF), aldosterone antagonists (resistant HTN), alpha blockers, central agonists, vasodilators
  • Avoid combining ACE + ARB (hyperkalemia, renal injury)

Nursing care:

  • Accurate BP measurement and trending
  • Monitor electrolytes, renal function with RAAS agents and diuretics
  • Assess for orthostatic hypotension (especially older adults, alpha blockers)
  • Medication adherence support (asymptomatic disease → poor adherence)
  • Lifestyle counseling reinforcement

Medications

  • Thiazide diuretics (HCTZ, chlorthalidone)
  • ACE inhibitors (lisinopril) or ARBs (losartan)
  • Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine)
  • Initial choice varies: ACE/ARB or CCB often preferred; thiazide or CCB first-line in Black clients (per guidelines); ACE/ARB preferred in diabetes/CKD (renal protection)
  • Stage 2 or BP > 20/10 above goal: start with 2 agents
  • Add-ons: beta blockers (if compelling indication like CAD/HF), aldosterone antagonists (resistant HTN), alpha blockers, central agonists, vasodilators
  • Avoid combining ACE + ARB (hyperkalemia, renal injury)

Client Education

  • HTN is usually asymptomatic — take medication even when you feel fine
  • Do NOT stop medications abruptly (rebound HTN, especially beta blockers and clonidine)
  • DASH diet: rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy; reduce saturated fat
  • Sodium restriction (< 2,300 mg/day, ideally < 1,500 mg)
  • Limit alcohol; quit smoking
  • Regular aerobic exercise (150 min/week)
  • Weight loss if overweight (~1 mmHg per kg lost)
  • Home BP monitoring; keep a log; bring to appointments
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic dizziness
  • Report: severe headache, chest pain, vision changes, shortness of breath (possible crisis)
  • ACE inhibitors: report dry cough, facial/lip swelling (angioedema), avoid salt substitutes (K+)
  • Manage stress; adequate sleep (screen for sleep apnea)
  • Keep all follow-up appointments and labs

Therapeutic Procedures

  • No routine therapeutic procedure treats uncomplicated primary HTN; management centers on lifestyle change plus long-term pharmacotherapy.
  • Home BP monitoring and ambulatory BP monitoring support diagnosis and treatment adjustment.
  • If hypertensive emergency or secondary HTN is suspected, prepare for ordered emergency evaluation, IV antihypertensive therapy, renal/endocrine workup, or specialty referral.
  • Reinforce follow-up visits for medication titration, target-organ screening, and adherence support.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider and pharmacist for medication selection, titration, interaction screening, orthostatic risk, renal function, and electrolyte monitoring.
  • Involve dietitian, diabetes educator, smoking-cessation resources, sleep-medicine evaluation, or exercise/cardiac rehabilitation resources when indicated.
  • Refer to cardiology or nephrology for resistant HTN, target-organ damage, CKD, secondary-cause concern, or complex comorbid disease.
  • Communicate home BP logs, severe readings, symptoms, adherence barriers, renal/electrolyte abnormalities, and adverse effects.
Worked Example Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) — persistent, excessive worry about multiple life areas (work, health, family, finances) for ≥ 6 months that is difficult to control and interferes with daily functioning.

  • DSM-5 criteria: excessive anxiety + 3+ physical symptoms (restlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance)
  • Distinct from panic disorder (acute episodes) and OCD (specific intrusive thoughts)
  • Lifetime prevalence ~6%; twice as common in women
  • Often comorbid with depression (~50%) and substance use disorders

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Neurotransmitter dysregulation: reduced GABA (inhibitory) activity, altered serotonin/norepinephrine signaling
  • HPA axis dysfunction: chronic activation → elevated cortisol → physical and cognitive effects
  • Amygdala hyperactivity: fear-processing center over-responds to perceived threats
  • Prefrontal cortex underactivity: diminished top-down regulation of fear responses
  • Genetic predisposition — heritability ~30–40%
  • Environmental: childhood adversity, chronic stress, substance use (caffeine, stimulants exacerbate)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote CBT skills, mindfulness, relaxation practice, sleep hygiene, regular exercise, and limiting caffeine, stimulants, and alcohol.
  • Teach that SSRIs/SNRIs and buspirone take weeks for full effect and should not be stopped abruptly.
  • Encourage a crisis plan and routine suicide-risk check-ins due to high depression comorbidity.
  • Support stress-management routines and early reporting of worsening anxiety, substance use, or medication adverse effects.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess female sex, family/genetic predisposition, childhood adversity, chronic stress, and substance/caffeine/stimulant use.
  • Screen for depression, substance-use disorder, insomnia, panic disorder, OCD, and medical causes of anxiety-like symptoms.
  • Review benzodiazepine risk factors including falls, sedation, alcohol use, substance-use history, and abrupt-withdrawal risk.
  • Assess suicide risk, functional impairment, sleep disturbance, and ability to access therapy/support.

Expected Findings

Psychological:

  • Excessive, uncontrollable worry across multiple domains
  • Difficulty concentrating, mind “going blank”
  • Irritability, feeling on edge
  • Catastrophizing, hypervigilance for threat

Physical:

  • Muscle tension (headaches, back/neck pain)
  • Restlessness, fatigue
  • Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, restless sleep)
  • GI symptoms (IBS-like)
  • Sympathetic activation: palpitations, sweating, tremor

Assessment tools: GAD-7 questionnaire (score ≥ 10 suggests moderate-severe GAD).

Laboratory Tests

  • No routine laboratory test diagnoses GAD; diagnosis is clinical using symptom duration, distress, impairment, and assessment tools.
  • Use labs only when ordered to rule out medical contributors such as thyroid disease, stimulant/substance effects, or medication-related concerns.
  • Monitor medication-safety labs when required by comorbid conditions or prescribed adjunctive agents.
  • Trend symptom scales and adverse effects as the main response-monitoring data.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use DSM-5 criteria: excessive anxiety/worry for at least 6 months plus physical symptoms and difficulty controlling worry.
  • Use GAD-7 scoring to quantify severity and follow response to therapy.
  • Differentiate GAD from panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, depression, stimulant/substance effects, and medical causes.
  • Assess suicide risk at each visit, especially when depression or substance use is present.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Suicide risk: assess ideation, plan, intent, means, and protective factors because depression commonly co-occurs.
  • Benzodiazepine safety: short-term only when used; avoid alcohol/driving until response is known and never stop abruptly.
  • SSRI/SNRI safety: teach delayed onset, discontinuation syndrome with abrupt stopping, and report worsening mood or suicidal thoughts.
  • Substance/caffeine safety: alcohol, stimulants, and excess caffeine can worsen anxiety and increase medication risk.

Complications

  • Untreated GAD can cause chronic sleep disturbance, fatigue, impaired concentration, irritability, muscle tension, GI symptoms, and functional impairment.
  • Comorbid depression and substance use increase suicide and treatment-complexity risk.
  • Benzodiazepines can cause sedation, falls, dependence, withdrawal, and dangerous effects with alcohol.
  • Stopping SSRIs/SNRIs abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms and relapse.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

First-line treatment: combination of psychotherapy + pharmacology

Pharmacotherapy:

  • SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine) — first-line; 2–6 weeks for full effect; start low, go slow
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) — alternative first-line
  • Buspirone — non-addictive; 2–4 weeks to effect
  • Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, alprazolam) — SHORT-TERM ONLY for acute distress while SSRI takes effect; high addiction risk
  • Hydroxyzine — non-addictive option for acute anxiety
  • Gabapentin/pregabalin — adjunct options
  • Beta blockers — for performance/situational anxiety (physical symptoms)

Non-pharm: CBT (gold standard), exposure therapy, mindfulness, sleep hygiene, exercise, limit caffeine/alcohol.

Suicide risk assessment — comorbidity with depression elevates risk; assess at every visit.

Medications

  • SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine) — first-line; 2–6 weeks for full effect; start low, go slow
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) — alternative first-line
  • Buspirone — non-addictive; 2–4 weeks to effect
  • Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, alprazolam) — SHORT-TERM ONLY for acute distress while SSRI takes effect; high addiction risk
  • Hydroxyzine — non-addictive option for acute anxiety
  • Gabapentin/pregabalin — adjunct options
  • Beta blockers — for performance/situational anxiety (physical symptoms)

Non-pharm: CBT (gold standard), exposure therapy, mindfulness, sleep hygiene, exercise, limit caffeine/alcohol.

Suicide risk assessment — comorbidity with depression elevates risk; assess at every visit.

Client Education

  • SSRIs/SNRIs take 2–6 weeks for full effect — do NOT stop because they “aren’t working”
  • Side effects (GI, sexual, insomnia) often improve after 1–2 weeks
  • Do NOT stop abruptly — discontinuation syndrome (flu-like, dizziness, electric-shock sensations) — taper
  • Avoid alcohol (worsens anxiety, dangerous with benzos)
  • Limit caffeine; avoid stimulants
  • Practice relaxation techniques daily; engage in regular exercise
  • Crisis plan: contact provider/hotline if suicidal thoughts emerge
  • If on benzodiazepines: NO alcohol, NO driving until known response, NEVER stop abruptly

Therapeutic Procedures

  • CBT is a gold-standard nonpharmacologic treatment; exposure-based and cognitive skills reduce worry and avoidance.
  • Mindfulness, relaxation training, sleep hygiene, exercise, and limiting caffeine/alcohol support symptom control.
  • Use safety planning and crisis resources when suicidal thoughts or severe distress occur.
  • Medication follow-up should track onset, adherence, side effects, suicidality, and function rather than expecting immediate relief.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with prescriber, pharmacist, therapist/psychologist, and primary care to balance medication and psychotherapy.
  • Refer to behavioral health for CBT, comorbid depression/substance use, suicidality, or poor response to initial therapy.
  • Use social work/case management when access, cost, school/work stressors, or safety planning needs interfere with care.
  • Communicate GAD-7 trends, sleep/function changes, medication effects, benzodiazepine use, substance use, and suicide-risk findings.
Worked Example Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) — develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence (direct, witnessing, or learning of an event affecting a loved one).

  • DSM-5 requires 4 symptom clusters for > 1 month: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, negative cognitions/mood, alterations in arousal/reactivity
  • Onset may be delayed (years after trauma)
  • Lifetime prevalence ~7–8% (higher in military veterans, abuse survivors)
  • Frequently comorbid with depression, substance use, anxiety, suicide risk
  • Children may exhibit through play, regression, or behavioral changes

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • HPA axis dysregulation: chronic stress hormone exposure alters cortisol response
  • Amygdala hyperreactivity: heightened threat detection persists after danger has passed
  • Hippocampal volume reduction: impairs memory consolidation; trauma memories remain “raw”
  • Prefrontal cortex hypoactivity: reduced capacity to inhibit fear response
  • Conditioned fear response: environmental cues become associated with trauma → triggered re-experiencing
  • Risk factors: prior trauma, lack of social support, severity/duration of trauma, female sex, genetic predisposition

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Use trauma-informed care: safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, empowerment, and cultural humility.
  • Promote trauma-focused therapy, EMDR/CPT/PE when appropriate, sleep hygiene, exercise, support systems, and trigger/safety planning.
  • Teach that SSRIs/SNRIs can take 4-12 weeks for PTSD response and therapy remains essential.
  • Limit alcohol/substance use, reinforce crisis resources, and assess suicide risk at every visit.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess trauma exposure type, severity, duration, prior trauma, lack of social support, female sex, and genetic/family predisposition.
  • Screen for depression, substance use, anxiety, sleep disturbance, nightmares, dissociation, and suicide risk.
  • Assess trigger patterns, avoidance behaviors, hypervigilance, reckless behavior, and interpersonal safety.
  • Review medication risks: avoid benzodiazepines when possible; monitor prazosin hypotension/falls.

Expected Findings

Intrusion symptoms:

  • Recurrent intrusive memories, distressing dreams/nightmares
  • Flashbacks (dissociative reactions) — feel/act as if reliving trauma
  • Intense psychological/physiological distress at trauma reminders

Avoidance:

  • Avoidance of trauma-related memories, thoughts, feelings
  • Avoidance of external reminders (people, places, situations)

Negative cognitions/mood:

  • Inability to remember key aspects of trauma
  • Persistent negative beliefs (“I am bad,” “the world is dangerous”)
  • Distorted blame of self/others
  • Detachment, anhedonia, restricted positive affect

Arousal/reactivity:

  • Irritability, anger outbursts, reckless behavior
  • Hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response
  • Sleep disturbance, concentration problems

Laboratory Tests

  • No routine laboratory test diagnoses PTSD; diagnosis is clinical using trauma exposure and symptom clusters.
  • Use labs only when ordered for comorbid substance use, medication safety, or medical contributors to sleep/mood symptoms.
  • Monitor BP/orthostatic findings clinically with prazosin rather than relying on labs.
  • Track symptom scales, nightmares, sleep, avoidance, and arousal symptoms as response data.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Assess the four DSM-5 symptom clusters: intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, and arousal/reactivity for more than 1 month.
  • Screen for flashbacks, nightmares, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, avoidance, detachment, guilt/blame, and reckless behavior.
  • Assess suicide risk and substance use at every visit due to high comorbidity.
  • Use validated PTSD symptom measures when available to trend severity and treatment response.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Suicide risk: assess ideation, plan, intent, means, prior attempts, and crisis supports at each contact.
  • Trauma-informed safety: avoid retraumatization, explain care before acting, and preserve client choice/control when possible.
  • Medication safety: avoid benzodiazepines when possible due to worsening PTSD/addiction risk; monitor prazosin first-dose/orthostatic hypotension.
  • Trigger safety: develop coping and safety plans for flashbacks, dissociation, severe nightmares, or reckless behavior.

Complications

  • PTSD can lead to severe sleep disturbance, impaired relationships/work, depression, substance use, reckless behavior, and suicide risk.
  • Nightmares, flashbacks, and dissociation can impair safety and daily functioning.
  • Benzodiazepines can worsen outcomes and increase dependence risk in this population.
  • Prazosin can cause dizziness/orthostatic hypotension, especially when starting or increasing dose.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Trauma-informed care principles: safety, trustworthiness, peer support, collaboration, empowerment, cultural humility. Survivor never to blame.

Pharmacotherapy:

  • SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) — FDA-approved for PTSD; first-line
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine) — alternative
  • Prazosin — specifically for trauma-related nightmares (alpha-1 blocker)
  • Mirtazapine — for insomnia/appetite
  • AVOID benzodiazepines — may worsen PTSD; high addiction risk in this population
  • Atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, quetiapine) — adjunct for refractory cases

Non-pharm (gold standards):

  • Trauma-focused CBT, Prolonged Exposure (PE), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT)
  • EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing)
  • Group therapy with trauma survivors
  • Suicide risk assessment at every visit

Medications

  • SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) — FDA-approved for PTSD; first-line
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine) — alternative
  • Prazosin — specifically for trauma-related nightmares (alpha-1 blocker)
  • Mirtazapine — for insomnia/appetite
  • AVOID benzodiazepines — may worsen PTSD; high addiction risk in this population
  • Atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, quetiapine) — adjunct for refractory cases

Non-pharm (gold standards):

  • Trauma-focused CBT, Prolonged Exposure (PE), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT)
  • EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing)
  • Group therapy with trauma survivors
  • Suicide risk assessment at every visit

Client Education

  • Recovery is possible — evidence-based treatments work; many recover or significantly improve
  • SSRIs/SNRIs take 4–12 weeks for PTSD response (longer than depression)
  • Prazosin: take at bedtime; start low to avoid first-dose hypotension; report dizziness
  • Sleep hygiene, regular exercise, limit alcohol/substances (worsen PTSD)
  • Identify and use coping strategies; build social support
  • Recognize triggers; develop a safety plan for distress episodes
  • Therapy is essential adjunct to medication
  • Crisis lines: 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; Veterans Crisis Line

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Trauma-focused CBT, prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, and EMDR are evidence-based treatments.
  • Group therapy with trauma survivors can support recovery when appropriate and safe.
  • Safety planning, grounding techniques, sleep routines, and trigger-management plans support acute distress episodes.
  • Medication follow-up should review nightmares, sleep, arousal, avoidance, mood, suicidality, BP with prazosin, and adverse effects.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with prescriber, pharmacist, trauma therapist/psychologist, primary care, and crisis resources.
  • Involve social work/case management for safety planning, housing, legal advocacy, veteran/community resources, and access barriers.
  • Refer urgently for suicidal ideation with intent/plan, severe dissociation, unsafe home situation, or uncontrolled substance use.
  • Communicate symptom clusters, triggers, sleep/nightmare response, medication effects, BP/orthostasis, substance use, and suicide-risk findings.
Worked Example Parkinson’s Disease Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · Parkinson’s section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Parkinson’s Disease
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Parkinson’s Disease (PD) — progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain.

  • Classic motor tetrad: TRAP — Tremor (resting, “pill-rolling”), Rigidity (cogwheel), Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural instability
  • Onset typically > 60 yr; affects ~1% over 60
  • Diagnosis is clinical; no specific test confirms
  • Non-motor symptoms often precede motor: anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, constipation, depression
  • Progressive course; medications manage symptoms but do not halt disease

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta → reduced dopamine in basal ganglia (nigrostriatal pathway)
  • Imbalance of dopamine (deficient) and acetylcholine (relatively excess) → motor symptoms
  • Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein protein aggregates) in remaining neurons
  • Symptoms appear when ~70–80% of dopaminergic neurons are lost
  • Multi-system involvement — autonomic, cognitive, mood regulation pathways affected
  • Etiology: combination of genetic predisposition + environmental factors (pesticides, head trauma)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote regular physical activity, fall prevention, assistive devices, home safety, constipation prevention, and caregiver education.
  • Teach exact levodopa timing, avoiding missed doses, and separating high-protein meals from levodopa when needed.
  • Encourage early speech/swallowing therapy and mental-health screening for depression, anxiety, hallucinations, and cognitive changes.
  • Reinforce not abruptly stopping dopaminergic medications because severe symptom rebound/parkinsonian crisis can occur.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess age over 60, family/genetic predisposition, pesticide exposure, head trauma, and nonmotor prodrome such as anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, constipation, or depression.
  • Screen for falls, orthostatic hypotension, dysphagia/aspiration risk, cognitive decline, hallucinations, and caregiver strain.
  • Review medications that worsen parkinsonism, especially first-generation antipsychotics and dopamine-blocking agents.
  • Assess nutrition/protein timing, adherence, on/off fluctuations, dyskinesias, and access to specialty care.

Expected Findings

Motor symptoms (TRAP):

  • Resting tremor (pill-rolling); diminishes with movement
  • Cogwheel rigidity (ratcheting resistance to passive motion)
  • Bradykinesia (slowness initiating/completing movements); shuffling gait, micrographia (small handwriting), masked facies (hypomimia)
  • Postural instability (later stage); falls; festinating gait

Non-motor symptoms:

  • Autonomic: constipation, orthostatic hypotension, urinary urgency, drooling
  • Cognitive: dementia (50%+ at late stages); executive dysfunction
  • Mood: depression (~50%), anxiety, apathy
  • Sleep: REM behavior disorder, insomnia, daytime sleepiness
  • Sensory: anosmia (loss of smell — often early)

Laboratory Tests

  • No specific laboratory test confirms Parkinson's disease; diagnosis is clinical.
  • Use labs only when ordered to rule out alternate causes of tremor, weakness, cognitive change, or medication adverse effects.
  • Monitor hydration/nutrition status and medication-safety labs when comorbidities or adjunct drugs require it.
  • Trend orthostatic vital signs, falls, dyskinesias, hallucinations, and symptom timing as practical response data.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Diagnosis is clinical based on resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability, and response to dopaminergic therapy.
  • Assess gait, balance, handwriting, facial expression, swallowing, speech, orthostatic BP, cognition, mood, and sleep.
  • Use neurologic evaluation to distinguish Parkinson's disease from medication-induced parkinsonism or other movement disorders.
  • Swallowing assessment is indicated when coughing, choking, weight loss, or aspiration risk appears.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Fall risk: bradykinesia, rigidity, postural instability, orthostatic hypotension, and freezing episodes require home safety and assistive support.
  • Medication timing: missed or delayed levodopa can cause off periods; abrupt dopaminergic withdrawal can precipitate severe crisis.
  • Aspiration risk: dysphagia, drooling, weak cough, or weight loss needs prompt evaluation.
  • Neuropsychiatric safety: monitor hallucinations, impulse-control effects, depression, anxiety, and cognitive decline.

Complications

  • Parkinson's disease can progress to falls, fractures, aspiration pneumonia, dysphagia, malnutrition, constipation, cognitive decline, dementia, depression, and caregiver burnout.
  • Levodopa can cause wearing-off, on/off fluctuations, dyskinesias, nausea, orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations, and impulse-control concerns with dopamine agonists.
  • Anticholinergics can worsen cognition, especially in older adults.
  • Medication interruption can cause sudden severe symptom return and functional decline.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Levodopa/carbidopa (Sinemet) — GOLD STANDARD; carbidopa prevents peripheral levodopa breakdown, reducing peripheral side effects
  • Dopamine agonists: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine (early disease; may delay levodopa start)
  • MAO-B inhibitors: selegiline, rasagiline
  • COMT inhibitors: entacapone, tolcapone (extend levodopa effect)
  • Anticholinergics: benztropine, trihexyphenidyl (for tremor in younger clients; avoid in older adults — cognitive impairment)
  • Amantadine (for dyskinesias)
  • Deep brain stimulation (DBS) for advanced disease

Nursing care:

  • Fall prevention: assistive devices, environmental modification, PT/OT
  • Swallowing assessment (aspiration risk); speech therapy
  • Constipation management: fluids, fiber, mobility
  • Nutrition: protein can compete with levodopa absorption — separate protein meals
  • Mental health screening: depression, anxiety, hallucinations
  • Caregiver support and education

Medications

  • Levodopa/carbidopa (Sinemet) — GOLD STANDARD; carbidopa prevents peripheral levodopa breakdown, reducing peripheral side effects
  • Dopamine agonists: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine (early disease; may delay levodopa start)
  • MAO-B inhibitors: selegiline, rasagiline
  • COMT inhibitors: entacapone, tolcapone (extend levodopa effect)
  • Anticholinergics: benztropine, trihexyphenidyl (for tremor in younger clients; avoid in older adults — cognitive impairment)
  • Amantadine (for dyskinesias)
  • Deep brain stimulation (DBS) for advanced disease

Client Education

  • Take levodopa exactly on schedule — missed doses cause “off” periods (sudden return of symptoms)
  • Take on empty stomach if possible (high-protein meals reduce absorption) — separate from protein by ≥ 30 min
  • Expect “wearing off” and on/off fluctuations as disease progresses; report to provider for dose adjustment
  • Report dyskinesias (involuntary movements), hallucinations, severe nausea
  • Rise slowly to prevent orthostatic hypotension
  • Increase fiber and fluids for constipation
  • Maintain physical activity (walking, tai chi, dancing — shown to slow motor decline)
  • Speech and swallowing therapy as needed
  • Do NOT abruptly stop dopaminergic medications (can precipitate parkinsonian crisis)
  • Avoid first-generation antipsychotics (worsen PD); if antipsychotic needed for hallucinations, use pimavanserin or quetiapine/clozapine
  • Carry medical ID; inform all providers

Therapeutic Procedures

  • PT/OT support gait training, balance, assistive devices, home safety, joint mobility, and ADL adaptation.
  • Speech and swallowing therapy address dysphagia, aspiration risk, hypophonia, and communication decline.
  • Deep brain stimulation may be used for advanced disease when medication response is inadequate or fluctuations are severe.
  • Bowel routines, nutrition/protein timing, and caregiver training support long-term function.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with neurology, pharmacist, PT/OT, speech therapy, dietitian, mental health, and caregiver resources.
  • Review medication schedules carefully across settings to avoid missed levodopa doses.
  • Refer for swallowing evaluation, fall-prevention support, DBS evaluation, or behavioral health when symptoms indicate.
  • Communicate on/off timing, falls, orthostasis, dyskinesias, hallucinations, swallowing issues, constipation, and caregiver strain.
Worked Example Alzheimer’s Disease Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · Alzheimer’s section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Alzheimer’s Disease
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) — the most common cause of dementia in older adults; a progressive, irreversible neurodegenerative disorder characterized by gradual loss of memory, cognition, language, and ultimately motor function.

  • Onset typically > 65 yr; prevalence doubles every 5 years after 65
  • Three stages: mild (early), moderate (middle), severe (late)
  • Mean duration ~8–10 years from diagnosis to death
  • Diagnosis: clinical assessment + cognitive testing (MMSE, MoCA) + imaging to rule out other causes; definitive only on autopsy
  • Risk factors: age, family history, ApoE4 allele, cardiovascular risk factors, head trauma, low education

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Amyloid-beta plaques — extracellular protein aggregates disrupt neuronal communication
  • Neurofibrillary tangles — intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau protein
  • Cholinergic deficit — loss of cholinergic neurons in basal nucleus of Meynert → reduced acetylcholine
  • Glutamate excitotoxicity — excess glutamate damages neurons
  • Brain atrophy progresses from medial temporal lobe (memory) outward
  • Synaptic dysfunction → neurotransmitter loss → cell death

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote structured routine, orientation cues, safe environment, physical activity, social engagement, cognitive stimulation, sleep routine, and caregiver support.
  • Plan early for advance directives, power of attorney, driving safety, medication management, and long-term care needs while the client can participate.
  • Reduce anticholinergic burden and alcohol use because they can worsen cognition and safety.
  • Teach that medications may slow decline, not restore lost function, and follow-up is needed to monitor benefit and adverse effects.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess age over 65, family history, ApoE4 risk, cardiovascular risk factors, head trauma, and lower education/social engagement history.
  • Screen for depression, delirium, sleep disturbance, medication adverse effects, anticholinergic burden, and caregiver safety concerns.
  • Assess wandering, falls, driving risk, medication mismanagement, dysphagia/aspiration risk, and nutrition/hydration status.
  • Review caregiver capacity and home safety because progression increases dependence.

Expected Findings

Early/mild:

  • Short-term memory loss; difficulty learning new info
  • Word-finding difficulty
  • Mild executive dysfunction; difficulty with complex tasks (finances, planning)
  • Mood changes: depression, anxiety, social withdrawal

Moderate:

  • Confusion, disorientation to time and place
  • Apraxia (difficulty with familiar tasks), agnosia
  • Behavioral disturbances: agitation, wandering, sundowning, paranoia, hallucinations
  • Sleep disturbance
  • Inability to manage ADLs independently

Severe/late:

  • Severe memory loss; inability to recognize family
  • Loss of communication (aphasia, mutism)
  • Loss of motor function: incontinence, immobility
  • Dysphagia; aspiration risk
  • Total dependence; eventually bed-bound

Laboratory Tests

  • No single routine lab confirms Alzheimer's disease; diagnosis is clinical with exclusion of reversible causes.
  • Use ordered labs to evaluate contributors to cognitive change, such as thyroid dysfunction, B12 deficiency, infection, dehydration, anemia, or medication effects.
  • Monitor medication-safety labs only when required by comorbidities or prescribed therapies.
  • Trend cognitive/functional assessments and caregiver reports as primary response data.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use cognitive testing such as MMSE or MoCA plus history of progressive memory, language, executive, and functional decline.
  • Use imaging when ordered to rule out alternate causes of dementia or cognitive decline.
  • Assess ADLs/IADLs, wandering, sleep, behavior, dysphagia, falls, and caregiver burden at each stage.
  • Differentiate dementia progression from delirium, depression, medication effects, infection, or metabolic problems.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Home safety: wandering, falls, driving, cooking, medication errors, and financial vulnerability require supervision and environmental controls.
  • Medication safety: cholinesterase inhibitors can cause GI effects, bradycardia, and syncope; antipsychotics carry increased mortality risk in dementia.
  • Dysphagia safety: late-stage swallowing difficulty increases aspiration and malnutrition risk.
  • Caregiver safety: monitor caregiver burnout, unsafe behaviors, agitation, and need for respite/support.

Complications

  • Alzheimer's disease progresses to loss of independence, wandering, falls, malnutrition, dysphagia, aspiration, incontinence, immobility, and total dependence.
  • Behavioral symptoms can include agitation, sundowning, paranoia, hallucinations, and sleep disturbance.
  • Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause GI upset, bradycardia, and syncope; antipsychotics increase mortality risk in dementia.
  • Caregiver burden and delayed planning can compromise safety and continuity of care.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) — mild-moderate AD; slow decline by ~6–12 months
  • NMDA antagonist (memantine) — moderate-severe AD; can combine with cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Newer disease-modifying agents (aducanumab, lecanemab) — controversial; high cost, modest benefit, brain edema risk
  • Symptomatic: SSRIs for depression; antipsychotics (cautious) for severe agitation/psychosis — BBW for increased mortality in dementia

Non-pharm (more important than meds):

  • Structured environment, consistent routine, orientation cues
  • Safety: door alarms (wandering), remove hazards, supervision
  • Communication: short sentences, eye contact, validation rather than correction
  • Caregiver education and support
  • Adult day programs, respite care
  • Advance care planning EARLY (while client can participate)
  • Avoid restraints; minimize anticholinergic burden (worsens cognition)

Medications

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) — mild-moderate AD; slow decline by ~6–12 months
  • NMDA antagonist (memantine) — moderate-severe AD; can combine with cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Newer disease-modifying agents (aducanumab, lecanemab) — controversial; high cost, modest benefit, brain edema risk
  • Symptomatic: SSRIs for depression; antipsychotics (cautious) for severe agitation/psychosis — BBW for increased mortality in dementia

Non-pharm (more important than meds):

  • Structured environment, consistent routine, orientation cues
  • Safety: door alarms (wandering), remove hazards, supervision
  • Communication: short sentences, eye contact, validation rather than correction
  • Caregiver education and support
  • Adult day programs, respite care
  • Advance care planning EARLY (while client can participate)
  • Avoid restraints; minimize anticholinergic burden (worsens cognition)

Client Education

  • Diagnosis and prognosis discussed honestly; engage in advance directives and POA decisions while still able
  • Medication takes weeks to show effect; expect slowed decline, not improvement
  • Cholinesterase inhibitor side effects: GI (most common — titrate slowly), bradycardia, syncope
  • Use memory aids: calendars, labels, simple lists
  • Maintain physical activity, social engagement, cognitive stimulation
  • Mediterranean-style diet may slow progression
  • Sleep regularly; avoid alcohol
  • Caregivers: join support groups (Alzheimer’s Association); learn de-escalation techniques; address own self-care
  • Driving cessation conversations — safety priority
  • Plan for eventual long-term care needs

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Structured routine, orientation cues, validation communication, environmental safety measures, door alarms, and supervision are central interventions.
  • Adult day programs, respite care, caregiver training, and support groups help maintain care at home when safe.
  • Speech/swallow evaluation, nutrition support, and aspiration precautions are needed as swallowing declines.
  • Advance care planning should occur early while the client can participate.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with neurology/geriatrics, pharmacist, primary care, social work, OT, speech therapy, dietitian, and caregiver support resources.
  • Use pharmacist review to reduce anticholinergic burden and monitor cholinesterase inhibitor/memantine tolerability.
  • Refer to Alzheimer support organizations, adult day care, respite, home safety evaluation, and long-term care planning resources.
  • Communicate cognitive/functional changes, wandering/falls, driving concerns, swallowing issues, behavior changes, medication effects, and caregiver strain.
Worked Example Asthma Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Asthma
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Asthma — chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterized by reversible airflow obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and episodes of wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, and cough.

  • Affects ~8% of US population; common in children
  • Triggers vary: allergens, exercise, cold air, viral infections, irritants (smoke), aspirin/NSAIDs, stress
  • Severity classified by symptom frequency and pulmonary function (NAEPP/GINA guidelines): intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, severe persistent
  • Goal of management: control inflammation, prevent attacks, maintain normal activity, minimize medication side effects

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Airway inflammation — mast cells, eosinophils, T-lymphocytes release inflammatory mediators
  • Bronchospasm — smooth muscle contraction narrows airways
  • Airway edema from inflammation
  • Mucus hypersecretion — thick mucus plugs further narrow airways
  • Airway remodeling (chronic) — permanent thickening of airway walls
  • Result: increased airway resistance, decreased airflow, particularly on expiration (air trapping)
  • Triggers: allergens (dust mites, pollen, pet dander), irritants (smoke, pollution), exercise, infection, cold air, emotional stress, GERD, certain meds (aspirin, beta blockers)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote trigger avoidance, smoking cessation, dust-mite and environmental control, HEPA filtration when helpful, and cold-air/exercise pre-treatment plans as prescribed.
  • Reinforce annual influenza vaccination, pneumococcal vaccination as indicated, and routine follow-up with pulmonary function review.
  • Teach asthma action plan use with green/yellow/red zones, peak-flow monitoring, and early reporting of increased rescue inhaler use.
  • Emphasize controller adherence even when asymptomatic and correct inhaler/nebulizer/spacer technique.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess personal triggers: allergens, smoke, respiratory infections, exercise, cold air, occupational exposures, stress, and medication triggers.
  • Review atopy/allergy history, elevated IgE/eosinophilia pattern, family history, and prior exacerbation or hospitalization history.
  • Assess adherence, inhaler technique, access to controller/rescue medications, and misunderstanding of quick-relief vs long-term therapy.
  • Screen comorbidities that worsen control, such as GERD, obesity, sleep apnea, sinus disease, or anxiety when clinically relevant.

Expected Findings

Asthma attack symptoms:

  • Wheezing (expiratory; may be inspiratory in severe)
  • Dyspnea, shortness of breath
  • Chest tightness
  • Persistent cough (especially at night/early morning)
  • Use of accessory muscles, retractions (severe)
  • Tachypnea, tachycardia
  • Pulsus paradoxus (severe)
  • Cyanosis, decreased oxygen saturation
  • Silent chest (extremely severe — ominous; cannot move air)

Diagnostic findings:

  • Spirometry: reduced FEV1, reduced FEV1/FVC ratio, reversibility (≥ 12% improvement after bronchodilator)
  • Peak flow monitoring at home (personal best, zones)
  • Eosinophilia on CBC
  • Elevated IgE in atopic asthma
  • Methacholine challenge if diagnosis unclear

Laboratory Tests

  • CBC can show eosinophilia in allergic/eosinophilic asthma patterns.
  • IgE can be elevated in atopic asthma and can support biologic-therapy evaluation when ordered.
  • Monitor medication-safety labs when systemic corticosteroids, methylxanthines, or biologics require provider-directed monitoring.
  • During severe exacerbations, use ordered oxygenation/ventilation labs to assess respiratory compromise and response to therapy.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Spirometry shows reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1/FVC ratio with reversibility after bronchodilator.
  • Peak-flow monitoring compares current readings with personal best and action-plan zones.
  • Methacholine challenge may be used when the diagnosis is unclear.
  • Assess pulse oximetry, work of breathing, accessory muscle use, and silent chest during exacerbations to determine severity.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Emergency signs: severe shortness of breath unrelieved by rescue medication, peak flow <50% personal best, inability to speak in full sentences, cyanosis, or silent chest requires urgent care.
  • Rescue vs controller safety: teach SABA for quick relief and inhaled glucocorticoids/montelukast/cromolyn for prevention; inhaled glucocorticoids are not for acute attacks.
  • Medication precautions: rinse mouth and use spacer with inhaled glucocorticoids, taper oral steroids as ordered, monitor mood/behavior changes with montelukast, and use cromolyn only for prophylaxis.
  • Trend control: keep a log of exacerbation frequency/intensity and report increasing rescue use or worsening symptoms.

Complications

  • Uncontrolled asthma can progress to acute exacerbation, hypoxemia, respiratory failure, or need for ICU/intubation in refractory severe cases.
  • Inhaled glucocorticoids can cause oral candidiasis if the client does not rinse the mouth after use.
  • Oral corticosteroids can cause systemic effects with longer-term use and must be tapered as ordered.
  • Montelukast can be associated with mood or behavior changes; underuse of controller therapy or overreliance on rescue therapy increases exacerbation risk.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Stepwise pharmacologic management (NAEPP/GINA):

  • Step 1 (intermittent): SABA (albuterol) PRN; ICS-formoterol as PRN reliever per GINA
  • Step 2 (mild persistent): Low-dose ICS daily + SABA PRN
  • Step 3: Low-dose ICS + LABA, or medium-dose ICS
  • Step 4: Medium-dose ICS + LABA
  • Step 5: High-dose ICS + LABA; consider biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab) for severe
  • Step 6: + oral corticosteroids
  • Leukotriene modifiers (montelukast) — alternative or add-on

Acute exacerbation:

  • SABA via nebulizer or MDI with spacer (albuterol)
  • Ipratropium (anticholinergic) in moderate-severe
  • Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone, methylprednisolone)
  • Oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 90–94%
  • IV magnesium for severe
  • Heliox, ICU/intubation for refractory severe

Non-pharm:

  • Trigger avoidance: HEPA filters, dust-mite covers, smoking cessation
  • Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines
  • Asthma Action Plan with green/yellow/red zones
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation for severe cases

Medications

  • Short-acting beta2 agonists (albuterol): quick-relief bronchodilators for acute symptoms; increased use can signal poor asthma control.
  • Long-acting beta2 agonists: provide long-term bronchodilation and are used with controller therapy as prescribed.
  • Inhaled glucocorticoids (fluticasone, beclomethasone): first-line controllers; rinse mouth after use, use a spacer, and do not use for an acute attack.
  • Oral glucocorticoids (prednisone): used for exacerbations; taper as ordered and monitor systemic effects with longer-term use.
  • Leukotriene modifiers (montelukast): oral long-term control, often taken in the evening; not for acute attack; monitor mood or behavior changes.
  • Cromolyn: mast-cell stabilizer for prophylaxis, including exercise-induced symptoms; teach fixed vs PRN schedule and correct inhaler/nebulizer technique.
  • Other options: anticholinergics, methylxanthines, and biologics such as omalizumab may be used for selected airflow disorders.

Client Education

  • Distinguish reliever (rescue) vs controller medications — rescue (SABA) for symptoms; controllers (ICS) DAILY even when feeling well
  • Use of MDI/DPI with proper technique; spacer with MDI improves delivery
  • Rinse mouth after ICS to prevent thrush
  • Peak flow monitoring: know personal best; act on zones (green/yellow/red)
  • Asthma Action Plan: when to take rescue, when to add steroids, when to seek emergency care
  • Identify and avoid personal triggers
  • Cold air: cover mouth with scarf; exercise: pre-treat with SABA 15–30 min before
  • Vaccinations: annual flu shot, pneumococcal series
  • NEVER use only SABA as monotherapy in chronic asthma (linked to mortality)
  • Seek emergency care for: severe shortness of breath unrelieved by rescue, peak flow < 50% personal best, cannot speak in full sentences, cyanosis
  • Regular follow-up with provider; PFTs annually

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Acute exacerbation support: administer nebulized SABA/MDI with spacer, add ipratropium for moderate-severe exacerbations when ordered, provide oxygen, and give systemic corticosteroids as prescribed.
  • Severe refractory exacerbation: prepare for IV magnesium, ICU-level care, or intubation/ventilatory support if ordered.
  • Monitoring procedures: use peak-flow monitoring and spirometry/PFT follow-up to guide control and action-plan zones.
  • Long-term support: pulmonary rehabilitation may be used for severe disease, while trigger control and vaccination reduce exacerbation risk.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider, pharmacist, and respiratory therapist for inhaler selection, spacer/nebulizer teaching, action-plan review, and stepwise therapy adjustment.
  • Involve pulmonology/allergy specialists for severe asthma, biologic therapy such as omalizumab, frequent exacerbations, or unclear diagnosis.
  • Use school/workplace resources, smoking-cessation support, and environmental-control counseling to reduce trigger exposure.
  • Communicate peak-flow trends, rescue inhaler use, exacerbation frequency, inhaler technique problems, and steroid/biologic adverse effects.
Worked Example Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
COPD
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Airflow Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) — preventable and treatable disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation that is usually progressive, associated with enhanced chronic inflammatory response.

  • Includes emphysema (alveolar destruction; loss of elastic recoil) and chronic bronchitis (chronic productive cough ≥ 3 months in 2 consecutive years)
  • Primary cause: cigarette smoking (85–90%); also environmental pollutants, occupational dusts, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
  • 3rd leading cause of death in US
  • GOLD staging based on FEV1 % predicted:
    • GOLD 1 (mild): FEV1 ≥ 80%
    • GOLD 2 (moderate): 50–80%
    • GOLD 3 (severe): 30–50%
    • GOLD 4 (very severe): < 30%

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Chronic inflammation from noxious particles/gases (tobacco smoke)
  • Emphysema: destruction of alveolar walls → loss of elasticity → air trapping; barrel chest from hyperinflation
  • Chronic bronchitis: goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → chronic productive cough
  • Small airway disease: peripheral airway narrowing from inflammation and fibrosis
  • V/Q mismatch: impaired gas exchange → hypoxemia, hypercapnia (later stages)
  • Pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale (right heart failure)
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in some clients

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote smoking cessation as the most important intervention to slow disease progression.
  • Encourage influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, Tdap, and RSV vaccination as appropriate, plus hand hygiene and avoidance of respiratory infections.
  • Support pulmonary rehabilitation, activity pacing, pursed-lip breathing, adequate hydration, and high-protein small frequent meals.
  • Teach correct inhaler technique, rinse mouth after ICS, oxygen safety, and early reporting of exacerbation symptoms.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess cigarette smoking history, secondhand smoke, occupational dust/chemical exposure, air pollution, and biomass/environmental exposures.
  • Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, especially in younger clients or nonsmokers with COPD.
  • Screen for recurrent respiratory infection, asthma overlap, poor inhaler technique, and access barriers to maintenance inhalers or oxygen.
  • Assess nutritional decline, cachexia, fatigue, and activity intolerance that can worsen outcomes.

Expected Findings

Symptoms (progressive over years):

  • Dyspnea on exertion (early), then at rest (late)
  • Chronic productive cough (often clear/white sputum)
  • Wheezing, prolonged expiration
  • Pursed-lip breathing (compensatory)
  • Fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance
  • Weight loss, cachexia (late)

Physical exam:

  • Barrel chest (increased AP diameter)
  • Use of accessory muscles, tripod position
  • Decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance on percussion
  • Wheezing, rhonchi, prolonged expiratory phase
  • Clubbing (chronic hypoxia)
  • Cyanosis (late)
  • Edema (cor pulmonale)

Diagnostic:

  • Spirometry: FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70 (post-bronchodilator) — CONFIRMS COPD
  • Chest X-ray: hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm
  • ABG: hypoxemia, hypercapnia (later stages)
  • CBC: polycythemia (chronic hypoxia)
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin level (especially < 45 yo or non-smoker COPD)

Laboratory Tests

  • ABGs can show hypoxemia and later hypercapnia during advanced disease or exacerbation.
  • CBC can show polycythemia from chronic hypoxia or infection-related changes during exacerbation.
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin level is used when early-onset COPD or COPD in a nonsmoker is suspected.
  • Monitor medication-safety labs when systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, or other acute-exacerbation therapies are prescribed.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Post-bronchodilator spirometry confirms COPD when FEV1/FVC is <0.70.
  • Chest x-ray can show hyperinflation and flattened diaphragm and helps evaluate alternate or acute causes.
  • Pulse oximetry and ABG help assess severity during exacerbations and oxygen needs.
  • Use GOLD staging with FEV1 percent predicted and symptom/exacerbation history to guide therapy intensity.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Exacerbation warning: increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, color change, fever, worsening wheeze, or reduced SpO2 needs prompt provider contact.
  • Oxygen safety: target SpO2 is often 88-92%; avoid smoking/open flames and follow prescribed flow rates.
  • Medication safety: use SABA for acute symptoms, LAMA/LABA for maintenance, rinse mouth after ICS, and monitor systemic steroid effects during exacerbations.
  • Respiratory failure signs: severe fatigue, confusion, cyanosis, silent/poor air movement, or worsening hypercapnia requires urgent escalation.

Complications

  • COPD can progress to hypoxemia, hypercapnia, acute exacerbations, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, cachexia, and death.
  • Frequent exacerbations accelerate decline and can require antibiotics, systemic steroids, hospitalization, or ventilatory support.
  • ICS can increase oral candidiasis risk; systemic steroids can cause glucose, mood, infection, and bone effects.
  • Unsafe oxygen use creates fire risk and inappropriate oxygen delivery can worsen CO2 retention in susceptible clients.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (stepwise per GOLD):

  • SABA (albuterol) for acute symptoms; PRN
  • LAMA (tiotropium, umeclidinium) — first-line maintenance; long-acting bronchodilator
  • LABA (salmeterol, formoterol) — long-acting bronchodilator
  • LAMA/LABA combinations (umeclidinium/vilanterol)
  • ICS add-on for frequent exacerbations or with asthma overlap
  • Triple therapy (ICS/LAMA/LABA) for severe with frequent exacerbations
  • Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor (roflumilast) for severe chronic bronchitis with exacerbations
  • Oral steroids for acute exacerbations (5–7 days)
  • Antibiotics for infectious exacerbations (azithromycin sometimes used preventively)

Oxygen therapy:

  • Indicated when PaO2 ≤ 55 mmHg or SpO2 ≤ 88%
  • Target SpO2 88–92% (avoid over-oxygenation — can suppress hypoxic drive)
  • Long-term home oxygen if criteria met (improves survival)

Non-pharm:

  • Smoking cessation — the single most important intervention
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation — improves QOL, exercise tolerance
  • Vaccines: influenza annually, pneumococcal, COVID-19, Tdap, RSV (older adults)
  • Nutrition: high-protein, smaller frequent meals (large meals worsen dyspnea)
  • Breathing techniques: pursed-lip, diaphragmatic breathing
  • End-stage: palliative care discussion, lung transplant for select patients

Medications

  • SABA (albuterol) for acute symptoms; PRN
  • LAMA (tiotropium, umeclidinium) — first-line maintenance; long-acting bronchodilator
  • LABA (salmeterol, formoterol) — long-acting bronchodilator
  • LAMA/LABA combinations (umeclidinium/vilanterol)
  • ICS add-on for frequent exacerbations or with asthma overlap
  • Triple therapy (ICS/LAMA/LABA) for severe with frequent exacerbations
  • Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor (roflumilast) for severe chronic bronchitis with exacerbations
  • Oral steroids for acute exacerbations (5–7 days)
  • Antibiotics for infectious exacerbations (azithromycin sometimes used preventively)

Oxygen therapy:

  • Indicated when PaO2 ≤ 55 mmHg or SpO2 ≤ 88%
  • Target SpO2 88–92% (avoid over-oxygenation — can suppress hypoxic drive)
  • Long-term home oxygen if criteria met (improves survival)

Non-pharm:

  • Smoking cessation — the single most important intervention
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation — improves QOL, exercise tolerance
  • Vaccines: influenza annually, pneumococcal, COVID-19, Tdap, RSV (older adults)
  • Nutrition: high-protein, smaller frequent meals (large meals worsen dyspnea)
  • Breathing techniques: pursed-lip, diaphragmatic breathing
  • End-stage: palliative care discussion, lung transplant for select patients

Client Education

  • Stop smoking — this is the most important step for slowing disease progression
  • Use inhalers with proper technique; demonstrate at every visit
  • Rinse mouth after ICS (oral candidiasis prevention)
  • Recognize exacerbation signs: increased dyspnea, sputum color change, increased volume; contact provider promptly
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation participation improves quality of life
  • Annual flu shot; one-time pneumococcal vaccines
  • Pursed-lip breathing during dyspnea episodes; tripod position to ease breathing
  • Activity pacing; energy conservation strategies
  • Adequate hydration to thin secretions
  • Cor pulmonale signs: peripheral edema, weight gain, JVD — report
  • Home oxygen safety: no smoking, no open flames, keep away from heat
  • Avoid people with respiratory infections; hand hygiene
  • Advance directives and end-of-life planning conversations EARLY

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Use pulmonary rehabilitation, pursed-lip breathing, diaphragmatic breathing, tripod positioning, activity pacing, and nutrition support to improve function.
  • Oxygen therapy is indicated when criteria are met and can improve survival with long-term home use.
  • During exacerbations, prepare for nebulized bronchodilators, systemic steroids, antibiotics when infectious signs are present, oxygen titration, and ABG monitoring.
  • End-stage COPD may require palliative-care planning or lung-transplant referral for selected clients.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider, pharmacist, and respiratory therapist for inhaler selection, technique checks, oxygen orders, and exacerbation action plans.
  • Involve pulmonology for severe disease, frequent exacerbations, oxygen qualification, alpha-1 antitrypsin concern, or transplant/palliative discussions.
  • Use smoking-cessation resources, pulmonary rehabilitation, dietitian, home oxygen supplier, and social work/case management support.
  • Communicate spirometry, SpO2/ABG results, exacerbation frequency, sputum changes, oxygen safety concerns, and medication access barriers.
Worked Example Allergic Rhinitis Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Allergic Rhinitis
Review Module Chapter
Ch 18 — Upper Respiratory Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Allergic Rhinitis — IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction of the nasal mucosa to environmental allergens, characterized by sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and itching.

  • Seasonal (hay fever): triggered by pollens (trees in spring, grasses in summer, weeds in fall, ragweed)
  • Perennial: year-round; triggered by dust mites, pet dander, mold, cockroaches
  • Affects ~15–30% of population; often onset in childhood/adolescence
  • Strong association with asthma, eczema (atopic march); ~30% of allergic rhinitis clients develop asthma
  • Family history of atopy is a major risk factor

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Sensitization phase: initial allergen exposure → IgE production by B-cells → IgE binds to mast cells
  • Early-phase reaction (within minutes): allergen re-exposure crosslinks IgE on mast cells → histamine release + other mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins, tryptase) → vasodilation, edema, mucus, itching, sneezing
  • Late-phase reaction (4–8 hr later): eosinophils, neutrophils, T-cells infiltrate → sustained nasal congestion, hyperresponsiveness
  • Chronic exposure → mucosal hypertrophy, polyp formation

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Identify and reduce allergen exposure, including pollen, dust mites, pet dander, mold, and cockroaches when relevant.
  • Use routine intranasal corticosteroid technique and adherence during symptom seasons or perennial exposure as prescribed.
  • Teach saline irrigation, trigger avoidance, and early treatment before symptoms progress to congestion, sleep disruption, or asthma worsening.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Family history of atopy, asthma, eczema, childhood or adolescent onset, and repeated environmental allergen exposure increase risk.
  • Seasonal pollen exposure causes intermittent symptoms; dust mites, pets, mold, and cockroaches can cause perennial symptoms.
  • Chronic mucosal inflammation can worsen nasal obstruction and is associated with asthma and eczema in the atopic pattern.

Expected Findings

Classic symptoms:

  • Sneezing (often paroxysmal)
  • Rhinorrhea (clear, watery)
  • Nasal congestion
  • Nasal itching
  • Itchy/watery eyes (allergic conjunctivitis)
  • Postnasal drip, throat clearing, cough
  • Mild fatigue, headache
  • Decreased sense of smell

Physical signs:

  • Allergic shiners — dark periorbital circles (venous congestion)
  • Allergic salute — transverse nasal crease from rubbing
  • Pale, boggy, blue-gray nasal mucosa with clear discharge
  • Cobblestone appearance of posterior pharynx
  • Mouth breathing in children — can cause dental malocclusion

Diagnostic:

  • Clinical history (often sufficient)
  • Skin prick testing — gold standard for specific allergen identification
  • Serum-specific IgE testing (RAST or ImmunoCAP) — alternative if skin testing contraindicated
  • Nasal smear (eosinophils > 10%)

Laboratory Tests

  • Routine labs are not required for uncomplicated allergic rhinitis.
  • Allergy-related testing such as IgE or eosinophil evaluation may be used when ordered for unclear or persistent symptoms.
  • Monitor medication-specific safety needs when systemic therapy or interacting medications are used.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Diagnosis is mainly clinical, based on sneezing, rhinorrhea, congestion, itching, timing, and allergen exposure pattern.
  • Allergy skin testing or specific IgE testing can identify triggers when symptoms are persistent, severe, or immunotherapy is being considered.
  • Evaluate for sinusitis, nasal polyps, or asthma when symptoms are refractory or lower-airway symptoms occur.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Monitor first-generation antihistamines for sedation and anticholinergic effects, especially in older adults.
  • Use decongestants cautiously in hypertension, cardiac disease, glaucoma, and BPH because they can worsen BP, palpitations, or urinary retention.
  • Teach intranasal steroid technique to reduce epistaxis and report wheezing, shortness of breath, fever, facial pain, or purulent drainage.

Complications

  • Sinusitis, otitis media, sleep disruption, impaired concentration, nasal polyps, and reduced quality of life.
  • Asthma exacerbation or worsening lower-airway symptoms in clients with atopic disease.
  • Medication harm such as sedation, falls, anticholinergic effects, rebound congestion from overused topical decongestants, or decongestant-related BP elevation.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (stepwise):

  • Intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone, mometasone, budesonide) — MOST EFFECTIVE for moderate-severe; daily use; takes days for full effect
  • Second-generation antihistamines (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine) — first-line for mild-moderate; less sedating
  • Intranasal antihistamines (azelastine) — alternative or add-on
  • Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) — if asthma + allergic rhinitis
  • Nasal decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, oxymetazoline spray) — SHORT-TERM only; rhinitis medicamentosa risk with topical > 3–5 days
  • Saline nasal irrigation (neti pot, NeilMed) — mechanical removal of allergens
  • Allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual) — for severe persistent symptoms; modifies underlying immune response
  • First-gen antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) — very sedating; avoid in older adults (Beers list)

Non-pharm:

  • Allergen avoidance/reduction (HEPA filters, dust mite covers, hardwood floors, no carpets)
  • Shower after outdoor activity during pollen season
  • Keep windows closed during high pollen days
  • Wear sunglasses outdoors (reduces ocular exposure)
  • Vacuum with HEPA filter
  • Remove pets from bedroom if pet allergy

Medications

  • Intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone, mometasone, budesonide) — MOST EFFECTIVE for moderate-severe; daily use; takes days for full effect
  • Second-generation antihistamines (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine) — first-line for mild-moderate; less sedating
  • Intranasal antihistamines (azelastine) — alternative or add-on
  • Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) — if asthma + allergic rhinitis
  • Nasal decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, oxymetazoline spray) — SHORT-TERM only; rhinitis medicamentosa risk with topical > 3–5 days
  • Saline nasal irrigation (neti pot, NeilMed) — mechanical removal of allergens
  • Allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual) — for severe persistent symptoms; modifies underlying immune response
  • First-gen antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) — very sedating; avoid in older adults (Beers list)

Non-pharm:

  • Allergen avoidance/reduction (HEPA filters, dust mite covers, hardwood floors, no carpets)
  • Shower after outdoor activity during pollen season
  • Keep windows closed during high pollen days
  • Wear sunglasses outdoors (reduces ocular exposure)
  • Vacuum with HEPA filter
  • Remove pets from bedroom if pet allergy

Client Education

  • Allergic rhinitis is not infectious; family/coworkers cannot catch it
  • Most effective treatment: intranasal corticosteroids — daily, takes days for full effect
  • Combine medication with allergen avoidance for best results
  • Start medications BEFORE peak season (1–2 weeks); continue throughout
  • Proper nasal spray technique: tilt head slightly forward, spray AWAY from septum (lateral) to avoid epistaxis
  • Identify and avoid your specific allergens
  • Monitor for asthma symptoms (often co-occurs); use rescue inhaler if prescribed
  • Decongestants only short-term (≤ 3 days for nasal sprays to avoid rebound)
  • Consider allergist referral for severe symptoms or immunotherapy
  • Track symptoms in a diary; identify patterns
  • For children: discuss with school nurse for medication during school hours

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Allergen avoidance and environmental control are core nonpharmacologic interventions.
  • Nasal saline irrigation can support symptom control and reduce irritant burden.
  • Allergen immunotherapy may be considered through allergy specialty care when symptoms remain uncontrolled or triggers are confirmed.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the pharmacist for antihistamine selection, intranasal steroid technique, decongestant precautions, and OTC duplication screening.
  • Refer to allergy/immunology for testing or immunotherapy when symptoms are severe, persistent, or trigger identification is needed.
  • Coordinate with primary care or respiratory care when asthma symptoms, wheezing, or frequent sinus complications are present.
Worked Example Heart Failure Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Heart Failure
Review Module Chapter
Ch 19 — Medications Affecting Urinary Output

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Heart Failure (HF) — clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s metabolic demands, resulting in fluid congestion and/or inadequate tissue perfusion.

  • HFrEF (reduced ejection fraction, ≤ 40%) — systolic dysfunction; impaired contractility
  • HFpEF (preserved ejection fraction, ≥ 50%) — diastolic dysfunction; impaired filling
  • Left-sided HF → pulmonary congestion (most common)
  • Right-sided HF → systemic venous congestion (often from left-sided)
  • NYHA Functional Classification I–IV based on activity limitation
  • Common causes: CAD/MI, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, diabetes

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Decreased cardiac output → compensatory mechanisms become maladaptive over time
  • RAAS activation: low renal perfusion → renin → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) → aldosterone (sodium/water retention) → increased preload and afterload
  • Sympathetic activation: increased HR and contractility (initially helpful, eventually harmful; increases myocardial oxygen demand)
  • Ventricular remodeling: hypertrophy and dilation → worsening function
  • Natriuretic peptides (BNP) released in response to ventricular stretch
  • Fluid backs up: left HF → lungs (pulmonary edema); right HF → periphery (edema, ascites, hepatomegaly)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Prevent worsening HF through daily weights, sodium restriction, fluid restriction if ordered, medication adherence, smoking cessation, alcohol limitation, and vaccination.
  • Teach early reporting of weight gain, increasing dyspnea, swelling, fatigue, cough when lying down, or orthopnea.
  • Encourage gradual activity progression, energy conservation, and cardiac rehabilitation when available.
  • Promote control of HTN, CAD, diabetes, valvular disease, and other causes that worsen cardiac workload.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess CAD/MI, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, dysrhythmias, renal disease, and prior HF hospitalization.
  • Screen for fluid overload triggers: high sodium intake, missed diuretics, NSAID use, infection, uncontrolled BP, or medication nonadherence.
  • Review renal function and potassium risk before RAAS, ARNI, mineralocorticoid antagonist, SGLT2 inhibitor, or diuretic therapy.
  • Assess functional status, NYHA class symptoms, weight trend, and ability to obtain/understand medications.

Expected Findings

Left-sided HF (pulmonary congestion):

  • Dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  • Crackles (rales), wheezing
  • Pink frothy sputum (pulmonary edema)
  • Fatigue, weakness
  • S3 gallop, tachycardia
  • Cough (especially when lying down)

Right-sided HF (systemic congestion):

  • Peripheral edema (dependent: ankles, sacrum)
  • Jugular venous distension (JVD)
