  • Hepatomegaly, ascites
  • Weight gain (fluid retention)
  • Nausea, anorexia (GI congestion)

Diagnostic:

  • BNP / NT-proBNP elevated (key marker; correlates with severity)
  • Echocardiogram: ejection fraction, wall motion, valve function
  • Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, pleural effusion
  • EKG: arrhythmias, ischemia, hypertrophy
  • Labs: electrolytes, renal function, troponin

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor BNP/NT-proBNP to support HF severity assessment and response trends.
  • Trend electrolytes, especially potassium, and renal function with loop diuretics, RAAS/ARNI therapy, and mineralocorticoid antagonists.
  • Check troponin when ischemia or acute decompensation is suspected.
  • Monitor medication-specific levels or labs when ordered, including digoxin level if used because of its narrow therapeutic index.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Echocardiogram evaluates ejection fraction, wall motion, valve function, and HFrEF vs HFpEF pattern.
  • Chest x-ray can show cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, or pleural effusion.
  • EKG assesses dysrhythmias, ischemia, or hypertrophy that can worsen HF.
  • Assess daily weight, lung sounds, edema, JVD, oxygen saturation, and I&O as bedside indicators of congestion/perfusion.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Pulmonary edema warning: worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, pink frothy sputum, or low SpO2 requires prompt escalation.
  • Daily weight safety: report gain >2-3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week.
  • Medication monitoring: monitor potassium and renal function with diuretics/RAAS therapies; watch for hypotension, dizziness, dehydration, and digoxin toxicity if prescribed.
  • Fluid safety: follow sodium/fluid restriction, strict I&O when ordered, and high Fowler's positioning for dyspnea.

Complications

  • HF can progress to pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, cardiogenic shock, dysrhythmias, renal hypoperfusion, recurrent hospitalization, and death.
  • Fluid overload can cause respiratory distress, JVD, ascites, edema, hepatomegaly, and rapid weight gain.
  • Therapy complications include electrolyte imbalance, renal dysfunction, hypotension, dehydration, and digoxin toxicity when used.
  • Missed medications or high-sodium intake can trigger acute decompensation.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy — GDMT for HFrEF):

  • ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACE inhibitor/ARB — reduce afterload, block RAAS
  • Beta blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol) — reduce sympathetic effects; improve survival
  • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduce mortality
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) — reduce hospitalization/mortality
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) — symptom relief (congestion); do NOT improve survival but essential for fluid control
  • Digoxin — symptom control in select cases (narrow therapeutic index)
  • Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate — especially in Black clients or ACE/ARB intolerant

Nursing care:

  • Daily weights (same time, same scale, same clothing) — report gain > 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week
  • Strict I&O; fluid restriction if ordered (often 2 L/day)
  • Sodium restriction (2–3 g/day)
  • Position: high Fowler’s for dyspnea
  • Oxygen as needed; monitor SpO2
  • Monitor electrolytes (especially K+ with diuretics), renal function, BNP
  • Energy conservation; gradual activity progression

Medications

  • ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACE inhibitor/ARB — reduce afterload, block RAAS
  • Beta blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol) — reduce sympathetic effects; improve survival
  • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduce mortality
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) — reduce hospitalization/mortality
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) — symptom relief (congestion); do NOT improve survival but essential for fluid control
  • Digoxin — symptom control in select cases (narrow therapeutic index)
  • Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate — especially in Black clients or ACE/ARB intolerant

Client Education

  • Daily weights — same time each morning; report gain of 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week
  • Low-sodium diet (read labels; avoid processed/canned foods, deli meats)
  • Fluid restriction if prescribed
  • Take all medications as prescribed (do not skip even when feeling well)
  • Recognize worsening HF: increased SOB, swelling, weight gain, fatigue, orthopnea — report promptly
  • Diuretics: take in the morning (avoid nocturia); monitor for dizziness; eat potassium-rich foods if on loop diuretics (unless on K-sparing)
  • Daily activity as tolerated; cardiac rehab if available
  • Smoking cessation; limit alcohol
  • Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines
  • Weigh medications’ benefits (improved survival, fewer hospitalizations)
  • Advance directives discussion as appropriate
  • Keep all follow-up appointments; lab monitoring essential

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Use high Fowler's positioning, oxygen as needed, strict I&O, daily weights, sodium restriction, and fluid restriction when ordered to manage congestion.
  • Prepare for IV diuretic therapy, electrolyte replacement, or acute decompensation protocols when symptoms worsen.
  • Cardiac rehabilitation and gradual activity progression can improve function and self-management.
  • For advanced disease, coordinate provider-directed discussions about specialty HF care, palliative care, and advance directives.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with cardiology/provider and pharmacist for GDMT titration, diuretic adjustment, renal/electrolyte monitoring, and interaction review.
  • Involve dietitian for sodium/fluid teaching and diabetes/renal nutrition needs.
  • Use cardiac rehabilitation, home health, case management, and social work to support daily weights, medication access, and readmission prevention.
  • Communicate weight trends, I&O, lung sounds, edema, BNP/renal/electrolyte results, and worsening symptoms promptly.
Worked Example Atrial Fibrillation Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Atrial Fibrillation
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Atrial Fibrillation (AFib) — the most common sustained cardiac dysrhythmia, characterized by rapid, disorganized atrial electrical activity causing an irregularly irregular ventricular response and loss of effective atrial contraction.

  • No discernible P waves on EKG; irregularly irregular rhythm
  • Classifications: paroxysmal (self-terminating < 7 days), persistent (> 7 days), long-standing persistent (> 1 yr), permanent
  • Major risk: thromboembolism / stroke (blood stasis in atria → clots)
  • Prevalence increases with age; common in HTN, HF, valvular disease, hyperthyroidism

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Multiple ectopic foci in the atria (often near pulmonary veins) fire chaotically → disorganized atrial depolarization (400–600/min)
  • AV node filters impulses → irregular ventricular response (often rapid)
  • Loss of “atrial kick” → reduced cardiac output (up to 20–30%)
  • Blood stasis in fibrillating atria (especially left atrial appendage) → thrombus formation → embolic stroke risk
  • Triggers: HTN, CAD, HF, valvular disease, hyperthyroidism, alcohol (“holiday heart”), sleep apnea, sepsis, post-cardiac surgery, pulmonary disease

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote control of hypertension, heart failure, CAD, thyroid disease, sleep apnea, diabetes, obesity, and alcohol/caffeine triggers that can worsen AFib.
  • Teach anticoagulant adherence and stroke-warning recognition using FAST because AFib increases thromboembolic stroke risk.
  • Encourage pulse self-checks, symptom tracking, medication-list/anticoagulant alert ID, and keeping ECG/lab follow-up appointments.
  • Reinforce not stopping rate/rhythm medications or anticoagulants abruptly without provider guidance.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess age, hypertension, heart failure, CAD, valvular disease, hyperthyroidism, sleep apnea, pulmonary disease, sepsis, post-cardiac surgery status, and alcohol use.
  • Use CHA2DS2-VASc risk factors to support stroke-prevention planning: CHF, HTN, age, diabetes, stroke history, vascular disease, and sex category.
  • Review electrolyte imbalance, renal/hepatic impairment, and drug-interaction risk before antidysrhythmic or anticoagulant therapy.
  • Assess asthma/COPD history before beta blockers and bradycardia/AV block history before rate-control therapy.

Expected Findings

Symptoms (may be asymptomatic):

  • Palpitations
  • Fatigue, weakness
  • Dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, syncope
  • Chest discomfort
  • Anxiety

Physical/diagnostic:

  • Irregularly irregular pulse; pulse deficit (apical > radial)
  • EKG: irregularly irregular R-R intervals, absent P waves, fibrillatory waves
  • Echocardiogram: assess for structural disease, atrial size, thrombus (TEE)
  • Labs: thyroid function, electrolytes, BNP
  • Holter monitor for paroxysmal AFib

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor thyroid function and electrolytes because thyroid disease and electrolyte imbalance can trigger or worsen dysrhythmias.
  • Check renal and hepatic function for dosing and safety of antidysrhythmics and anticoagulants.
  • Monitor INR for warfarin therapy with target range per provider plan, and CBC/bleeding indicators when anticoagulated.
  • Trend BNP or other ordered labs when heart failure is suspected or symptoms worsen.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • ECG confirms irregularly irregular R-R intervals, absent P waves, and fibrillatory waves.
  • Assess apical-radial pulse deficit and monitor rhythm continuously or intermittently based on acuity.
  • Echocardiogram evaluates structural disease and atrial size; TEE can assess for thrombus before cardioversion when ordered.
  • Holter or ambulatory monitoring can detect paroxysmal AFib and correlate symptoms with rhythm.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Proarrhythmia risk: all antidysrhythmics can worsen or cause dysrhythmias; use continuous ECG monitoring during IV administration and correct electrolyte imbalances.
  • Rate-control safety: check apical pulse before beta blockers and hold/notify for pulse <50/min; monitor for hypotension, bradycardia, AV block, heart failure, and bronchospasm in asthma.
  • Amiodarone safety: obtain baseline chest x-ray and pulmonary function tests; report dyspnea, cough, chest pain, visual disturbances, or bradycardia symptoms.
  • Stroke/bleeding safety: monitor for FAST stroke findings and bleeding precautions when anticoagulation is prescribed.

Complications

  • Atrial fibrillation increases thromboembolic stroke risk, especially when anticoagulation is missed or not indicated/managed correctly.
  • Rapid or uncontrolled rate can contribute to hypotension, chest discomfort, syncope, reduced exercise tolerance, or heart failure.
  • Antidysrhythmics can cause new/worsening dysrhythmias, bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, pulmonary toxicity, visual disturbances, and drug interactions.
  • Anticoagulant therapy can cause bleeding complications that require prompt reporting.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Three pillars of management:

1. Rate control:

  • Beta blockers (metoprolol)
  • Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil)
  • Digoxin (especially with HF)
  • Goal: resting HR < 110 (lenient) or < 80 (strict)

2. Rhythm control (restore sinus rhythm):

  • Antidysrhythmics: amiodarone, flecainide, propafenone, sotalol, dofetilide
  • Electrical cardioversion (anticoagulate first or TEE to rule out clot)
  • Catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation)

3. Anticoagulation (stroke prevention):

  • CHA2DS2-VASc score determines anticoagulation need (CHF, HTN, Age, Diabetes, Stroke, Vascular, Sex)
  • DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) — preferred for non-valvular AFib
  • Warfarin (target INR 2–3) — for valvular AFib or mechanical valves
  • Left atrial appendage closure (Watchman) for anticoagulation-ineligible

Nursing care:

  • Continuous or intermittent cardiac monitoring
  • Assess apical-radial pulse deficit
  • Monitor for signs of stroke, HF, hemodynamic instability
  • Bleeding precautions if anticoagulated

Medications

  • Class II beta blockers (propranolol, esmolol, acebutolol): slow SA/AV conduction and decrease HR; used for atrial fibrillation/flutter rate control; check apical pulse and hold/notify for pulse <50/min.
  • Class III potassium channel blockers (amiodarone, sotalol, ibutilide, dofetilide, dronedarone): prolong the refractory period and are used for conversion of atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter.
  • Class IV calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem): slow SA/AV conduction and reduce HR; used for rate control in atrial fibrillation/flutter and SVT.
  • Digoxin: can be used for ventricular rate control.
  • Safety: antidysrhythmics can worsen or cause dysrhythmias; use continuous ECG during IV therapy, correct electrolytes, and monitor for heart failure.
  • Amiodarone monitoring: obtain baseline chest x-ray and pulmonary function tests; monitor BP/ECG; report dyspnea, cough, chest pain, visual disturbances, or bradycardia symptoms.

Client Education

  • AFib increases stroke risk — anticoagulation is critical even when you feel fine
  • Anticoagulant teaching: bleeding precautions, regular INR for warfarin, consistent vitamin K intake (warfarin), do not skip doses (DOACs have short action)
  • Recognize stroke (FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911)
  • Take rate/rhythm medications as prescribed; do not stop abruptly
  • Check pulse; report rates that are very high, very low, or with new symptoms
  • Limit alcohol and caffeine (triggers)
  • Manage underlying conditions: HTN, sleep apnea, thyroid, HF
  • Report palpitations, dizziness, chest pain, syncope, shortness of breath
  • Report bleeding: black stools, blood in urine, prolonged bleeding, severe bruising
  • Keep all follow-up and lab appointments
  • Carry medication list and anticoagulant alert ID

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Electrical cardioversion: may restore sinus rhythm; ensure anticoagulation first or TEE to rule out clot as ordered.
  • Catheter ablation: pulmonary vein isolation can be used for rhythm control when medication therapy is inadequate or not tolerated.
  • Left atrial appendage closure: may be used for stroke prevention in selected clients who cannot take long-term anticoagulation.
  • Maintain cardiac monitoring, assess apical-radial pulse deficit, and watch for stroke, heart failure, or hemodynamic instability before/after procedures.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with cardiology/electrophysiology for rate control, rhythm control, cardioversion, catheter ablation, and left atrial appendage closure decisions.
  • Work with the pharmacist for anticoagulant selection, warfarin/DOAC teaching, interaction review, renal/hepatic dosing, and antidysrhythmic safety monitoring.
  • Involve anticoagulation clinic, sleep-medicine services, cardiac rehabilitation, or chronic-disease educators when indicated.
  • Communicate ECG findings, pulse deficit, stroke symptoms, bleeding signs, electrolyte/thyroid results, and medication adverse effects promptly.
Worked Example Peptic Ulcer Disease Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) — erosion (ulceration) of the mucosal lining of the stomach (gastric ulcer) or duodenum (duodenal ulcer) due to imbalance between protective and damaging factors.

  • Duodenal ulcers (more common): pain 2–3 hr after meals; relieved BY eating; nocturnal pain
  • Gastric ulcers: pain DURING/shortly after eating; worsened by food; weight loss
  • Two main causes: H. pylori infection and NSAID use
  • Less common: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrin-secreting tumor)

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • H. pylori: bacteria colonize gastric mucosa, produce urease (ammonia), trigger inflammation, damage protective mucus layer
  • NSAIDs: inhibit COX-1 → decreased protective prostaglandins → reduced mucus/bicarbonate, reduced mucosal blood flow
  • Imbalance: aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm defensive factors (mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow, prostaglandins)
  • Mucosal erosion exposes underlying tissue to acid → ulcer
  • Risk factors: H. pylori, NSAIDs, smoking, alcohol, stress, corticosteroids, family history

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote full completion of H. pylori antibiotic therapy and follow-up eradication testing when ordered.
  • Avoid NSAIDs/aspirin unless specifically directed; use safer alternatives such as acetaminophen when appropriate.
  • Encourage smoking cessation, limiting alcohol/caffeine, individualized trigger-food avoidance, regular meals, and stress management.
  • Teach alarm symptoms requiring immediate care: black/tarry stools, hematemesis/coffee-ground emesis, sudden severe abdominal pain, dizziness, or fainting.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess H. pylori exposure/history, NSAID/aspirin use, smoking, alcohol, corticosteroid use, family history, and stress.
  • Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, older age, prior ulcer/GI bleed, and comorbid disease that raises bleeding risk.
  • Assess food-related pain timing to distinguish gastric vs duodenal patterns and identify nutrition/weight-loss concerns.
  • Review adherence barriers to multi-drug H. pylori regimens because incomplete therapy promotes failure/resistance.

Expected Findings

  • Epigastric pain (burning, gnawing) — timing differs by ulcer type
  • Dyspepsia, bloating, belching
  • Nausea; with gastric ulcers, food may worsen pain
  • Early satiety, weight loss (gastric)

Complications (alarm features):

  • GI bleeding: hematemesis (coffee-ground or bright red), melena (black tarry stools), anemia
  • Perforation: sudden severe pain, rigid board-like abdomen, signs of peritonitis (emergency)
  • Obstruction: vomiting, feeling of fullness

Diagnostic:

  • Upper endoscopy (EGD) — gold standard; visualize and biopsy
  • H. pylori testing: urea breath test, stool antigen, biopsy, serology
  • CBC (anemia), stool occult blood

Laboratory Tests

  • Use H. pylori testing such as urea breath test, stool antigen, biopsy testing, or serology as ordered.
  • Monitor CBC/hemoglobin/hematocrit for anemia or blood loss.
  • Use stool occult blood testing when GI bleeding is suspected or ordered.
  • Monitor medication-safety labs when prolonged PPI therapy, antibiotics, or comorbid renal/hepatic concerns require follow-up.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Upper endoscopy (EGD) is the gold standard to visualize ulcers and obtain biopsy when needed.
  • Assess epigastric burning/gnawing pain, timing with meals, nocturnal pain, nausea, early satiety, weight loss, and dyspepsia.
  • Evaluate alarm features: hematemesis, melena, anemia, obstruction symptoms, sudden severe pain, rigid abdomen, or peritonitis signs.
  • Follow up gastric ulcers as ordered to confirm healing and rule out malignancy.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • GI bleed warning: black/tarry stool, coffee-ground or bright-red emesis, pallor, dizziness, tachycardia, or dropping Hgb requires prompt escalation.
  • Perforation warning: sudden severe abdominal pain, rigid board-like abdomen, or peritonitis signs is an emergency.
  • Medication safety: complete H. pylori therapy, avoid NSAIDs/aspirin unless directed, and take PPIs before meals as instructed.
  • Resistance prevention: stopping antibiotics early can cause treatment failure and resistance.

Complications

  • PUD can cause GI bleeding, anemia, perforation, peritonitis, gastric outlet obstruction, and recurrent ulceration.
  • Gastric ulcer symptoms can reduce intake and cause weight loss.
  • Incomplete H. pylori treatment can lead to persistent infection, recurrence, and resistance.
  • Continued NSAID use or smoking delays healing and increases recurrence/bleeding risk.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • H. pylori triple therapy: PPI + two antibiotics (clarithromycin + amoxicillin or metronidazole) for 10–14 days; quadruple therapy (+ bismuth) if resistance
  • Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) — potent acid suppression; promote healing
  • H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine) — reduce acid
  • Mucosal protectants (sucralfate) — coat ulcer
  • Antacids — symptomatic relief
  • Discontinue NSAIDs; if needed, use COX-2 selective + PPI

Nursing care:

  • Pain assessment and management
  • Monitor for bleeding (vitals, Hgb, stool); be alert for perforation
  • Dietary counseling (avoid triggers)
  • Smoking and alcohol cessation
  • Medication adherence (especially completing H. pylori antibiotics)
  • Stress management

Medications

  • H. pylori triple therapy: PPI + two antibiotics (clarithromycin + amoxicillin or metronidazole) for 10–14 days; quadruple therapy (+ bismuth) if resistance
  • Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) — potent acid suppression; promote healing
  • H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine) — reduce acid
  • Mucosal protectants (sucralfate) — coat ulcer
  • Antacids — symptomatic relief
  • Discontinue NSAIDs; if needed, use COX-2 selective + PPI

Client Education

  • Complete the entire H. pylori antibiotic course — stopping early causes resistance and treatment failure
  • Take medications as scheduled (PPIs before meals)
  • Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin (use acetaminophen for pain unless directed otherwise)
  • Stop smoking (delays healing, increases recurrence)
  • Limit alcohol and caffeine
  • Avoid trigger foods (individualized — spicy, acidic, fatty if they worsen symptoms)
  • Eat regular meals; avoid eating right before bed
  • Manage stress
  • Report ALARM signs immediately: black/tarry stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, severe sudden abdominal pain, dizziness/fainting
  • Follow up for confirmation of H. pylori eradication if treated
  • Keep follow-up endoscopy appointments (especially gastric ulcers — rule out malignancy)

Therapeutic Procedures

  • EGD allows visualization, biopsy, and possible endoscopic control of bleeding when indicated.
  • H. pylori eradication uses PPI-based antibiotic combinations; adherence through the full course is essential.
  • Acute bleeding may require IV access, fluid/blood support, medication therapy, and endoscopic intervention per provider orders.
  • Perforation or obstruction requires urgent surgical/provider evaluation.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with provider, pharmacist, gastroenterology, and lab for H. pylori therapy, interaction review, EGD, biopsy, and eradication follow-up.
  • Involve dietitian when weight loss, poor intake, or trigger-food planning affects nutrition.
  • Use smoking-cessation and alcohol-use resources when these delay healing or increase recurrence.
  • Communicate pain pattern, NSAID/anticoagulant use, bleeding signs, Hgb/CBC trends, H. pylori results, and adherence barriers.
Worked Example Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease · Acid suppression section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
GERD
Review Module Chapter
Ch 28 — Peptic Ulcer Disease

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — chronic condition where stomach contents reflux into the esophagus, causing symptoms and/or mucosal damage, due to incompetent lower esophageal sphincter (LES).

  • Very common; affects ~20% of adults
  • Spectrum: occasional heartburn → erosive esophagitis → Barrett’s esophagus (premalignant) → esophageal adenocarcinoma
  • Risk factors: obesity, hiatal hernia, pregnancy, smoking, certain foods, large/late meals, medications that relax LES

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Incompetent or relaxed lower esophageal sphincter (LES) → gastric acid refluxes upward
  • Esophageal mucosa lacks protection against acid → inflammation (esophagitis)
  • Delayed gastric emptying increases reflux
  • Hiatal hernia disrupts the anatomic barrier
  • Chronic acid exposure → metaplasia (Barrett’s esophagus) → increased cancer risk
  • LES-relaxing factors: fatty/spicy foods, caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, nicotine, certain meds (CCBs, anticholinergics, nitrates)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Encourage weight loss when overweight, smoking cessation, smaller meals, and avoidance of individual trigger foods.
  • Teach the client to avoid lying down for 2–3 hr after meals and elevate the head of the bed 6–8 inches with blocks or a wedge.
  • Reinforce taking PPIs 30–60 min before the first meal and using the lowest effective long-term regimen with provider follow-up.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Overweight status, large or late meals, tight waist clothing, smoking, alcohol, caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, fatty, fried, spicy, acidic, or carbonated foods can worsen reflux.
  • Hiatal hernia, delayed gastric emptying, pregnancy, and reduced lower esophageal sphincter tone increase reflux risk.
  • Long-term or high-dose acid suppression requires review for adverse effects and ongoing need.

Expected Findings

  • Heartburn (pyrosis) — burning retrosternal sensation, often after meals or lying down
  • Regurgitation of sour/bitter material
  • Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing)
  • Chest pain (can mimic cardiac — rule out)
  • Chronic cough, hoarseness, sore throat (laryngopharyngeal reflux)
  • Worsening when supine or bending over
  • Water brash (excess salivation)

Alarm features (warrant endoscopy):

  • Dysphagia, odynophagia (painful swallowing)
  • Weight loss, anemia, GI bleeding
  • Persistent symptoms despite therapy

Diagnostic:

  • Clinical diagnosis often sufficient; PPI trial
  • Upper endoscopy (esophagitis, Barrett’s, complications)
  • Ambulatory pH monitoring; esophageal manometry

Laboratory Tests

  • GERD is usually diagnosed clinically; routine labs are not required for uncomplicated symptoms.
  • Monitor magnesium, B12, renal function, or other labs when long-term PPI therapy or adverse effects are a concern.
  • Evaluate bleeding indicators such as anemia when black stools, vomiting blood, or other alarm symptoms are reported.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use endoscopy for persistent symptoms despite treatment, Barrett screening, or alarm symptoms such as dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, or painful swallowing.
  • Ambulatory pH monitoring may be used when diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms continue despite therapy.
  • Esophageal manometry may support evaluation before antireflux procedures or when motility disorder is suspected.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Treat dysphagia, painful swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools, or chest pain as warning signs requiring prompt evaluation.
  • Teach correct PPI timing and discuss long-term risks such as B12 deficiency, fractures, C. diff, and hypomagnesemia with the provider.
  • Use caution with metoclopramide because of neurologic adverse effects and with antacids or H2 blockers when interactions or renal issues are present.

Complications

  • Erosive esophagitis, ulceration, bleeding, stricture, dysphagia, Barrett esophagus, and increased cancer surveillance needs.
  • Aspiration, chronic cough, hoarseness, dental erosion, and sleep disruption from persistent reflux.
  • Long-term acid suppression adverse effects or continued symptoms when lifestyle measures and correct medication timing are not followed.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole) — first-line for moderate-severe; most effective
  • H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine) — mild/intermittent symptoms
  • Antacids — rapid, short-term relief
  • Prokinetics (metoclopramide) — select cases (delayed emptying)

Lifestyle modifications (cornerstone):

  • Weight loss if overweight
  • Elevate head of bed 6–8 inches
  • Avoid eating 2–3 hours before lying down
  • Smaller, more frequent meals
  • Avoid trigger foods
  • Smoking cessation; limit alcohol

Severe/refractory: surgical fundoplication (Nissen).

Medications

  • Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole) — first-line for moderate-severe; most effective
  • H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine) — mild/intermittent symptoms
  • Antacids — rapid, short-term relief
  • Prokinetics (metoclopramide) — select cases (delayed emptying)

Lifestyle modifications (cornerstone):

  • Weight loss if overweight
  • Elevate head of bed 6–8 inches
  • Avoid eating 2–3 hours before lying down
  • Smaller, more frequent meals
  • Avoid trigger foods
  • Smoking cessation; limit alcohol

Severe/refractory: surgical fundoplication (Nissen).

Client Education

  • Lifestyle changes are essential:
  • Elevate the head of the bed 6–8 inches (blocks/wedge, not just extra pillows)
  • Do not lie down for 2–3 hours after eating
  • Eat smaller, more frequent meals; avoid large/late meals
  • Avoid trigger foods: fatty, fried, spicy, acidic, caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, carbonated drinks
  • Lose weight if overweight
  • Stop smoking
  • Avoid tight clothing around the waist
  • Take PPIs 30–60 min before the first meal of the day
  • Report difficulty/pain swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, or black stools (need evaluation)
  • Long-term PPI risks (discuss with provider): B12 deficiency, fractures, C. diff, hypomagnesemia — use lowest effective dose
  • Persistent symptoms despite treatment warrant endoscopy (Barrett’s screening)

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Endoscopy supports evaluation of alarm symptoms, refractory GERD, esophagitis, stricture, or Barrett esophagus.
  • Ambulatory pH monitoring and manometry may be used for refractory symptoms or pre-procedure evaluation.
  • Fundoplication, such as Nissen fundoplication, may be considered for severe or refractory GERD.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the prescriber and pharmacist for PPI timing, drug interactions, step-down therapy, and long-term safety monitoring.
  • Refer to gastroenterology for alarm symptoms, refractory symptoms, Barrett screening, or procedure evaluation.
  • Use dietitian support when trigger identification, weight loss, or nutrition planning would improve symptom control.
Worked Example Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Depressive Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) — mood disorder characterized by persistent depressed mood and/or anhedonia plus additional symptoms for ≥ 2 weeks, causing significant impairment.

  • DSM-5 requires ≥ 5 of 9 symptoms (one must be depressed mood OR anhedonia): SIG E CAPS — Sleep changes, Interest loss, Guilt/worthlessness, Energy loss, Concentration impaired, Appetite changes, Psychomotor changes, Suicidality
  • Lifetime prevalence ~17%; twice as common in women
  • Subtypes: melancholic, atypical, peripartum, seasonal, with psychotic features, treatment-resistant
  • High rate of recurrence; comorbid with anxiety, substance use, medical illness

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Monoamine hypothesis: reduced serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine activity
  • HPA axis hyperactivity: elevated cortisol; impaired feedback
  • Neuroplasticity deficits: reduced BDNF; hippocampal volume loss
  • Inflammation hypothesis: elevated inflammatory cytokines
  • Genetic predisposition — heritability ~40%
  • Psychosocial: trauma, loss, chronic stress, social isolation
  • Medical contributors: hypothyroidism, vitamin D/B12 deficiency, chronic pain, neurological disease

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote medication adherence, psychotherapy, behavioral activation, sleep hygiene, exercise, social support, and crisis/safety planning.
  • Teach that antidepressants take weeks for full effect and should not be stopped abruptly.
  • Encourage early reporting of worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, serotonin syndrome symptoms, or medication side effects.
  • Support management of contributors such as hypothyroidism, B12/vitamin D deficiency, chronic pain, substance use, and social isolation.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess personal/family history, prior episodes, trauma/loss, chronic stress, social isolation, medical illness, chronic pain, and substance use.
  • Screen for anxiety, substance use, bipolar history/mania, psychotic features, peripartum/seasonal pattern, and treatment resistance.
  • Review suicide risk, access to lethal means broadly, prior attempts, and protective factors.
  • Consider medical contributors such as hypothyroidism, vitamin B12/D deficiency, neurologic disease, and medication effects.

Expected Findings

Psychological: depressed mood, anhedonia, hopelessness, worthlessness, guilt, suicidal ideation, concentration difficulty, indecisiveness.

Physical: fatigue, sleep disturbance (insomnia or hypersomnia), appetite/weight changes, psychomotor agitation or retardation, decreased libido, somatic complaints (headache, GI distress).

Severity tools:

  • PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire): ≥ 10 moderate; ≥ 20 severe
  • Beck Depression Inventory
  • Hamilton Depression Rating Scale

Always assess suicide risk — ideation, plan, intent, means, history.

Laboratory Tests

  • No routine laboratory test diagnoses MDD; diagnosis is clinical using DSM-5 symptoms and functional impairment.
  • Use ordered labs to assess contributors such as thyroid function, B12, vitamin D, anemia, or other medical causes of depressive symptoms.
  • Monitor medication-safety labs when using lithium, antipsychotic augmentation, TCAs, MAOIs, or other higher-risk agents.
  • Trend PHQ-9 or other rating scales with side effects and functioning to evaluate response.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use DSM-5 criteria: at least 5 symptoms for at least 2 weeks, including depressed mood or anhedonia, with impairment.
  • Use PHQ-9, Beck Depression Inventory, or Hamilton Depression Rating Scale to quantify severity.
  • Always assess suicide risk: ideation, plan, intent, means, past attempts, and supports.
  • Screen for bipolar disorder before antidepressant therapy because antidepressants can precipitate mania in susceptible clients.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Suicide safety: assess every visit; create a safety plan and escalate urgently for imminent risk.
  • Antidepressant safety: monitor for worsening mood/suicidality early in therapy, especially in younger clients.
  • Serotonin syndrome: report agitation, fever, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, clonus, or confusion when serotonergic drugs are combined.
  • High-risk medications: TCAs are dangerous in overdose; MAOIs require tyramine and interaction precautions.

Complications

  • MDD can cause severe functional impairment, sleep/appetite disturbance, substance use, psychosis in severe cases, recurrence, and suicide.
  • Untreated depression can worsen chronic medical illness and self-care adherence.
  • Antidepressants can cause discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly and may initially worsen agitation or suicidal thoughts.
  • TCAs, MAOIs, lithium, antipsychotic augmentation, and ketamine/esketamine require additional safety monitoring.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (first-line):

  • SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine) — best tolerated
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) — effective; may help with pain
  • Atypical: bupropion (no sexual side effects; lowers seizure threshold), mirtazapine (sleep/appetite)
  • TCAs — effective but anticholinergic burden; LETHAL IN OVERDOSE
  • MAOIs — reserved; tyramine diet, drug interactions
  • Augmentation: lithium, atypical antipsychotics, T3
  • Ketamine/esketamine for treatment-resistant depression
  • ECT for severe/refractory cases

Non-pharm:

  • CBT, IPT (interpersonal therapy), behavioral activation
  • Light therapy for seasonal affective disorder
  • Exercise (as effective as medication for mild-moderate)
  • Sleep hygiene, social support

Suicide safety: assess risk every visit; safety plan; lethal-means counseling (restricting access generally, not naming methods); hospitalize if imminent risk; involve trusted support persons.

Medications

  • SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine) — best tolerated
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) — effective; may help with pain
  • Atypical: bupropion (no sexual side effects; lowers seizure threshold), mirtazapine (sleep/appetite)
  • TCAs — effective but anticholinergic burden; LETHAL IN OVERDOSE
  • MAOIs — reserved; tyramine diet, drug interactions
  • Augmentation: lithium, atypical antipsychotics, T3
  • Ketamine/esketamine for treatment-resistant depression
  • ECT for severe/refractory cases

Non-pharm:

  • CBT, IPT (interpersonal therapy), behavioral activation
  • Light therapy for seasonal affective disorder
  • Exercise (as effective as medication for mild-moderate)
  • Sleep hygiene, social support

Suicide safety: assess risk every visit; safety plan; lethal-means counseling (restricting access generally, not naming methods); hospitalize if imminent risk; involve trusted support persons.

Client Education

  • Antidepressants take 4–6 weeks for full effect — do not stop early
  • Side effects often improve in 1–2 weeks
  • Do NOT stop abruptly — discontinuation syndrome; taper with provider
  • Black box warning: increased suicidal thoughts in clients < 25 yr in first weeks — closer monitoring needed
  • Avoid alcohol (worsens depression, sedating combination)
  • Engage in therapy alongside medication
  • Identify support system; attend follow-up
  • Crisis line: 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline)
  • Report worsening symptoms, suicidal thoughts, unusual bleeding, or signs of serotonin syndrome

Therapeutic Procedures

  • CBT, interpersonal therapy, behavioral activation, exercise, sleep hygiene, and social support are core nonpharmacologic treatments.
  • ECT is used for severe, psychotic, catatonic, suicidal, or treatment-resistant depression when indicated.
  • Light therapy can support seasonal affective patterns; ketamine/esketamine may be used for treatment-resistant depression under specialty protocol.
  • Use safety planning and lethal-means counseling in general terms when suicide risk is present.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with prescriber, pharmacist, therapist/psychologist, primary care, and crisis resources for medication, psychotherapy, and safety planning.
  • Refer to psychiatry for suicidality, psychosis, bipolar concern, treatment resistance, ECT/ketamine consideration, or complex augmentation.
  • Use social work/case management for access barriers, support systems, transportation, financial stressors, and safe follow-up.
  • Communicate PHQ-9/severity trends, suicide-risk findings, side effects, adherence, sleep/appetite changes, and medical-contributor labs.
Worked Example Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn’s / Ulcerative Colitis) Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 29 — Gastrointestinal Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) — chronic, relapsing autoimmune inflammation of the GI tract. Two main types:

  • Crohn’s disease: can affect ANY part of GI tract (mouth to anus); transmural (full-thickness); “skip lesions” (patchy); commonly terminal ileum
  • Ulcerative colitis (UC): affects ONLY the colon and rectum; continuous mucosal/submucosal inflammation starting at rectum; no skip lesions

Chronic course with flares and remissions. Onset often young adulthood. Increased colorectal cancer risk (especially UC).

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Dysregulated immune response to gut microbiota in genetically susceptible individuals
  • Chronic inflammation damages the intestinal wall
  • Crohn’s: transmural inflammation → strictures, fistulas, abscesses, “cobblestone” mucosa
  • UC: superficial continuous inflammation → ulcerations, friable mucosa, pseudopolyps
  • Contributing factors: genetics (NOD2/CARD15), environment, smoking (worsens Crohn’s, paradoxically protective in UC), altered microbiome, immune dysregulation

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Reinforce maintenance medication adherence during remission to reduce flares.
  • Teach flare recognition, hydration, adequate protein/calories, trigger-food tracking, stress management, and smoking cessation for Crohn disease.
  • Keep vaccination and colonoscopy surveillance current, avoiding live vaccines during immunosuppressive therapy as directed.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Genetic susceptibility, altered microbiome, immune dysregulation, environmental factors, and young-adult onset contribute to IBD risk.
  • Smoking worsens Crohn disease and should be addressed directly during teaching.
  • Immunomodulators, biologics, and corticosteroids increase infection and medication-safety risks that require monitoring.

Expected Findings

Crohn’s disease:

  • Abdominal pain (often RLQ), often non-bloody diarrhea
  • Weight loss, malnutrition, malabsorption (B12, fat-soluble vitamins)
  • Fistulas, perianal disease, strictures, abscesses
  • Fewer bloody stools than UC

Ulcerative colitis:

  • Bloody diarrhea with mucus (hallmark)
  • Lower abdominal cramping, urgency, tenesmus
  • Frequent small-volume stools
  • Weight loss, fatigue

Both: fever, fatigue, extraintestinal manifestations (arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis).

Diagnostic: colonoscopy with biopsy, CT/MR enterography (Crohn’s), labs (CRP, ESR, fecal calprotectin, anemia), stool studies to exclude infection.

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor CBC for anemia, infection, and medication effects during flares and immunosuppressive therapy.
  • Trend inflammatory markers such as ESR or CRP when ordered to support flare assessment and response to therapy.
  • Use electrolytes, renal/liver function, stool testing, and nutrient labs such as iron or B12 as indicated by diarrhea, dehydration, ileal disease, or medication regimen.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Colonoscopy with biopsy supports diagnosis, disease extent, surveillance, and differentiation of Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis.
  • Use imaging as ordered for suspected Crohn complications such as strictures, fistulas, abscesses, or obstruction.
  • Stool studies help rule out infection when diarrhea, fever, or flare-like symptoms occur.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Report fever, severe abdominal pain, increased bleeding, dehydration, persistent vomiting, or signs of obstruction promptly.
  • Monitor biologics, immunomodulators, and corticosteroids for infection risk; avoid live vaccines while immunosuppressed unless specifically cleared.
  • Use antidiarrheals cautiously during active ulcerative colitis because of toxic megacolon risk.

Complications

  • Crohn disease can cause strictures, fistulas, abscesses, obstruction, malabsorption, and B12 deficiency with ileal involvement.
  • Ulcerative colitis can cause severe bleeding, toxic megacolon, perforation, and increased colorectal cancer risk.
  • Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, anemia, malnutrition, infection, and medication toxicity can occur during flares or intensive therapy.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (step-up):

  • 5-aminosalicylates (sulfasalazine, mesalamine) — mild-moderate UC; maintenance
  • Corticosteroids (prednisone, budesonide) — acute flares (short-term; not maintenance)
  • Immunomodulators (azathioprine, methotrexate) — steroid-sparing maintenance
  • Biologics (infliximab, adalimumab — anti-TNF; vedolizumab; ustekinumab) — moderate-severe
  • Antibiotics (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin) for Crohn’s complications
  • Antidiarrheals — with CAUTION (toxic megacolon risk in active UC)

Nursing care:

  • Monitor bowel pattern, hydration, electrolytes, nutrition, weight
  • Assess for complications: toxic megacolon, perforation, obstruction, hemorrhage
  • Nutritional support (may need TPN in severe Crohn’s); vitamin supplementation
  • Monitor for medication side effects (immunosuppression → infection)
  • Skin/ostomy care if surgical
  • Emotional support (chronic disease, body image)
  • Surgery: colectomy can cure UC; Crohn’s recurs

Medications

  • 5-aminosalicylates (sulfasalazine, mesalamine) — mild-moderate UC; maintenance
  • Corticosteroids (prednisone, budesonide) — acute flares (short-term; not maintenance)
  • Immunomodulators (azathioprine, methotrexate) — steroid-sparing maintenance
  • Biologics (infliximab, adalimumab — anti-TNF; vedolizumab; ustekinumab) — moderate-severe
  • Antibiotics (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin) for Crohn’s complications
  • Antidiarrheals — with CAUTION (toxic megacolon risk in active UC)

Client Education

  • IBD is a chronic, relapsing condition — adherence to maintenance therapy reduces flares
  • Do not stop medications during remission without provider guidance
  • Recognize flare symptoms; report increased pain, bleeding, fever, dehydration
  • Dietary management: identify trigger foods; low-residue diet during flares; adequate protein/calories; stay hydrated
  • Vitamin/mineral supplementation (B12 for Crohn’s ileal disease, iron, calcium/vitamin D with steroids)
  • Smoking cessation (especially Crohn’s)
  • Biologics/immunomodulators increase infection risk: report fever, signs of infection; stay current on vaccines (no live vaccines while immunosuppressed)
  • Regular colonoscopy surveillance (increased colorectal cancer risk)
  • Stress management (can trigger flares)
  • Support groups (Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation)
  • Ostomy education if surgical

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Colonoscopy with biopsy is central for diagnosis, disease monitoring, and cancer surveillance.
  • Surgery, colectomy, bowel resection, drainage, or ostomy creation may be required for refractory disease or complications.
  • Provide ostomy and postoperative teaching when surgical management is planned or completed.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with gastroenterology for flare management, biologic or immunomodulator therapy, endoscopy, surveillance, and escalation decisions.
  • Involve dietitian support for low-residue intake during flares, hydration, protein/calorie needs, and vitamin or mineral replacement.
  • Include pharmacist, infusion services, surgery, wound/ostomy nursing, and behavioral health when medication safety, biologic administration, surgery, or coping needs arise.
Worked Example Rheumatoid Arthritis Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) — chronic, systemic autoimmune disease causing symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, primarily affecting synovial joints, with potential extra-articular involvement.

  • Autoimmune; more common in women; onset typically 30–60 yr
  • Symmetric joint involvement (both sides)
  • Affects small joints first (hands, wrists, feet), then larger joints
  • Systemic: fatigue, fever, weight loss; can affect lungs, heart, eyes, vessels
  • Progressive joint destruction and deformity if untreated

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Autoimmune attack on synovium — immune cells infiltrate the joint lining
  • Chronic inflammation → pannus formation (inflammatory granulation tissue)
  • Pannus erodes cartilage and bone → joint destruction, deformity
  • Autoantibodies: rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-CCP (more specific)
  • Cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6) drive inflammation (targets for biologics)
  • Genetic predisposition (HLA-DR4) + environmental triggers (smoking)

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote early, consistent DMARD therapy to slow progression and prevent joint damage.
  • Encourage smoking cessation, low-impact exercise, balanced rest/activity, joint protection, assistive devices, and heat/cold use as appropriate.
  • Teach infection prevention and vaccine planning before/while using biologics or other immunosuppressants; avoid live vaccines when contraindicated.
  • Reinforce lab follow-up and contraception counseling with teratogenic medications such as methotrexate.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess female sex, age 30-60, family/genetic risk, smoking, and autoimmune/inflammatory history.
  • Screen for symmetric small-joint pain/swelling, morning stiffness over 1 hr, fatigue, fever, weight loss, nodules, and extra-articular symptoms.
  • Review infection history, TB risk, liver disease, pregnancy plans, alcohol use, and vaccine status before DMARD/biologic therapy.
  • Assess functional limitations, pain, hand/foot deformity, work/home demands, and adherence barriers.

Expected Findings

  • Symmetric joint pain, swelling, warmth, stiffness
  • Morning stiffness > 1 hour (hallmark; improves with activity)
  • Small joints of hands (MCP, PIP), wrists, feet
  • Joint deformities: ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, hallux valgus
  • Rheumatoid nodules (subcutaneous)
  • Fatigue, low-grade fever, malaise, weight loss
  • Extra-articular: pleuritis, pericarditis, dry eyes (Sjogren’s), vasculitis, anemia

Diagnostic:

  • RF and anti-CCP antibodies
  • Elevated ESR, CRP (inflammation)
  • X-rays: joint space narrowing, erosions
  • CBC: anemia of chronic disease
  • Clinical criteria (ACR/EULAR)

Laboratory Tests

  • Use RF and anti-CCP antibodies to support diagnosis; anti-CCP is more specific.
  • Monitor ESR and CRP as inflammation/activity markers.
  • Monitor CBC and liver function with methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, biologics, or JAK inhibitors as ordered.
  • Screen for TB and other infection risks before biologic DMARDs; monitor renal function when NSAIDs or comorbid disease require it.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Use ACR/EULAR clinical criteria with joint involvement, serology, inflammatory markers, and symptom duration.
  • X-rays can show joint space narrowing, erosions, and deformity as disease progresses.
  • Assess symmetric MCP/PIP/wrist/foot involvement, morning stiffness, nodules, deformities, and extra-articular lung/heart/eye/vascular findings.
  • Trend function, pain, swelling, stiffness duration, and ability to perform ADLs to guide treat-to-target adjustments.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Methotrexate safety: weekly dosing only, folic acid as prescribed, avoid alcohol, use effective contraception, and keep CBC/LFT monitoring.
  • Biologic/JAK safety: increased infection risk; report fever or infection signs, avoid live vaccines when contraindicated, and screen for TB before therapy.
  • Steroid/NSAID safety: monitor GI, renal, BP, glucose, and bone effects; use the lowest effective duration when possible.
  • Function safety: protect inflamed joints, prevent falls, and use assistive devices during flares.

Complications

  • Untreated RA can cause progressive joint erosion, deformity, disability, chronic pain, fatigue, anemia, and reduced quality of life.
  • Extra-articular complications can involve lungs, heart, eyes, vessels, nodules, and systemic inflammation.
  • DMARDs/biologics can cause infection risk, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression, teratogenicity, and other therapy-specific adverse effects.
  • Long-term corticosteroids and NSAIDs can cause bone, glucose, BP, GI, renal, and cardiovascular complications.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (treat-to-target, early DMARDs):

  • DMARDs (disease-modifying) — methotrexate is first-line/anchor; also hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide
  • Biologic DMARDs — TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab), IL-6 (tocilizumab), others — for inadequate response
  • JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib)
  • Corticosteroids — bridge therapy/flares (short-term; minimize)
  • NSAIDs — symptom relief (not disease-modifying)

Nursing care:

  • Pain and inflammation management; balance rest and activity
  • Joint protection; assistive devices; OT/PT referral
  • Heat/cold therapy
  • Monitor DMARD/biologic toxicity (LFTs, CBC, infection)
  • Promote function and independence
  • Emotional support (chronic disease, body image)

Medications

  • DMARDs (disease-modifying) — methotrexate is first-line/anchor; also hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide
  • Biologic DMARDs — TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab), IL-6 (tocilizumab), others — for inadequate response
  • JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib)
  • Corticosteroids — bridge therapy/flares (short-term; minimize)
  • NSAIDs — symptom relief (not disease-modifying)

Client Education

  • RA is a chronic autoimmune disease; early aggressive treatment prevents joint damage
  • Take DMARDs consistently even when feeling well (they slow disease progression)
  • Methotrexate: weekly dosing (NOT daily — fatal if daily); take folic acid; avoid alcohol; effective contraception (teratogenic); monitor labs
  • Biologics/immunosuppressants: increase infection risk — report fever/signs of infection; no live vaccines; screen for TB before starting
  • Balance activity and rest; protect joints (use larger joints, assistive devices)
  • Apply heat for stiffness, cold for acute inflammation
  • Morning stiffness routines (warm shower)
  • Regular exercise (low-impact: swimming, walking) maintains function
  • Smoking cessation (worsens RA)
  • Keep all lab/follow-up appointments for medication monitoring
  • Report increasing joint damage, new symptoms, medication side effects

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Treat-to-target medication adjustment with early DMARD use is the main disease-modifying strategy.
  • PT/OT support joint protection, splinting, assistive devices, energy conservation, ROM, strengthening, and ADL adaptation.
  • Heat can reduce stiffness; cold can reduce acute inflammation depending on symptoms.
  • Advanced joint damage may require orthopedic evaluation or surgical intervention when function is severely impaired.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with rheumatology/provider and pharmacist for DMARD/biologic selection, dosing, interaction review, vaccine planning, contraception counseling, and lab monitoring.
  • Involve PT/OT for joint protection, function, splints, exercise, assistive devices, and home/work adaptation.
  • Use dietitian, behavioral health, smoking-cessation resources, and social work/case management when chronic pain, fatigue, cost, or access affect care.
  • Communicate joint counts, pain/stiffness trends, function, CBC/LFT/ESR/CRP results, infection signs, pregnancy plans, and medication adverse effects.
Worked Example Gout Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders · Gout/SLE section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Gout
Review Module Chapter
Ch 33 — Connective Tissue Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Gout — a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and tissues, due to hyperuricemia.

  • More common in men; postmenopausal women
  • Acute gout: sudden, severe monoarticular attack (often great toe — podagra)
  • Chronic gout: recurrent attacks, tophi, chronic arthropathy
  • Associated with metabolic syndrome, obesity, HTN, CKD, alcohol use

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Hyperuricemia — serum urate > 6.8 mg/dL (saturation point)
  • Causes: underexcretion (~90%, renal) or overproduction (~10%) of uric acid
  • Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism
  • Urate crystals precipitate in cooler peripheral joints → trigger intense neutrophil-mediated inflammation
  • Chronic deposits form tophi (urate masses in tissues)
  • Triggers: purine-rich foods (red meat, organ meats, shellfish), alcohol (especially beer), fructose, dehydration, diuretics, rapid urate changes

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote hydration as appropriate, gradual weight management, and avoidance of dehydration or rapid weight loss that can trigger flares.
  • Teach dietary reduction of purine-rich foods, alcohol especially beer, and high-fructose drinks while encouraging individualized sustainable changes.
  • Reinforce daily long-term urate-lowering therapy adherence when prescribed, even when asymptomatic, and early use of acute therapy at the first sign of an attack.
  • Keep follow-up for serum urate and renal monitoring and report rash promptly with allopurinol.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess male sex, postmenopausal status, obesity, metabolic syndrome, hypertension, CKD, alcohol use, and family/personal gout history.
  • Review high-purine intake, organ/red meats, shellfish, anchovies, beer, high-fructose drinks, dehydration, and rapid urate shifts.
  • Review medications that can raise uric acid, including thiazide-type diuretics when present in the medication history.
  • Assess renal function and kidney-stone history before uricosuric therapy such as probenecid.

Expected Findings

Acute attack:

  • Sudden, excruciating joint pain (often at night)
  • First MTP joint of great toe (podagra) — classic
  • Joint red, hot, swollen, exquisitely tender (even sheet touch hurts)
  • Low-grade fever possible
  • Usually monoarticular early

Chronic gout:

  • Tophi (ears, joints, tendons) — firm nodules
  • Chronic joint pain, deformity
  • Uric acid kidney stones

Diagnostic:

  • Joint aspiration (gold standard): needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals
  • Serum uric acid (may be normal during acute attack)
  • X-ray (chronic: erosions, tophi)
  • 24-hr urine uric acid (over- vs under-excretion)

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor serum uric acid; levels can be normal during an acute attack, so interpret with symptoms and diagnostic findings.
  • Trend renal function because CKD affects gout risk and medication selection/dosing.
  • Use 24-hr urine uric acid testing when ordered to distinguish overproduction from underexcretion patterns.
  • Monitor medication-safety labs as ordered for NSAIDs, colchicine, allopurinol/febuxostat, or probenecid.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Joint aspiration is the diagnostic gold standard and shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals.
  • X-ray can show chronic erosions or tophi when gout is long-standing.
  • Assess classic podagra, red/hot/swollen exquisitely tender joint, tophi, and kidney-stone history as part of diagnostic evaluation.
  • Rule out infection when presentation is atypical, severe, febrile, or clinically concerning.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Acute vs chronic therapy: colchicine, NSAIDs, or glucocorticoids treat acute inflammation; allopurinol/febuxostat/probenecid lower uric acid for chronic prevention and do not relieve an acute attack immediately.
  • Allopurinol safety: teach that nausea/vomiting, rash, and increased gout attacks can occur when therapy starts; report rash promptly due to severe hypersensitivity risk.
  • Hydration safety: encourage fluids as appropriate to prevent urate stones, especially with uric-acid-lowering therapy.
  • Monitoring: follow uric acid and renal function, and review medications that can worsen hyperuricemia.

Complications

  • Recurrent uncontrolled gout can cause severe acute pain, chronic joint pain, deformity, and tophi in joints, tendons, or ears.
  • Uric acid kidney stones can occur, especially with inadequate hydration or persistent hyperuricemia.
  • Allopurinol can cause nausea/vomiting, rash, severe hypersensitivity reactions, and increased gout flares when therapy first starts.
  • Stopping or misunderstanding long-term urate-lowering therapy can increase future attack risk.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Acute attack treatment:

  • NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen) — first-line if no contraindication
  • Colchicine — especially early in attack
  • Corticosteroids (oral or intra-articular) — if NSAIDs/colchicine contraindicated
  • Rest and elevate joint; ice
  • Do NOT start or stop urate-lowering therapy during an acute attack (but continue if already on it)

Chronic/preventive (urate-lowering therapy):

  • Allopurinol or febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors) — reduce uric acid production
  • Probenecid (uricosuric) — increase excretion
  • Start prophylactic colchicine/NSAID when initiating (prevents flares)
  • Target serum urate < 6 mg/dL

Nursing care: pain management, hydration, dietary counseling, monitor renal function and uric acid.

Medications

  • Acute gout attack: colchicine, NSAIDs, or glucocorticoids reduce inflammation and pain from urate crystals.
  • Chronic uric-acid lowering: allopurinol and febuxostat reduce uric acid production; probenecid increases uric acid excretion.
  • Allopurinol teaching: nausea/vomiting, rash, and increased gout attacks can occur when therapy first starts; report rash promptly due to severe hypersensitivity risk.
  • Hydration: encourage fluids as appropriate to prevent urate stones while using antigout therapy.
  • Therapy distinction: separate acute-attack relief from chronic uric-acid control so the client does not stop long-term therapy during early flares without provider guidance.

Client Education

  • Dietary modifications: limit purine-rich foods (red/organ meats, shellfish, anchovies), limit alcohol (especially beer), avoid high-fructose drinks
  • Stay well hydrated (helps excrete uric acid, prevents stones)
  • Maintain healthy weight; gradual weight loss (rapid loss can trigger attacks)
  • Urate-lowering medications (allopurinol): take daily, long-term, even when no symptoms — they prevent future attacks but do NOT relieve an acute one
  • May initially cause more flares when starting — continue as directed; prophylaxis given
  • Report rash with allopurinol (serious hypersensitivity risk)
  • Take acute medications at the first sign of an attack
  • Rest and elevate the affected joint during attacks
  • Low-fat dairy and cherries may help
  • Keep follow-up for uric acid and renal monitoring
  • Tell providers about gout (some medications, like thiazides, raise uric acid)

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Joint aspiration: confirms diagnosis by identifying needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals and helps distinguish gout from infection.
  • Intra-articular corticosteroid injection: may be used for acute gout when NSAIDs or colchicine are contraindicated or inadequate.
  • Acute supportive care: rest, elevate, and ice the affected joint while prescribed anti-inflammatory therapy takes effect.
  • Chronic prevention: urate-lowering therapy is medication-based; keep follow-up for serum urate and renal monitoring.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider, pharmacist, and lab team for acute anti-inflammatory therapy, urate-lowering therapy, renal dosing, and flare prophylaxis when therapy starts.
  • Involve rheumatology for recurrent, tophaceous, refractory, or diagnostically uncertain gout.
  • Use dietitian support for purine reduction, alcohol/fructose counseling, weight management, and comorbidity-friendly nutrition.
  • Communicate serum urate trends, renal function, medication adherence, rash or hypersensitivity symptoms, kidney-stone symptoms, and flare frequency.
Worked Example Diabetes Mellitus (Type 1 & Type 2) Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Diabetes Mellitus
Review Module Chapter
Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Diabetes Mellitus — a group of metabolic disorders characterized by chronic hyperglycemia due to defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both.

  • Type 1: autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells → absolute insulin deficiency; requires insulin; usually younger onset; prone to DKA
  • Type 2: insulin resistance + relative insulin deficiency; associated with obesity/metabolic syndrome; managed with lifestyle, oral agents, sometimes insulin; prone to HHS
  • Gestational diabetes (pregnancy)

Diagnostic criteria: A1c ≥ 6.5%, fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL, 2-hr OGTT ≥ 200, or random ≥ 200 with symptoms.

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Insulin normally moves glucose into cells; deficiency/resistance → glucose stays in blood (hyperglycemia)
  • Cells starve despite high blood glucose → body breaks down fat/protein
  • Type 1: no insulin → lipolysis → ketones → DKA (metabolic acidosis)
  • Type 2: some insulin present (prevents ketosis usually) → severe hyperglycemia → HHS (hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state)
  • Chronic hyperglycemia → micro/macrovascular damage
  • Osmotic diuresis from glucosuria → dehydration, electrolyte loss

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote blood glucose self-monitoring, A1c follow-up, consistent carbohydrate intake, regular activity, weight management, smoking cessation, and BP/lipid control.
  • Teach daily foot inspection, protective footwear, annual eye exams, renal monitoring, and prompt wound/infection reporting.
  • Reinforce sick-day rules: continue insulin, monitor glucose/ketones more often, hydrate, and contact the provider for concerning values/symptoms.
  • Encourage medical alert ID and carrying fast carbohydrates for hypoglycemia.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Type 1 risk centers on autoimmune beta-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency with DKA risk.
  • Type 2 risk includes obesity, metabolic syndrome, sedentary lifestyle, family history, older age, insulin resistance, and related HTN/dyslipidemia.
  • Assess pregnancy/gestational diabetes history, recurrent infections, poor wound healing, food insecurity, medication access, and health-literacy barriers.
  • Review renal function, cardiovascular disease, and hypoglycemia risk before medication selection or insulin intensification.

Expected Findings

Classic (“3 Ps”):

  • Polyuria (excessive urination)
  • Polydipsia (excessive thirst)
  • Polyphagia (excessive hunger)
  • Weight loss (especially type 1), fatigue, blurred vision
  • Slow wound healing, recurrent infections
  • Type 1: rapid onset, may present in DKA
  • Type 2: gradual; often found on screening

Chronic complications:

  • Microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy
  • Macrovascular: CAD, stroke, PAD
  • Foot ulcers, increased infection risk

Diagnostic: A1c, fasting/random glucose, OGTT; monitor lipids, renal function, eye/foot exams.

Laboratory Tests

  • Use A1c, fasting glucose, random glucose with symptoms, or 2-hr OGTT criteria to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
  • Monitor renal function and urine albumin/renal markers for nephropathy and medication safety.
  • Trend lipids because macrovascular disease risk is high.
  • Use ketone testing, electrolytes, anion gap, and hydration/renal markers when DKA or severe hyperglycemia is suspected.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Diagnose diabetes using A1c >=6.5%, fasting glucose >=126 mg/dL, 2-hr OGTT >=200 mg/dL, or random glucose >=200 mg/dL with symptoms.
  • Perform routine foot exams for neuropathy, pulses, skin breakdown, and ulcer risk.
  • Schedule regular dilated eye exams to screen for diabetic retinopathy.
  • Assess for DKA/HHS patterns when hyperglycemia is accompanied by dehydration, nausea/vomiting, fruity breath, altered mentation, or severe illness.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Hypoglycemia: shakiness, sweating, confusion, or weakness requires rapid treatment with 15 g fast carbohydrate and recheck per rule of 15.
  • DKA/HHS warning: thirst, polyuria, nausea, fruity breath, ketones, dehydration, or altered mentation needs urgent evaluation.
  • Insulin safety: verify type/dose/timing, rotate sites, store correctly, match meals/activity, and never stop basal insulin during illness.
  • Foot safety: no barefoot walking; report wounds, infection, numbness, or color/temperature changes.

Complications

  • Acute complications include hypoglycemia, DKA, HHS, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and infection.
  • Chronic microvascular complications include retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy.
  • Macrovascular complications include CAD, stroke, PAD, foot ulcers, amputation risk, and delayed wound healing.
  • Medication complications include insulin-related hypoglycemia and therapy-specific renal/GI/genitourinary effects depending on the regimen.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Type 1: insulin (basal-bolus, pump) — lifelong; match to carbs/activity
  • Type 2: metformin first-line; add sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, insulin as needed
  • GLP-1 agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors have CV/renal benefits

Nursing care:

  • Blood glucose monitoring; A1c (goal generally < 7%)
  • Recognize/treat hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia (DKA/HHS)
  • Insulin administration teaching (rotation, storage, technique)
  • Foot care, eye exams, renal monitoring
  • Sick-day management; nutrition (carb counting); exercise
  • Cardiovascular risk reduction (BP, lipids)

Medications

  • Type 1: insulin (basal-bolus, pump) — lifelong; match to carbs/activity
  • Type 2: metformin first-line; add sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, insulin as needed
  • GLP-1 agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors have CV/renal benefits

Client Education

  • Blood glucose self-monitoring — technique, target ranges, when to check
  • Recognize hypoglycemia (shaky, sweaty, confused) — treat with 15 g fast carbs (rule of 15); carry a source
  • Recognize hyperglycemia/DKA (thirst, frequent urination, fruity breath, nausea) — seek care
  • Sick-day rules: continue insulin (do NOT stop), monitor glucose/ketones more often, hydrate, contact provider
  • Nutrition: consistent carbohydrate intake, balanced meals
  • Regular physical activity (monitor glucose around exercise)
  • Daily foot care: inspect feet, proper footwear, no going barefoot, report wounds
  • Annual eye and regular foot/renal exams
  • Take medications/insulin as prescribed; proper insulin storage and site rotation
  • Manage BP and cholesterol; smoking cessation
  • Wear medical alert ID

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Blood glucose self-monitoring or continuous glucose monitoring guides daily therapy decisions.
  • Insulin administration, pump therapy, site rotation, and safe injection technique are core treatment skills for insulin-requiring clients.
  • Foot care procedures include daily inspection, routine provider foot exams, wound care referral, and protective footwear when indicated.
  • DKA/HHS management may require IV fluids, insulin therapy, electrolyte correction, and close monitoring in acute care.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider/endocrinology team and pharmacist for insulin/oral agent selection, renal dosing, hypoglycemia risk, and interaction review.
  • Involve diabetes educator for glucose monitoring, insulin technique, sick-day rules, nutrition, exercise, and foot care.
  • Use dietitian, ophthalmology, podiatry/wound care, nephrology, and cardiology referrals based on complications and risk factors.
  • Communicate A1c/glucose trends, hypoglycemia events, ketones, renal/lipid results, foot findings, adherence barriers, and access problems.
Worked Example Hypothyroidism Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Hypothyroidism
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Hypothyroidism — deficiency of thyroid hormone, slowing metabolic processes throughout the body.

  • Primary (most common): thyroid gland failure — Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (autoimmune) is leading cause; also post-thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine, iodine deficiency
  • Secondary: pituitary failure (low TSH)
  • Myxedema coma: severe, life-threatening decompensated hypothyroidism
  • More common in women; increases with age

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Insufficient thyroid hormone (T3, T4) → decreased metabolic rate in all tissues
  • Reduced energy production, slowed body functions
  • In primary hypothyroidism: low T4 → elevated TSH (pituitary tries to stimulate thyroid)
  • Accumulation of mucopolysaccharides → myxedema (non-pitting edema)
  • Hashimoto’s: autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Teach lifelong levothyroxine adherence at the same time each day and regular TSH follow-up.
  • Take levothyroxine with water on an empty stomach 30–60 min before breakfast and separate calcium, iron, and antacids by 4 hr.
  • Report pregnancy, brand changes, new cardiac symptoms, or symptoms of over-replacement so the dose and labs can be reassessed.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Hashimoto thyroiditis, female sex, older age, thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine therapy, pituitary disease, and iodine deficiency increase risk.
  • Cardiac disease and older age increase risk when starting or increasing thyroid replacement too quickly.
  • Calcium, iron, antacids, inconsistent brand use, and missed doses can reduce medication effectiveness.

Expected Findings

Slowed metabolism:

  • Fatigue, lethargy, weakness
  • Cold intolerance
  • Weight gain (despite poor appetite)
  • Bradycardia
  • Constipation
  • Dry skin, brittle hair/nails, hair loss
  • Cognitive slowing, depression, memory issues
  • Menstrual irregularities
  • Periorbital edema, puffy face (myxedema)
  • Hoarseness, enlarged tongue

Myxedema coma: hypothermia, hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory depression, altered mental status (emergency).

Diagnostic:

  • Elevated TSH, low free T4 (primary)
  • Thyroid antibodies (Hashimoto’s)
  • Lipid panel (often elevated)

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor TSH to diagnose primary hypothyroidism and titrate levothyroxine therapy.
  • Use free T4 with TSH, especially when secondary hypothyroidism or dose response is unclear.
  • Trend labs after dose changes, pregnancy changes, brand changes, or symptoms of under- or over-replacement.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Diagnosis is primarily laboratory based, with elevated TSH and low T4 expected in primary hypothyroidism.
  • Thyroid antibody testing may support Hashimoto thyroiditis when ordered.
  • Assess for myxedema coma clinically when severe hypothyroid symptoms occur with altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia, or respiratory compromise.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Myxedema coma is life-threatening; monitor for severe lethargy, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, respiratory depression, and altered mental status.
  • Start low and titrate slowly in older adults or clients with cardiac disease to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmias.
  • Teach symptoms of over-replacement such as palpitations, weight loss, nervousness, heat intolerance, insomnia, or chest pain.

Complications

  • Myxedema coma, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, respiratory depression, and altered mental status in severe untreated disease.
  • Dyslipidemia, weight gain, fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, infertility concerns, and worsening quality of life with undertreatment.
  • Over-replacement can cause palpitations, insomnia, heat intolerance, weight loss, angina, arrhythmias, and bone loss.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) — lifelong replacement; titrate to TSH
  • Start low and increase slowly in older adults / cardiac disease (avoid precipitating angina/arrhythmia)
  • Myxedema coma: IV levothyroxine, supportive care (warming, ventilation, fluids, corticosteroids)

Nursing care:

  • Monitor TSH/T4 to guide dosing
  • Monitor cardiovascular response (especially when starting)
  • Warmth for cold intolerance
  • Promote bowel regularity
  • Energy conservation
  • Monitor for over-replacement (hyperthyroid symptoms)

Medications

  • Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) — lifelong replacement; titrate to TSH
  • Start low and increase slowly in older adults / cardiac disease (avoid precipitating angina/arrhythmia)
  • Myxedema coma: IV levothyroxine, supportive care (warming, ventilation, fluids, corticosteroids)

Client Education

  • Take levothyroxine in the morning on an empty stomach, 30–60 min before breakfast, with water
  • This is lifelong therapy — do not stop even when feeling well
  • Take at the same time daily; be consistent with brand
  • Separate from calcium, iron, antacids by 4 hours (reduce absorption)
  • It may take weeks to feel full effect
  • Report symptoms of over-replacement (palpitations, weight loss, nervousness, heat intolerance, insomnia)
  • Report chest pain (especially if older/cardiac disease)
  • Keep regular lab appointments for TSH monitoring
  • Do not switch brands without provider/lab follow-up
  • Inform provider if pregnant (dose usually increases)

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Routine management is medication replacement and laboratory monitoring rather than a procedure.
  • Myxedema coma requires emergency supportive care, IV levothyroxine, warming, ventilation, fluids, and corticosteroids as ordered.
  • Use follow-up visits after dose changes to reassess symptoms, adherence, interactions, and TSH response.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the prescriber and pharmacist for dose titration, brand consistency, absorption interactions, and cardiac precautions.
  • Involve endocrinology for pregnancy, secondary hypothyroidism, unstable labs, myxedema coma, or difficult titration.
  • Communicate pregnancy status, cardiac symptoms, missed doses, supplement use, and lab trends across the care team.
Worked Example Hyperthyroidism (Graves’ Disease) Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Hyperthyroidism
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Hyperthyroidism — excess thyroid hormone, accelerating metabolic processes.

  • Graves’ disease (most common): autoimmune; antibodies stimulate the thyroid (TSI); associated with exophthalmos and goiter
  • Toxic multinodular goiter; toxic adenoma
  • Thyroiditis (transient)
  • Excess thyroid hormone intake
  • Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis): life-threatening severe hyperthyroidism

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Excess T3/T4 → increased metabolic rate in all tissues
  • Increased oxygen consumption, heat production, sympathetic activity
  • Graves’: autoantibodies (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins) bind TSH receptors → continuous stimulation
  • Primary: low TSH, high free T4/T3
  • Exophthalmos: immune-mediated retro-orbital tissue changes

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote medication adherence, thyroid-level follow-up, adequate calories, rest periods, reduced stimulation, and avoidance of caffeine/stimulants.
  • Teach early reporting of fever, sore throat, jaundice, severe palpitations, high fever, agitation, or worsening symptoms.
  • Protect eyes with lubricants, sunglasses, and head elevation when exophthalmos is present.
  • After radioactive iodine, reinforce radiation precautions and likely lifelong monitoring/replacement for hypothyroidism.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess Graves' disease features, goiter, exophthalmos, autoimmune history, toxic nodular disease, thyroiditis, and excess thyroid hormone exposure.
  • Screen for triggers or risks for thyroid storm such as infection, surgery, trauma, severe stress, or untreated/worsening hyperthyroidism.
  • Review pregnancy status because PTU is preferred in the first trimester and therapy selection changes.
  • Assess cardiac risk, especially tachycardia, palpitations, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and older age.

Expected Findings

Accelerated metabolism:
