  • Weight loss despite increased appetite
  • Heat intolerance, sweating
  • Tachycardia, palpitations, atrial fibrillation, hypertension
  • Nervousness, anxiety, irritability, tremor
  • Insomnia
  • Diarrhea/frequent stools
  • Warm, moist skin; fine hair
  • Goiter (enlarged thyroid)
  • Graves’: exophthalmos (bulging eyes), lid lag

Thyroid storm: high fever, severe tachycardia, hypertension then hypotension, agitation/delirium, vomiting (emergency).

Diagnostic: low TSH, elevated free T4/T3; thyroid antibodies (Graves’); radioactive iodine uptake.

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor TSH, free T4, and T3; primary hyperthyroidism typically shows low TSH with elevated free T4/T3.
  • Check thyroid antibodies when Graves' disease is suspected.
  • Monitor CBC for agranulocytosis risk and liver function for hepatotoxicity with antithyroid drugs, especially PTU.
  • Trend thyroid levels after radioactive iodine, surgery, or medication changes to detect hypothyroidism or persistent hyperthyroidism.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Radioactive iodine uptake testing helps distinguish Graves' disease, toxic nodular disease, and thyroiditis patterns when ordered.
  • Assess thyroid size/goiter, tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss, tachycardia, and eye findings.
  • Monitor ECG or cardiac status when palpitations, atrial fibrillation, or severe tachycardia is present.
  • Recognize thyroid storm clinically: high fever, severe tachycardia, hypertension then hypotension, agitation/delirium, vomiting, and acute deterioration.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Thyroid storm: high fever, severe tachycardia, agitation/delirium, vomiting, or hypotension is an emergency.
  • Antithyroid-drug safety: report sore throat/fever for agranulocytosis and jaundice/dark urine for hepatotoxicity.
  • Cardiac safety: monitor HR/rhythm, palpitations, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation; beta blockers should not be stopped abruptly.
  • Radioactive iodine safety: follow temporary radiation precautions and avoid close contact with children/pregnant people as instructed.

Complications

  • Untreated hyperthyroidism can cause atrial fibrillation, hypertension, heart failure, weight loss, bone loss, and severe anxiety/insomnia.
  • Thyroid storm is life-threatening and can progress to severe hyperthermia, dysrhythmias, shock, and death.
  • Antithyroid medications can cause agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity.
  • Radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy can lead to hypothyroidism requiring lifelong levothyroxine monitoring/replacement.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil/PTU) — block hormone synthesis; PTU preferred in 1st trimester pregnancy
  • Beta blockers (propranolol) — control symptoms (tachycardia, tremor)
  • Radioactive iodine (I-131) — destroys thyroid tissue (common definitive treatment; leads to hypothyroidism → need replacement)
  • Iodine solutions (SSKI) — before surgery / thyroid storm
  • Thyroidectomy (surgical)

Nursing care:

  • Monitor cardiac status (afib, HR), weight, temperature
  • Cool environment; promote rest; reduce stimulation
  • Adequate nutrition/calories
  • Eye care for exophthalmos (lubricants, elevate HOB)
  • Monitor for thyroid storm; agranulocytosis (antithyroid drugs)

Medications

  • Antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil/PTU) — block hormone synthesis; PTU preferred in 1st trimester pregnancy
  • Beta blockers (propranolol) — control symptoms (tachycardia, tremor)
  • Radioactive iodine (I-131) — destroys thyroid tissue (common definitive treatment; leads to hypothyroidism → need replacement)
  • Iodine solutions (SSKI) — before surgery / thyroid storm
  • Thyroidectomy (surgical)

Client Education

  • Antithyroid drugs: take consistently; effects take weeks; report sore throat, fever (agranulocytosis); report jaundice (hepatotoxicity, especially PTU)
  • Beta blockers: control symptoms; do not stop abruptly
  • Radioactive iodine: radiation precautions (limit close contact, especially children/pregnant women, for several days); will likely become hypothyroid → need lifelong levothyroxine
  • Eat a high-calorie, nutritious diet (increased metabolism)
  • Avoid caffeine and stimulants
  • Cool, calm, restful environment
  • Eye protection if exophthalmos (sunglasses, artificial tears, elevate head)
  • Report worsening symptoms: high fever, severe palpitations, agitation (thyroid storm — emergency)
  • Keep follow-up for thyroid levels
  • PTU preferred if pregnant in first trimester

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Radioactive iodine destroys thyroid tissue and is a common definitive treatment; prepare the client for radiation precautions and later hypothyroid monitoring.
  • Thyroidectomy may be used when surgery is indicated; iodine solutions can be used before surgery or during thyroid storm as ordered.
  • During thyroid storm, prepare for emergency cooling/supportive care plus provider-directed antithyroid, beta-blocker, iodine, and glucocorticoid therapy.
  • Eye care for Graves' ophthalmopathy includes lubricants, head elevation, sunglasses, and specialty referral when needed.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with endocrinology/provider and pharmacist for antithyroid dosing, beta-blocker use, radioactive iodine planning, pregnancy considerations, and lab monitoring.
  • Involve ophthalmology for exophthalmos, eye irritation, visual changes, or severe Graves' ophthalmopathy.
  • Use dietitian support for high-calorie nutrition and weight loss concerns.
  • Communicate HR/rhythm, temperature, weight, thyroid labs, CBC/LFT abnormalities, pregnancy status, and thyroid-storm symptoms promptly.
Worked Example Addison’s Disease & Adrenal Crisis Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Addison’s Disease (Adrenal Insufficiency)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 40 — Endocrine Disorders

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Addison’s Disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) — deficiency of adrenal cortex hormones: cortisol (glucocorticoid) and often aldosterone (mineralocorticoid).

  • Primary: adrenal gland destruction (autoimmune most common; also TB, hemorrhage)
  • Secondary: pituitary ACTH deficiency (or abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal — common iatrogenic cause)
  • Adrenal (Addisonian) crisis: acute, life-threatening insufficiency — medical emergency

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Cortisol deficiency → impaired stress response, hypoglycemia, hypotension, GI symptoms
  • Aldosterone deficiency → sodium loss, potassium retention, water loss → hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, hypotension
  • Loss of negative feedback → high ACTH (primary) → hyperpigmentation (ACTH stimulates melanocytes)
  • Crisis triggered by stress (infection, surgery, trauma) when cortisol cannot increase, or abrupt steroid withdrawal

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Teach lifelong daily steroid replacement, never stopping abruptly, and never running out of medication.
  • Reinforce sick-day stress dosing during illness, fever, surgery, trauma, or major stress according to the provider plan.
  • Promote medical alert identification, emergency injectable hydrocortisone kit use, and informing all providers before procedures.
  • Encourage infection prevention, adequate salt/fluid intake when prescribed, and follow-up for BP, weight, electrolytes, and glucose.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess primary adrenal destruction causes such as autoimmune disease, TB history, adrenal hemorrhage, or other adrenal disease.
  • Review secondary causes including pituitary ACTH deficiency and abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal.
  • Identify crisis triggers: infection, surgery, trauma, vomiting/dehydration, major stress, missed steroids, or inability to keep medications down.
  • Assess orthostatic hypotension, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, salt craving, hypoglycemia symptoms, and medication access.

Expected Findings

  • Chronic fatigue, weakness, lethargy
  • Hyperpigmentation (bronze skin, especially creases, scars, mucous membranes) — primary
  • Weight loss, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
  • Hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, salt craving
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Labs: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia

Adrenal crisis:

  • Severe hypotension → shock
  • Severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia
  • Profound weakness, confusion
  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal/flank pain, fever (emergency)

Diagnostic: low cortisol, high ACTH (primary), ACTH stimulation test, electrolytes.

Laboratory Tests

  • Monitor sodium, potassium, glucose, cortisol, and ACTH; primary adrenal insufficiency often has low cortisol and high ACTH.
  • During crisis, trend severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and dehydration/renal indicators.
  • Monitor weight, I&O, and BP alongside labs to evaluate fluid and mineralocorticoid status.
  • Evaluate therapy response and over-/under-replacement through ordered endocrine labs and symptom trends.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • ACTH stimulation testing helps evaluate adrenal response when adrenal insufficiency is suspected.
  • Assess for chronic findings such as hyperpigmentation, fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, salt craving, nausea/vomiting, and abdominal pain.
  • Recognize adrenal crisis clinically: severe hypotension/shock, severe weakness, confusion, vomiting, fever, flank/abdominal pain, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia.
  • Review medication history for corticosteroid withdrawal or inadequate stress dosing.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Adrenal crisis: severe weakness, dizziness, vomiting, confusion, hypotension/shock, fever, or abdominal/flank pain requires emergency care.
  • Do not stop steroids abruptly: missed or abruptly stopped glucocorticoids can precipitate crisis.
  • Emergency kit: carry injectable hydrocortisone and medical alert ID; teach when and how to use the injection if trained.
  • Monitoring: watch BP, orthostasis, glucose, sodium, potassium, weight, and signs of over-replacement such as swelling/weight gain/Cushingoid changes.

Complications

  • Adrenal crisis can cause shock, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, dehydration, confusion, and death if untreated.
  • Chronic undertreatment causes fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, GI symptoms, salt craving, and poor stress tolerance.
  • Over-replacement can cause Cushingoid effects, weight gain, edema, hypertension, and hyperglycemia.
  • Vomiting, infection, surgery, or missed stress dosing can quickly destabilize the client.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone, prednisone) — lifelong
  • Mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) — if aldosterone deficient
  • Adrenal crisis: immediate IV hydrocortisone, IV fluids (NS), dextrose for hypoglycemia, correct electrolytes

Nursing care:

  • Monitor vital signs (hypotension), electrolytes, glucose, weight, I&O
  • Stress-dose steroids during illness/surgery (increased need)
  • Recognize and treat adrenal crisis promptly
  • Avoid abrupt steroid discontinuation
  • Promote rest; prevent infection

Medications

  • Glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone, prednisone) — lifelong
  • Mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) — if aldosterone deficient
  • Adrenal crisis: immediate IV hydrocortisone, IV fluids (NS), dextrose for hypoglycemia, correct electrolytes

Client Education

  • Take replacement steroids every day for life — NEVER abruptly stop (can precipitate crisis)
  • “Sick-day” stress dosing: increase glucocorticoid dose during illness, fever, surgery, or major stress (per provider instructions)
  • Take glucocorticoid with food; often larger dose in morning (mimic natural rhythm)
  • Wear a medical alert bracelet (adrenal insufficiency)
  • Carry an emergency injectable hydrocortisone kit and know how to use it
  • Recognize adrenal crisis (severe weakness, dizziness, vomiting, confusion) — seek emergency care; give emergency injection if trained
  • Maintain adequate salt intake (especially if on fludrocortisone)
  • Report signs of over-replacement (Cushingoid: weight gain, moon face, swelling)
  • Keep follow-up appointments; do not run out of medication
  • Inform all providers of the condition before procedures

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Adrenal crisis requires immediate IV hydrocortisone, IV normal saline, dextrose for hypoglycemia, and electrolyte correction as ordered.
  • Stress-dose steroid plans are used before procedures, surgery, severe illness, or major physiologic stress.
  • Teach and rehearse emergency hydrocortisone injection procedure and when to seek emergency care afterward.
  • Routine management is medication-based with glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement and ongoing monitoring.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with endocrinology/provider and pharmacist for glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid dosing, stress-dose instructions, emergency kit supply, and interaction review.
  • Involve emergency care promptly for suspected adrenal crisis and ensure perioperative teams know the client requires stress-dose steroids.
  • Use dietitian support when salt/fluid guidance, weight changes, or comorbid diabetes/HTN complicate therapy.
  • Communicate BP/orthostasis, glucose/electrolytes, vomiting/illness, missed doses, crisis symptoms, and over-replacement findings.
Worked Example Urinary Tract Infection Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) — infection of any part of the urinary system, most commonly bacterial.

  • Lower UTI (cystitis): bladder; urethritis
  • Upper UTI (pyelonephritis): kidneys — more serious
  • Uncomplicated: healthy, non-pregnant women, normal tract
  • Complicated: men, pregnancy, catheters, abnormalities, immunocompromise
  • Most common cause: E. coli
  • More common in women (shorter urethra)

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Bacteria (usually from perineal/fecal flora) ascend the urethra into the bladder
  • Adhere to and colonize urinary epithelium → inflammation
  • May ascend ureters to kidneys (pyelonephritis)
  • Risk factors: female anatomy, sexual activity, urinary stasis (obstruction, incomplete emptying), catheters (CAUTI), pregnancy, diabetes, menopause (low estrogen), poor hygiene
  • Indwelling catheters provide a direct route and biofilm for bacteria

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Encourage fluids, regular voiding, not delaying urination, and urinating after intercourse when relevant.
  • Teach front-to-back wiping, avoiding douches or bubble baths, wearing cotton underwear, and addressing recurrent triggers.
  • Reinforce completing the full antibiotic course and seeking care for recurrent UTIs rather than self-treating repeated symptoms.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Female anatomy, sexual activity, poor hygiene, menopause, pregnancy, diabetes, urinary stasis, obstruction, incomplete emptying, and immunocompromise increase risk.
  • Indwelling catheters increase CAUTI risk by providing a direct route and biofilm for bacteria.
  • Complicated UTI risk is higher in men, pregnancy, catheters, urinary abnormalities, and immunocompromised clients.

Expected Findings

Lower UTI (cystitis):

  • Dysuria (painful urination)
  • Frequency, urgency
  • Suprapubic pain/pressure
  • Cloudy, foul-smelling urine; hematuria
  • Nocturia

Upper UTI (pyelonephritis):

  • Flank pain, costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness
  • High fever, chills
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Systemic illness (can lead to sepsis)

Older adults: may present atypically — confusion, altered mental status, falls (instead of classic symptoms).

Diagnostic: urinalysis (nitrites, leukocyte esterase, WBCs, bacteria), urine culture and sensitivity, sometimes imaging (complicated/recurrent).

Laboratory Tests

  • Use urinalysis to assess leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria, hematuria, and bacteriuria when UTI is suspected.
  • Obtain urine culture and sensitivity for recurrent, complicated, pyelonephritis, pregnancy, or treatment-failure cases to guide antibiotics.
  • Monitor renal function, CBC, or other labs when pyelonephritis, sepsis, dehydration, complicated infection, or nephrotoxic therapy is a concern.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Diagnose uncomplicated cystitis by symptoms and urinalysis when appropriate.
  • Use urine culture for complicated infection, recurrence, treatment failure, pregnancy, or suspected pyelonephritis.
  • Imaging or urology evaluation may be needed for recurrent infection, obstruction, stones, anatomic abnormality, or persistent pyelonephritis symptoms.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Report high fever, flank pain, chills, nausea/vomiting, worsening symptoms, or confusion promptly because these can indicate pyelonephritis or sepsis.
  • Tailor antibiotics to culture and sensitivity when needed and teach full-course adherence even when symptoms improve.
  • Teach that phenazopyridine turns urine orange/red, can stain clothing or contacts, and treats dysuria symptoms only, not the infection.

Complications

  • Pyelonephritis, sepsis, recurrent UTI, renal involvement, dehydration, and treatment failure from resistant organisms or incomplete antibiotics.
  • Pregnancy-associated complications and complicated infection in catheterized, obstructed, diabetic, or immunocompromised clients.
  • CAUTI risk and biofilm formation with indwelling catheters.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Uncomplicated cystitis: nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, or fosfomycin (first-line); short course
  • Pyelonephritis/complicated: fluoroquinolones or others per culture; longer course; sometimes IV
  • Phenazopyridine — urinary analgesic for dysuria (symptomatic only; turns urine orange)
  • Tailor to culture and sensitivity

Nursing care:

  • Obtain urine culture before antibiotics
  • Encourage fluids (flush bacteria)
  • Pain management; monitor for systemic infection/sepsis (pyelonephritis)
  • CAUTI prevention: remove catheters ASAP, aseptic insertion/care
  • Monitor response and renal function

Medications

  • Uncomplicated cystitis: nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, or fosfomycin (first-line); short course
  • Pyelonephritis/complicated: fluoroquinolones or others per culture; longer course; sometimes IV
  • Phenazopyridine — urinary analgesic for dysuria (symptomatic only; turns urine orange)
  • Tailor to culture and sensitivity

Client Education

  • Complete the full antibiotic course even if symptoms resolve
  • Drink plenty of fluids (water) to flush bacteria
  • Prevention: wipe front to back, urinate after intercourse, avoid irritants (douches, bubble baths), wear cotton underwear, do not delay urination
  • Cranberry products may help prevent recurrence (not treat)
  • Phenazopyridine: turns urine orange/red (harmless; can stain clothing/contacts); short-term only; treats symptoms not infection
  • Report worsening symptoms: high fever, flank pain, nausea/vomiting (possible kidney infection)
  • Take antibiotics as scheduled
  • Postmenopausal women: vaginal estrogen may reduce recurrence (per provider)
  • Seek care for recurrent UTIs (evaluation)

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Collect a clean-catch or catheter urine specimen correctly before antibiotics when culture is ordered.
  • Remove unnecessary urinary catheters promptly and maintain catheter care protocols when a catheter is required.
  • Use imaging, urology referral, or catheter/obstruction management when recurrent, complicated, or upper-tract infection is suspected.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the prescriber and pharmacist for empiric therapy, culture-guided antibiotic adjustment, renal dosing, and adverse-effect counseling.
  • Work with laboratory staff to ensure timely urine culture collection and sensitivity reporting.
  • Involve urology or obstetric care for recurrent, complicated, obstructive, pregnancy-related, or upper-tract infections.
Worked Example Tuberculosis Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections · TB section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
Tuberculosis (TB)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 47 — Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Tuberculosis (TB) — an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs, spread by airborne droplet nuclei.

  • Latent TB infection (LTBI): infected but asymptomatic, not contagious, positive test
  • Active TB disease: symptomatic, contagious
  • Higher risk: immunocompromised (HIV), crowded living, healthcare workers, foreign-born from high-prevalence areas, homeless
  • Drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) is a growing concern

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • Inhaled droplet nuclei reach alveoli → bacteria multiply
  • Immune response walls off bacteria in granulomas (tubercles) → latent infection (bacteria dormant)
  • If immunity falls (HIV, age, immunosuppression) → reactivation → active disease
  • Caseating necrosis in lung tissue; can spread (miliary/extrapulmonary TB)
  • Slow-growing; requires prolonged multi-drug therapy

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Prevent transmission with airborne precautions for active TB, cough etiquette, ventilation, masking during transport, and contact testing.
  • Promote full-course adherence to RIPE or latent-TB therapy; stopping early risks treatment failure and drug-resistant TB.
  • Use DOT when indicated to support adherence and resistance prevention.
  • Teach nutrition support, avoidance of alcohol with hepatotoxic therapy, and prompt reporting of vision changes, neuropathy, or hepatitis symptoms.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess HIV/immunocompromise, close contact with active TB, crowded living, homelessness, correctional or shelter exposure, healthcare work, and birth/travel from high-prevalence areas.
  • Screen for latent TB in high-risk clients and for reactivation risk when immunity falls.
  • Review prior TB treatment, medication adherence history, and drug-resistant TB exposure risk.
  • Assess liver disease, alcohol use, pregnancy, and medication interactions before RIPE or latent-TB therapy.

Expected Findings

Active TB symptoms:

  • Persistent cough (> 3 weeks), productive, may be blood-tinged (hemoptysis)
  • Night sweats
  • Unintentional weight loss, anorexia
  • Low-grade fever, fatigue, malaise
  • Chest pain

Diagnostic:

  • Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST/PPD) — measure induration at 48–72 hr (not redness)
  • Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) — blood test (not affected by BCG)
  • Chest X-ray (infiltrates, cavitation, upper lobes)
  • Sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture — confirms active disease (gold standard)

Laboratory Tests

  • Use IGRA blood testing or TST/PPD screening; TST induration is read at 48-72 hr and IGRA is not affected by BCG vaccination.
  • Obtain sputum AFB smear and culture to confirm active TB and monitor conversion when ordered.
  • Monitor liver function because INH, rifampin, and pyrazinamide are hepatotoxic.
  • Use HIV testing and other immune-status evaluation when clinically indicated because HIV increases TB risk and changes care needs.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Chest x-ray can show infiltrates, cavitation, or upper-lobe disease suggestive of active pulmonary TB.
  • Collect ordered sputum specimens, often early morning and repeated, for AFB smear/culture.
  • Differentiate latent TB from active disease using symptoms, imaging, and microbiologic testing.
  • Assess persistent cough >3 weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, fever, fatigue, and chest pain.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Airborne isolation: active TB requires negative-pressure room, N95 respirator for staff, and surgical mask for client transport.
  • Adherence safety: incomplete therapy increases relapse, transmission, and MDR-TB risk.
  • RIPE toxicity: monitor hepatotoxicity, INH neuropathy, rifampin interactions/orange fluids, pyrazinamide hyperuricemia, and ethambutol optic neuritis.
  • Public health: report active TB and support contact tracing per local requirements.

Complications

  • Untreated active TB can cause cavitary lung disease, hemoptysis, respiratory compromise, miliary/extrapulmonary spread, transmission to contacts, and death.
  • Incomplete treatment can lead to relapse and multidrug-resistant TB.
  • TB medications can cause hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis, hyperuricemia, drug interactions, and reduced oral contraceptive effectiveness with rifampin.
  • Immunocompromised clients have higher risk for reactivation and severe/disseminated disease.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy (active TB — multi-drug, prolonged):

  • RIPE regimen: Rifampin, Isoniazid (INH), Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol — typically 2 months, then INH + rifampin for 4 more months (6 months total)
  • Latent TB: usually INH (with B6) for months, or shorter rifampin-based regimens
  • Drug-resistant TB: extended specialized regimens

Nursing care:

  • Airborne precautions for active TB: negative-pressure room, N95 respirator, patient wears surgical mask when out of room
  • Obtain sputum samples (often 3 early-morning); monitor AFB conversion
  • Monitor liver function (hepatotoxic drugs)
  • Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) to ensure adherence
  • Report to public health; contact tracing
  • Nutrition support

Medications

  • RIPE regimen: Rifampin, Isoniazid (INH), Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol — typically 2 months, then INH + rifampin for 4 more months (6 months total)
  • Latent TB: usually INH (with B6) for months, or shorter rifampin-based regimens
  • Drug-resistant TB: extended specialized regimens

Client Education

  • Take ALL medications exactly as prescribed for the full duration (months) — stopping early causes treatment failure and drug-resistant TB
  • Directly observed therapy may be used to support adherence
  • Isoniazid: take B6 (pyridoxine) to prevent neuropathy; avoid alcohol (hepatotoxicity); report numbness/tingling
  • Rifampin: turns body fluids (urine, sweat, tears) orange-red (harmless; can stain contacts); reduces oral contraceptive effectiveness (use backup)
  • Ethambutol: report vision changes (optic neuritis)
  • Report yellowing skin/eyes, dark urine, anorexia (hepatotoxicity — common to several drugs)
  • Cover mouth when coughing; proper hand hygiene; ventilation
  • Once on effective therapy and no longer infectious (negative sputum), precautions may ease
  • Keep follow-up sputum tests and appointments
  • Inform close contacts to be tested

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Implement airborne isolation procedures for suspected or confirmed active pulmonary TB until criteria for discontinuation are met.
  • Collect serial sputum specimens and monitor AFB conversion as ordered.
  • Directly Observed Therapy is used to ensure adherence and prevent resistance.
  • Coordinate public-health contact tracing, testing, and treatment follow-up for exposed contacts.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with the provider, pharmacist, infection prevention, respiratory therapy, lab, and public health department for isolation, sputum testing, RIPE therapy, DOT, and contact tracing.
  • Involve case management/social work to address housing, transportation, medication access, and adherence barriers during prolonged therapy.
  • Use dietitian support for weight loss, anorexia, and nutrition recovery.
  • Communicate cough/hemoptysis, fever/weight trends, AFB results, LFTs, vision changes, neuropathy, adherence barriers, and contact-exposure information.
Worked Example HIV / AIDS Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS · HIV section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Disorder
HIV / AIDS
Review Module Chapter
Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS

Alterations in Health (Diagnosis)

Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) — a retrovirus that infects and destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes, progressively weakening the immune system.

  • AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) — advanced HIV; defined by CD4 < 200 cells/mm³ or an AIDS-defining opportunistic illness
  • Transmission: blood, sexual contact, perinatal (pregnancy/birth/breastfeeding), needle sharing
  • NOT transmitted by casual contact
  • With effective treatment, HIV is now a manageable chronic condition

Pathophysiology Related to Client Problem

  • HIV binds CD4 receptors, enters T-cells, uses reverse transcriptase to integrate into host DNA
  • Viral replication destroys CD4 cells → progressive immunodeficiency
  • As CD4 declines → susceptibility to opportunistic infections and malignancies
  • Stages: acute infection (flu-like, high viral load) → clinical latency (asymptomatic, ongoing replication) → AIDS
  • Viral load reflects replication; CD4 reflects immune status

Health Promotion and Disease Prevention

  • Promote strict ART adherence to reach/maintain undetectable viral load, prevent resistance, preserve CD4 count, and reduce transmission.
  • Teach safer sex, no needle sharing, partner notification/testing, PrEP/PEP awareness for contacts, and U=U counseling when viral load is undetectable.
  • Encourage recommended vaccinations while avoiding live vaccines if severely immunocompromised.
  • Prevent opportunistic infections through CD4/viral-load monitoring, prophylaxis when indicated, nutrition support, and prompt infection reporting.
ASSESSMENT

Risk Factors

  • Assess sexual exposure, blood exposure, needle sharing, perinatal exposure, STI history, and partner HIV status.
  • Review barriers to ART adherence such as stigma, mental health, substance use, housing instability, cost, side effects, or complex regimens.
  • Screen for opportunistic infection risk as CD4 count falls, especially CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness.
  • Assess pregnancy plans/status, breastfeeding counseling needs, and medication-interaction risk with all prescribed/OTC/herbal agents.

Expected Findings

Acute HIV (2–4 weeks after exposure):

  • Flu-like: fever, fatigue, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, rash, myalgia

Latency: often asymptomatic for years.

Advanced HIV/AIDS:

  • Persistent fever, night sweats, weight loss (wasting)
  • Chronic diarrhea, fatigue
  • Opportunistic infections: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), candidiasis (oral/esophageal), TB, CMV, toxoplasmosis
  • Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma
  • Neurocognitive decline

Diagnostic:

  • HIV antigen/antibody (4th-gen) screening → confirmatory testing
  • HIV RNA (viral load)
  • CD4 count (immune status, staging)

Laboratory Tests

  • Use 4th-generation HIV antigen/antibody screening with confirmatory testing for diagnosis.
  • Monitor HIV RNA viral load to evaluate replication, treatment response, and transmission risk.
  • Monitor CD4 count for immune status, AIDS staging, and opportunistic infection prophylaxis decisions.
  • Trend medication-safety labs according to ART regimen, including renal/hepatic function, CBC, glucose/lipids, or other ordered monitoring.

Diagnostic Procedures

  • Stage HIV using symptoms, CD4 count, viral load, and presence of AIDS-defining opportunistic infection or malignancy.
  • Assess for acute HIV after exposure with fever, fatigue, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, rash, and myalgia.
  • Evaluate advanced disease symptoms such as persistent fever, night sweats, wasting, chronic diarrhea, candidiasis, TB, PCP, CMV, toxoplasmosis, Kaposi sarcoma, lymphoma, or neurocognitive decline.
  • Use targeted testing for opportunistic infections based on symptoms and CD4 level.
SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
  • Adherence safety: missed ART doses can lead to viral rebound, resistance, progression, and transmission risk.
  • Infection safety: fever, cough, dyspnea, oral/esophageal candidiasis, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, or neurologic changes require prompt evaluation.
  • Transmission safety: use condoms, do not share needles, follow perinatal prevention plans, and avoid breastfeeding in resourced settings when advised.
  • Medication safety: review all drugs/supplements for ART interactions and monitor toxicity labs for the prescribed regimen.

Complications

  • Untreated HIV can progress to AIDS with opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, chronic diarrhea, neurocognitive decline, and death.
  • Low CD4 count increases risk for PCP, candidiasis, TB, CMV, toxoplasmosis, Kaposi sarcoma, and lymphoma.
  • Poor adherence can cause drug resistance and treatment failure.
  • ART can cause regimen-specific toxicities and interactions that require ongoing lab monitoring and medication review.
PATIENT-CENTERED CARE

Nursing Care

Pharmacotherapy:

  • Antiretroviral therapy (HAART) — combination regimen for ALL HIV+ individuals; goal undetectable viral load
  • Opportunistic infection prophylaxis (e.g., TMP-SMX for PCP when CD4 low) and treatment
  • Vaccinations (avoid live vaccines if severely immunocompromised)

Nursing care:

  • Standard precautions (prevent transmission)
  • Intensive adherence support (resistance prevention)
  • Monitor CD4, viral load, medication toxicities
  • Prevent/recognize opportunistic infections
  • Nutrition support; manage symptoms
  • Psychosocial support; address stigma; safe-sex/harm-reduction counseling

Medications

  • Antiretroviral therapy (HAART) — combination regimen for ALL HIV+ individuals; goal undetectable viral load
  • Opportunistic infection prophylaxis (e.g., TMP-SMX for PCP when CD4 low) and treatment
  • Vaccinations (avoid live vaccines if severely immunocompromised)

Client Education

  • Strict adherence to ART is essential — take every dose, do not stop; prevents resistance and progression
  • U=U: an undetectable viral load means HIV cannot be sexually transmitted
  • Prevent transmission: condoms, do not share needles, disclose status to partners; ART reduces transmission
  • Pregnancy: ART greatly reduces transmission to baby; avoid breastfeeding (in resourced settings)
  • Recognize and report signs of infection promptly (immunocompromised)
  • Avoid live vaccines if severely immunocompromised; stay current on recommended vaccines
  • Maintain nutrition, healthy lifestyle, avoid raw/undercooked foods if very low CD4
  • Keep all appointments for CD4/viral load monitoring
  • Tell providers about all medications (interactions)
  • Seek support resources; HIV is a manageable chronic condition with treatment

Therapeutic Procedures

  • Initiate and maintain combination ART for all clients with HIV; goal is undetectable viral load.
  • Use opportunistic infection prophylaxis, such as TMP-SMX for PCP when CD4 is low, and treat infections promptly when diagnosed.
  • Provide standard precautions and exposure-prevention procedures for blood/body-fluid contact.
  • Use routine CD4/viral-load monitoring and targeted opportunistic-infection evaluation to guide therapy and prevention.

Interprofessional Care

  • Coordinate with HIV specialist/provider and pharmacist for ART regimen selection, interaction screening, adherence support, resistance concerns, and toxicity monitoring.
  • Involve public health, partner services, case management, social work, behavioral health, and substance-use resources to address transmission prevention and adherence barriers.
  • Use dietitian support for weight loss, wasting, diarrhea, and food safety when severely immunocompromised.
  • Communicate viral load/CD4 trends, infection symptoms, medication side effects, pregnancy status, adherence barriers, and psychosocial needs.

Therapeutic Procedure

Active · 9 examples
Worked Example Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration
Review Module Chapter
Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration

Description of Procedure

Pharmacokinetics — what the body does TO the drug — encompasses four processes (ADME):

  • Absorption: movement of drug from administration site into bloodstream
    • Influenced by: route, formulation, GI factors (pH, motility, food), first-pass metabolism
  • Distribution: movement of drug from bloodstream to tissues
    • Influenced by: blood flow, lipid solubility, protein binding, blood-brain barrier, placenta
  • Metabolism (biotransformation): chemical alteration, mostly hepatic (CYP450 enzymes)
    • Active metabolites, prodrugs, drug-drug interactions occur here
  • Excretion: removal from body, primarily renal (urine), also bile, feces, lungs, sweat, breast milk

Pharmacodynamics — what the drug does TO the body — receptor binding, signal transduction, dose-response relationships.

Indications

  • Medication absorption pattern: Rapid absorption through the alveolar capillary network. A spacer keeps the medication in the device longer, increasing the amount delivered to the lungs and decreasing the amount deposited in the oropharynx.
  • Barrier to absorption: Inadequate respiratory effort.
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre:

  • Verify ordered route is appropriate for the drug and client (e.g., morphine: PO dose >> IV dose due to first-pass)
  • Assess client factors affecting PK: age (peds/elderly altered metabolism), weight (dosing), renal function (BUN, creatinine, eGFR), hepatic function (LFTs), pregnancy, comorbidities
  • Review all medications for interactions (CYP450, protein binding, additive effects)
  • Check timing relative to food, other meds, lab draws

Intra:

  • Administer by correct route with correct technique
  • Use proper IV infusion rate, site, equipment
  • For oral: check if must be on empty stomach, with food, separated from interacting meds
  • For sublingual: must be absorbed in mouth (not swallowed) — bypasses first-pass

Post:

  • Monitor for therapeutic effect (expected onset based on route)
  • Monitor for adverse effects, especially at peak time
  • For narrow-window drugs: obtain drug levels at appropriate times (peak, trough, steady state typically after 4-5 half-lives)
  • Adjust dosing based on response and labs
  • Educate client about timing, food/drug interactions, route-specific considerations

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Therapeutic drug levels achieved without toxicity (narrow-window drugs especially)
  • Effective drug concentration at site of action
  • Predictable onset, peak, and duration based on chosen route
  • Appropriate dose adjustments made for client factors (age, weight, renal/hepatic function)
  • Drug-drug interactions identified and managed

Client Education

  • Remove the covers from the mouthpieces of the inhaler and of the spacer
  • Insert the MDI into the end of the spacer
  • Shake the inhaler five or six times
  • Exhale completely, then close your mouth around the spacer's mouthpiece
  • Tilt your head back slightly, press the inhaler, and at the same time begin a slow, deep inhalation
  • Continue to breathe in slowly and deeply for 3 to 5 seconds to facilitate delivery to the air passages
  • Hold your breath for 10 seconds to allow the medication to deposit in your airways
  • Take the mouthpiece out of your mouth and slowly exhale through pursed lips
  • Resume normal breathing

Potential Complications

  • Subtherapeutic levels: failed treatment due to inadequate absorption, distribution, or excessive metabolism/excretion
  • Toxic levels: due to overdose, accumulation (renal/hepatic impairment), drug interactions, missed first-pass metabolism (IV vs PO)
  • First-pass effect: oral drugs metabolized extensively before reaching systemic circulation — much higher PO than IV dose needed (e.g., morphine, nitroglycerin)
  • Half-life accumulation: drugs with long half-life can accumulate to toxic levels in renal/hepatic impairment
  • CYP450 drug interactions: inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort) ↓ levels of substrates; inhibitors (cimetidine, fluconazole, erythromycin, grapefruit) ↑ levels
  • Protein-binding interactions: warfarin, phenytoin, valproic acid — displaced by other highly protein-bound drugs
  • Route-specific complications: IV (extravasation, infection, embolism), IM (sterile abscess, nerve injury), oral (variable absorption, GI upset)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor vital signs and clinical status closely
  • Assess for adverse effects related to the procedure
  • Provide post-procedure care per protocol; reposition and reassess regularly
  • Document findings, interventions, and patient response; notify provider of unexpected outcomes
Worked Example Blood and Blood Products Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products · ALS in book · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Blood and Blood Products
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products

Description of Procedure

Administration of blood and blood products through IV infusion for transfusion:

  • Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs): most common; ↑ oxygen-carrying capacity; ~250-350 mL/unit; ↑ Hgb ~1 g/dL per unit
  • Platelets: ↑ platelet count and clotting capacity
  • Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP): contains all clotting factors; for warfarin reversal, DIC, massive transfusion
  • Cryoprecipitate: fibrinogen, factors VIII, XIII, vWF, fibronectin
  • Albumin: colloid volume expander; hypoalbuminemia, burns, ascites
  • Granulocytes (rare): severe neutropenia
  • Factor concentrates: factor VIII for hemophilia A, factor IX for hemophilia B, prothrombin complex concentrate

Indications

A client who lost blood from a GI bleed can need a unit of PRBCs for a hgb level below 10 g/dL especially if demonstrating manifestations of hypovolemia (increase in pulse and respiration rate; decrease in blood pressure; low oxygen saturation; cool and pale or cyanotic; increased capillary refill time; increased urinary output). If hypoxic, the client will exhibit decreased level of consciousness and confusion. PRBCs restore red blood cells and improve oxygenation. If the client has lost a large amount of fluid volume, whole blood, rather than PRBCs, can be indicated.

Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-transfusion:

  • Verify provider order, indication, consent (informed consent required)
  • Ensure type and crossmatch completed; verify with second nurse at bedside (right product, right client, expiration, blood type compatibility — TWO RNs check)
  • Establish dedicated IV access — at least 20 ga (18 ga preferred for rapid infusion); avoid small-gauge unless necessary
  • Use Y-tubing with filter and 0.9% normal saline only (NOT D5W or lactated Ringer's — cause hemolysis or clotting)
  • Baseline vital signs (temperature, BP, HR, RR, SpO₂) immediately before starting
  • Assess for signs of fluid overload risk (CHF, renal failure, elderly)
  • Pre-medicate (acetaminophen, diphenhydramine) if ordered for clients with history of reactions

During transfusion:

  • Start slowly: 2 mL/min (~120 mL/hr) for first 15 minutes; stay with client during this critical period
  • Vital signs after 15 minutes; if stable, may increase rate
  • Complete unit within 4 hours (bacterial growth risk after); typical infusion 2-3 hr per unit
  • Monitor VS per protocol (q30 min or per institution)
  • Observe for transfusion reaction signs: fever, chills, back/flank pain, dyspnea, urticaria, hypotension, anxiety, dark urine
  • If reaction suspected:
    1. STOP transfusion immediately
    2. Keep IV line open with NS via NEW tubing
    3. Notify provider and blood bank
    4. Send blood bag and tubing to blood bank
    5. Collect blood and urine samples per protocol
    6. Treat symptoms (epinephrine for anaphylaxis, antihistamines, antipyretics, etc.)
    7. Complete transfusion reaction report

Post-transfusion:

  • Vital signs at end of transfusion and per protocol
  • Document: time started/completed, product type, amount, response, any reactions
  • Check post-transfusion CBC at appropriate interval (e.g., 1 hr post for platelets; with next AM labs for PRBCs)
  • Monitor for delayed reactions (24-48 hr; up to 10 days for delayed hemolytic)
  • Continue to assess for fluid overload

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • PRBCs: ↑ Hgb (1 g/dL per unit), ↓ symptoms of anemia (fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia), improved tissue oxygenation
  • Platelets: ↑ platelet count, ↓ bleeding
  • FFP: normalized INR/PTT, control of bleeding
  • Cryoprecipitate: ↑ fibrinogen, control of bleeding
  • No transfusion reactions
  • No fluid overload (esp. in elderly, HF, renal failure)
  • No transmission of blood-borne infections

Client Education

  • Report immediately: back/flank pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, fever or chills, itching or rash, dizziness, dark urine, difficulty breathing
  • You may feel slightly cool — this is normal (blood products are refrigerated; warming devices used when indicated)
  • Nurse will check on you frequently, especially in the first 15 minutes
  • Stay in bed during the transfusion; call before getting up
  • Refused transfusion (e.g., Jehovah's Witness): respect; document; plan alternatives with team
  • After: report any unusual symptoms — back pain, fever, jaundice, dark urine — within several days
  • Future transfusions: tell providers about any prior reactions; ID bracelet may be needed for severe reactions

Potential Complications

  • Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) — ABO incompatibility — most dangerous:
    • Fever, chills, flank/back pain, hypotension, tachycardia, dyspnea, hemoglobinuria, DIC, renal failure
    • Onset within minutes; STOP transfusion immediately
  • Febrile non-hemolytic reaction: fever, chills (most common; pre-medicate with acetaminophen if history)
  • Allergic reaction: urticaria, itching, mild — antihistamine; if severe → anaphylaxis
  • Anaphylaxis: severe respiratory distress, shock — often IgA-deficient clients
  • TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury): acute respiratory distress within 6 hr; non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema
  • TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload): rapid fluid overload — dyspnea, pulmonary edema, ↑ BP
  • Bacterial contamination/sepsis: fever, hypotension, often platelet products (room temp storage)
  • Delayed hemolytic reaction: 3-10 days post-transfusion
  • Transmission of infections (HIV, hepatitis B/C, CMV) — rare with current screening
  • Iron overload with chronic transfusion (sickle cell, thalassemia)
  • Graft-versus-host disease (rare; immunocompromised)

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor vital signs and clinical status closely
  • Assess for adverse effects related to the procedure
  • Provide post-procedure care per protocol; reposition and reassess regularly
  • Document findings, interventions, and patient response; notify provider of unexpected outcomes
Worked Example Anaphylaxis Recognition and Treatment Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications · Anaphylaxis section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Anaphylaxis Recognition and Treatment
Review Module Chapter
Ch 5 — Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications

Description of Procedure

Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening, IgE-mediated systemic hypersensitivity reaction. Onset is typically within minutes of exposure (may be delayed up to 30–60 min).

Classic presentation involves at least 2 of:

  • Skin/mucosa: urticaria (hives), pruritus, flushing, angioedema (lips, tongue, throat swelling)
  • Respiratory: wheezing, stridor, dyspnea, hypoxia, throat tightness
  • Cardiovascular: hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, shock
  • GI: abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhea

Epinephrine IM is FIRST-LINE. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are ADJUNCTS, not substitutes.

Indications

  • Any client with known severe allergy receiving a triggering medication (penicillins, sulfa, contrast dye, NSAIDs)
  • First-time IV antibiotics — especially penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin
  • Latex exposure in sensitized clients (banana, kiwi, avocado cross-reactivity)
  • Bee/wasp stings, food allergies (peanuts, shellfish, tree nuts)
  • ALL clinical settings — any nurse may encounter anaphylaxis
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre (prevention):

  • Document allergies thoroughly — type of reaction (rash vs anaphylaxis), severity, antidote used
  • Verify allergies before EVERY medication administration
  • For first IV doses of high-risk drugs: stay with client first 15 min; have emergency equipment ready
  • Skin test before penicillin if remote history of severe reaction

Intra (active anaphylaxis — act fast):

  1. STOP the offending agent immediately (clamp IV, remove patch, etc.)
  2. Call for help / activate rapid response
  3. Epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL strength, 0.3–0.5 mL) in lateral thigh — repeat every 5–15 min as needed
  4. Position: supine with legs elevated (Trendelenburg) unless respiratory distress — then high Fowler’s
  5. Establish airway — prepare for intubation if stridor/swelling
  6. High-flow oxygen 100% via non-rebreather
  7. Large-bore IV access; IV fluid bolus 1–2 L 0.9% NS
  8. Adjuncts (after epinephrine): diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV, methylprednisolone IV (delayed onset; prevents biphasic reaction)
  9. For bronchospasm: albuterol nebulizer
  10. If unresponsive to IM epinephrine: IV epinephrine drip (ICU)

Post:

  • Continuous monitoring (cardiac, oxygen sat, BP) for at least 4–6 hours (biphasic reaction risk)
  • Document the reaction in detail (time, signs, treatments, response)
  • Add the allergen to allergy list with severity
  • Discharge teaching: epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) use; medical alert ID; allergist referral

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Stabilization of airway, breathing, circulation
  • Resolution of urticaria, angioedema, hypotension within 30–60 min
  • No biphasic reaction in the observation window
  • Client and family demonstrate correct use of epinephrine auto-injector
  • Allergy properly documented to prevent future re-exposure

Client Education

  • Report hives, swelling of lips/tongue/throat, wheezing, shortness of breath, dizziness, or sense of impending doom immediately.
  • Carry and know how to use prescribed epinephrine auto-injectors; use epinephrine first for severe allergic reaction symptoms.
  • Seek emergency care after epinephrine use because symptoms can recur after initial improvement.
  • Avoid known triggers, read medication/food labels carefully, and wear medical alert identification when indicated.

Potential Complications

  • Death — respiratory or cardiovascular collapse if treatment delayed
  • Biphasic reaction — second episode 1–72 hr (most within 8 hr) after apparent resolution; observation required
  • Cerebral hypoxia — prolonged hypoxia or hypotension
  • Cardiac arrhythmias from epinephrine in clients with CAD
  • Adverse effects of epinephrine: tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, tremor
  • Recurrence on re-exposure if allergy not documented

Nursing Interventions

  • Recognize anaphylaxis rapidly and stop exposure to the suspected trigger when possible.
  • Maintain airway, breathing, and circulation; administer IM epinephrine promptly per protocol.
  • Provide oxygen, IV fluids, bronchodilators, antihistamines, corticosteroids, and vasopressors as ordered.
  • Monitor for biphasic reaction, document timing/response, and reinforce avoidance and emergency action teaching.
Worked Example Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) Ch 15 — Misc CNS Medications · NMB section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Malignant Hyperthermia Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 15 — Misc CNS Medications

Description of Procedure

Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) — a rare, life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle calcium regulation triggered by exposure to certain anesthetic agents. Autosomal dominant inheritance (RYR1 gene mutation in most cases).

Trigger agents:

  • Volatile inhaled anesthetics: halothane, sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, enflurane
  • Succinylcholine (depolarizing NMB)

Onset: from minutes to hours after exposure. Without rapid recognition and dantrolene treatment, mortality > 70%. With prompt treatment, mortality < 5%.

Indications

  • Suspected MH crisis during or after general anesthesia
  • Sudden unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 despite increased ventilation (often the EARLIEST sign)
  • Generalized muscle rigidity (especially masseter rigidity after succinylcholine)
  • Tachycardia, hyperthermia, mixed acidosis
  • Hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis
  • Family history of MH — preventive measures
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre (prevention — for known/suspected susceptible clients):

  • Detailed pre-op history: personal/family history of MH or anesthesia complications
  • Susceptibility testing: caffeine-halothane contracture test (CHCT) or RYR1 genetic testing
  • Plan: AVOID trigger agents; use total IV anesthesia (TIVA) with propofol; non-depolarizing NMBs (vecuronium, rocuronium); flush anesthesia machine
  • Have dantrolene available and team familiar with MH protocol

Intra (active MH crisis — act IMMEDIATELY):

  1. STOP all triggering agents immediately
  2. Call for help / activate MH cart and MHAUS hotline (1-800-MH-HYPER for US)
  3. Hyperventilate with 100% oxygen at high flow rates (10–15 L/min)
  4. DANTROLENE 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus — reconstitute rapidly with sterile water; repeat every 5–10 min as needed (max 10 mg/kg)
  5. Active cooling: cool IV fluids, cooling blanket, ice packs to groin/axilla, gastric lavage with cold saline (target temp < 38°C)
  6. Treat hyperkalemia: insulin + glucose, calcium gluconate, bicarbonate, hyperventilation
  7. Treat arrhythmias per ACLS (avoid CCBs — cardiac arrest risk with dantrolene)
  8. Foley catheter; monitor urine output (rhabdo → AKI risk)
  9. Continuous ABG, electrolytes, CK monitoring
  10. ICU admission post-stabilization

Post:

  • Continue dantrolene 1 mg/kg q6h for at least 24–48 hr (recrudescence risk)
  • Document MH crisis in chart; medical alert bracelet for client
  • Refer client AND first-degree relatives for MH susceptibility testing
  • Counsel future surgery precautions (non-trigger anesthesia)
  • Report to North American MH Registry

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Temperature returns to baseline < 38°C
  • Resolution of muscle rigidity
  • Hemodynamic stability
  • Electrolytes (especially potassium) within normal range
  • Acid-base balance restored
  • No recrudescence in 48 hours
  • Client survives and avoids permanent organ damage
  • Family members tested and counseled appropriately

Client Education

  • Tell all anesthesia and surgical providers about any personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia or unexplained anesthesia reaction.
  • Wear medical alert identification for malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
  • Ask about non-triggering anesthesia plans before surgery or procedures requiring sedation.
  • Encourage family screening/genetic counseling when malignant hyperthermia susceptibility is suspected.

Potential Complications

  • Death — from arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, multi-organ failure (mortality < 5% with prompt treatment; > 70% without)
  • Hyperthermia-induced multi-organ damage — CNS, hepatic, renal injury
  • Rhabdomyolysis → acute kidney injury (massive CK elevation)
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Cerebral edema, neurologic deficits
  • Recrudescence (recurrence) — 25% within 24–48 hr; requires ongoing dantrolene
  • Compartment syndrome from rigidity
  • Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest
  • If undiagnosed in family: future relatives at risk for crisis

Nursing Interventions

  • Recognize early signs such as rising end-tidal CO2, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, acidosis, and hyperthermia.
  • Stop triggering anesthetic agents, call for help, and administer dantrolene per malignant hyperthermia protocol.
  • Cool the client, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, correct acidosis/electrolytes, and monitor urine output.
  • Prepare for ICU monitoring, repeated dantrolene dosing, complication surveillance, and family education.
Worked Example Postpartum Hemorrhage Management Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery · Stimulants section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 32 — Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery

Description of Procedure

Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) — blood loss ≥ 1,000 mL (or blood loss with signs of hypovolemia) within 24 hours of birth (primary) or up to 12 weeks (secondary). A leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide.

Causes — the “4 Ts”:

  • Tone — uterine atony (most common, ~70–80%)
  • Trauma — lacerations, hematoma, uterine rupture
  • Tissue — retained placenta/products
  • Thrombin — coagulopathy (DIC)

Indications

  • Excessive postpartum bleeding (≥ 1,000 mL or symptomatic)
  • Boggy/soft uterus that does not firm with massage (atony)
  • Continuous bright-red bleeding, passing clots
  • Signs of hypovolemia: tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, decreased LOC
  • Risk factors present: prolonged labor, oxytocin use, multiple gestation, polyhydramnios, grand multiparity, retained placenta
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Prevention/early (pre):

  • Identify risk factors antenatally and in labor
  • Active management of third stage (prophylactic oxytocin after delivery)
  • Frequent fundal and lochia assessment postpartum

If PPH occurs (intra) — act FAST:

  1. Fundal massage — first action for atony (firm up the uterus)
  2. Call for help; notify provider
  3. Establish/ensure large-bore IV access; IV fluids; type and crossmatch
  4. Uterotonic medications in sequence:
    • Oxytocin (first-line) — IV/IM
    • Methylergonovine (Methergine) — IM; contraindicated in hypertension
    • Carboprost (Hemabate) — IM; contraindicated in asthma
    • Misoprostol — rectal/oral
  5. Empty bladder (full bladder displaces uterus)
  6. Monitor vital signs, oxygen, blood loss quantification
  7. Blood transfusion if needed
  8. Prepare for procedures: bimanual compression, uterine tamponade (balloon), surgical (B-Lynch suture, artery ligation, hysterectomy)

Post:

  • Continued monitoring of fundus, lochia, vitals, urine output
  • Monitor labs (Hgb, coagulation)
  • Emotional support; debrief
  • Iron supplementation for anemia

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Bleeding controlled; uterus firm and contracted
  • Hemodynamic stability restored (stable VS, adequate urine output)
  • Hemoglobin stabilized; no further transfusion needed
  • No progression to shock, DIC, or organ failure
  • Cause identified and addressed
  • Maternal survival without major morbidity

Client Education

  • Report heavy bleeding, soaking a pad quickly, large clots, dizziness, faintness, palpitations, or increasing weakness.
  • Ask for help before ambulating if lightheaded or bleeding heavily.
  • Keep the bladder empty as instructed because bladder distention can interfere with uterine contraction.
  • Review medication effects and warning signs before discharge, including delayed heavy bleeding or fever.

Potential Complications

  • Hypovolemic shock — can be rapid and fatal
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Acute kidney injury, multi-organ failure (Sheehan syndrome — pituitary necrosis)
  • Need for emergency hysterectomy (loss of fertility)
  • Death — PPH is a leading cause of maternal mortality
  • Transfusion reactions
  • Medication contraindication errors (methylergonovine in HTN; carboprost in asthma)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess fundus, lochia, vital signs, bladder status, uterine tone, and signs of shock.
  • Massage a boggy uterus, call for help, establish/maintain IV access, and administer uterotonics as prescribed.
  • Quantify blood loss, collect labs, prepare blood products, and support escalation to procedures if bleeding continues.
  • Document interventions, response, blood loss, medications, teaching, and provider notifications.
Worked Example Chemotherapy Extravasation Ch 42 — Chemotherapy Agents · Toxicity section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Chemotherapy Extravasation Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 42 — Chemotherapy Agents

Description of Procedure

Extravasation is the inadvertent leakage of a vesicant chemotherapy drug from the vein into surrounding tissue, causing pain, tissue damage, and potentially severe necrosis, ulceration, and loss of function.

  • Vesicants (e.g., anthracyclines like doxorubicin, vinca alkaloids like vincristine) cause severe tissue damage
  • Irritants cause inflammation/pain but less tissue destruction
  • Prevention and rapid recognition are critical — damage can progress for weeks

Indications

  • Any patient receiving vesicant/irritant chemotherapy (prevention/recognition)
  • Signs during infusion: pain, burning, stinging at IV site; swelling; redness; loss of blood return; resistance to flow; leaking
  • Suspected extravasation requires immediate action
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Prevention (pre):

  • Central line (CVAD) preferred for vesicants
  • If peripheral: choose a large, intact vein (avoid hand, wrist, antecubital, areas of flexion); avoid recently used veins
  • Verify blood return before and frequently during administration
  • Stay with patient; monitor site continuously

If extravasation occurs (intra) — act immediately:

  1. STOP the infusion immediately
  2. Do NOT remove the IV catheter yet — attempt to aspirate residual drug through it
  3. Disconnect tubing; aspirate any drug/blood from the catheter
  4. Notify provider; follow agent-specific extravasation protocol
  5. Administer antidote if indicated (e.g., dexrazoxane for anthracyclines; hyaluronidase for vinca alkaloids)
  6. Apply warm or cold compress per agent (cold for most vesicants like anthracyclines; warm for vinca alkaloids)
  7. Elevate the extremity
  8. Mark and photograph the area; measure

Post:

  • Continue monitoring (tissue damage can progress over days/weeks)
  • Document time, drug, estimated volume, site, appearance, interventions, antidote
  • Wound care / plastic surgery consult if severe
  • Patient education on ongoing monitoring and signs to report

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Extravasation recognized and infusion stopped promptly
  • Appropriate antidote and compress applied
  • Minimized tissue damage; healing without necrosis/functional loss
  • Accurate documentation and follow-up
  • Patient understands monitoring and reporting

Client Education

  • Report burning, pain, swelling, redness, blistering, leaking, or tightness at the IV site immediately during chemotherapy.
  • Do not rub the site or apply heat/cold unless specifically instructed by the oncology team.
  • Keep follow-up appointments for site assessment because tissue injury can worsen after the event.
  • Report increasing pain, skin color change, ulceration, drainage, fever, or decreased movement near the site.

Potential Complications

  • Tissue necrosis, ulceration (may require debridement, skin grafting)
  • Loss of function, contractures (especially over joints)
  • Infection
  • Chronic pain
  • Delayed/progressive damage (weeks)
  • Wrong compress (warm vs cold for the specific agent) → worse outcome
  • Removing catheter before aspirating → lost chance to remove drug

Nursing Interventions

  • Stop the infusion immediately for suspected extravasation while leaving the access device in place initially.
  • Aspirate residual drug if possible and follow drug-specific antidote and compress protocols.
  • Notify provider/oncology team, photograph or mark the site per policy, and monitor tissue status closely.
  • Document drug, dose, site findings, actions, client response, teaching, and follow-up plan.
Worked Example Status Epilepticus Management Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders · Status epilepticus section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Status Epilepticus Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 13 — Chronic Neurologic Disorders

Description of Procedure

Status epilepticus (SE) — a neurologic emergency defined as a single seizure lasting ≥ 5 minutes OR two or more seizures without return to baseline consciousness between them.

Time is brain — prolonged seizures cause neuronal injury via excitotoxicity. Treatment becomes progressively harder the longer SE continues (refractory SE after 2 lines of treatment; super-refractory after > 24 hr).

The treatment ladder uses progressively stronger anticonvulsants while supporting airway, breathing, and circulation.

Indications

  • Convulsive seizure activity lasting ≥ 5 minutes
  • Recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness in between
  • Subtle or non-convulsive SE (continuous EEG seizures with altered mental status)
  • Witnessed seizure plus continued altered mental status of unclear etiology
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre / immediate during seizure:

  • Call for help / activate rapid response
  • Note time of onset and duration
  • Protect airway: position lateral (recovery position), suction secretions, suppl. O2; do NOT insert anything into mouth
  • Protect from injury: pad rails, move objects; do NOT restrain
  • Continuous monitoring: pulse ox, cardiac, BP

Intra (treatment ladder):

  1. Stage 1 (0–5 min): ABCs; check glucose (give D50W if hypoglycemic, thiamine first if alcoholic); establish IV access
  2. Stage 2 (5–20 min): First-line: IV benzodiazepine
    • Lorazepam 4 mg IV (preferred — longer duration than diazepam)
    • Or diazepam 10 mg IV
    • Or midazolam 10 mg IM if no IV access
    • May repeat once after 5 min if seizure continues
  3. Stage 3 (20–40 min): Second-line: IV antiepileptic
    • Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (preferred — no cardiac effects, no interactions)
    • Or fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (cardiac monitoring; slower infusion)
    • Or valproate 40 mg/kg IV
  4. Stage 4 (> 40 min — refractory SE): ICU admission, continuous EEG; continuous IV infusion:
    • Midazolam infusion, propofol infusion, or pentobarbital
    • Intubation often required

Post:

  • Identify underlying cause: head CT, EEG, labs (glucose, electrolytes, drug levels, toxicology, infection workup)
  • If known epilepsy: check antiepileptic levels, adherence; restart home regimen
  • If new-onset: full workup for cause (stroke, tumor, infection, metabolic)
  • Document seizure characteristics for future reference
  • Continuous EEG monitoring if persistent altered mental status
  • Education for client and family on seizure precautions and medication adherence

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Seizure terminates within 5–30 min of treatment initiation
  • Return to baseline mental status
  • Stable airway, breathing, circulation throughout
  • No injury during seizure
  • Underlying cause identified and addressed
  • Discharge with appropriate antiepileptic regimen and follow-up

Client Education

  • Use prescribed antiseizure medications consistently and avoid abrupt discontinuation.
  • Follow the seizure action plan, including when and how to use rescue medication if prescribed.
  • Call emergency services for a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, repeated seizures without recovery, injury, pregnancy, or breathing difficulty.
  • Teach family to protect from injury, turn the client to the side when safe, time the seizure, and avoid putting anything in the mouth.

Potential Complications

  • Permanent neurologic injury — from prolonged excitotoxicity (mortality 10–30% for refractory SE)
  • Respiratory depression / failure — from seizure activity AND from treatment medications; need intubation
  • Aspiration pneumonia — from impaired airway protection
  • Rhabdomyolysis from sustained motor activity → AKI
  • Cardiac arrhythmias (especially with fosphenytoin/phenytoin or hypotension)
  • Hypoglycemia (especially in children)
  • Hyperthermia from prolonged activity
  • Hypotension from benzodiazepines, propofol, or barbiturates — vasopressor support may be needed

Nursing Interventions

  • Time seizure activity, protect from injury, maintain airway, position laterally when possible, and provide oxygen/suction as needed.
  • Establish IV access, monitor glucose/vital signs, and administer benzodiazepine rescue therapy promptly per protocol.
  • Prepare second-line antiseizure medications and escalation to airway support or ICU care if seizures continue.
  • Document onset, duration, medications, response, neurologic status, triggers, and client/family teaching.
Worked Example Alcohol Withdrawal Management (CIWA-Ar) Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders · Alcohol section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Alcohol Withdrawal Management (CIWA-Ar Protocol)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 12 — Substance Use Disorders

Description of Procedure

Management of alcohol withdrawal syndrome using the CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) protocol — a symptom-triggered or scheduled dosing approach to prevent and treat alcohol withdrawal.

CIWA-Ar is a 10-item scale (max score 67) assessing: nausea/vomiting, tremor, sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile/auditory/visual disturbances, headache, orientation. Scores guide benzodiazepine dosing.

  • < 10: mild withdrawal — supportive care only
  • 10–19: moderate — symptom-triggered benzo dosing
  • ≥ 20: severe — aggressive treatment, ICU consideration, scheduled benzo dosing

Indications

  • Hospitalized client with history of heavy alcohol use and stopping/reducing intake
  • Last drink within ~6–48 hours (withdrawal onset)
  • Symptoms: tremor, anxiety, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis)
  • Prevention of progression to seizures, delirium tremens (DTs), Wernicke encephalopathy
  • Planned detoxification before rehabilitation
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre (assessment):

  • Alcohol use history: amount, frequency, last drink time, prior withdrawal history (seizures, DTs)
  • Baseline vital signs, mental status
  • Labs: CBC, BMP, magnesium, phosphate, LFTs, ammonia, urine drug screen
  • Assess for Wernicke risk: nystagmus, ataxia, confusion
  • Administer thiamine 100 mg IV/IM BEFORE giving any glucose (prevents Wernicke); also folate, multivitamin

Intra (treatment per CIWA-Ar):

  • Assess CIWA-Ar every 1–4 hours; more frequently if score increasing
  • Benzodiazepines first-line: chlordiazepoxide (long-acting, smooth taper) or lorazepam (preferred in liver disease — not metabolized by liver)
  • Symptom-triggered: give benzo dose when CIWA ≥ 8–10; reassess in 1 hr
  • Adjunct: alpha-2 agonist (clonidine, dexmedetomidine) for autonomic symptoms; antipsychotic (haloperidol) for hallucinations (NOT instead of benzos)
  • Hydration with IV fluids if dehydrated; correct electrolytes (especially magnesium)
  • Monitor for seizures (peak 24–48 hr); DTs (peak 48–96 hr): severe agitation, hallucinations, autonomic instability
  • Maintain quiet environment; orient frequently

Post:

  • Transition to outpatient: motivational interviewing, referral to AA/treatment program
  • Maintenance medications: naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram
  • Address underlying co-occurring mental health, social issues
  • Family/support involvement

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • CIWA-Ar score decreases over 48–72 hours
  • No seizures, DTs, or Wernicke encephalopathy
  • Stable vital signs return to baseline
  • Client tolerates oral intake; electrolytes normalize
  • Engagement in continued treatment plan
  • Safe transition to outpatient or rehab setting

Client Education

  • Do not stop heavy alcohol use abruptly without medical guidance because withdrawal can cause seizures or delirium tremens.
  • Report tremors, sweating, anxiety, hallucinations, fever, confusion, vomiting, or seizure activity immediately.
  • Take prescribed withdrawal medications only as directed and avoid alcohol or other sedatives with them.
  • Engage support resources such as detoxification services, counseling, relapse-prevention treatment, and follow-up care.

Potential Complications

  • Withdrawal seizures — typically tonic-clonic, single or in flurries; peak 12–48 hr; require IV benzo
  • Delirium Tremens (DTs) — severe withdrawal: confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability, fever; mortality 5–15% without treatment; peak 48–96 hr
  • Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency) — triad: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; can progress to permanent Korsakoff psychosis
  • Aspiration pneumonia from altered mental status
  • Trauma from falls during agitation/confusion
  • Cardiac arrhythmias from electrolyte imbalance and autonomic surges
  • Hypoglycemia, especially if thiamine delayed
  • Over-sedation from benzodiazepines (respiratory depression)

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess withdrawal severity using CIWA-Ar or ordered protocol and monitor vital signs, orientation, hydration, and seizure risk.
  • Administer benzodiazepines, thiamine, fluids, electrolytes, nutrition, and symptom medications as prescribed.
  • Maintain seizure/fall precautions, reduce stimulation, and escalate rapidly for delirium tremens or unstable vital signs.
  • Document scores, medication response, safety measures, teaching, and referral planning.
Worked Example Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products · Reactions section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure
Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction Management
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products

Description of Procedure

Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) is a life-threatening emergency caused by ABO incompatibility — recipient antibodies attack and destroy transfused donor RBCs.

Usually results from clerical/identification error (wrong blood to wrong patient). Onset is rapid — often within the first 15 minutes, which is why nurses stay with the client during the initial phase.

Can rapidly progress to shock, DIC, acute kidney injury, and death.

Indications

  • Any client receiving a blood transfusion (recognition)
  • Sudden fever, chills, flank/back pain during transfusion
  • Hypotension, tachycardia, sense of impending doom
  • Dark/red urine (hemoglobinuria)
  • Chest pain, dyspnea
  • Oozing from IV site (DIC)
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Prevention (pre):

  • Meticulous two-person bedside verification of client identity and blood compatibility
  • Use two patient identifiers
  • Stay with client during first 15 minutes; baseline and frequent vital signs

If reaction occurs (intra) — act IMMEDIATELY:

  1. STOP the transfusion immediately
  2. Keep the IV line open with 0.9% normal saline using NEW tubing (do not flush remaining blood into client)
  3. Stay with client; notify provider and blood bank STAT
  4. Recheck identification of client and blood product (verify clerical error)
  5. Monitor vital signs frequently; assess for shock
  6. Maintain airway, oxygen, prepare for emergency support
  7. Administer ordered medications: IV fluids (maintain BP/renal perfusion), diuretics (maintain urine output), vasopressors if needed
  8. Insert/monitor indwelling catheter; monitor urine output and color
  9. Send blood bag, tubing, and blood/urine samples to lab per protocol
  10. Treat DIC if it develops

Post:

  • Continuous monitoring (ICU if severe)
  • Monitor renal function (AKI from hemoglobin), coagulation (DIC)
  • Complete transfusion reaction report and incident documentation
  • Investigate root cause (clerical error)
  • Update records to prevent recurrence

Outcomes/Evaluation

  • Transfusion stopped promptly at first signs
  • Hemodynamic stability restored
  • Adequate urine output maintained (renal protection)
  • No progression to DIC, renal failure, or death
  • Root cause identified; system error corrected
  • Accurate documentation and reporting completed

Client Education

  • Report fever, chills, back or flank pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, anxiety, itching, rash, dark urine, or feeling suddenly unwell during transfusion.
  • Expect the nurse to stop the transfusion and continue monitoring if a reaction is suspected.
  • Report delayed fever, jaundice, dark urine, back pain, or unusual fatigue after a transfusion.
  • Tell healthcare providers about any previous transfusion reaction before future transfusions.

Potential Complications

  • Shock and cardiovascular collapse
  • Acute kidney injury — free hemoglobin damages renal tubules
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Death — AHTR has significant mortality
  • Multi-organ failure
  • Hyperkalemia (from cell lysis)
  • If transfusion not stopped promptly — outcomes worsen dramatically

Nursing Interventions

  • Stop the transfusion immediately at first signs of acute hemolytic reaction and keep IV access open with normal saline using new tubing.
  • Notify provider and blood bank, recheck client/product identification, and send required blood product, tubing, blood, and urine specimens.
  • Monitor airway, vital signs, urine output, renal function, coagulation, and signs of shock or DIC.
  • Document reaction findings, timing, interventions, client response, reporting, and prevention steps.

Worked Example Medication Adherence Concept spans Ch 1 (Pharmacokinetics & Routes), Ch 2 (Individual Considerations), and every drug-class chapter · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Medication Adherence

Defining Characteristics

The extent to which a person takes medication as prescribed — correct dose, correct interval, correct duration. Distinguished from the older term "compliance" — adherence emphasizes the patient as an active partner in the therapeutic plan.

Two complementary domains:

  • Initiation — filling the prescription and starting the medication
  • Persistence — continuing the medication as prescribed over time

Estimated at ~50% globally for chronic-disease medications — a major modifiable contributor to treatment failure.

Antecedents

  • Understanding of the indication and expected benefit
  • Manageable regimen — fewer pills, fewer daily doses, simpler timing
  • Affordability — cost is a major modifiable antecedent
  • Tolerable side effects
  • Trust in the prescriber and therapeutic relationship
  • Health literacy and language access
  • Social support, reminders, pill organizers
  • Stable housing, food, and routine

Negative Consequences

  • Treatment failure and disease progression
  • Antimicrobial resistance when antibiotic courses are not completed
  • Withdrawal or rebound with abrupt discontinuation (e.g., SSRIs, beta-blockers, benzodiazepines, opioids)
  • Avoidable hospitalization and mortality
  • Wasted medications and rising healthcare cost
  • "Diagnostic creep" — prescribers add more medications to address apparent treatment failure, when the underlying issue is non-adherence — masking and worsening polypharmacy

Related Concepts

  • Health literacy, language access, affordability, therapeutic relationship, and shared decision-making all influence whether the client can start and continue therapy.
  • Pill burden, regimen complexity, reminders, pill organizers, and simplified dosing connect adherence to practical medication-management planning.
  • Polypharmacy, deprescribing, side effects, withdrawal or rebound effects, and medication reconciliation help explain why clients may stop or change therapy.
  • Antimicrobial stewardship is related because incomplete antibiotic courses can contribute to treatment failure and resistance.

Exemplars

  • Positive (system-level): client uses a 7-day pill organizer and smartphone reminder; prescriber selects an affordable generic; nurse simplifies the regimen to once-daily where pharmacokinetically possible
