  • Acute kidney injury
  • Death without treatment

Related Concepts

NAPQI metabolite, glutathione, Rumack-Matthew nomogram, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), liver function tests, INR/coagulopathy, combination products, hepatic failure, activated charcoal, maximum daily dose.

Exemplars

  • Mechanism: NAPQI (toxic metabolite) is normally neutralized by glutathione. Overdose depletes glutathione → NAPQI damages liver. NAC replenishes glutathione and binds NAPQI.
  • Rumack-Matthew nomogram: plots serum acetaminophen level vs time since ingestion (use level drawn ≥ 4 hr post-ingestion) to determine NAC need.
  • N-acetylcysteine (NAC): most effective within 8–10 hours of ingestion; still beneficial later. Oral (rotten-egg smell/taste — may cause nausea; dilute) or IV (anaphylactoid reactions possible).
  • Acute overdose management: activated charcoal if within ~1–2 hr; draw acetaminophen level at 4 hr; plot on nomogram; start NAC if indicated (do not delay if presentation late or level pending in massive ingestion).
  • Monitoring: serial LFTs, INR, renal function, mental status.
  • Prevention/teaching: never exceed 4 g/day (less with liver risk/alcohol); read labels for hidden acetaminophen in combination products; limit alcohol; report dark urine, jaundice, RUQ pain.
  • Chronic toxicity can occur from repeated supratherapeutic dosing, not just single overdose.
Worked Example NSAID Therapy & GI/Renal Risk Ch 35 — Non-Opioid Analgesics · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
NSAID Therapy & GI/Renal Risk

Defining Characteristics

NSAID therapy uses nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac, aspirin, celecoxib) for anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects by inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes.

  • COX-1: protective (gastric mucosa, platelets, renal flow)
  • COX-2: inflammation/pain
  • Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both → efficacy + GI/renal/bleeding risks
  • COX-2 selective (celecoxib) → less GI risk but cardiovascular concerns

Antecedents

  • Pain, inflammation, fever requiring treatment
  • Chronic conditions: arthritis, musculoskeletal pain
  • Risk factors for complications: older age, history of GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, heart failure, dehydration, concurrent anticoagulants/corticosteroids
  • Long-term or high-dose use
  • OTC availability → unmonitored use

Negative Consequences

  • GI: dyspepsia, peptic ulcers, GI bleeding/perforation (reduced protective prostaglandins)
  • Renal: acute kidney injury, sodium/water retention, hyperkalemia (reduced renal prostaglandins, decreased perfusion); worsens HF and HTN
  • Cardiovascular: increased MI/stroke risk (BLACK BOX, especially with prolonged use; not low-dose aspirin)
  • Bleeding: platelet inhibition (aspirin irreversible; others reversible)
  • Hypersensitivity (especially aspirin — asthma/nasal polyps triad)
  • Masking of fever/infection signs

Related Concepts

COX-1/COX-2, prostaglandins, peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding, acute kidney injury, platelet aggregation, anticoagulants, proton pump inhibitors (gastroprotection), Reye syndrome (aspirin in children), heart failure, hyperkalemia, Samter’s triad.

Exemplars

  • GI protection: high-risk clients on NSAIDs → add a PPI; take NSAIDs with food; use lowest effective dose for shortest time.
  • Renal caution: avoid NSAIDs in CKD, HF, dehydration, and with ACE inhibitors/ARBs + diuretics (“triple whammy” → AKI). Monitor renal function and BP.
  • Bleeding: hold NSAIDs before surgery; caution with warfarin/anticoagulants/corticosteroids (additive bleed risk); aspirin’s antiplatelet effect lasts the platelet lifespan (~7–10 days).
  • Ketorolac: potent; limit to ≤ 5 days (high GI/renal risk).
  • Aspirin + children: avoid with viral illness/fever (Reye syndrome).
  • Cardiovascular: NSAIDs (except aspirin) increase CV events; avoid/limit in heart disease; naproxen may have lower CV risk.
  • Patient teaching: take with food, report black/tarry stools, abdominal pain, decreased urine output, swelling, weight gain; avoid combining NSAIDs; limit alcohol; tell providers before surgery; know hidden NSAID content.
  • Monitoring: renal function, BP, signs of GI bleeding (Hgb, stool), edema.
Worked Example Opioid Toxicity & Reversal Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Opioid Toxicity & Reversal

Defining Characteristics

Opioid toxicity (overdose) is potentially fatal CNS and respiratory depression from excessive opioid effect.

Classic toxidrome triad:

  • Respiratory depression (the lethal feature — decreased rate/depth)
  • CNS depression / coma (decreased LOC, sedation)
  • Miosis (pinpoint pupils)

Other: hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia, decreased bowel sounds. Antidote: naloxone (Narcan) — competitive opioid antagonist.

Antecedents

  • Accidental or intentional overdose
  • Opioid-naive patients given too high a dose
  • Combining opioids with CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol)
  • Renal/hepatic impairment (accumulation)
  • Loss of tolerance (after abstinence/incarceration/rehab) then resuming prior dose
  • Potent illicit opioids (fentanyl analogs)
  • Dosing/route errors (e.g., crushing ER for IV)

Negative Consequences

  • Respiratory arrest and death (primary cause of opioid death)
  • Hypoxic brain injury
  • Aspiration pneumonia
  • Cardiac arrest
  • If reversed too aggressively: acute withdrawal (agitation, pain, hypertension, tachycardia, vomiting) and loss of needed analgesia
  • Re-sedation when naloxone wears off (shorter half-life than many opioids)

Related Concepts

Naloxone (Narcan), mu-opioid receptor, respiratory depression, sedation scales (POSS), capnography, opioid withdrawal, half-life mismatch, harm reduction, take-home naloxone, CNS depressant interactions.

Exemplars

  • Recognition: unresponsive patient with RR < 8–10, pinpoint pupils, after opioid use → suspect overdose.
  • Immediate care: support airway/ventilation (bag-mask, oxygen), call for help, administer naloxone (IV, IM, SC, or intranasal); repeat every 2–3 min as needed.
  • Naloxone titration: in a hospitalized patient on opioids for pain, titrate carefully (dilute, small increments) to restore breathing WITHOUT precipitating severe withdrawal/pain; in pure overdose, prioritize reversing respiratory depression.
  • Re-sedation risk: naloxone’s duration (~30–90 min) is often SHORTER than the opioid → monitor closely; repeat doses or infusion may be needed (especially long-acting opioids, fentanyl).
  • Monitoring: continuous respiratory rate, SpO2, capnography, sedation level, LOC.
  • Prevention: sedation/respiratory assessment with opioids, avoid concurrent CNS depressants, use lowest effective dose, take-home naloxone for high-risk patients, patient/family education.
  • Withdrawal after reversal: manage symptoms supportively; balance is reversing toxicity vs comfort.
Worked Example Opioid-Induced Constipation Management Ch 36 — Opioid Agonists and Antagonists · Overview section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Opioid-Induced Constipation Management

Defining Characteristics

Opioid-induced constipation (OIC) is the most common and persistent opioid side effect, caused by opioid action on mu-receptors in the GI tract.

  • Reduced peristalsis, increased fluid absorption, increased sphincter tone → hard, infrequent stools
  • Tolerance does NOT develop — persists for the duration of opioid therapy (unlike sedation/respiratory depression)
  • Affects most patients on chronic opioids
  • Requires PROACTIVE (prophylactic) management, not just treatment

Antecedents

  • Any opioid therapy (acute or chronic)
  • Higher doses, longer duration
  • Reduced mobility, dehydration, low-fiber diet
  • Older age
  • Concurrent anticholinergics, other constipating drugs
  • Pre-existing constipation or GI disorders

Negative Consequences

  • Abdominal pain, bloating, distension
  • Fecal impaction
  • Bowel obstruction (severe)
  • Hemorrhoids, anal fissures (straining)
  • Nausea, decreased appetite
  • Reduced quality of life; some patients reduce/stop needed pain medication
  • Increased healthcare utilization

Related Concepts

Mu-opioid receptors, peristalsis, stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl), osmotic laxatives (PEG), stool softeners (docusate), PAMORAs (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol), bowel regimen, fecal impaction, fluid/fiber intake, mobility.

Exemplars

  • Prophylactic bowel regimen (KEY): start a stimulant laxative (senna, bisacodyl) at the same time opioids begin — do not wait for constipation. A stool softener (docusate) alone is often insufficient.
  • Stepwise approach: stimulant laxative +/- osmotic (PEG/MiraLAX) → if inadequate, add/escalate → if refractory, a PAMORA (peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist: methylnaltrexone, naloxegol) that blocks GI opioid effects without reversing analgesia.
  • Non-pharm: increase fluids, dietary fiber (if appropriate), mobility/ambulation, privacy and routine for toileting.
  • Avoid bulk-forming laxatives (psyllium) alone in OIC if fluid intake is low or motility severely reduced — can worsen impaction.
  • Assessment: establish baseline bowel pattern; monitor frequency, consistency, distension, bowel sounds; assess for impaction.
  • Patient teaching: expect constipation; take the bowel regimen proactively (not PRN only); report no bowel movement in 3 days, severe pain, or distension; maintain fluids, fiber, and activity.
  • Distinguish: OIC management differs from naloxone reversal — PAMORAs treat constipation without reversing pain relief.
Worked Example Hypoglycemia & Glucagon Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · Injectable section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Hypoglycemia & Glucagon

Defining Characteristics

Hypoglycemia — abnormally low blood glucose (typically < 70 mg/dL), a common and potentially dangerous complication of diabetes treatment.

Signs (adrenergic + neuroglycopenic):

  • Early (adrenergic): shakiness, sweating, tachycardia, palpitations, hunger, anxiety, tremor
  • Neuroglycopenic: confusion, difficulty concentrating, slurred speech, irritability, blurred vision
  • Severe: seizures, loss of consciousness, coma

Hypoglycemia unawareness can occur (especially long-standing diabetes, beta blockers mask symptoms).

Antecedents

  • Too much insulin or oral hypoglycemic (especially sulfonylureas)
  • Skipped/delayed meals or inadequate carbohydrate intake
  • Increased physical activity without dose/food adjustment
  • Alcohol consumption (impairs gluconeogenesis)
  • Renal/hepatic impairment (reduced drug clearance)
  • Incorrect insulin timing or dosing error
  • Beta blockers (mask symptoms)

Negative Consequences

  • Seizures, coma
  • Falls and injury
  • Brain injury or death if severe/prolonged (brain depends on glucose)
  • Cardiac arrhythmias
  • Hypoglycemia unawareness with recurrent episodes
  • Fear of hypoglycemia → poor glycemic control (overcompensation)

Related Concepts

  • The Rule of 15, fast-acting carbohydrate, repeat glucose checks, complex carbohydrate/protein follow-up snack, and prevention of recurrence guide care for conscious clients.
  • Glucagon, IV dextrose, aspiration precautions, unconsciousness, seizures, coma, and emergency response guide care for severe hypoglycemia.
  • Insulin, sulfonylureas, skipped meals, exercise, alcohol use, renal/hepatic impairment, and dosing errors are common antecedents nurses assess.
  • Neuroglycopenic symptoms, adrenergic symptoms, beta blocker masking, hypoglycemia unawareness, sick-day management, and client teaching support early recognition and prevention.

Exemplars

  • Rule of 15 (conscious, able to swallow): give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (4 oz juice/regular soda, glucose tablets, 1 tbsp honey) → recheck glucose in 15 min → repeat if still < 70 → once normalized, give a complex carb/protein snack to prevent recurrence.
  • Severe (unconscious or cannot swallow): do NOT give oral anything (aspiration). Give glucagon (IM, SC, or intranasal) OR IV dextrose (D50) if IV access; position on side; call for help.
  • Glucagon: raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis; may cause nausea/vomiting (position on side); less effective if glycogen stores depleted (malnutrition, alcohol, prolonged fasting).
  • After glucagon: patient may vomit; give carbohydrate when alert and able to swallow; monitor (glucose may drop again).
  • Prevention: consistent meals, adjust insulin for activity, monitor glucose, limit alcohol, recognize early symptoms, carry fast carbs and glucagon, family education.
  • Hospital: IV D50 for severe hypoglycemia with IV access; recheck and treat cause.
  • Teaching: family/caregivers learn to administer glucagon; never give oral glucose to an unconscious person.
Worked Example Insulin Therapy (Onset / Peak / Duration) Ch 39 — Diabetes Mellitus · Insulin section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Insulin Therapy (Onset / Peak / Duration)

Defining Characteristics

Insulin therapy replaces or supplements insulin to control blood glucose. Insulins are classified by onset, peak, and duration — understanding the time-action profile is critical for timing, hypoglycemia prevention, and meal coordination.

  • Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart, glulisine): onset ~15 min, peak ~1 hr, duration 3–5 hr — give with meals
  • Short-acting (Regular): onset ~30 min, peak 2–3 hr, duration 5–8 hr — give 30 min before meals; ONLY insulin given IV
  • Intermediate (NPH): onset 1–2 hr, peak 4–12 hr, duration 12–18 hr; cloudy
  • Long-acting (glargine, detemir): onset ~1–2 hr, no pronounced peak, duration ~24 hr; do NOT mix

Antecedents

  • Type 1 diabetes (required)
  • Type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by oral agents
  • Gestational diabetes
  • DKA/HHS (IV regular insulin)
  • Hyperkalemia (insulin + dextrose to shift potassium)
  • Acute illness/stress hyperglycemia

Negative Consequences

  • Hypoglycemia — especially at the insulin’s PEAK time (know when to watch)
  • Hyperglycemia/DKA if dose missed or insufficient
  • Dosing/timing errors (high-alert medication)
  • Lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy at injection sites (poor rotation)
  • Weight gain
  • Errors from mixing incompatible insulins or wrong concentration

Related Concepts

Onset/peak/duration, basal-bolus regimen, sliding scale, insulin mixing (“clear before cloudy”), high-alert medication, site rotation, U-100/U-500 concentration, hypoglycemia, DKA, carbohydrate counting.

Exemplars

  • Peak = hypoglycemia risk window: teach patients when each insulin peaks so they can recognize/prevent lows (e.g., NPH peaks 4–12 hr → watch mid-afternoon if given at breakfast).
  • Mixing NPH + Regular: draw up clear (Regular) before cloudy (NPH) — “RN” / “clear before cloudy” — to avoid contaminating the rapid vial.
  • Do NOT mix long-acting (glargine, detemir) with other insulins.
  • Only Regular insulin is given IV (DKA, hyperkalemia).
  • Rapid-acting: give right before/with meals (onset ~15 min) — ensure food is available to avoid hypoglycemia.
  • Site rotation: rotate within and between sites (abdomen fastest absorption) to prevent lipohypertrophy.
  • High-alert safety: independent double-check for insulin doses; use insulin-specific syringes; never use “U” abbreviation (write “units”); verify concentration.
  • Storage: unopened insulin refrigerated; in-use vials/pens room temperature ~28 days; do not freeze; roll (don’t shake) cloudy insulin.
  • Nursing assessment: verify type, dose, timing relative to meals; monitor glucose; assess injection sites; educate on time-action profile.
Worked Example Vancomycin Therapy & Monitoring Ch 44 — Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Vancomycin Therapy & Monitoring

Defining Characteristics

Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, used for serious gram-positive infections, notably MRSA. It has a narrow therapeutic index requiring monitoring.

  • IV for systemic infections (MRSA, serious gram-positive)
  • Oral vancomycin is NOT absorbed systemically — used specifically for C. difficile colitis (acts locally in gut)
  • Requires trough level monitoring for efficacy and toxicity

Antecedents

  • MRSA or serious gram-positive infection
  • Beta-lactam allergy requiring alternative for gram-positives
  • C. difficile colitis (oral form)
  • Renal impairment (affects dosing — renally cleared)
  • Older age, concurrent nephrotoxic/ototoxic drugs

Negative Consequences

  • Nephrotoxicity — especially with high troughs, prolonged therapy, other nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides)
  • Ototoxicity — hearing loss, tinnitus (high levels)
  • “Red man syndrome” — flushing, erythema of face/neck/torso from rapid infusion (histamine release; NOT a true allergy)
  • Thrombophlebitis at IV site
  • Subtherapeutic levels → treatment failure/resistance (VRE)
  • Hypersensitivity reactions

Related Concepts

  • Therapeutic drug monitoring, trough timing, renal clearance, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, infusion-rate safety, and MRSA coverage are central to IV vancomycin therapy.
  • Oral vancomycin, C. difficile colitis, poor systemic absorption, and IV-versus-PO route selection are key concepts because route determines therapeutic site.
  • Red man syndrome, phlebitis, hypersensitivity, antimicrobial resistance, VRE, and concurrent nephrotoxic medications shape nursing monitoring and teaching.
  • Culture results, renal function, dose adjustment, infusion duration, and completion of therapy connect vancomycin monitoring to antimicrobial stewardship.

Exemplars

  • Trough monitoring: draw the trough level just before the next dose; used to guide dosing for efficacy (adequate level for MRSA) and to avoid toxicity. Adjust dose based on trough and renal function.
  • Red man syndrome prevention: infuse slowly (over at least 60 minutes); if flushing occurs, stop/slow the infusion, give antihistamine, then resume slower. Distinguish from true allergy.
  • Nephrotoxicity monitoring: baseline and periodic BUN/creatinine; monitor urine output; caution with other nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, NSAIDs).
  • Ototoxicity: assess for hearing changes, tinnitus, vertigo — report.
  • Oral vs IV: use ORAL vancomycin for C. difficile (stays in gut); IV vancomycin does NOT treat C. diff. Conversely, oral does not treat systemic infection.
  • IV site care: assess for phlebitis; central line for prolonged therapy.
  • Patient teaching: report flushing/itching during infusion, hearing changes, decreased urination; the importance of blood-level monitoring; complete therapy.
  • Nursing role: ensure correct infusion rate, draw troughs at correct time, monitor renal function and levels, recognize red man syndrome vs allergy.
Worked Example Aminoglycoside Toxicity Monitoring Ch 45 — Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis · Other section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Aminoglycoside Toxicity Monitoring

Defining Characteristics

Aminoglycoside toxicity monitoring is essential because aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) have a narrow therapeutic index with serious, dose-related toxicities.

Two signature toxicities:

  • Nephrotoxicity — usually reversible; from drug accumulation in renal tubules
  • Ototoxicity — often IRREVERSIBLE; cochlear (hearing) and vestibular (balance) damage

Serum peak (efficacy) and trough (safety) levels guide dosing.

Antecedents

  • Aminoglycoside therapy for serious gram-negative infection
  • Renal impairment (reduced clearance → accumulation)
  • Prolonged therapy or high doses
  • Dehydration
  • Older age
  • Concurrent nephrotoxic (vancomycin, NSAIDs, contrast) or ototoxic (loop diuretics) drugs
  • Pre-existing hearing/vestibular impairment

Negative Consequences

  • Permanent hearing loss / deafness (cochlear ototoxicity)
  • Vestibular damage — vertigo, ataxia, balance problems, fall risk
  • Acute kidney injury (usually reversible if caught early)
  • Treatment failure if subtherapeutic peaks
  • Toxicity if elevated troughs
  • Neuromuscular blockade (rare; respiratory)

Related Concepts

Peak and trough levels, narrow therapeutic index, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity (cochlear/vestibular), therapeutic drug monitoring, extended-interval dosing, creatinine clearance, additive toxicity, fall prevention.

Exemplars

  • Peak level: drawn ~30 min after the IV infusion completes — reflects efficacy (must be high enough to kill the organism).
  • Trough level: drawn just before the next dose — reflects clearance/safety (must be LOW enough to avoid toxicity). Elevated trough = toxicity risk → hold/adjust dose.
  • Renal monitoring: baseline and regular BUN/creatinine, urine output, I&O, daily weights; rising creatinine signals nephrotoxicity → notify provider.
  • Ototoxicity monitoring: assess hearing (tinnitus, decreased hearing) and vestibular function (vertigo, ataxia, nystagmus); baseline audiometry for prolonged therapy; report changes immediately (may be permanent).
  • Reduce risk: ensure hydration, avoid concurrent nephro/ototoxic drugs, dose by renal function, limit duration.
  • Extended-interval (once-daily) dosing: uses concentration-dependent killing and post-antibiotic effect; may reduce toxicity; uses different level monitoring.
  • Fall precautions if vestibular effects occur.
  • Nursing role: draw levels at the correct times, hold dose if trough elevated and notify provider, monitor renal and auditory/vestibular status, educate patient to report hearing/balance changes.
Worked Example Fluoroquinolone Black Box Warnings Ch 46 — Urinary Tract Infections · Urinary section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Fluoroquinolone Black Box Warnings

Defining Characteristics

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are broad-spectrum antibiotics carrying multiple FDA black box warnings for serious, sometimes permanent or disabling adverse effects.

Because of these risks, the FDA recommends reserving them for serious infections when no alternative exists — NOT first-line for uncomplicated UTI, sinusitis, or bronchitis.

Antecedents

  • Prescription of a fluoroquinolone (oral or IV)
  • Risk factors: older age (> 60), corticosteroid use, organ transplant, renal impairment
  • Concurrent QT-prolonging drugs
  • Diabetes (dysglycemia)
  • Myasthenia gravis (exacerbation)
  • Strenuous physical activity (tendon stress)

Negative Consequences

  • Tendinitis and tendon rupture (especially Achilles) — can occur during or months after therapy
  • Peripheral neuropathy — can be irreversible/permanent
  • CNS effects — seizures, confusion, hallucinations, psychosis; myasthenia gravis exacerbation (can cause respiratory failure)
  • QT prolongation → torsades, sudden death
  • Aortic aneurysm/dissection
  • Dysglycemia (severe hypo- or hyperglycemia)
  • C. difficile, photosensitivity

Related Concepts

Black box warning, Achilles tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, QT prolongation, myasthenia gravis, aortic aneurysm, antimicrobial stewardship, chelation (drug-mineral interactions), photosensitivity.

Exemplars

  • Tendon rupture teaching: instruct patient to stop the drug and report immediately any tendon pain, swelling, or inflammation (commonly Achilles); avoid strenuous activity; higher risk in older adults and those on corticosteroids.
  • Peripheral neuropathy: report numbness, tingling, burning, weakness promptly — may be permanent; discontinue.
  • CNS/seizure: caution in seizure history; avoid with NSAIDs (lower seizure threshold); avoid in myasthenia gravis (can precipitate severe weakness/respiratory failure).
  • QT prolongation: review concurrent QT drugs; caution with electrolyte abnormalities; monitor at-risk patients.
  • Dysglycemia: diabetics should monitor glucose closely (both hypo- and hyperglycemia reported).
  • Aortic risk: caution in older adults, hypertension, known aneurysm; report sudden severe chest/back/abdominal pain.
  • Stewardship: reserve for serious infections; not first-line for uncomplicated UTI/sinusitis/bronchitis given the risk profile.
  • Nursing role: educate on warning signs, assess risk factors, avoid in contraindicated patients, monitor for the specific toxicities.
Worked Example Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) Ch 48 — Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS · HIV section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART)

Defining Characteristics

Antiretroviral therapy (ART/HAART) uses combinations of drugs targeting different steps of the HIV life cycle to suppress viral replication, preserve immune function, and prevent transmission.

Major classes:

  • NRTIs (zidovudine, tenofovir, emtricitabine) — block reverse transcriptase
  • NNRTIs (efavirenz) — bind reverse transcriptase differently
  • Protease inhibitors (-navir; ritonavir) — block protease enzyme
  • Integrase inhibitors (-tegravir; dolutegravir) — block integration
  • Entry/fusion inhibitors and CCR5 antagonists

Typically ≥ 3 drugs from ≥ 2 classes (combination = HAART).

Antecedents

  • HIV diagnosis (ART recommended for ALL, regardless of CD4)
  • Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in high-risk individuals
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after exposure
  • Prevention of perinatal transmission (pregnancy)
  • Need to suppress viral load and preserve CD4 count

Negative Consequences

  • Resistance if adherence is poor (missed doses → resistant virus → treatment failure)
  • Class-specific toxicities: lactic acidosis/lipodystrophy (NRTIs), rash/CNS (NNRTIs), metabolic effects/hyperlipidemia (PIs), hepatotoxicity
  • Numerous drug interactions (especially PIs/NNRTIs — CYP)
  • Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)
  • Without effective ART: progression to AIDS, opportunistic infections, death

Related Concepts

HIV life cycle, CD4 count, viral load, drug resistance, adherence, HAART, PrEP/PEP, perinatal transmission, opportunistic infections, IRIS, U=U (undetectable = untransmittable), CYP interactions.

Exemplars

  • Adherence is critical: strict, consistent adherence (often described as needing very high adherence) prevents resistance; missed doses allow the virus to mutate. Emphasize in all teaching.
  • U=U: sustained undetectable viral load means the virus is not sexually transmissible — major motivation for adherence.
  • Monitoring: CD4 count (immune status) and viral load (treatment response); goal is undetectable viral load and rising/stable CD4.
  • Drug interactions: protease inhibitors and NNRTIs have extensive CYP interactions — review ALL medications (including OTC/herbal, e.g., St. John’s wort reduces levels).
  • Perinatal prevention: ART during pregnancy + intrapartum + neonatal prophylaxis (e.g., zidovudine) dramatically reduces mother-to-child transmission.
  • PrEP/PEP: PrEP (daily tenofovir/emtricitabine) for prevention in high-risk; PEP started ASAP (within 72 hr) after exposure for 28 days.
  • Nursing role: intensive adherence counseling, monitor CD4/viral load and toxicities, screen interactions, support coping, prevent/treat opportunistic infections, address stigma.
  • Patient teaching: take every dose on schedule, do not stop, report side effects rather than self-discontinuing, keep all appointments and labs.
Worked Example Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · First-gen section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)

Defining Characteristics

Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) is a rare but life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotic medications (or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medications).

Classic tetrad:

  • Fever (hyperthermia, often > 38°C / 100.4°F — can exceed 41°C)
  • Encephalopathy / altered mental status (confusion, stupor, coma)
  • Vitals unstable / autonomic instability (BP fluctuations, tachycardia, diaphoresis)
  • Elevated enzymes / muscle rigidity (“lead pipe” rigidity, elevated CK, rhabdomyolysis)

Mnemonic: FEVER — Fever, Encephalopathy, Vitals unstable, Elevated enzymes, Rigidity.

Onset is typically within hours to days of starting or increasing antipsychotic; can occur at any point.

Antecedents

  • Initiation or dose increase of any antipsychotic (more common with typicals like haloperidol, but ALL antipsychotics can cause NMS)
  • High-potency dopamine receptor antagonists
  • Long-acting injectable antipsychotics
  • Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medications (levodopa, dopamine agonists in Parkinson’s)
  • Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance (hyponatremia)
  • Concurrent illness, agitation, restraint use
  • Genetic predisposition (probable)
  • Previous episode of NMS (recurrence risk)

Negative Consequences

  • Death — mortality 5–20% even with treatment
  • Rhabdomyolysis → acute kidney injury
  • Aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary embolism
  • Hyperthermia-related multi-organ damage
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Permanent neurological deficits
  • Need for ICU admission, mechanical ventilation
  • Future need for non-antipsychotic alternatives to manage psychosis

Related Concepts

Serotonin syndrome (differential), malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic toxicity, antipsychotic medications (typical and atypical), dopamine agonists, dantrolene, bromocriptine, supportive care, hyperthermia management, rhabdomyolysis.

Exemplars

  • Classic case: Client started on haloperidol IM 2 days ago presents with temp 39.5°C, BP 180/110, HR 130, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, sweating, CK 25,000. Diagnosis: NMS.
  • Treatment:
    • (1) STOP the antipsychotic IMMEDIATELY
    • (2) Aggressive cooling (cooling blanket, ice packs, IV fluids)
    • (3) IV hydration to prevent renal failure from rhabdomyolysis
    • (4) Dantrolene — muscle relaxant (also used in malignant hyperthermia)
    • (5) Bromocriptine — dopamine agonist to counteract D2 blockade
    • (6) Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) for agitation
    • (7) ICU admission; mechanical ventilation if needed
    • (8) Monitor CK, renal function, electrolytes
  • Differential from serotonin syndrome: NMS has “lead-pipe” rigidity; serotonin syndrome has clonus and hyperreflexia. NMS onset slower (days); serotonin syndrome faster (hours). NMS — recent antipsychotic; serotonin syndrome — serotonergic drug interaction.
  • Recovery: 7–10 days typically. After recovery, consider clozapine or different drug class (NEVER restart the offending antipsychotic without specialist consultation).
Worked Example Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS) & Tardive Dyskinesia Ch 10 — Psychotic Disorders · First-gen section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS) & Tardive Dyskinesia

Defining Characteristics

Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS) are movement disorders caused by D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway, primarily from antipsychotics.

Four classic EPS syndromes (in order of typical onset):

  1. Acute dystonia (hours to days) — sudden muscle spasms, oculogyric crisis, torticollis, opisthotonos. Treat with IM benztropine or diphenhydramine.
  2. Akathisia (days to weeks) — subjective restlessness, inability to sit still, pacing. Treat with dose reduction, beta blockers (propranolol), or benzodiazepines.
  3. Pseudoparkinsonism (weeks) — tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, masked facies. Treat with anticholinergics (benztropine) or dose reduction.
  4. Tardive dyskinesia (TD) (months to years) — involuntary repetitive movements of face, tongue, lips, jaw, fingers. OFTEN PERMANENT; key concern.

Antecedents

  • Antipsychotic use, especially high-potency typicals (haloperidol, fluphenazine)
  • Atypicals can cause EPS but lower risk (highest risk with risperidone)
  • Higher doses, longer duration of treatment
  • Older adults (especially women) at higher risk for TD
  • Patients with mood disorders may be more susceptible
  • Other dopamine antagonists: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine

Negative Consequences

  • Tardive dyskinesia is often irreversible — even after stopping the offending drug
  • Social stigma, functional impairment, embarrassment
  • Pain and physical discomfort (dystonia can affect breathing if laryngeal)
  • Falls (from pseudoparkinsonism, akathisia)
  • Nonadherence due to side effects → relapse of psychosis
  • Acute dystonia can be life-threatening if airway involved (laryngospasm)
  • Akathisia is sometimes associated with increased suicide risk

Related Concepts

Antipsychotic medications (typical vs atypical), dopamine D2 receptor blockade, anticholinergic medications (benztropine, diphenhydramine), AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale), VMAT-2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine for TD), neuroleptic malignant syndrome (differential).

Exemplars

  • Acute dystonia case: Young adult started on haloperidol 5 mg IM for agitation; 4 hours later develops sustained upward gaze (oculogyric crisis) and neck twisting (torticollis). Treat: IM benztropine 1–2 mg or IM/IV diphenhydramine 25–50 mg — rapid resolution.
  • Akathisia case: Client on risperidone 6 mg/day reports inability to sit still; pacing constantly; says they feel “like jumping out of their skin.” Treat: reduce dose, add propranolol 10–20 mg BID.
  • Pseudoparkinsonism case: Older adult on haloperidol develops tremor, shuffling gait, masked face. Treat: switch to atypical OR add benztropine 1–2 mg PO BID.
  • Tardive dyskinesia case: Long-term haloperidol user develops chewing-like movements of tongue and lip-smacking. Reduce/stop antipsychotic if possible; switch to clozapine (lower TD risk); consider VMAT-2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) for TD treatment.
  • AIMS scale — performed every 3–6 months on all clients on antipsychotics to detect TD early.
  • Prevention: use atypicals when possible; lowest effective dose; periodic dose reduction trials; AIMS monitoring; switch to clozapine if TD develops.
Worked Example First-Pass Effect Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration · Metabolism section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
First-Pass Effect

Defining Characteristics

The first-pass effect (also called first-pass metabolism or pre-systemic metabolism) is the extensive hepatic metabolism of an orally administered drug BEFORE it reaches systemic circulation.

Path: oral drug → GI absorption → portal vein → liver (CYP450 enzymes) → systemic circulation.

The result: a substantial portion of an oral dose may be metabolized to inactive compounds before reaching its target tissue — meaning the oral dose must be significantly higher than the IV dose to achieve the same therapeutic effect.

Antecedents

  • Oral route of administration (only affects drugs absorbed via the GI tract that drain to portal circulation)
  • Lipid-soluble drugs that are metabolized by hepatic CYP450 enzymes
  • Hepatic CYP450 activity — affected by age, genetics (poor vs ultra-rapid metabolizers), liver disease, drug interactions (inducers/inhibitors)
  • Drug-specific factors: extent of hepatic extraction ratio (high-extraction drugs have the most pronounced first-pass effect)

Negative Consequences

  • Reduced bioavailability — only a fraction of the oral dose reaches systemic circulation
  • Requires higher oral doses than equivalent parenteral doses (e.g., morphine: PO 30 mg ≈ IV 10 mg)
  • Variable drug levels due to inter-individual differences in CYP450 activity
  • Drug interactions — CYP450 inhibitors (e.g., grapefruit juice, erythromycin) can dramatically increase drug levels by blocking first-pass metabolism
  • Generation of active or toxic metabolites (e.g., codeine → morphine via CYP2D6)

Related Concepts

Bioavailability, hepatic extraction ratio, CYP450 metabolism, pharmacogenomics, drug interactions, prodrugs, routes that BYPASS first-pass (sublingual, buccal, rectal lower 2/3, IV, IM, SC, transdermal, inhaled).

Exemplars

  • High first-pass drugs (low oral bioavailability): morphine (~25%), lidocaine (negligible orally — must be parenteral), propranolol, nitroglycerin (~0% orally — use sublingual/transdermal), verapamil
  • Bypassing first-pass: sublingual nitroglycerin enters venous return directly without portal circulation passage — immediate systemic effect
  • Prodrug strategy: codeine is converted to morphine (active) by hepatic CYP2D6 — clients with reduced CYP2D6 activity get little pain relief
  • Drug interaction: grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, blocking first-pass metabolism of calcium channel blockers and statins → elevated drug levels and toxicity risk
Worked Example Half-Life and Steady State Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration · Half-life section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Half-Life and Steady State

Defining Characteristics

Half-life (t½) — the time required for the plasma drug concentration to decrease by 50%. Determined by the drug’s clearance and volume of distribution.

Steady state — the dynamic equilibrium reached when the amount of drug administered per dosing interval equals the amount eliminated. At steady state, peak and trough levels are predictable and stable.

Key rule: it takes approximately 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state with regular dosing, and similarly 4–5 half-lives to eliminate a drug after stopping it.

Antecedents

  • Drug-specific: intrinsic clearance, volume of distribution, protein binding
  • Hepatic function — CYP450 metabolism affects clearance of many drugs
  • Renal function — eGFR affects renally cleared drugs (digoxin, gentamicin, vancomycin, lithium)
  • Age — neonates and older adults often have reduced clearance → longer half-life
  • Drug interactions affecting metabolism or excretion
  • Dosing regimen — interval should align with half-life to maintain steady-state levels

Negative Consequences

  • Sub-therapeutic levels if dosing interval is too long relative to half-life — clinical failure
  • Toxicity / accumulation if dosing interval is too short or clearance is impaired — drug builds up beyond therapeutic range (especially for narrow-TI drugs like digoxin, lithium, warfarin, vancomycin)
  • Delayed onset of full effect — clients may stop a medication too early because they don’t feel an effect (e.g., antidepressants take weeks)
  • Delayed offset — withdrawal/effect persists after discontinuation (e.g., amiodarone t½ ~58 days)
  • Missed doses cause level drops that take time to recover at steady state

Related Concepts

  • Clearance, volume of distribution, protein binding, renal function, hepatic metabolism, and CYP450 interactions determine half-life and time to steady state.
  • Loading doses, maintenance doses, dosing intervals, peak and trough levels, and therapeutic drug monitoring connect half-life to practical medication scheduling.
  • Drug accumulation, delayed onset, delayed offset, withdrawal or rebound effects, and organ impairment explain why timing matters for safety and effectiveness.
  • Narrow therapeutic index medications such as digoxin, lithium, vancomycin, gentamicin, and warfarin require closer monitoring when half-life or clearance changes.

Exemplars

  • Short half-life: adenosine (~10 seconds — rapid IV push, immediate effect, brief duration); nitroglycerin SL (~1–3 min)
  • Intermediate half-life: digoxin (~36–40 hr — reaches steady state in ~5–7 days; daily dosing maintains levels)
  • Long half-life: amiodarone (~58 days — effects persist for weeks after discontinuation; loading dose used to reach therapeutic levels faster); fluoxetine (4–6 day half-life of active metabolite)
  • Loading dose rationale: for drugs with long half-lives (digoxin, amiodarone, vancomycin), a higher initial dose “loads” the drug to therapeutic range, avoiding the 5-half-life wait
  • Trough timing: draw 30 min BEFORE the next dose at steady state — this reflects the lowest concentration to avoid toxicity
Worked Example Therapeutic Index (TI) Ch 1 — Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration · Half-life section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Therapeutic Index (TI)

Defining Characteristics

Therapeutic Index (TI) is the safety margin of a drug — the ratio of the toxic dose to the therapeutic dose. Mathematically: TI = TD50 / ED50 (median toxic dose / median effective dose).

A wide TI = large safety margin between effective and toxic doses (forgiving). A narrow TI = small margin; small dose changes can cause toxicity. Narrow-TI drugs require therapeutic drug monitoring (peak/trough levels) and dose adjustment for organ dysfunction.

Antecedents

  • Drug-specific: pharmacokinetic properties (absorption variability, protein binding, metabolism, excretion) and pharmacodynamic dose-response curve
  • Genetic factors: CYP450 polymorphisms (poor vs ultra-rapid metabolizers)
  • Organ dysfunction: reduced renal or hepatic function narrows the effective TI for drugs cleared by those organs
  • Drug interactions: inducers/inhibitors of metabolism can push levels out of the therapeutic window
  • Comorbidities and age extremes (neonates, older adults)

Negative Consequences

  • Toxicity at therapeutic-appearing doses (especially with comorbidities or drug interactions)
  • Sub-therapeutic levels causing treatment failure
  • Required intensive monitoring (peak/trough levels, INR, drug levels, organ function tests) adds cost and complexity
  • Risk of medication errors — narrow-TI drugs are on the ISMP “high-alert medications” list
  • Patient burden from frequent labs, dose changes, and adverse effects

Related Concepts

  • Therapeutic range, toxic dose, effective dose, narrow therapeutic index, and wide therapeutic index define how much margin exists between benefit and harm.
  • Therapeutic drug monitoring, peak and trough levels, INR for warfarin, serum drug levels, and organ-function tests help keep narrow-index drugs in range.
  • Renal impairment, hepatic impairment, age extremes, drug interactions, protein binding, and CYP450 variation can narrow the safety margin for a given client.
  • High-alert medication safeguards, dose adjustment, medication reconciliation, client teaching, and toxicity recognition reduce harm from narrow-index drugs.

Exemplars

  • Narrow-TI drugs requiring monitoring: warfarin (INR 2–3), digoxin (level 0.5–2 ng/mL), lithium (0.6–1.2 mEq/L), phenytoin (10–20 mcg/mL), theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin (peaks and troughs)
  • Wide-TI drugs: penicillins, most NSAIDs, most antihistamines — generally well-tolerated even with dose variability
  • Narrow-TI in renal impairment: digoxin and lithium accumulate dangerously; reduce dose or extend interval based on creatinine clearance
  • Narrow-TI in hepatic impairment: warfarin (clotting factors reduced), benzodiazepines (slower clearance), acetaminophen (depleted glutathione)
  • Drug interaction example: amiodarone raises digoxin level by ~50–100% — must reduce digoxin dose and monitor
Worked Example Blood Typing & Compatibility Ch 27 — Blood and Blood Products · Products section · Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Blood Typing & Compatibility

Defining Characteristics

Blood typing and compatibility determine which blood products a recipient can safely receive, based on ABO and Rh antigen systems on RBC surfaces and corresponding antibodies in plasma.

ABO system:

  • Type A: A antigen; anti-B antibodies
  • Type B: B antigen; anti-A antibodies
  • Type AB: both antigens; NO antibodies (universal recipient)
  • Type O: no antigens; both anti-A and anti-B antibodies (universal donor)

Rh system: Rh-positive (D antigen present) or Rh-negative (absent). Rh-negative people can develop anti-D antibodies if exposed to Rh-positive blood.

Antecedents

  • Need for transfusion (anemia, bleeding, surgery)
  • Type and screen or type and crossmatch ordered
  • Pregnancy (Rh status critical for hemolytic disease of newborn)
  • History of prior transfusions or pregnancies (alloantibody formation)
  • Emergency situations (may use O-negative before full typing)

Negative Consequences

  • ABO incompatibility → acute hemolytic reaction (life-threatening)
  • Rh incompatibility: sensitization; hemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive fetus)
  • Alloimmunization from repeated exposure → harder to find compatible blood
  • Delayed hemolytic reactions
  • Death from incompatible transfusion

Related Concepts

Type and crossmatch, universal donor (O-negative), universal recipient (AB-positive), Rh factor, RhoGAM (Rh immune globulin), hemolytic disease of the newborn, acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, antibody screen, emergency transfusion.

Exemplars

  • Universal RBC donor: O-negative — no A, B, or Rh antigens; used in emergencies before typing complete
  • Universal RBC recipient: AB-positive — no anti-A or anti-B antibodies; can receive any ABO type
  • Plasma compatibility is OPPOSITE of RBC: AB plasma is the universal donor (no antibodies); O is universal recipient for plasma
  • Rh-negative recipient should receive Rh-negative blood (especially women of childbearing age) to prevent sensitization
  • RhoGAM example: Rh-negative mother carrying Rh-positive fetus receives Rh immune globulin (RhoGAM) at 28 weeks and after delivery to prevent maternal sensitization and protect future pregnancies
  • Crossmatch: donor RBCs mixed with recipient serum to confirm compatibility before transfusion (detects agglutination)
  • Type and screen: determines ABO/Rh and screens for unexpected antibodies; type and crossmatch reserves specific compatible units
  • Verification: two licensed personnel confirm blood type matches recipient before every transfusion — the critical error-prevention step
